Pulse oximeters gained prominence during the Covid-19 pandemic, offering anyone a handheld tool to take stock of their blood oxygen level.
But their newfound popularity also brought new attention to their limitations — several studies have shown that pulse oximeters overestimate blood oxygen levels when used on darker skin tones. This can make patients of color appear more healthy than they really are, resulting in worse health outcomes and exacerbated inequality.
In the years since, researchers have tried to unpack what exactly is going wrong with these commonly used tools. A recent study, published in the Annals of the American Thoracic Society, adds to a growing body of evidence showing the issues with pulse oximeters are more than skin deep. In a retrospective study reviewing five years of data, researchers found that pulse oximeters at Johns Hopkins Hospital inexplicably went from overestimating blood oxygen levels to underestimating them in all patients at higher oxygen levels, though the inaccuracies were worse in patients of color.
“One of the biggest problems with pulse oximeters is that they are this black box. I have no idea why we found what we found in this paper, and why it’s changing year over year,” said Ashraf Fawzy, a pulmonologist and critical care physician at Hopkins who is an author on the paper.
In response, a spokesperson for Masimo, which manufactures the pulse oximeters used in the study, said it is “unaware of any sensor, software, or manufacturing changes during the study period evaluated in the publications that would explain the reported results.” They added that there are multiple factors that can affect a reading, including what type of sensor is used, where it is placed, signal quality, and perfusion.
“The study’s available data do not establish the cause of the reported shift from overestimation to underestimation,” they said. In addition, they pointed to two studies supported by the company that have not found differences in pulse oximeter efficacy based on skin tone.
Pulse oximeters work by shining a light through the skin at two wavelengths, one of which is absorbed by oxygenated blood and the other by deoxygenated blood. The device then compares how much of each is absorbed, and calculates what percent of the blood is oxygenated.
Using data from intensive care units across Hopkins, Fawzy’s study found that the same make of oximeter was not consistent in its readings throughout the years.
The paper was trying to answer a question posed by a Food and Drug Administration-funded study of pulse oximeters, which was published earlier this year. That paper, called EquiOx, was intended to help researchers understand why pulse oximeters overestimated blood oxygen levels in patients with darker skin tones.
Instead, it found that the devices were underestimating blood oxygen levels, a result the authors and outside commentators struggled to justify. It was one of the first studies to proactively take pulse oximeter readings from patients and compare them to an arterial blood gas test, which is the gold standard for blood oxygen levels, but much more invasive.
Taken together, these findings make it difficult for clinicians to know how to interpret pulse oximeter results. If they only over or underestimated oxygen levels in patients with darker skin tones, physicians could adjust accordingly. But if pulse oximeters are inconsistent, it makes it more difficult to work around.
Thomas Valley, a health services researcher and pulmonologist at University of Colorado Anschutz who was involved in a seminal 2020 New England Journal of Medicine paper bringing attention to pulse oximeters’ racial bias, compares pulse oximeters to a broken clock. “If you have a broken clock and you know how it’s going to be five minutes slow every time, you can adjust your routines to take care of that,” he said. But now, it’s unclear whether that metaphorical clock is running fast or slow. “That’s a huge problem, given how important these devices are,” he added.
In the Hopkins study, pulse oximeters gradually shifted from overestimates to underestimates over the course of the five years when compared to arterial blood gas tests. When oximeters overestimate oxygen levels, clinicians run the risk of not providing care to patients when they need it. But underestimating can also come with issues, like providing unnecessary care or keeping patients in the hospital longer than necessary. Overall, “it is not at all clear these things are fit for use in the way that we’re using them,” said Jack Iwashyna, a pulmonologist and critical care physician who is an author on the Hopkins paper.
The recent crop of papers also raises a question about how to best study the shortcomings of pulse oximeters. The landmark 2020 paper brought renewed attention to the devices’ bias was a retrospective, gleaning a trend from past data. Researchers at the time hoped prospective studies, where scientists actively collect data to get to the root of a problem, would be more helpful in understanding why pulse oximeters fell short in the way they do.
But thus far, such studies have mostly raised more questions than answers. Another prospective study, from Emory University, found evidence of racial bias, but that the inaccurate results were not fully accounted for by variations in skin tone. Readings are likely impacted by factors other than molecules that impact skin pigmentation, such as conditions like anemia, cardiovascular disease, or liver disease, which are more common in patients of color, said Sivasubramanium Bhavani, an ICU physician at Emory who led that study.
“It is more complicated than just skin tone,” he said. “We don’t know all the different causalities and how these things work. But, we do know that if you had the next generation of pulse oximeters, and you can claim that it was 100% calibrated for skin tone, all these other pathways are still going to affect it, and you may still have the same racial bias.”

In the decade since its launch, India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has evolved from a promising digital experiment into critical economic infrastructure. Against this backdrop, the Union Finance Ministry has notified that the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) will operationalise a 0.4% Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on specified merchant transactions above ₹2,000 from October 15. While consumers will not be charged directly, this marks a significant departure from UPI’s zero-MDR model for merchants. While the reasoning is understandable, considering the costs to run UPI, one question deserves an answer: what has UPI cost India, and what has it saved?
Editorial | Complex priorities: On UPI transactions, MDR charges
The costs are easy to see as servers, security and fraud controls show up on balance sheets, while the savings are scattered across the economy. For example, take a small shopkeeper. Before digital payments, taking cash meant counting notes, keeping change, guarding the till and making trips to the bank, with the added risk of theft. UPI removed most of that, with customers also saving themselves a few trips to the ATM. Further, banks now handle less physical cash, businesses reconcile accounts faster, lenders are able to read a small trader’s cash flow from digital records, and most importantly, the government gets a trail that helps with formalisation and tax compliance. None of this is revenue to UPI; it is spread across banks, consumers and the exchequer.
The case for MDR is that the payments ecosystem needs a steady income to maintain and expand UPI, which is a fair point. Yet this logic assumes that most of UPI’s cost should be recovered from the transactions on it; the wider benefits are not accounted for. Every payment that moves from cash to UPI cuts handling costs elsewhere while every merchant who joins adds to formalisation. Further, the increase in UPI users makes the network more useful to those already on it. India has acted on this logic before: the government approved ₹1,500 crore in 2024-25 alone to incentivise low-value merchant transactions, with the view that moving cash through digital networks was worth paying for.
Balancing benefits
On September 28, the Supreme Court, while declining to stay the levy, asked the Centre, the RBI and the NPCI to explain, on affidavit, the legal basis for the levy, including whether the MDR was a tax or a fee. In response, the government stated that nothing reaches the exchequer and that the money was a settlement between banks and service providers. This answers the legal question but not the economic one — what is India giving up?
Consider a highway between an industrial region and a port. A toll can be perfectly reasonable, but toll collections say little about the highway’s real return, which is the faster movement of goods and the businesses that grow with it. A port is similar; while container fees pay for operations, its larger contribution is the trade that it enables. UPI also deserves the same lens. Any plan to recover its maintenance bill should ask what happens to the activity it supports once a toll is introduced. That calculation is largely missing from the MDR debate.
MDR might raise money that lets banks and payment providers invest more in resilience and expansion. But it would also lead to a change in behaviour. Some merchants may prefer cash for transactions, while others may nudge customers towards a different payment instrument. When payments slip back to cash, the costs UPI had removed come back, such as handling, reconciliation, cash logistics, and less digital visibility. Some of the formalisation gains go too. If ₹100 collected in MDR causes more than ₹100 of economic value to disappear elsewhere, the payment system ends up better funded and the country poorer.
Additionally, UPI and RuPay had helped India build a domestic payments ecosystem at the expense of global card networks. The USTR had earlier called India’s zero-MDR policy a market-access barrier for Visa and Mastercard; these players now stand to gain from any drift back to cards. A lasting domestic advantage should not be conceded for trade terms that can later be revised.
A network that millions of Indians rely on has to be secure, resilient and able to grow. The harder question is what “self-sustaining” should mean. The test for the new toll should be straightforward: does it increase India’s overall economic return from UPI after accounting for the behaviour it may change and the wider benefits the network creates? This is the question policymakers should answer.
Americai V. Narayanan is National Spokesperson of the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), a certified public accountant (CPA) and a certified management accountant (CMA)

8 public officers in Singapore referred to police after property review
The review identified officers in agencies involved in rail planning who bought property between 2007 and 2014 close to unannounced MRT stations
Eight public service officers have been referred to Singapore police after a review of 191 officers’ property transactions, Coordinating Minister for Public Services Chan Chun Sing has told parliament.
The review followed a working paper by the US-based National Bureau of Economic Research, which identified 2007 to 2011 as the period of concern.
The Public Service Division (PSD) extended the scope to 2014 as a matter of prudence, Chan said on Tuesday, because many new MRT station locations continued to be announced after 2011.
Based on administrative records, PSD identified officers in agencies involved in rail planning who bought property between 2007 and 2014 close to locations later announced as MRT stations, he said.

Supporters of jailed ex-PM Imran Khan march to Pakistan capital
- Published
Thousands of supporters of Pakistan's jailed ex-prime minister Imran Khan are marching to the capital Islamabad as they call for his release.
Concerns over the 73-year-old's health have grown louder in recent months. His family claims he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
The cricket star-turned-politician, who faces charges in more than 100 cases, was jailed for 17 years over corruption last year. Khan said all the cases against him are politically motivated.
Even behind bars, he remains a force in Pakistani politics, and demonstrations in support for him have led to deadly violence and crackdowns in the past.
Sunday's march, which began in Lakki Marwat, a city 275km away from Islamabad, had paused for the night and is expected to resume around midday local time on Monday.
Originally scheduled for last week, it was postponed to allow for talks between the government and Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party but the talks ended in a deadlock.
Khan, who faces charges ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts, was first imprisoned in August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year.
Sohail Afridi, chief minister for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province ruled by PTI, expects that the march will make its way to a town about 80km (50 miles) west of Islamabad by Thursday.
"[By then] this movement will have reached every corner of the country and every square will have become a centre of activity," he said on Sunday, urging the people to "play an active role in the political process".
Authorities in Islamabad have stacked up shipping containers to block key access routes to the capital city.
The PTI said talks with government failed because authorities rejected the party's request for access to Khan so that its leaders could consult him on national and political issues.
The party also said it had demanded that Khan be given an immediate medical examination and treatment.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi meanwhile accused Afridi of "sabotaging" negotiations, saying the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government had backed out of earlier commitments on counter-terrorism issues, according to Pakistan's local media reports.
In August, Khan was briefly transferred from jail to a state-run hospital for medical examination and treatment following complaints about his deteriorating health. The doctors later deemed him "medically fit".
The intervention was the most significant relief Khan has received from the courts since he was imprisoned in 2023 on corruption charges, which he says were politically motivated.
Khan's family and the PTI, however, criticised the authorities for defying a court order that he be examined by physicians at a specific private hospital.
On 20 September, Khan's sister Aleema Khanum was arrested in the eastern city of Lahore.
The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government".
Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as the country's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.
His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.
At least eight people died in the protests and the army had to be called in to quell the violence.
Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif urging Khan be accorded proper medical care.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

Suzuki Motor has unveiled its first fully electric minicar, fueling competition in Japan’s most important vehicle segment.
Including government subsidies, the “e SKY” model will cost around ¥1.6 million ($10,120) when sales start in November, Suzuki said Tuesday. That’s cheaper than Nissan Motor’s top-selling Sakura EV and BYD’s first minicar, introduced by the Chinese company in July.
Minicars are affordable, ultracompact vehicles that account for more than a third of automobile sales in Japan.
The arrival of the e SKY adds to signs that the country is becoming a key battleground for electric versions of the tiny cars, with Nissan, Honda, Daihatsu and now Suzuki offering them. Together, the Japanese brands control about 80% of the market.
Suzuki targets around 1,000 monthly sales for the tiny EV, which has a battery range of 310 kilometers and a base price of ¥2.1 million. Government subsidies can bring its sticker down by around half a million yen. BYD said in July that its Racco minicar, which offers a minimum range of 210 kilometers, will cost less than ¥2 million including subsidies.
In Japan, where EV uptake is far lower than in the U.S., Europe or China, Suzuki is betting that its first electric minicar can help lower the barrier for customers to make the switch from gasoline vehicles.
“We asked ourselves what kind of product would convince minicar drivers to shift to an EV, and this is our answer,” the model’s chief engineer Tomoyuki Tsubata told reporters in Tokyo. “We’re hoping this will help them recognize that option.”

Uproar escalated on Friday (October 2, 2026) after a video went viral showing a Dalit woman who was allegedly denied admission at the government hospital in Bhadohi district during labour pain and forced to deliver outside the hospital in public.
While the victim’s family and Opposition parties alleged untouchability, claiming feudal elements are running the government in Uttar Pradesh, the authorities said disciplinary action has been taken against personnel found guilty of partial negligence.
“The family categorically alleged that hospital staff failed to provide timely treatment and did not admit due to her caste affiliation, this is so sad and inhuman that even after 79 years of independence, untouchability and discrimination prevails in government system, forcing a Dalit woman to give birth on the roadside, outside a government hospital. The feudal elements within the administrative system are emboldened by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government. The fight of the Samajwadi Party (SP) for justice, equality is against such tendencies,” said Sunil Singh Yadav ‘Sajan’, the SP spokesperson.
“The incident is a cruel, evil act, which is unacceptable in a civilised society,” said Ajay Kumar Lallu, a senior U.P. Congress leader.
In the matter, Rani Vanvasi, a 20-year-old pregnant woman gave birth on the roadside outside government district hospital in Bhadohi on September 29, after she was allegedly denied admission for delivery. The victim’s family also alleged that hospital staff failed to provide timely treatment and did not admit her.
Ms. Vanvasi eventually went into labour near the hospital gate while she and her family were leaving. Women accompanying her used saris or a sheet to provide privacy as she delivered the baby beside the road.
“The victim had a hemoglobin level of around five grams per deciliter, indicating severe anemia. She was referred to a higher-level facility in Mirzapur but in the meantime the pain started. Upon learning of the incident, I immediately arrived at the scene and provided appropriate medical assistance. Currently, both the infant and mother are completely healthy and recovering at the district hospital. Disciplinary action has also been taken against personnel found guilty of partial negligence. The remaining statements were found to be untrue,” said the Chief Medical Officer of the Hospital.

Googlebooks are Google’s latest attempt to carve out a piece of the premium laptop market, and tight integration with Android phones is a key part of that effort. Now that Googlebooks are available, we’re learning of some frustrating limitations of that plan. For now, Googlebooks will only play nicely with your phone if you have a Pixel.
When Google announced the launch window for Googlebooks, it said the laptops were “engineered to work with your Android phone right out of the box.” But as with many things Google, the truth is more convoluted. We have since learned that you need Android 17 for any of the nifty integrations to work. With a compatible Android 17 phone, you can seamlessly stream apps to your laptop, access files on your phone, mirror notifications, and continue where you left off in certain apps when switching from phone to laptop.
You might think that the latest Samsung phones, which shipped with Android 17, would be ready for this experience. You’d be wrong, though. Some early Googlebook adopters have complained that phones like the Z Fold 8 won’t work with the laptops. While the devices appear to see each other, the phone doesn’t stay connected. Google representatives have since confirmed that these “Better Together” features are not currently supported on even the latest Samsung phones. An update that brings support to Samsung phones will roll out in “the coming weeks.”

CM: AI training in govt schools to start from Class 6
Karnataka is considering extending artificial intelligence training in government schools to Class 6, with Chief Minister D K Shivakumar asking officials on Monday to work with the Information Technology department and private companies to expand the programme.
Karnataka is considering extending artificial intelligence training in government schools to Class 6, with chief minister DK Shivakumar asking officials on Monday to work with the Information Technology department and private companies to expand the programme.
“AI training has already started for Class 9 students in government schools,” Shivakumar said, adding that “officials have been asked to work toward extending it to students from Class 6.” He gave the directions during a review meeting on the government’s 100 day programmes, recruitments and priority schemes.
Google has expressed interest in providing AI training in government schools, and officials have been asked to study the company’s initiatives in Telangana before working out a programme for Karnataka, according to a statement from the chief minister’s office.
Shivakumar also asked officials to identify land for an AI university in the state. The government is separately preparing to recruit 956 teachers on an outsourcing basis. The review also covered a plan to take Class 9 and 11 students from 941 urban government schools to progressive farmers’ fields.
Officials have been asked to arrange overnight stays in villages, including in community halls and hostels. Private schools will also be required to implement the programme, which is to be completed by December.
For the proposed development of 1,000 Karnataka Public Schools, the CM directed officials to complete preparations for laying foundation stones by November 14. Deputy commissioners have been authorised to approve detailed project reports and tenders for the schools.
The government also plans to develop 100 KPS schools through corporate social responsibility funds. Companies have already expressed interest in developing 60 schools.
In agriculture, Shivakumar said 25 lakh SMS messages had been sent to farmers under the CM Raitha Chaitanya Agritech Mission. Officials were asked to send video messages explaining the scheme in simple terms. A chatbot is being integrated into the programme, while preparations are under way to invite tenders for drone and satellite based crop estimation and digital crop surveys.
The CM Negilu Yogi scheme, aimed at promoting farm mechanisation, will use the JFarm app to connect farmers with service providers. About 2.5 lakh people have registered to provide services through the platform, and officials have been directed to launch it from November 1.
The government has set a target of training and preparing 2,000 farmers to become agricultural and horticultural exporters by March 2027, including guidance on certification and other requirements. Officials were asked to promote group farming, scientific processing and storage, and floriculture, and identify at least five acres for marketing purposes.
In the animal husbandry sector, Shivakumar directed officials to establish four protein parks in Chamarajanagar, Chitradurga, Haveri and Koppal under the Protein Mission.
The government also plans to increase egg production. A proposal to provide a 50% subsidy for installing solar power systems to address electricity related problems will be placed before the cabinet on Tuesday for a decision.

A video has gone viral on social media platforms, showing two women slapping a man wearing a saffron scarf. Users claim that it shows a Muslim man masquerading as Hindu by wearing a saffron scarf, and that he was allegedly caught stalking college girls in an attempt to snatch their phones.
Right-wing handle @MeghUpdates posted the clip, which garnered more than 116,000 views, and has been shared around 2,000 times at the time of this article being written. (Archive)
A “Peaceful” in a saffron scarf was allegedly STALKING college girls and ATTEMPTING to snatch their phones before the Hindu girls CAUGHT him RED-HANDED and BEAT him up. 👏 https://t.co/EK2q3vkgN1
— Megh Updates 🚨™ (@MeghUpdates) September 25, 2026
In Right-wing social-media discourse, the term ‘peaceful’ is used as a a code word for Muslims as a negative stereotype, while avoiding saying ‘Muslim’ directly.
An X user with the handle @Hinduspirit0 had also posted the viral clip on September 24 with the same claim that a Muslim boy pretending to be Hindu while wearing a saffron scarf had been “caught red-handed and beaten up badly”.
Other users who shared this clip with the same claim included the user ‘Boiled Anda’ (@AmitLeliSlayer), Vishal Deep Singh (@VishalDeep5151), Amitabh Chaudhary (@MithilaWaaala), and (@singh31919). Archives: 1, 2, 3, 4
The readers should note that many of this handles, like ‘Boiled Anda’, Amitabh Chaudhary, and MeghUpdates, have been found sharing misinformation and communal propaganda several times in the past.
Fact Check
To verify the veracity of the claims, we broke down the viral video into several keyframes. A reverse image search on one such keyframe led us to a news report by Aaj Tak, published on August 10.
According to the report, the viral clip is from Gwalior in Madhya Pradesh. On August 8, twin sisters Harshita and Rashita Agarwal, while on their way to college on a scooter, had one of their phones snatched by a miscreant trailing them on another scooter.
A chase ensued, after which the sisters were able to apprehend the man at an intersection and proceeded to thrash him, visuals of which began to circulate on social media soon after. The report identifies the culprit as a resident of Jalandhar, Punjab, named Manpreet. We found another news report published by The Free Press Journal, on August 9, which corroborated this finding.
On using relevant keywords, we also came across a video uploaded by ANI Bharat, in which Gwalior SSP Dharamveer Singh lauded the bravery of the twin sisters in nabbing the motorcycle-borne mobile snatcher.
So, to sum up, the viral claims suggesting that the man being slapped in the clip is Muslim, is false. The man in the viral video was identified as Manpreet.

Nicaragua torture victim imprisoned for second time after being deported by U.S.
A Nicaraguan exile who was imprisoned and tortured after protesting against that country's government was deported by the U.S. back to his country, where he was immediately imprisoned once again by authorities
MEXICO CITY -- A Nicaraguan exile who was imprisoned and tortured after protesting against the government was deported by the U.S. back to his country, where he was immediately imprisoned once again by authorities, family members and his lawyer confirmed Monday.
Upon climbing off the U.S. deportation flight in Managua, Nicaragua's capital, last week, 35-year-old Jeffrey Jarquín was taken by authorities back to the same prison where he was once tortured, confirmed one family member.
The family member spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity, fearing persecution by the government. Local media first reported on Jarquín’s deportation and detention.
Jarquín was a prominent figure in anti-government protests in 2018, which set off a yearslong campaign by husband-and-wife co-Presidents Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo to crush dissent.
The government’s crackdown on critics, civil society, religious groups and virtually anyone who raised their voice has fueled the flight of more than 800,000 people from the country, according to U.N. figures.
Osley Sallent, Jarquín’s lawyer in the U.S., confirmed the Nicaraguan exile was deported after seeking asylum in the United States.
Jarquín was detained in 2018 with other protesters and thrown into a maximum-security prison known as El Modelo. Until he was released a year later and fled to the U.S., Jarquín and others were tortured in chambers known as “tiny hell,” according to a 2019 report by the Organization of American States.
Sallent said Jarquín was living in Miami when he was detained. Before Jarquín's asylum case was rejected by a Louisiana court in July, Sallent said he was held in Alligator Alcatraz, the Florida immigration detention center in the Everglades plagued by reports of harsh conditions. Sallent wasn't able to provide more details of the asylum case.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Following a request by the AP for more details on why Jarquín was imprisoned for a second time, a spokesperson for Nicaragua's government responded: “Thank you very much! Hugs."
The Trump administration has long criticized the Nicaraguan government and labeled it a dictatorship, especially after authorities there canceled elections scheduled for next year. Just last week, Deputy U.S. Secretary of State Christopher Landau said in remarks before the OAS that what was happening in Nicaragua was “intolerable.”
“Murillo and Ortega’s dictatorship has no place in our hemisphere,” he added.
Despite that, ICE has ramped up deportations to the Central American country in recent months, according to a recent Human Rights Watch report, which said the Trump administration had deported 6,300 Nicaraguans between January and July 2026.
The organization documented that ICE had detained least eight Nicaraguan exiles who were stripped of their citizenship in a move observers say was intended to punish critics, the report said. Some of those detained had pending asylum applications.
Juan Pappier, deputy director of the Americas for Human Rights Watch, said the simultaneous criticisms of Nicaragua's government and deportations of those forced to flee its repression “makes Washington look hypocritical.”
“Nicaragua has the most brutal government in the Western Hemisphere, and any government critic who is sent back is at real risk of torture or persecution," Pappier said.
——
Associated Press reporter Gisela Salomon contributed to this report from Miami.

Millions of US seniors are checking their bank accounts this week after unexpected $90 payments began appearing through the Social Security Administration. The money is real, but it is not a new Social Security benefit. The one-time payment is a Medicare rebate announced by President Donald Trump, intended to help eligible beneficiaries offset their October Medicare Part B premium. The Centres for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) says 20.8 million people qualify for the payment. For many recipients, the arrival may look like an ordinary Social Security deposit, as the vast majority of eligible beneficiaries will receive the rebate via direct deposit from the Social Security Administration. CBS News reported that some seniors had already seen the money or pending deposits on Tuesday, ahead of the main payment date. If you are enrolled in Original Medicare Part B, live in the United States, do not receive Medicaid premium assistance and do not pay an income-related monthly adjustment amount (IRMAA), you may be eligible. People enrolled in Medicare Advantage are not included. CMS says most eligible beneficiaries should receive the $90 direct deposit on or around 08/10. Those without direct deposit will receive a paper cheque later in October from the US Treasury. The cheque is expected to identify the payment as coming from the Medicare Improvement Fund and say it is intended to offset the October premium. The payment comes from the Medicare Improvement Fund, a pool created by Congress to support improvements to the original fee-for-service Medicare programme. The White House said the fund contains about $2 billion and that the administration is using it to put money directly towards seniors’ healthcare costs. The payment is relatively small against the cost of Medicare. CBS News noted that Part B premiums increased by more than $200 annually in 2026 and are projected to rise again in 2027. The timing has also attracted political attention. Trump announced the payments weeks before the 03/11 midterm elections, framing them as help for older Americans facing healthcare costs. Reuters reported that the move comes as the administration makes a series of financial proposals and payments ahead of the elections. Not every senior will see the $90, however. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

The zardozi embroidery on a Dior dress, the T-strap leather sandals at a Prada show, the mirror-work technique used on a Fendi bag – for decades, the skill of Indian artisans has been an invisible force behind some of the world’s most coveted fashion.
Now, that work is beginning to claim its own place in the spotlight, and the Mumbai-based textile and embroidery atelier Chanakya International is at the forefront.
Chanakya marked its 40th anniversary this month, celebrating with three exhibitions that trace its journey from an embroidery powerhouse to a present-day craft and cultural institution. The person steering it is 49-year-old Karishma Swali, whose father set up the group’s operations in the 1980s.
“What we have as a country is unique,” she tells me of India’s rich textile and craft heritage. “It’s unparalleled in many ways, and it’s the only place where we continue to practise it.” During the Renaissance, she says, France and Italy had established and varied traditions. “But what we have in India today is [what] other parts of the world have lost.”
Chanakya has a network of 1,400 artisans, and says that some are 13th-generation craftspeople, skilled in hundreds of embroidery traditions and supplying almost every luxury label you can imagine. Among the techniques they have revived is the Mughal-era silver filigree lace, or chaand jaal, reintroduced in a lighter form that has since become a regular feature in couture collections.
In 2023, Dior held a show at Mumbai’s Gateway of India, showcasing its partnership with Chanakya, in a high-profile acknowledgment of Indian craftsmanship. The runway saw sari-inspired skirts, vibrant madras-checks sets and Nehru-collar jackets.
These collaborations are supported by expert craft knowledge passed down and refined over generations, and they need institutional support to survive. The Kalhath Institute, a craft-preservation centre in Lucknow, runs residencies that pair artists from across the world with local artisans.
Kalhath’s co-founder Mohammed Amine Dadda tells me that Indian craftsmanship’s defining quality is “intelligence of the hand” – a sensitive, slow and cumulative process underpinned by patience and dexterity. “Without this technical mastery, and the considerable time required to create the most demanding pieces, haute couture and contemporary luxury simply could not bring their most ambitious creative visions to life.”
This mastery is not limited to textiles. When it comes to jewellery, global luxury brands have long sought Jaipur-based the Gem Palace, established in 1852 by the Kasliwal family, who still run it today. Samarth Kasliwal, 33, says part of the appeal lies in the visual language of Indian artistry itself. “There is something about Indian artistry that is inspired by nature,” he tells me, pointing to the recurring use of floral patterns and animals across Indian art and design. These motifs are universal, and travel across the lines of culture and language.
One recent collaboration Kasliwal is particularly proud of is a collection for Dior featuring green onyx and rock crystals, with engravings of birds, animals and flowers. The combination, he says, is reminiscent of traditional Indian jewellery, while drawing on techniques that remain central to the atelier’s work today.
With increased visibility, the question of credit and appropriation has become harder to ignore. Last week, a Ralph Lauren gown from the designer’s spring 2027 collection attracted criticism after many Indians pointed out that the embroidery the brand described as “embellishments” looked a lot like Indian zardozi, but without any accompanying credit. (Ralph Lauren did not respond to my request for comment.)
Then, Fendi came under fire when people noticed that a baguette bag from its autumn/winter collection featured mirrorwork often seen in Gujarati crafts. In April, Fendi credited Chanakya artisans in a social media video showcasing the same embroidery. But the product description on its site failed to mention any Indian inspiration, and its final label read “Made in Italy”.
After I asked Fendi about the discrepancy, the brand cited its “creative partnership” with Chanakya of more than three decades, saying it “remains committed to supporting and recognizing India’s rich craft heritage”. The website descriptor now reads: “Made in Italy and India with Chanakya”.
A recent Financial Times report noted that under EU rules, garments embroidered in India can still end up with a European label – so long as the final construction and finishing take place in Europe.
Last year, Prada was accused of appropriating Indian culture with Kolhapuri-inspired sandals, a controversy that showed us these debates around recognition can sometimes produce a more structural response. “We acknowledge the sandals … are inspired by traditional Indian handcrafted footwear, with a centuries-old heritage,” Lorenzo Bertelli, the corporate social responsibility chief at the Italian fashion house, had written in a letter to the Maharashtra chamber of commerce at the time.
Prada subsequently partnered with state-backed organisations in Maharashtra and Karnataka to produce a limited-edition collection, Made in India, and committed to a three-year training programme for artisans specialising in the craft.
Might these collaborations, controversies and corrections represent a shift in India’s place in the fashion industry? Anthropologist Phyllida Jay, author of Inspired by India: How India Transformed Global Design, appears to think so, placing the debate in a longer arc. “The stories of the ateliers producing highly skilled Indian craft in the elevated realm of European luxury and high fashion is part of a broader paradigm shift,” she writes, “where over 70 years after the end of colonial rule, India is being looked at in a different way on the world stage.” It is, in a way, a reversal, moving from a colonial history of extraction toward one in which Indians themselves get a voice in how their craft is represented.
Swali is ensuring this visibility also lives on through the Chanakya School of Craft, which she set up in 2016. Its 18-month programme provides free embroidery training and a travel honorarium to dozens of women, some of whom have gone on to work at the main atelier. Others have set up their own independent studios.
I had a chance to visit the space – inside a high-rise in Lower Parel, where those as young as 18 learn intricate needlework alongside grandmothers in their 60s. “Craft in India has never been institutionalised,” Swali says of the ethos behind the initiative. “It’s intergenerational,” she says, adding that women have often been excluded.
India’s culture of craft has always been precious. Growing up, I loved having the choice to affordably create any type of clothing. At one point, I had a small army of tailors, each with a different specialisation, whom I’d go to for different needs. I’d buy ajrakh and mashru silks from Dastkar or Nalli, and hand it to the right Masterji to stitch, embroider and tweak to my size. So, to me, Indian craftsmanship is not just a part of luxury, but a luxury itself.

Giant underwater Kelvin wave could 'pack a punch' for B.C. in mid-October
El Niño phenomenon could worsen the effects of storm surges and high tides
A giant underwater wave of water connected to this year's El Niño weather pattern is moving up the west coast of the Americas, raising alarm bells among scientists about how climate change is magnifying the impacts of the naturally occurring phenomenon.
The so-called Kelvin wave is not unexpected. But like El Niño as a whole, it is happening on top of human-caused climate change that has already warmed the oceans and atmosphere.
A smaller wave already reached B.C. earlier this summer, and the next one is expected to arrive within one to two weeks, according to Bill Merryfield, a research scientist at Environment and Climate Change Canada.
"We actually did already see over 30 centimetres in some locations in June. And so the coming wave looks like it'll be a stronger one," Merryfield said.
What causes it?
The Kelvin wave is a naturally occurring weather phenomenon, just like El Niño itself. In normal years, winds blow from east to west along the equator in the Pacific Ocean, generally pushing water from South America toward Asia.
During El Niño years, however, those east-to-west winds weaken or can reverse direction, allowing water to move east instead.
"When these Kelvin waves reach the coast of South America, there's nowhere further east for this pile up of water to go. And so it splits and starts running up and down the coasts of the Americas" and eventually all the way up to Canada, Merryfield said.
Sea-level monitoring data collected at Tofino, on Vancouver Island's Pacific coast, shows the impact of the earlier Kelvin wave in June.
Rather than a giant tsunami-like wave, the Kelvin wave temporarily raises sea levels.
"You can think of it more like a very broad, hundreds of miles wide, but very shallow bulge in the height of the ocean surface, so by maybe a foot or so," University of California climate scientist Daniel Swain told CBS News last month.
What will it do to the West Coast?
Merryfield said the impacts are most pronounced during king tides, particularly high tides that happen when the gravitational pull of the sun and moon combine to produce higher-than-normal tides.
"So if you put that 30 centimetres of sea level rise on top of a king tide, and then maybe you add a winter storm to that, which causes a storm surge, that's when you really start to get into trouble," he said.
"This extra foot or so of sea level rise due to El Niño can pack a punch."
Those surges could be intensified by another effect of El Niño, further raising sea levels along the B.C coast. El Niño can strengthen northward winds along the coast, pushing even more water toward shore.
These compounding effects — the Kelvin wave, stronger northward winds and winter storms, on top of climate change already raising sea levels and intensifying extreme weather — could worsen flooding and erosion along the coast. Strong El Niños in the past have caused widespread erosion on California's beaches.
Local authorities there are placing emergency sand on beaches and expect the Kelvin wave to raise water levels six to 12 inches, the Associated Press reports.
The impacts of the Kelvin wave — and El Niño more broadly — could extend far beyond this season, Merryfield warned.
The oceans absorb much of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases, moderating global warming as humans continue to burn fossil fuels. During El Niños, however, some of that stored heat is released from the ocean into the atmosphere.
This will likely lead to 2027 becoming the warmest year on record "by quite a significant margin," Merryfield said, echoing similar warnings from other climate research organizations and scientists.

There must be some mistake. A company studies its cancer blood test in a randomized trial of 140,000 people using a suboptimal surrogate endpoint, fails to meet that endpoint, yet is recommended for approval by a Food and Drug Administration advisory panel. And because of the Medicare Multi-Cancer Early Detection Screening Coverage Act passed earlier this year, the company appears to be on track to have taxpayers foot the bill.
How does this happen?
The company is Grail, named to reflect the promise of its product: a simple blood test to screen for multiple cancers — the so-called holy grail of cancer screening. Grail has made remarkable claims for its test: that it will save tens of thousands of lives and save money.
It has also been sued by its own investors twice: in 2024 and 2026. Furthermore, the company’s friendly relationship with England’s National Health Service has been criticized — a former Prime Minister David Cameron was a paid adviser, and NHS provided Grail with the public imprimatur of a high-profile trial of 140,000 Britons. All for a test that had shown little promise in early studies.
I have been writing about Grail for quite some time. In 2021, David Carr and I raised concerns about the lack of control group in the initial announcement of the trial (it was later clarified that there was a control group) and later that year were joined by David Kent in an investigation demonstrating that the trial was large enough to test the most relevant question for patients: Will it save lives? In 2022, Barnett Kramer and I questioned the confluence of Congress and multicancer screening and went on to criticize the design of the taxpayer-funded Grail/Medicare study the following year.
I agree that the underlying technology is truly remarkable. This test, as well as others like it, can detect tiny fragments of free-floating DNA in the blood. More remarkably, the technology can distinguish a little bit of tumor DNA from the sea of normal DNA in our blood. It may prove quite useful for cancer patients by helping discern who has been completely treated (no tumor DNA) from those who need more treatment (persistent tumor DNA).
But Grail’s interest is in screening. Why? Because screening means a huge market. While there are only so many cancer patients, all of us are candidates for screening.
Screening is an easy sell. It taps into a widely held belief: the sooner, the better. It always finds more cancer patients, which is interpreted as helping people. It always produces more “cancer survivors” — powerful stories of individuals found to have cancer by the test who are currently doing well. And it is always accompanied by longer survival times and thus higher five-year survival rates.
Easy sell, but horribly deceptive. Telling more people they have cancer is not progress; progress is having fewer people die from cancer. Some survive because treatment works, not because the cancer was detected earlier; others survive because they were overdiagnosed (diagnosed with a cancer not destined to cause symptoms or death). And survival statistics always go up because the survival clock is started earlier and because overdiagnosed patients do really well.
Because of this deceptive feedback, the gold standard for evaluating cancer screening has been a randomized trial of screening vs. no screening to determine the effect on cancer death. That is the standard that has been applied to breast, colorectal, lung, and prostate cancer screening. Even Grail investigators agree: Practice-changing level of evidence requires a randomized trial testing cancer death. Other Grail investigators modeled the likely impact of their multicancer test, estimating a 25% reduction in the death rate for all cancers combined.
But the Grail/National Health Service trial did not investigate the effect of screening on cancer death. Instead, it tested the effect on how many patients were found to have late-stage cancer. That’s a surrogate outcome: While effective screening should reduce the number of patients who present with late-stage disease (because aggressive cancers are found earlier) that doesn’t necessarily mean cancer deaths will fall (because aggressive cancers may be no more treatable when found earlier). That’s what happened with ovarian cancer screening: fewer late-stage patients, but no change in death.
Nevertheless, the Grail/National Health Service trial was negative. No reduction in late-stage cancer. The trial provided no evidence that this test will reduce cancer deaths by 25%. Yet the FDA advisory panel recommends approval.
Don’t ask me why. I don’t pretend to know. But I do know that FDA approval would trigger a tsunami of public and private expenditure.
The reason is the Medicare Multi-Cancer Early Detection Screening Coverage Act, signed into law earlier this year. It mandates Medicare coverage of multicancer screening tests following FDA approval — bypassing the usual role of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. And private insurers will undoubtedly face enormous pressure to follow suit.
There was widespread, bipartisan support in Congress. Why? The juxtaposition of the words “cancer” and “early detection” has obvious political appeal. Furthermore, Grail spearheaded a massive lobbying effort — even going so far as to suggest that multicancer screening will reduce health disparities and the American Cancer Society echoed the claim.
Seriously? We can screen away health disparities? I don’t think so.
While the advisory panel has recommended that the FDA approve Grail’s test, the FDA itself has yet to render judgment. Hopefully, the agency will question why it should approve an expensive test whose benefit has not been demonstrated — especially given the prospect of a cascade of coverage decisions bound to make health insurance more expensive at a time when fewer and fewer Americans can afford it.
And with the National Cancer Institute preparing a major randomized trial of multicancer screening tests using cancer death as the endpoint, the agency should also consider whether approving Grail’s test will impede that work. (Why volunteer for the trial if multicancer screening is already covered by insurance?)
Almost forgot: I estimate that screening all Americans 50 and older would have a ballpark cost of $60-$100 billion per year. Here’s the math: There are more than 120 million Americans over 50 — the population for whom Grail recommends annual screening. The test will cost somewhere between about $500 (the current Medicare payment for Cologuard, the benchmark specified in the MCED Coverage Act) and $949 (Grail’s current list price).
To the FDA: Don’t approve the test. Test the tests. Let the National Cancer Institute do its work. And don’t make Americans pay even more for health care.
H. Gilbert Welch is a physician and cancer screening researcher at the Center for Surgery and Public Health at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston.

Mumbai: A Class 7 student was allegedly threatened with a knife and injected with an unidentified substance in the neck by a group of four to five boys in Barve Nagar, Ghatkopar West, on October 5 around 7.30 pm, police said.
Incident Near School Playground
The boy’s father, Ramu Chaurasia, said his son, a student of Municipal School No. 3 in Barve Nagar, had gone to a playground opposite his school in Bhatwadi to play with his friends. While he was leaving the ground with his cousin, a group of four to five boys allegedly confronted them and asked them to leave.
One of the boys allegedly punched the student on his back before another member of the group injected a syringe containing a white-coloured liquid into his neck. The student reportedly felt dizzy and collapsed shortly thereafter.
Student Taken To Hospital
Local residents informed the boy’s family, following which he was taken to the nearby Sant Muktabai General Hospital for treatment. His family said his condition is now out of danger.
Ghatkopar police visited the hospital, recorded the student’s statement and registered a case under Sections 115, 118(1) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). Police said the boys involved are believed to be school students and that the victim recognises one of them but does not know his name.
Police are examining CCTV footage from the area to identify those involved and establish the sequence of events. Police are also awaiting the reports of the medical tests conducted on the victim.
The incident has also raised concerns among residents about substance abuse in the Barve Nagar area. Rajesh Sawant, president of the Mokalā Shwas organisation, called for strict action against those responsible and said a protest march has been planned in Ghatkopar on Sunday in response to the incident.

A 1-kg mass of hair was removed from the stomach and small intestine of a nine-year-old girl in a rare surgery at a private hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam, authorities said on Saturday.
The girl, who was diagnosed with Rapunzel syndrome, underwent the surgery at NIMS Medicity in nearby Neyyattinkara, they said.
She was admitted to the hospital with persistent abdominal pain and vomiting, according to a statement issued by the hospital. Ultrasound and CT scans revealed severe intestinal obstruction, and a subsequent endoscopy confirmed a large mass of hair accumulated in the stomach and small intestine.
The hairball was completely removed through a complex surgical procedure led by Dr Biju I G Nair, senior consultant in the Department of Paediatric Surgery at the hospital. The girl recovered well, resumed eating normally and was discharged, the doctor said.
Dr Nair said a trichobezoar, or hairball, forms when a person repeatedly pulls out and swallows hair. The swallowed hair cannot be digested and can gradually accumulate in the stomach, forming a hard mass that may cause intestinal obstruction over time, he said.
Rare condition
Rapunzel syndrome is an extremely rare condition in which a trichobezoar extends from the stomach into the small intestine. It is usually seen in adolescent girls, according to medical literature. Hospital authorities said fewer than 100 cases have been reported worldwide.
