TPG continues to dilute its shareholding in Shadowfax. The private equity (PE) giant has now sold more shares of the listed logistics company via an open-market transaction for ₹114.8 Cr. According to BSE data, the PE major, via its entity NewQuest Asia Fund IV (Singapore), sold 40 Lakh shares of Shadowfax at ₹287 apiece to rake in the amount. There was no clarity on who lapped up the shares that flooded the market. The bulk deal was undertaken at a discount of 0.3% to the stock’s last closing price on Tuesday. This is the fourth time that TPG has sold its stake in the logistics company in the past three months. Last week, the PE firm offloaded Shadowfax shares worth ₹113.6 Cr. In September, the PE firm offloaded more shares of the company worth ₹200 Cr. A month prior in August, TPG also sold Shadowfax stake in a bulk deal worth ₹300 Cr. The bulk deals come as investors look to book profits amid a sharp jump in Shadowfax’s share prices. The stock hit an all-time high ₹291.90 on September 24. Overall, shares of the company have surged 10.96% in the past month, and are up more than 144.38% in the last six months. This jump has come on the back of healthy performance by the startup on the financial front. The logistics major reported an 8X surge in its consolidated net profit to ₹65.4 Cr in Q1 FY27 compared to ₹8 Cr in the year ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue jumped 65% YoY and 10% QoQ to ₹1,358.1 Cr in the quarter under review. Following the results, Shadowfax also revised its FY27 revenue growth forecast to 38-40%, a significant jump from the 28-30% guidance projected just a quarter ago. Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Bansal and Vaibhav Khandelwal, Shadowfax operates a logistics network serving ecommerce, quick commerce and D2C brands. The company was listed on the stock exchanges earlier this year. It currently operates across more than 16,372 pincodes and plans to increase its network of dark stores from 47 to 100 by March 2027 as it looks to strengthen its quick commerce business. Shares of Shadowfax closed Tuesday’s trading session 0.4% lower at ₹287.75 on the BSE.

Govt employee caught recording Bombay High Court proceedings, fined Rs 10,000
Bombay High Court judges noticed a person in the last row holding a mobile phone with its flash on during proceedings. The court treated it as suspected unauthorised recording and fined a government official Rs 10,000.
The Bombay High Court on Tuesday imposed a Rs. 10,000 fine on a government employee for recording court proceedings without permission, warning that such violations could attract severe legal action, including contempt proceedings.
The action came after the bench detected the unauthorised recording during a hearing and found that the official had attempted to delete the footage after being caught.
A division bench of Justices GS Kulkarni and Dr Neela Gokhale noticed a person seated in the last row of the courtroom on Tuesday, holding a mobile phone with its flash switched on. Suspecting that he was recording the proceedings, the court had him apprehended.
The person was identified as Dilip Wagh, an employee of the Office of the Education Inspector. The bench noted that Wagh had no case listed before it.
After being caught, he attempted to delete the footage from his phone. However, the court’s IT department recovered the recording from the device’s deleted items.
The bench observed that unauthorised recordings of court proceedings can be manipulated and distorted before being circulated on social media.
Referring to Wagh’s conduct, the court remarked that he acted "as if he was sitting in a garden or on the roadside".
The judges said the conduct warranted contempt proceedings but accepted Wagh’s apology subject to conditions. The court stressed that recording proceedings without written permission violates Rules 9.2 and 9.3 of the Rules Governing Live-Streaming and Recording of Court Proceedings.
The bench further observed that Wagh, being a government employee, had a "more onerous" responsibility to follow the rules.
It also expressed concern over the growing trend of unauthorised recordings being shared and distorted on social media.
As part of its directions, the court ordered Wagh’s mobile phone to be seized and confiscated. His personal data will be wiped in his presence by the Registrar (Judicial-I) and the IT department before the device is disposed of.
Wagh has been directed to deposit Rs. 10,000 with the Secretary of the High Court Legal Services Authority, Mumbai, within two weeks.
If he fails to pay, the amount will be recovered directly from his salary. The court also warned that any future violation could lead to formal contempt proceedings and other severe legal action.

England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender
- Published
Harry Kane will write another chapter in his illustrious England history by equalling Peter Shilton's record tally of 125 caps if he plays a part in the Uefa Nations League meeting with the Czech Republic at Wembley.
England's captain is already his country's record scorer with 89 goals in 124 appearances in a full international career he started by opening his account 79 seconds into his debut.
Since that 4-0 win against Lithuania at Wembley in March 2015, he has been England's mainstay. He is still irreplaceable at 33 and their top scorer in major tournaments with 21 goals in 36 appearances across six of those showpieces, ahead of Gary Lineker's 10 goals in 18 appearances.
He is in the process of building a monument to his goalscoring brilliance at elite level as he currently stands 36 goals ahead of England's second-highest scorer Wayne Rooney, who boasts a record of 53 goals in 120 games.
Kane is unquestionably England men's most important and influential player of the modern era. The only blemish on his magnificent career is the failure – not his alone it must be stressed – to add to the one men's World Cup won in 1966.
Irrespective of that space for silverware on his CV, how highly does Kane rank in the pantheon of greats who have represented the England men's team? Could he even be the greatest? He has made himself a serious contender.
- The great number nine decline - where have England's strikers gone? 
  - Published13 November 2025
- Can Kane buck history and win Ballon d'Or? 
  - Published7 September
Moore? Charlton? Rooney? - where does Kane rank?
This argument will instantly cut away from Kane to Bobby Moore, the elegant, unflappable defender who remains the only England captain to lift the World Cup, leading his team to triumph at Wembley in July 1966 as West Germany were beaten 4-2.
Moore was only 25 at the time, and had enjoyed success at club level with West Ham United, winning the FA Cup and European Cup Winners' Cup before the World Cup. He won 108 caps between May 1962 and November 1973.
And then, of course, the conversation must turn to Sir Bobby Charlton, who survived the Munich Air Disaster with Manchester United in 1958 to become arguably England's most famous footballer of his era.
Charlton was a global beacon of dignity and world-class ability, winning the World Cup then, two years later, captaining Manchester United when they became the first English team to win the European Cup, scoring twice as Benfica were beaten 4-1 at Wembley.
He remains third on England's list of scorers, with 49 goals in 106 games.
Sir Geoff Hurst will always claim a special place with his hat-trick in the World Cup final win, while many others will have their supporters from recent times, including the likes of Wayne Rooney and David Beckham.
Former England midfielder Danny Murphy, said: "Bobby Moore will always be in people's conversation. Sir Bobby Charlton also, because of what they did and the memories they created.
"As you move forward, for me as a kid Gazza [Paul Gascoigne] burst on the scene and became a hero, especially as a creative midfield player myself.
"I think Rooney was arguably the most all-round footballer we have ever had, the most talented I've seen – but no-one can argue with Harry Kane's quality, numbers and longevity. It is the record of an England great."
He added: "There is one thing there is no debate about. Harry Kane is England's greatest goalscorer.
"No-one can take that away from him. The numbers over such a period of longevity are incredible. This, in itself, deserves all the accolades in the world. To stay at that level and not have anybody displace him is testimony to his ability and professionalism.
"He's a born goalscorer. He's a super professional. He's technically brilliant. He's been an absolute credit to himself and his family in the way he's conducted himself and the longevity he's had in his career.
"Is he England's greatest player? This is all about opinions and eras, but his record and longevity alone informs you that he is an England great. He is in that elite group."
'We are guilty of underestimating what is in front of us'
Kane's status as an England great is beyond question. Where he stands in that list of greats will be shaped by eras and opinions, according to former internationals Paul Robinson and Murphy.
Robinson told BBC Sport that the scale of Kane's greatness may only be fully appreciated in years to come.
He said: "Harry Kane is an England great. There is no argument. He will always be part of that conversation now.
"I think we are guilty in the modern era of underestimating what we've got in front of us. We are quite happy to look through rose-tinted spectacles at what we had in the past.
"We will talk about Bobby Moore and Sir Bobby Charlton, but football now is a completely different game. The life of a footballer is completely different and it's almost like they are playing a different game.
"What Bobby Moore and Sir Bobby Charlton achieved, nobody in an England shirt has done since. You respect what they did in the era, and the status and legacy that comes with winning the World Cup and everything else they did, but we must also say it is a different game now."
Kane's double in Saturday's 7-0 win in Croatia took his tally to 11 goals in 12 games for England in this calendar year. He has also scored in six consecutive England away games, with only Sir Tom Finney having a longer run, seven between September 1946 and May 1948.
Last season alone, Ballon d'Or contender Kane scored a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for England and his club Bayern Munich.
He has scored five hat-tricks in an England career which includes 110 starts, with a 66% win rate.
"The biggest compliment you can pay Harry Kane is to ask yourself how long we've been pondering the question 'what will England do if Harry Kane gets injured?'," Robinson added.
"There is no-one close to his class in that position. It is taken as read the captain is playing and without the captain, we would be in trouble.
"I think we'll appreciate him even more in another 10,15, 20 years when you look back and see what he has achieved. People will point to the lack of silverware with England, but he can't play everywhere can he?
"We look back with nostalgia and fondness, saying we've had this great and that great – and England have – but make no mistake Kane is right in that debate and will be for years to come."
'The big moments haven't yet happened for him'
Kane's lack of a major international trophy will undoubtedly be the argument used to counter suggestions he is England's greatest.
He has come close, only to lose two World Cup semi-finals and two European Championship finals.
The next Euros in the United Kingdom and Ireland in 2028 could be his last chance to change that unwanted record.
Murphy, said: "The only thing really missing from him is the icing on the cake, namely getting over the line in a major tournament, which is looking less likely for him as the years go by.
"I suppose that will always be one criticism of him, as well as many England players and generations. Nobody has managed to get them over the line since 1966, and the responsibility usually does fall on the strikers or the captain.
"He didn't score in the World Cup semi-final against Croatia 2018 or in the Euros final against Italy at Wembley. He missed a penalty against France in the World Cup quarter-final in 2022, then obviously he didn't score in the Euro 2024 final against Spain or the World Cup semi-final against Argentina.
"People will look at that and say in the big moments, it didn't happen for him.
"I don't adhere to that observation at all because it's not just him and he did so much to get England in those positions. Anyone can miss a penalty. The reality is the team itself, the tactics, all those things factor into why England haven't got over the line."
As Kane stands on the brink of equalling the England caps record, he still has time – and the enduring quality - to state his case as an all-time great even more forcefully in the future.

- U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced the creation of an Office of Religious Affairs at the Department of Defense on Sept. 30, 2026, during a speech he called the "State of the Force" address.
- Hegseth suggested the Office of Religious Affairs would address urgent spiritual needs among the troops, which he said had long been neglected. He said the office would report directly to him and that budgets would be guaranteed both for chaplaincy and infrastructure, such as "base chapels."

In October 2026, a rumor spread that U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had announced the creation of an Office of Religious Affairs at the Pentagon.
The claim spread on social media, including X. One X post included a video of Hegseth speaking on a stage with a U.S. flag background (archived):
"Today, at my direction, I am establishing the Office of Religious Affairs," Hegseth says in the video. "Starting today, and for secretaries of war after me, the Office of Religious Affairs will report straight to the top. No staff filters. No bureaucratic dilution. A direct line to the secretary."
Meanwhile, several Snopes readers searched the website seeking more information about the supposed Office of Religious Affairs.
It is true that on Sept. 30, 2026, Hegseth gave a speech he called the "State of the Force" address. In this speech, he said he had ordered the creation of an office dedicated to religious affairs, which Department of Defense spokesperson Sean Parnell confirmed in an X post (archived):
We reached out to the DOD seeking more details about the initiative and will update this story if we learn more.
Here's what we know about the new DOD office so far:
Office of Religious Affairs
In his speech, Hegseth said the initiative would address what he described as long-neglected spiritual needs among the troops (starting around the 50:25 mark of the DOD's recording of the speech):
After describing how significant the loss of a religious community could be for military personnel assigned to a new location or deployed abroad, Hegseth said that "political correctness and secular humanism" had allowed budgets for religious support to dwindle and infrastructure such as "base chapels" to go into disarray.
Religious diversity in the force
Hegseth said that "less than 5% of our force identifies as non-religious," without citing his source for the number. A 2019 congressional report found that while 2.3% of the force identified as agnostic or atheist, the affiliation of 24.4% of active duty personnel fell under "Other/Unclassified/Unknown" (PDF Page 51).
Meanwhile, the Military Association of Atheists and Freethinkers, an organization that advocates for nonreligious military members but is not associated with the DOD, said 2.05% of the force identified as "Humanists" in 2018 (Humanism is a non-theistic belief; Humanists believe in a moral and ethical code without believing in God). That report also said the chaplaincy did not represent the religious diversity of the military, with an overrepresentation of evangelistic Christians, when only 13.31% of the troops identified as such.
We reached out to the MAAF for comment on the creation of the office. A spokesperson told us the group was in the process of dissolving and directed us to the American Humanist Association, a nonprofit that advocates for secular humanism. We will update this story if the AHA returns our request for a statement on the possible impact of the creation of the office on nonreligious service members.
In May 2026, the DOD released a list of recognized religions in a memorandum signed by Undersecretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata. The memo included 31 religions, down from 211, according to Military.com, the news outlet dedicated to reporting on the U.S. Military. Twenty-two of those 31 were Christian denominations.
Hegseth then announced the creation of the Office of Religious Affairs, designed to report directly to him in the Pentagon organizational chart. In his announcement, he said (around 52:32 of the video embedded above):
This won't be a paper pushing shop. It will have real teeth. It will protect budgets, demand infrastructure, and strengthen religious support. The experts, our chaplains, will finally have an advocate at the highest levels. Policy and resources will serve the mission, not smother the mission.
'Spiritual readiness' and 'spiritual resilience'
A memo issued on the same day confirmed the creation of the office. It read, in part:
The Department of War is committed to fulfilling its duty to support the Department's Service members, their families, and the Department's civilian personnel in the free exercise of religion as protected by the Constitution of the United States and applicable Federal law. While the Department accomplishes this mission primarily through the chaplaincies of the Military Departments established under title 10, U.S. Code, the establishment of the ORA will ensure resources are adequately provided and, where necessary, policy is properly aligned to prioritize the free exercise of religion and the spiritual readiness across the Total Force.
Still, Hegseth's memo said, this effort to support the spirituality of military personnel should not "be construed to compel religious participation or to diminish the free exercise rights of any Service member, civilian employee, or family member of any faith or no faith."
The memo also said the new office had 90 days to present a plan of action to rebuild the spiritual force of the military:
Within 90 days of the date of this memorandum, the Secretaries of the Military Departments, in coordination with their respective Chiefs of Chaplains, will submit to the Director a comprehensive baseline report of all unfunded and underfunded religious affairs requirements, including, but not limited to, delivery ofreligious ministry, facilities and infrastructure, logistics, chaplain-led programs, chapel youth programs, faith-based homeschool support for military families, programs related to suicide reduction, and contracted services from faith-based non-Federal entities; research, technology, and analytical tools to support spiritual fitness, spiritual readiness, and spiritual resilience; chaplain in-service procurement programs, chaplain and religious support team training and education.
For further reading, Snopes examined another announcement Hegseth made that day, the launch of "Project Meridian," set to study the "future of warfare."

Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad - a first for US military since World War Two
- Published
The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first such military execution in more than 60 years.
Nidal Malik Hasan, a US Army major and physician, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it.
It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Hasan was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder by a jury panel of 13 officers, which unanimously recommended his death sentence.
Parnell said the Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution.
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," he wrote on X.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes".
He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.
It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.
The US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces deemed the military death penalty unconstitutional in 1983 but it was reinstated the following year by an executive order under then-President Ronald Reagan.
Military executions differ from those carried out at the state level.
The majority of executions in the US are carried out on the state level, with 27 states, the military and the federal government still having capital punishment as a legally available option.
Death by firing squad is rather uncommon. There was an execution by firing squad carried out last year in South Carolina, a first for the state and the first time the method was used in the US in 15 years.
Four other states allow the use of a firing squad, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Utah.
Trump has been a proponent of the federal death penalty and re-instated it through an executive order on the first day of his administration in January 2025.
Under his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, the justice department had issued a moratorium on the federal use of the death penalty.
The executive order signed by Trump describes capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

The National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings for parts of southern California, including Los Angeles, until Thursday, as temperatures are expected to hit the high 30s celsius. Burbank, a suburb north of Los Angeles, recorded 39C on Saturday, a few degrees shy of the October record for the region set in 1987. A persistent area of high pressure will remain in place this week, leading to further hazardous hot weather and increased fire risk.
Parts of Indonesia are in the midst of an extreme wildfire season, which has peaked over the past month. Western Kalimantan (Borneo) and southern Sumatra have been particularly badly affected. The lack of rainfall has dried the usually water-logged tropical soils, meaning that fires have been able to spread quickly, above and below the surface. Indonesia’s soils are also extremely rich in peat, meaning that the smoke produced from the fires contain higher levels of toxic gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Cities in surrounding areas and as far as Malaysia and Singapore have experienced reduced air quality in recent weeks as a result. Drought and wildfires are more common in this part of the world during El Niño events owing to suppressed thunderstorm activity.
On the flip side, El Niño is contributing to an extremely active period for tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean. After recent hurricanes in the eastern half of the basin, Super Typhoon Choi-Wan is now active and a category 4 typhoon to the south-east of Japan, while on a strengthening trend. After developing on 30 September, Choi-Wan moved through the Northern Mariana Islands as a tropical storm, causing power outages on the island of Tinian, forcing the closure of schools and government offices. Choi-Wan underwent rapid intensification after clearing the islands on Sunday, and as of Sunday night has sustained winds of 150mph, and gusts of up to 180mph. The system is expected to curve away from mainland Japan and areas affected by Typhoon Dujuan last month, while steadily weakening over the coming week.

Roughly 200 people are under medical observation, several hospitals are under quarantine, and dozens are in isolation in Russia following the unexplained death of an infectious disease researcher at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia, in the town of Shelekhov, according to early reports of the situation on Sunday and Monday.
Researcher Darya Shipilova reportedly died last week from pneumonia of “unknown” cause, according to Rospotrebnadzor, a Russian public health agency.
Unconfirmed information regarding her death has swirled. Some reports have claimed she accidentally broke a test tube containing the plague pathogen, Yersinia pestis, on September 25. She subsequently fell ill, was admitted to a hospital September 29 with severe pneumonia and died overnight between October 1 and Oct. 2. The head of the Russian region that neighbors Irkutsk, Alexey Tsydenov, initially reported that she had died of plague but later altered his statement to say she “possibly” died of the disease.
Y. pestis can cause several forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic—the latter of which can be aggressive and quickly fatal. However, the pathogen is generally easily treated by antibiotics. In the US, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that anyone exposed to the pathogen should undergo an immediate 7-day post-exposure antibiotic prophylaxis treatment. Additionally, though pneumonic plague is spread via respiratory particles from coughing, it is not considered highly infectious; it requires direct, close contact for the bacteria to be transmitted.

Vaxcyte said Monday that its experimental pneumococcal vaccine hit the primary endpoints in a Phase 3 clinical trial, setting up the California-based biotech to compete with Pfizer and Merck.
Vaxcyte’s shot, VAX-31, is designed to protect against 31 serotypes, or strains, of bacteria that can cause pneumococcal disease, including pneumonia, compared to 20 strains for Pfizer’s Prevnar and 21 strains for Merck’s Capvaxive.
In the trial, just over 3,500 adults age 50 and older were randomized to receive VAX-31, Prevnar, or Capvaxive. Investigators then measured the strength of their antibody responses against different strains.

Newcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.
The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.
Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.
Anant Amabani, 31, who is leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.
Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species. Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing.
The university’s announcement was met with incredulity and derision from academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists.
Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.
“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”
Bhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator into illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”
Prof Matt Perry, the chair of the University and College Union branch at Newcastle University, said staff members had objected to the appointment citing environmental concerns.
Prof Lyla Mehta, the head of the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.
She said: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”
In April, Anant Ambani launched Vantara University, billed as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.
Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”
In 2025, an investigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung found that many animals delivered to Vantara arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been illegally trafficked.
In August last year, an investigation by India’s supreme court, which lasted less than three weeks, cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing. A subsequent fact-finding mission into the zoo by Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were probably forged.
Its report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”
Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals. However, it subsequently reversed its decision after objections from India, the US and Japan at a Cites meeting after they argued there was not enough proof of illegal imports.
In August, the zoo launched a “reset” in its operations by appointing a former Cites head to oversee its operations and said it would voluntarily pause all wildlife imports until June next year.
Vantara has declined to comment. The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking. They have said: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.”
A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”

The disclosure of BJP’s West Bengal election expenditure has sparked a storm on social media after revealing a Rs 2.5 lakh payment to Bengali actor and vlogger Sayak Chakraborty, who was involved in a controversial beef-steak incident at Kolkata’s Olypub in January 2026.
The report, published on the party’s letterhead and signed by office secretary at the BJP headquarters Mahendra Kumar Pandey details the party’s expenditure between March 15, the date of announcement of West Bengal assembly elections, and May 6, 2026, the official completion of the polls. The report shows that the BJP paid Rs 2,50,000 to a person named Sayak Chakraborty.
The payment appears under Schedule 3, titled “Expense(s) on Media Advertisement (print and electronic, bulk SMS, cable, website and TV channel etc.) on General Party propaganda authorised/incurred by Party Central Headquarters”. Chakraborty is listed at serial number 23 under the “electronic media” category.
The disclosure has drawn particular attention because Chakraborty was involved in a beef-related controversy at the iconic Park Street pub, Olypub, on January 30, 2026.
Following the publication of the expenditure report, Chakraborty acknowledged that he had been paid by the BJP, but claimed it had nothing to do with the Olypub incident.
The Olypub Incident & Why the Expenditure Disclosure Raises Eyebrows
On January 30, Chakraborty alleged that he had been served beef steak instead of a mutton dish at the restaurant. He subsequently lodged an FIR against Olypub and the concerned waiter who allegedly served him beef.
Sayak recorded the heated interaction on a live video and posted it on his Facebook page. His page, ‘Sayakk’, has 1.5 million followers. The 3-minute-47-second video has since been deleted from the page but remains available across social media. The clip can be watched here:
According to Chakraborty, while having dinner at Olypub, he and two friends ordered a mutton steak. The server placed a plate of food on their table without telling them what it was. Unaware of what they had been served, they ate it. After they had finished the dish, the waiter returned with another plate and said, “This is your mutton steak.” When they questioned him about the earlier dish, the waiter allegedly said it had been a beef steak.
Trouble started after that.
In the viral video, Chakraborty can be heard saying, “I ordered mutton steak; how could you mess it up and serve me beef instead? How could you hear beef instead of mutton? Do you know I am a Brahmin? I ate beef instead of mutton because of you!”
He also asked the server, Nasimuddin Sheikh, about his religion, before saying, “You made me eat Go-Mata!”
Following the altercation with the server, the actor lodged an FIR at Park Street police station. Kolkata Police arrested Nasimuddin based on the complaint. He was released on bail four days later.
The disclosure of the BJP’s expenditure immediately raised questions about whether Chakraborty had been paid by the party for his role in the Olypub episode. The questions gained further significance given that the incident had the potential to fuel a communal debate around beef, religion and Hindu identity — ideas that could serve the BJP’s broader political messaging.
They also arose because the immediate relatives of another person who was with Sayak during the incident appear in the BJP’s expenditure list.
At Olypub, while the beef controversy was unfolding, Sayak was accompanied by fellow social media influencer Sukanta Kundu and Kundu’s female friend. The BJP’s list includes the names of Sikha Kundu and Subrata Kundu, identified as Sukanta’s parents. Sikha and Subrata were paid Rs 4,50,000 and Rs 3,00,000 respectively.
Sayak Chakraborty’s Disclosure
As social media posts questioning Chakraborty’s association with the BJP gained traction, and media reports on the issue emerged, Sayak made a Facebook post on the morning of September 26, admitting that he had received a payment from the party.
He, however, claimed that his reaction at Olypub was a genuine outburst and not paid promotion.
He pointed to Olypub’s statement apologising for the meat mix-up as evidence that the episode was not scripted to evoke emotions. According to him, the BJP and others who shared his views simply supported him after the incident.
Chakraborty said the BJP and a few other political parties had subsequently approached him to make promotional content. He accepted the BJP’s offer and made several videos, including content on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), possible reasons behind Narendra Modi’s silence during the conflict, and a congratulatory message for Suvendu Adhikari after he became chief minister.
He reiterated that these videos were made between March and May, the period covered by the BJP’s expenditure report, while the Olypub incident took place in January. Alt News tried calling up Chakraborty on his mobile number, but his phone was switched off.
Kundu, too, shared a Facebook post on September 26, acknowledging that the payment details being linked to him were indeed genuine. At the same time, he asserted that the Olypub incident was not part of his political campaign.

The Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI) has said that the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India’s (IRDAI) recently proposed norms could trigger a 60-70% revenue collapse across the insurance broking sector. Addressing a press briefing, the industry body representatives also said that the insurance distribution sector, which employs over 83 Lakh people, could see the loss of up to 10 Lakh jobs lost as a result of the economic impact of the proposed policies. This comes days after IRDAI proposed reintroducing product-wise commission caps for insurance distributors. The regulator also proposed tighter limits on insurers’ overall expenses over concerns related to disproportionate increases in commissions paid to distributors. The industry body has also sought an extension of the deadline to submit feedback on the proposed norms to December-end from October 25 currently. While noting that the association supports the regulator’s goal of making insurance more affordable and accessible, the IBAI representatives noted that the proposed sweeping changes threaten small businesses and MSMEs. The resulting job losses could impact insurance awareness, policy renewals, assistance to policyholders, and penetration of insurance among underserved communities, the representatives added. The brokers also countered IRDAI’s data that showed that general insurance premiums sourced through brokers had risen 37% whereas commission payouts zoomed 173% between FY23 and FY27. The industry body argued that the rise in commissions since FY23 largely reflected the reclassification of off-book marketing expenses following regularisation, and did not reflect inflationary pressures on insurance consumers. The IBAI also claimed that the entire general insurance industry’s operating expenses averaged around 26.5% of gross premiums as against the mandated limit of 30%. Making its point, the representatives also claimed that policyholders received back ₹84.4 in non-life insurance claim payouts for every ₹100 of premium paid over a five-year period. This is more than the global average of 72-75%, demonstrating the efficiency of the market in delivering value, the body’s representatives claimed. The industry body said it was ready to work with IRDAI to address specific market anomalies, such as misselling or disproportionate remuneration. It has also submitted formal letters to the Prime Minister’s Office and the Finance Ministry on the matter. Notably, the pushback comes as insurtech platforms continue to be up in arms against the proposed norms. Last week, Sanjib Jha, founder of insurtech startup Coverfox, said that the proposal could impact the viability of distributing insurance to rural and low-income borrowers. Pune-based insurance broker Quickinsure has also trimmed more than 100 jobs in response to the proposal as its founder Anand Shrikhande projected that the industry would see more than 1 Lakh jobs affected due to the changing economics. The news has also triggered a major sell-off in listed insurtech majors PB Fintech, which operates Policybazaar, and Turtlemint over fears that the IRDAI’s new policies would dent their core businesses.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
Today’s newsletter answers some pressing questions — what is optogenetics? When should I get my flu shot, as cases rise in parts of the United States? And perhaps most importantly — why do longevity clinics include scratch-and-sniff smell tests as part of their treatments? All will be revealed if you read on.
The story of optogenetics, and how it has reshaped brain science
The brain is wildly complex. So it makes sense that the tools required to study it must be remarkably complex as well. As newsletter readers know, one of those foundational tools — optogenetics — won the Nobel Prize for medicine yesterday. (Karl Deisseroth, who shared the prize with two other scientists, is pictured above.) The discovery was decades in the making, STAT’s Megan Molteni and Annalisa Merelli write, born out of a scientist’s curiosity about how a single-celled alga is able to swim toward light.
The answer turned out to be channelrhodopsin, a protein that makes any cell it is inserted into light sensitive. The discovery “jumpstarted the development of a whole range of new tools that let us selectively turn on and off brain cells with incredible precision. It has let us go from a Rand McNally road atlas of the brain to something more akin to Google Earth,” one professor told Megan and Annalisa.
Read more about the incredible history and impact of this innovation.
What to know about when to get your flu shot
It’s the perennial fall question for those of you who get flu shots: When’s the best time to be vaccinated? Predicting what this mercurial virus will do is always tough. But here are some thoughts that may help you make your decision.
There’s been a ticking up of flu activity in the Pacific Northwest, which is leading to some calls for people to get vaccinated now. But the latest national data from the CDC still shows minimal activity in the vast majority of the country.
Michael Osterholm, director of the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy, says people in the west or those who have plans to travel there should probably think about getting vaccinated now. And people in other parts of the country should make arrangements to get their shots within the next two or three weeks, because booking appointments will get more challenging as flu activity starts to heat up elsewhere. But there’s nothing to suggest this is unusual or alarming at this point. “What I see now is a flu year starting out as a pretty normal flu year,” Osterholm said. — Helen Branswell
Pulse oximeters are unreliable in different ways, new study finds
Pulse oximeters gained prominence during the Covid-19 pandemic as an easy way to track oxygen levels in the blood. But studies have shown they can be unreliable, especially at estimating the oxygen levels for people with darker skin.
A recent paper adds another layer, finding that over five years, pulse oximeters went from overestimating blood oxygen levels to underestimating them at one hopspital. One of the authors of the paper called the device a “black box,” saying “I have no idea why we found what we found in this paper, and why it’s changing year over year.” Read more about this strange finding and what it means for standards of care.
A STAT reporter’s day at the longevity clinic: Treadmill tests, fancy snacks, and a scratch-and-sniff test
STAT reporters will do a lot to get the story. Sarah Todd, for example, recently subjected herself to a barrage of tests and treatments at one of the longevity clinics popping up in medical centers across the country.
Sarah ran on a treadmill to the point of exhaustion (to find her VO2 max); tested her sense of smell (since olfactory loss is a sign of rapid aging); and sat through all manner of scans and blood draws. She wanted to understand what these nonprofit hospitals — which receive tax benefits and other perks in exchange for nominally serving the public — are offering, and how they justify the steep price tag of $5,500 to $45,000.
Critics see hypocrisy in these hospitals’ efforts to cater to the well-off. (“For me, this just reinforces the impression that not-for-profit hospitals are really for-profits masquerading in not-for-profit clothing,” one Carnegie Mellon University professor said.) Others question whether all the offerings (like full body MRIs) are scientifically sound. Where did Sarah come out on all this? Read more.
66%
That’s the proportion of U.S. adults who now support “Medicare for All,” according to a new poll from KFF. That’s a big jump from 2020, when 53 percent of adults supported the policy. The reason for the shift might be tied to another one of the poll’s findings — 6 in 10 voters are worried about being able to afford their health care.
Dig deeper into that Medicare for All number and you’ll find the expected partisan split. While 84% of Democrats and 72% of independents favor the policy, 66% of Republicans are opposed. Read the full poll results here.
A doctor’s inside account of how AI tools jack up health care costs
After Leah Pierson sees a patient, she often receives a message from a hospital administrator. The emails encourage her to add certain comorbidities or complications to the medical record, allowing the hospital to bill more for treatment. These requests inquire about legitimate issues turned up in lab work or through other diagnostics, Pierson writes. And yet, she wonders what it’s costing the patient.
“Risk adjustment specialists ask us to document real diagnoses that we know could increase the cost of a patient’s bill, but we have no idea by how much,” she writes. “Moreover, there’s no medical school module on how much any of these comorbidities affects the true cost of the hospitalization. Against this backdrop, it makes sense that doctors try to just tell the truth: yes, this patient has low sodium, and we are monitoring it, even though this probably allows hospitals to code some patients as being more complicated than they truly are.”
Please give Pierson’s insightful piece a read, for an inside look on how doctors have gotten caught up in the billing arms race, and the pressures they face on the ground.

SEOUL – South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday that AI models are believed to have been used in some recent hacking incidents against banks and called for the country to develop cybersecurity methods suited to the AI era.
“In some hacking incidents, signs have emerged of AI being used, causing considerable public concern and anxiety,” Lee said during a cabinet meeting.
“Please establish the circumstances swiftly and clearly, and concentrate personnel and resources on minimizing the damage.”
South Korea’s police have launched a full-scale investigation into the hacking attacks against commercial banks that led to a breach of customers’ personal information, the Yonhap news agency reported on Tuesday.
Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and others had reported cyberattacks, the Financial Services Commission (FSC) said on Friday, while Yonhap reported that Hana Bank and Woori Bank also suffered breaches.
Authorities have not yet disclosed details on what kind of AI tools were used in the hacking incidents or the full scale of the breaches.
On Sunday, FSC Chairman Lee Eog-weon convened an emergency meeting with financial industry associations, regulators and executives from affected institutions, warning that the sector must respond with the highest level of vigilance.
Financial watchdog the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) and the Financial Security Institute shared data about 28 unique IP addresses and some country information linked to the recent hacking attempts with the financial sector, the FSS said on Tuesday.
In September, Australia said an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorized access to files, in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.
An artificial intelligence research firm said last week that AI agents tried to hack into a Canadian government website, casting the effort as a failed hacking attempt, while Canada said there were no indications its systems were compromised.

People fret about the buses India has missed in its technological growth. The list is familiar: aircraft, advanced weapons, new materials, and biotechnology. In each, we look at what others built decades ago and ask why we did not. There is value in this introspection, and there is danger. The value is that it forces us to ask whether our systems can be streamlined and enabled. Catching up is not a bad thing. Much of the world’s industrial history is a history of catching up. The danger is that catch-up-itis can become a habit. If our ambition is always defined by what someone else has already done, we will always arrive late, pay for licences and know-how, and build on foundations laid elsewhere. The costs of technological catch-up are a heavy burden, and they recur with every new wave.
Also read | India has a research blindspot: its own science system
There is a better question to ask, and it arises from a tectonic change in the relationship between science and technology. By science, we mean discovery, curiosity, the effort to explain the universe, and the development of abstract ideas in mathematics. By technology, we mean the development of tools that enable humans to transform the world. For much of history, these were treated as separate enterprises, with technology following science at a distance, sometimes by a century.
However, over the past 50 years or so, we have increasingly seen fundamental research and application sewn together at the hip. Much of our understanding of how genes are regulated came from studying viruses that infect bacteria. More recently, studying how bacteria defend themselves gave us CRISPR technology within just a few years, which has an extraordinary range of applications. Today, the distance and time from curiosity to application are short. This shift lets thinking and training lead, and it shows that investing in fundamental research will enable leading than playing catch-up. The bus we need to board is the next one, and it has not yet left.
Get on the bus first
For science from India to have global impact by developing transformative technologies, four things need to be addressed.
First, invest in high-quality education at scale. The features of AI that democratise access to learning allow us to reach millions of students poorly served by our moribund institutions, and to bypass those institutions where necessary. But learning science requires doing science. Hundreds of experimental “foundries” in engineering, physics, biology, chemistry and math should be created; places where young people work with real instruments on real problems.
Second, national laboratories need to be liberated from insularity. The bulk of our national labs are currently poorly accessible to researchers, students and companies outside their walls. This can easily change, benefiting both labs and universities. All national labs need to be organised around three zones: green for open interaction, amber for collaboration, and red for strategic work. Much of what India’s labs do belong in the green and amber zones.
Third is flexibility. Many say we are a low-trust society and that our regulators should trust our research system more and be more flexible. The response to this is to point out that trust is low because compliance with guidelines is poor, necessitating onerous rules. However, India does have many high-quality islands of excellence in universities, institutes and laboratories. These institutions do comply with the rules and regulations, and should be freed from the weight of General Financial Rules compliance, a weight few other countries place on their scientists. Accountability should be measured by outcomes, and not by procedure at every step. Flexibility can allow these institutions to leap ahead.
Fourth, our regulatory system still needs much reform. Approvals for research with biological materials and for clinical trials remain slow and unpredictable. The more hoops companies and researchers must jump through, the less likely small and medium-sized institutions are to succeed, since only those with deep pockets can afford the time and costs. Thus, high-quality, speedy regulation is important.
None of this is beyond us; they can be achieved step by step. Many are already doing so in pockets. What is missing is the decision to make those pockets the norm, and a few who dedicate themselves to this task. How long will it take to become a science-driven nation with global impact? If we improve just 10% in each sector, field, and every year, we will be nearly seven times better in 20 years.
K. VijayRaghavan is Former Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India and chairs Ashoka University’s Science Advisory Council; Archish Mittal is Vice-President, Iron Pillar

'I have never felt heat like that' - a survivor on watching 33 cellmates die in Nigeria
- Published
Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak.
The day before he had been trapped inside the stifling room, measuring roughly 6m (19.7ft) by 3m (9.8ft), with more than 50 other prisoners.
Thirty-three of his cellmates died in the cramped conditions in the prison in Minna, the capital of Nigeria's Niger state - and four died later in hospital.
The mass deaths caused an outcry and sparked protests, including attacks on public buildings, as relatives and locals demanded answers.
Federal officials had initially blamed the deaths on a diphtheria outbreak but exactly what happened is now the subject of an investigation.
"I have never felt heat like that in my life. When we touched each other's bodies, it felt like fire burning," Muhammad tells the BBC once he is able to gather his thoughts.
When he was locked inside, there was standing room only amid humidity levels of more than 90%, which in some circumstances can be dangerous to human health as it prevents the natural cooling mechanism of sweat drying on the skin.
The temperature outside was above 25C and the only ventilation came from a small, high-up window.
"One of us fainted and we started knocking at the [cell] door. When [a guard] came we asked him for water. He looked at the guy that fainted and closed the door. That's how they started dying one after the other," Muhammad says.
Like the others who had been detained, the young man, in his 20s, is an artisanal miner, eking out a living searching for precious metals at mine sites.
The federal government has tried to crack down on this alleged illegal activity as it says it costs the country revenue, damages the environment and can be linked to wider criminal activity.
Officers from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) had arrested a large group of miners near Minna last Tuesday and Wednesday.
The prisoners were held at its detention centre in the city, but the NSCDC has not shared either the names or the number of those it was holding.
As the hours inside the cell wore on, the heat and dehydration became unbearable and Muhammad says some of the detainees began drinking their own urine and collecting sweat from their bodies to try to stay alive.
He describes seeing people in distress and struggling to breathe.
"People were calling for help, some were already very weak."
But no-one came to help, he and others allege.
"While in the cell, we were shouting and telling them that people were dying," another survivor Adamu Isah told the Reuters news agency.
"We tried to break down the door when they refused to open it… At one point, a security officer came to the door.
"We were shouting and telling him that people were dying, but he said it wasn't his problem if people died."
Finally, on Thursday, the cell door was opened and the guards saw the dead bodies.
The NSCDC has not directly responded to the accusations of neglect and maltreatment but has said that 24 of its personnel are now in custody in connection with the deaths, including its suspended Niger state commandant Suberu Aniviye.
"The people who were killed are not flies. How can this go unlooked? We will get to the bottom of this," Niger state Governor Umaru Bago told the BBC.
As the organisation involved is a federal body rather than a force under his jurisdiction, such as the police, the governor is unable to exert direct influence but he welcomes the investigation that has been ordered by the government in capital, Abuja.
A 10-member committee has now been set-up to determine exactly what happened.
It has two weeks to establish the causes of the deaths and identify who was responsible and can recommend legal action against anyone found culpable.
No officer, regardless of rank, would be protected and any attempt to obstruct the investigation would be taken seriously, Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said.
As he leaves the cell after talking to the BBC, Muhammad says he hopes that by speaking out he can help find justice and bring some closure to this traumatic event.

Pakistan-made cosmetics that continued to find their way to Hyderabad more than a year after India shut the door on imports from the neighbouring country have now led investigators to Mumbai’s Crawford Market, pointing to a wider supply chain behind the banned products.
The development comes amid a separate public-health concern over some of the skin-whitening products. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) last month specifically warned consumers against two Pakistan-made creams after tests found excessive levels of heavy metals.
Both ‘Goree Beauty Cream’ and ‘Chandni Whitening Cream’, named in the September 8 CDSCO alert, were among the products found during raids on three shops in Hyderabad this week.
An officer involved in the investigation said the cosmetics seized in Hyderabad were allegedly being sourced from Crawford Market in Mumbai. “Investigators are now looking further up the chain to establish how the products entered India and reached wholesale and retail markets despite restrictions on their import.
Imports from Pakistan prohibited since May 2025
India prohibited the direct or indirect import or transit of all goods originating in or exported from Pakistan on May 2, 2025. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade imposed the restriction through a notification, citing national security and public policy.
The prohibition extends to goods entering India indirectly, meaning routing Pakistan-origin products through another country does not by itself make their import permissible.
Cosmetics imported into India are additionally governed by the Cosmetics Rules, 2020. Products must be registered with the Central Licensing Authority before import and are required to comply with prescribed quality and safety standards.
The CDSCO had stepped up scrutiny even before the latest Hyderabad seizure. In July, it directed its zonal offices, State licensing authorities and officers at ports to maintain enhanced surveillance following instances of imported cosmetics being sold in domestic markets without valid import registration certificates.
Heavy metals found in two creams
The health regulator followed this with a more pointed warning on September 8. After testing Goree Beauty Cream and Chandni Whitening Cream, it said neither had been issued a registration certificate for import and that the products contained heavy metals beyond specified limits, which could pose health risks, including toxic effects. Consumers were advised not to purchase or use them.
The Hyderabad investigation has meanwhile opened another line of inquiry. According to the officer, investigators found that an ointment originating from the United Kingdom was allegedly being mixed with cosmetic products and the resulting preparation sold for skin-lightening purposes.
Samples of the products have been sent for forensic examination, and investigators are awaiting the laboratory findings to establish their composition and determine the substances present in them.
Officials have raised concerns about potentially carcinogenic substances, but the forensic results are awaited. The precise health implications of the seized preparations are therefore yet to be established.
The latest investigation follows raids by the Hyderabad police and CDSCO at Beauty Ladies Emporium, Beauty Queen Shop and S.J. Medical Shop in the Habeeb Nagar and Nampally areas, where cosmetics valued at about ₹7 lakh were seized.
The stock included several Pakistan-made whitening creams, soaps and other cosmetic products. Five persons were identified in connection with their alleged sale and distribution.
The Crawford Market link also comes against the backdrop of enforcement action in Mumbai itself, where Pakistan-made cosmetics valued at about ₹12 lakh were seized during a raid in July.

For a long time, fungal infections have meant itchy skin, discoloured nails and sometimes hair loss.
These symptoms are collectively called dermatophytosis and are caused by a group of fungi called dermatophytes.
‘’Unfortunately, immunocompromised patients can get lesions all over their body. The itchiness and the lesions can get so severe that people even get suicidal thoughts,” said Shivaprakash Rudramurthy, professor of medical mycology at the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER), Chandigarh.
Global warming
Dermatophytes are molds: fungi that grow in long strands. The other common category of fungi is yeast, which are single, oval-shaped cells. Among the yeasts, Candida auris is rapidly emerging as a multidrug resistant pathogen in ICU facilities. It enters the blood stream and causes severe infections, most of which are untreatable by the available antifungals. According to Prof. Rudramurthy, those infected suffer a 30-40% mortality rate.
C. auris has become a menace only in the last two decades. The first report was in 2009 in Japan. Several other fungal species have become more pathogenic only in recent times. The cause of this rise remains unresolved but scientists and medical doctors have some ideas.
Fungi grow best in damp places below 30° C, so they can grow on our skin, especially in moist areas of the body, like armpits and the genital area. However, bloodstream infections in humans were rare because they could not survive in the body’s 37° C temperature.
“Fungal infections are common in cold-blooded animals with lower body temperatures,” Sriram Varahan, a mycologist at CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad, said.
“But global warming puts a selective pressure on fungi such that only the more heat-tolerant ones survive. These ones can survive inside our bodies too, if they gain access to it. This is called the fungal infection — mammalian selection hypothesis.”
Clinical samples
Today, roughly 20% of infections reported in hospitals are fungal in nature — yet most hospitals in India lack the capabilities and infrastructure to identify fungal pathogens, Prof Rudramurthy said.
This prompted PGIMER to begin storing fungal pathogens some 25 years ago. Today, the institute holds a stock of 15,000 clinical fungal isolates across India and helps other medical centres and clinicians identify and culture them for study, free of cost.
The C. auris isolates from PGIMER’s repository have come handy for Kaustuv Sanyal and his research associate Aswathy Narayanan, both at the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research, Bengaluru. They study how fungal pathogens divide and their genomes evolve.
In a recent study published in Nature Communications, they characterised the clinical isolates of C. auris found across India. Their focus was the pathogen’s ability to resist antifungals. They were able to establish their findings in patient samples and go beyond earlier studies in model systems.
“More than 90% clinical isolates of C. auris are resistant to common azole-based antifungals, such as fluconazole,” Prof. Sanyal said. Some “30% of them are resistant to another class of antifungals called the polyenes. They mostly respond to a different class of antifungals called the echinocandins.”
A drug may not work on a pathogen for many reasons, including the drug’s target becoming mutated or the drug’s effect being negated by the pathogen’s own biomolecules. Dr. Narayanan and her collaborators at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Thiruvananthapuram, found significant changes in drug-resistant C. auris genomes that could explain why Indian clinical isolates were able to resist azoles and echinocandins.
Susceptibility tests
A fungal cell has two protective layers surrounding it. The outermost is the cell wall and the inner one is the cell membrane. Azole and polyene antifungals target a fat called ergosterol that is enriched in the cell membrane. Echinocandins target the cell wall.
“When we grow C. auris isolates in the presence of fluconazole, the pathogen fights back by making extra copies of the Erg 11 gene. This in turn helps in higher production of ergosterol, thereby eliminating the effect of the azole drug,” Dr Narayanan said.
The study found parts in the C. auris genome where additional copies of the Erg11 gene were present.
With echinocandin drugs such as caspofungin, the team found mutations in the Fks1 gene that allowed the pathogen to resist the drug’s action. The team also found genetic changes promoting higher tolerance of echinocandins.
“Fks1 mutations can enable C. auris to survive even caspofungin doses up to 16 ug/ml. That means a patient with such a pathogen will need the drug at a concentration higher than 16 ug/ml,” Prof. Sanyal said. “Today, clinicians would not know that because they test the pathogen’s ability to survive only until 2 µg/mL of caspofungin — as defined by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and followed globally.”
The logical thing for clinicians would be to look for mutations like in the Fks1 gene and decide the limits for tests to decide the antifungal dose for patients. But due to associated costs, a more practical way is to increase the limits of susceptibility tests for caspofungin to higher than 16 ug/ml, Prof. Sanyal added.
C. auris, without any specific gene mutation or gene duplication, still responds to high concentrations of caspofungin in unexpected ways. While the pathogen dies at lower concentrations of the drug, at exceptionally high ones, it survives. This is paradoxical.
“This is because caspofungin at high doses activates compensatory pathways in the fungus,” Prof. Sanyal explained. “The fungus starts producing chitin, the raw material of the fungal cell wall, in large quantities. Any damage that caspofungin brings about on the cell wall is compensated by the extra chitin production. And thus the cell wall remains intact despite the antifungal.”
Such examples of paradoxical growth are called the Eagle effect, named for the U.S. pathologist Harry Eagle.
Beyond the arms race
The studies underline the importance of clinicians conducting more nuanced susceptibility tests to decide the antifungal doses. They show that fungi are protected from antifungals by genetic mutations as well as by making more copies of protective genes.
Prof. Sanyal also stressed on the need for a combination of therapies to target cellular compensatory pathways, keeping the major antifungals effective against drug-tolerant species.
However, Dr. Varahan said he believed scientists and doctors need to think of gentler alternatives: “When we target [a molecule] without which an organism cannot live at all, evolution ensures that its population survives with a changed molecule. So instead of participating in an arms race, it is perhaps better to target the less critical molecular pathways, inhibition of which will allow the pathogen to still survive but not cause a disease.”
It seems the idea of dousing fungal pathogens with antifungals is nearing its end. The next-generation of antifungals will need more planning.
Somdatta Karak heads science communication at CSIR-CCMB.

The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.
The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.
Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.
Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”
“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”
The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination”.
The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates, where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.
Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.
The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.
He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.
“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”
