OriginOS 7 adds useful upgrades like a customizable Control Center, Pet Pals themes, custom stickers, Liquid Glass controls, and Vivo Office Kit for seamless file sharing, clipboard sync, and screen mirroring across Windows and Mac.
Chinese smartphone makers replicate their software to look like iOS, aiming to appeal to users who want something familiar with an iPhone-like design. Vivo is no different. Their newly announced OriginOS 6 is a slight departure from the older Funtouch OS, which mimics iOS.
Vivo recently unveiled Origin OS 7 based on Android 17. Once again, Vivo gets heavily inspired by iOS and brought some of the biggest changes, many of which are welcome, while some I wish they had never made. You can view the full changelog here.
I have been using Origin OS 7 on my Vivo V80 for the past several days. Here are the 5 best Origin OS 7 features I found genuinely useful.
Table of Contents
5 Best OriginOS 7 Features
Adjust Liquid Glass Design
With iOS 26, Apple introduced a Liquid Glass design that most people hated.
The new glossy design made text harder to read and requires more power to render. Many Android skins have quickly adopted the Liquid Glass design, whether users like it or not, and Vivo is no different.
Vivo OriginOS 7 has incorporated the Liquid Glass design throughout the system. Unlike Apple, which introduced Liquid Glass transparency control a year after launch, OriginOS 7 offers three modes out of the box. You can set it to Realistic, Neutral, and Soft. If you are not a fan of Liquid Glass design, you can set it to Tinted.
One big note: the new Liquid Glass design seems limited to high-end smartphones, and the Vivo V80 lacks the feature entirely. It runs on Snapdragon 7 Gen 4. The biggest reason might be that mid-range chips can’t handle the heavy rendering required by the new glass design. Believing this, Vivo might have restricted this feature on other older and mid-range devices too.
Customizable Control Center
Another feature that Vivo borrowed from iOS is the ability to customize Control Center. For years, Android Control Center has remained the same. But with OriginOS 7, Vivo has taken a similar approach to Apple, letting you fully customize the layout and individual tiles.
The biggest change is that you can no longer be forced to use the default layout. You can rearrange or resize tiles however you want. With this functionality, you can also change the connectivity cards and media player, and remove them completely from the Control Center.
You can also rearrange the volume and brightness sliders, and even the network and media player, similar to what Apple allowed in iOS 26. If you’re not a fan of this new approach, Vivo also lets you choose the older Control Center layout in Settings.
However, by default, it is set to the old controls, and to change the layout, follow the steps below. Plus, you can also resize app icons on the home screen. You can simply long-press and drag them to your preferred size.
Lock Screen Customization and Pet Pals
Customization is the biggest focus on OriginOS 7. Vivo has brought several new theme options. I particularly liked the Pet Pals themes, where cute little pets appear on your home and lock screen and perform different actions based on the time of day, such as while the screen is on, tilting your phone, tapping, while your phone is on low battery, and also while you are doing actions such as listening to music and charging, and much more.
Stickers
In addition to more themes and lock screen customization, Vivo also added the ability to add custom stickers to the Home or lock screens; you can even add them to the always-on display.
Like widgets, you can drag and drop these stickers anywhere on the screen and resize them as you like. But these stickers won’t have any functionality like widgets or let you tap them to open an app. They are purely there for looks. Vivo offers some built-in stickers to get you started. However, you can also create any sticker using AI or photos already on your phone. You can tap it, convert it, and add it to your stickers; once done, you can add it anywhere on supported screens. Vivo also designed dedicated themes for adding stickers.
Vivo Office Kit
Vivo introduced Vivo Office Kit with OriginOS 6, and while it isn’t particularly new in OriginOS 7, it still remains one of the favorite features if you want to create an ecosystem. It lets your Vivo connect to your computer and sync the clipboard, share files, remote control, mirror your screen, sync your notes, and much more, similar to what you can do if you have an iPhone or Mac with the Apple ecosystem.
The best part is that it also works on Mac and other Windows devices. So unlike Apple, you don’t need to own a Mac and iPhone combination to use it. Whether you use Windows or Mac, your Vivo phone can connect to either of them and get all those handy features.
Even if you have never been in the Apple ecosystem, you might find these features very useful. Especially since every company has tried hard to bring an ecosystem between Android and Windows, or Android and macOS, or vice versa, and failed.
But somehow, many Chinese brands have figured out how to break the Apple ecosystem and connect a Vivo phone to an Apple device. And not just Vivo; OnePlus did the same with O+ Connect. Similarly, OPPO devices can connect to any PC or Mac apps.
Final Thoughts
Those are the five best features I truly love about OriginOS 7. To sum it up, OriginOS 7 brought Liquid Glass design to the OS. If you don’t like it, Vivo does offer options to disable it.
Next, it offers plenty of customization options, including the ability to add stickers (which I found unique) and new Pet Pals themes, which are my favorite. Plus, it has plenty of AI features, some of which run locally on your device, that can help with tasks like formatting text, plus AI features in the Photos app to edit and remove unwanted backgrounds.
Finally, the Vivo Office Kit is a great way to connect the Vivo phone to any PC, including Windows or Mac, and it lets you easily sync your clipboard and share files. Finally, Android’s Control Center is also customizable, similar to iOS, where you can set different sizes for each tile and rearrange them to suit your preferences.
Another feature that is missing on my Vivo V80 is a workbench feature. It is designed for power users who multitask a lot. You can place apps side by side and switch between them easily, just like windows on a PC. The best part is that you can rearrange them the way you want with different layouts, which makes proper multitasking possible on a small screen.
Another feature I really like is the ability to connect your Apple Watch or AirPods directly to your Vivo phone. Previously, Apple Watch only worked with an iPhone. With OriginOS 7, you can pair your Apple Watch and sync your data with a Vivo phone; for AirPods, it also shows the battery level and total, just like on iPhones.
Vivo officially announced OriginOS 7 globally, but still hasn’t announced an official global supported device list. However, we keep track of all the latest OriginOS 7 updates in a separate timeline post. You can bookmark the post for the latest OriginOS 7 updates.

While thousands of Indian students head overseas annually for medical degrees, comprising a heavily monitored segment under the National Medical Commission (NMC) and the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS), parliamentary disclosures indicate that centralised tracking of specific discipline-wise student outflows remains complex.
But for many, the journey culminates in a grueling, high-stakes afternoon inside an Indian examination hall. When the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) released the results for the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE) June 2026, the pass rate had plummeted sharply to just 12.4%, triggering nationwide discussions, student protests, and scrutiny over what is locking foreign medical graduates out of medical practice.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
The panic after the paper
Dr. Chaynika Soni, a medical intern in a Government Hospital in Rajasthan who cleared the exam in her second attempt after graduating from Belarus in 2024, recalls, “Every single year after the exam, you’ll see the same thing. Students come out saying, ‘The paper was impossible.’ ‘It was too hard.’ ‘Nobody could solve it.’ Coaching centers will upload videos saying, ‘The paper was unexpected.’ Telegram groups will be filled with panic.”
This panic was visible during the June session, where candidates faced sudden structural shifts. Describing his experience with the exam pattern, Dr. Kshitij Anand said, “The questions were relatively long and time-consuming. I felt the questions were completely unrelated to what I studied. There were some questions I could get direct answers for, but it wasn’t much. They give you questions and options in a way that you take time to figure out answers but not enough time to think.”
He adds that the introduction of unfamiliar video modules caught aspirants off guard: “The Board gave us video questions which I agreed were manageable, but it was a new pattern. The FMGE conducted last January was way more image-based, and the options were comparatively easier to tap than this one. Also, the diagrams I have never seen before.”
Acknowledging these pressures, Professor Dr. Karan Juneja, National Convenor of IMA Junior Doctors’ Network, points out that “More video-based questions (this time), clinical-based questions will be tough for FMG’s [as they are] not exposed to Indian setting and less time make the exam tough.”
Inside the recall analysis
As the National Board of Examinations does not release official FMGE question papers, student-reconstructed “recall” papers serve as the baseline for preparation. A look at the high-weightage sections — Community Medicine (PSM), Internal Medicine, and Obstetrics and Gynaecology — reveals distinct hurdles.
Community Medicine heavily tests India-specific public health administration, including domestic health committees like the Bhore or Kartar Singh committees, local staffing norms at Primary Health Centres, and administrative schemes that foreign universities naturally omit. For a student trained overseas, this often translates to unfamiliar civic administration rather than core medicine.
Conversely, Internal Medicine acts as a control case focused on universal clinical reasoning, ranging from ABG analysis to emergency cardiac protocols. Meanwhile, Obstetrics and Gynaecology balances international diagnostic criteria with clinical application, though candidate performance frequently hinges on interpreting embedded clinical images, manoeuvres, or diagnostic scans.
Weighing these system dynamics, Dr. Samar Kumar, National FMG In-charge for the Federation of All India Medical Association (FAIMA), explains, “In departments such as Medicine, Surgery, and Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Indian hospitals generally see a very large number of patients. This gives doctors and students exposure to a wide variety of clinical presentations and allows them to learn how to manage patients even when resources are limited. I would particularly highlight Community Medicine... If an FMG studies Medicine, Surgery, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, and Community Medicine properly, focuses on clinical concepts, and practices clinical and image-based questions, they should find these areas much more manageable in the FMGE.”
Conceptual depth and the gap in coaching materials
Beyond traditional curriculum differences, candidates found that the depth of questioning defied standard coaching modules. Dr. Ruhi Kumari, who appeared in the June session, explains, “We weren’t trained that way. For example, there was a question on cholera; the answer was an increase in cAMP. I knew it was an increase in cAMP (cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate), but the options were given in biochemistry language. Like, you have to know what cAMP is in biochemistry; only then can you answer that. No coaching institute is teaching anyone like this. Only USMLE tutors do. Because USMLE has always asked in-depth questions. Many clinical questions expect you to have clinical experience. But that’s just unfair, because I will only get that experience after I visit the clinic.”
Dr. Kumari further notes the obsolescence of traditional prep material: “Marrow [an online platform) questions were considered the standard before this exam, but I can tell you they are not anymore. There were a lot of questions that weren’t even asked in many previous years' papers, that flustered everyone... Honestly, I am not sure which resource would give me the most apt training, because no institute is teaching you like that at present. Doing INICET papers is not going to help you, or even NEET-PG papers.”
Logistics, exam conditions, and the transparency debate
The academic difficulty was further compounded by severe logistical hurdles on test day. Dr. Samar Kumar outlines the physical toll: “The first issue was related to examination centres. Multiple centres had inadequate facilities. Some did not have coolers or fans, and in some cases, even drinking water was not adequately available. As you know, the FMG examination is five hours, and overall it takes eight hours. Maintaining concentration in such tough conditions, especially during extreme summer, is something beyond the capacity of many students and FMG doctors particularly when they are not provided with adequate facilities.”
He added regarding the sudden format changes, “The second and most important issue was the sudden introduction of video-based questions in the FMG June 2026 examination. FMGs opposed this later as well and conducted protests regarding this issue in Delhi, Gautam Nagar. The demand of the students was to provide compensation for the sudden introduction of video-based questions, but NBEMS denied the demand.”
Adding to student frustration is a perceived lack of institutional accountability. Dr. Kumar said, “Moreover, the FMG examination does not have any kind of transparency. The questions and answers have never been shown to FMGs. Thus, no one knows how they failed by just one mark, five marks, or ten marks... Then why does NBEMS say that they cannot show the questions and answers together? Why can’t the examination questions and their corresponding answers be disclosed?”
FMGE versus NEET-PG and the time crunch
Comparing the screening test to domestic evaluations, Professor Dr. Karan Juneja, National Convenor of IMA Junior Doctors’ Network, notes that “NEET PG exam standard is being given in FMGE exam as the board-making exam is the same NBE.”
While Indian MBBS graduates prepping for NEET-PG sit within a mature ecosystem of shared question banks and peer networks, foreign-trained graduates often experience thinner access to these informal pipelines.
Dr. Samar Kumar contrasts the two exams, “Recently, FMGE has also included video-based and lengthy clinically oriented questions, which adds another dimension to the examination... FMGE continues to have 300 questions, whereas NEET-PG has moved from the earlier 200-question format to 180 questions. Therefore, FMGE tests not only clinical knowledge and application but also a candidate’s ability to maintain concentration and consistency throughout a long examination. NEET-PG, on the other hand, has its own competitive dynamics, including negative marking and a highly competitive selection process. But if you remove these factors from NEET-PG, then it becomes easier than FMGE.”
This time crunch is intensified by structural scheduling. Dr. Anjali Ayappan from Kochi points out, “Two months is simply not enough preparation time for FMG students, especially considering the amount of syllabus and the situation most FMGs are already in. And bringing the next exam forward to October is especially bad for the June pass-outs. They barely get any time to prepare after the result, and then suddenly they’re expected to appear again in October.”
The long road to registration
Clearing the exam is only the first milestone; graduates face a complex administrative labyrinth before they can practice. Dr. Parvathy Sabu, who cleared the exam and works in a Government Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, said, “Internship posts for FMGs are fewer across almost every State, and protests to increase seats are seen often... By the time you get PR [permanent registration], best-case scenario, approximately 8 years have gone by (including course duration) and a lot of money. Abroad MBBS is a very long-term investment that many don’t realise initially. I think the integration into Indian healthcare and internship issues are the biggest challenges faced by FMGs.”
Reflecting on these cumulative pressures, Dr. Madhavi Gurung, an FMG aspirant who studied in the U.K., concludes, “Many of my friends skipped FMGE and are now doing residency in the U.S., some are working non-training jobs in the U.K., and some are on track to settle in Australia. The struggle doesn’t end after NEET-UG. And with rising competition and reservation quotas, the system is tough. Every year wasted in endless NEET attempts can drain your mental health and confidence. I’m now planning to take AMC Part 1 by the end of this year and hopefully move abroad permanently.”

The vanishing world of India's street magicians
- Published
Sitting in his cramped Delhi home, Ishamuddin Khan can still make a rope appear to rise into the air.
The 55-year-old magician spent decades performing a trick once dismissed as legend, and still keeps photographs and newspaper clippings from his years of international fame.
These days, he spends more time looking back at those memories than performing the trick.
"The times have changed," he says. "Street magic is dying a slow death. It is on a ventilator."
Khan's story reflects a wider change in India, where traditional street performers are finding it increasingly difficult to make a living from their craft.
Magicians, jugglers, puppeteers and acrobats once made a living from crowds in public spaces. Changing entertainment habits and tighter restrictions have made audiences harder to find, pushing many out of the profession.
Khan, one of India's best-known magicians, comes from the Madari community, which has a long tradition of performing in public spaces.
There are no official figures, but Khan says community records identify about 400 Madari families in Delhi, with hundreds more in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Telangana.
Despite their small numbers today, the Madaris trace their roots back centuries.
Historian Ashok Mathur says Madari traditions have roots in Indian folklore, mythology and the long history of travelling performers.
"For generations, these skills were passed through families," he explains.
Khan followed the same path, learning magic from his father and uncles and performing from the age of 12. By his early 20s, he had mastered the rope trick that would later make him famous.
The trick – in which a rope appears to rise into the air before a boy climbs it – was long associated with the mythology of Indian street magic and widely considered impossible, until Khan performed it.
He says it took six years to master the trick, which he first performed publicly in 1995 outside Delhi's iconic Qutub Minar. Two years later, he performed it before 30,000 people on a beach in Karnataka.
His trick brought international attention, and that led to tours to the UK, France, Germany and Japan.
Khan hoped the fame would shine a light on India's traditional performers. For a while, it did. But the attention faded.
As audiences turned to new forms of entertainment and public performance opportunities dwindled, many magicians found it harder to make a living from skills passed down through generations.
One of them is 40-year-old Imam Khan.
Once a magician, Imam now makes a living collecting bottles and recyclables from Delhi's streets. He spends much of his time rag-picking near a western Delhi dump, earning about 200 rupees ($2; £1.57) a day.
Experts say the decline in street performance has multiple causes, chief among them the changing nature of public spaces.
Anurupa Roy, founder of Katkatha Puppet Arts Trust, says performers increasingly struggle to find audiences as public spaces shrink.
"Closed parks and residential societies that bar outsiders are limiting spaces for performance."
Researcher and performer Komita Dhanda says changing attitudes to public spaces are also driving the decline.
"With tighter security, especially in busy town and city centres, there is little space left for street performers," she says.
It is not just individual artists who struggle to get permission. Dhanda says her well-known street theatre group, Jana Natya Manch, often faces hurdles performing in public spaces.
For many artists, the challenge is not just finding a venue but navigating unclear rules over what is allowed.
Most street performers rely on voluntary payments, but experts say the line between performing for money and begging can blur.
Unlike the UK, India has no federal busking framework. Performers instead navigate state-level rules on public order, obstruction, noise and public land.
"This is why street performers often have to face municipal and police regulations governing public spaces, as well as state-specific anti-begging laws," says lawyer Kaushik Mitra.
For many artists, Covid made a bad situation worse.
When India imposed its 2020 lockdown, public performances stopped. Many magicians returned to their villages; some never came back.
"We saw a decline in public performances after this period," Dhanda says. "The brunt was especially harsh for street magicians and performers, many of whom did not return to cities."
For the artists who did return and continue the trade, the challenges only increased.
Shahim Khan, 42, still performs magic on Delhi's streets, sometimes with his 12-year-old daughter, Alia.
Much of his work is now confined to industrial areas, far from the busy public spaces where he once performed, hitting his earnings hard.
Before the pandemic, he could stage four or five shows a day, earning 1,000-1,200 rupees.
"Now I barely manage two shows and earn 200-400 rupees," he says.
The rise of short-form digital entertainment has added to the pressures on traditional performers, experts say. So have changing attitudes towards street arts.
"There was a lot of Western interest in things like the rope trick decades ago. But forms and tastes have changed, and so has what India chooses to showcase," Dhanda says.
For Khan, the loss is about more than money. He fears an art passed down generations could disappear if no-one learns it.
"A trick can survive only if someone learns it," he says.
His son, Altamash, began performing with him as a teenager but now works decorating parties with balloons. In his 30s, he has largely left performing behind.
Years without regular practice have dulled his skills. When he demonstrated his juggling for the BBC, he struggled to find the rhythm.
"I am slowly forgetting all the tricks," he said.
Khan had hoped his son would carry on the family tradition. Altamash had hoped to make a name for himself too, but it did not work out.
"I knew I may not achieve the fame my father has, but I did not think there would come a time when performing would not remain an option," he says.

A while back, I was at physical therapy, and the topic of tennis came up. Someone said something about yellow tennis balls, and I was like… “What? They’re green.” And then someone else chimed in, “No, they’re yellow!” And then someone across the room hollered, “No, they’re obviously green.”
What color is a tennis ball?
A neuroscientist and artist argue there’s no such thing as a color.
There was basically a physical therapy uproar. And when I started asking other people how they saw them — yellow or green — they told me they couldn’t even believe there was a debate. So I called up Bevil Conway. He’s a neuroscientist who heads up a lab at the National Eye Institute. He’s working on a book called Color Coded, which is due out next year. And he’s also a working artist — which is actually how he got into studying color in the first place.
Conway told me there’s a pretty good reason for why so many people disagree about tennis balls. He said it’s simple: “There’s no such thing as a color.”
In the latest episode of Unexplainable, I talked with Conway about what color even is, the viral dress fight (black and blue or white and gold?), and why we get so upset when people don’t see color the same way we do. Below is an excerpt of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. Listen to the episode anywhere you get your podcasts or you can watch on Netflix.
So you are an artist. You are also a neuroscientist. You study color. You’re also working on a book about color. Are there still color mysteries? Are there things science doesn’t know about color?
There are lots of mysteries about color. For a long time, people thought that color was a little bit like a filter, that everything that’s really important is in black and white, and then there’s a color filter you put on top of it.
But a bunch of years ago, my lab were blown away to discover that there’s as much brain involved in processing color as there is in face recognition.
The same amount of processing power?
Yeah, there’s tons and tons of tissue [and] pretty fancy bits of brain that are doing pretty high-level things — parts of brain we think of as being involved in social cognition and in high-level reasoning and visual memory. Color must be more than just this little add-on. It’s doing something much deeper. So we’re trying to understand what those bits of brain are doing.
So what is color? How does it work? How do our brains and eyes perceive it?
The classic definition would be: Color is the visual feature that you get from wavelength properties of the light entering your eye. People typically see the long wavelength end as red light, and then going through short wavelengths, you know, following ROYGBIV: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
If color were just wavelength, then an object under blue light would look blue, and the same object under yellow light would look yellow. And that wouldn’t be very helpful — because what you want is a signal that tells you about objects, immune to the lighting condition. You want them to always have that color.
A perfect example is a peach. If you look at a peach outside and you look at it inside, it’s always gonna look like a peach color. But if you looked at the pattern of wavelengths that are coming off of the peach, they’re very different under different lighting conditions. They should be different colors if color were just wavelength, but they’re not. Those two different compositions of wavelengths look the same color.
What I think is so cool about color is it’s so fundamental for how we need to experience the world — but the mechanics of how it does it teaches us a lot about the brain.
What we’re talking about is color constancy. That is, an object’s color is constant despite the viewing conditions.
So if the peach is fundamentally a different color inside and outside, and our brains are telling us that it is still, you know, peach colored, how are our brains deceiving us?
So it’s not fundamentally a different color. It’s the same color. That’s the cool thing. The problem is that you are carrying around, Noam, in your head an idea that color is wavelength, and that is the mistake.
Color is not wavelength! And we’ve known this for a long time. But the problem is that we want something that is an empirical, measurable number that’s outside of an observer, that’s a thing out there in the world, that would be the same number regardless of who looks at it. And color, at its core, is not that.
Color is dependent on your own visual system interacting with the world. And that doesn’t mean it’s any less real. It just means that its reality is dependent on psychological neural brain processes. And that’s what makes color fascinating.
Color is, you’re saying, something that is essentially created in the brain.
Absolutely, yes. Color is a generative product of the brain that gives us reliable, useful, true, meaningful, objective information, but it itself is not [those things]. It’s some generative product of your brain in order to come up with this information that’s useful and meaningful about the world.
[Your brain is] actually creating that thing that is a color. Colors don’t exist out there in the world independent of a viewer to see them.
Is this related to “the dress” — you know, like 10 years ago when that photo of a dress went viral, and a bunch of people on the internet thought it was blue and black, and a bunch of other people thought it was white and gold, and everyone got super upset? Is this the same type of thing, of seeing something in different lighting or different contexts and perceiving a different color?
It is. So the dress was fascinating because people with normal color vision looking at exactly the same thing were asserting very different perceptions.
And, you know, from a deep kind of philosophical point of view, it’s important because they weren’t saying, “Yeah, it kinda looks different to me, but I understand how you could see it as different.” They were like, “No, it is white and gold.” And other people were saying, “It is different colors.” That was, for me professionally and personally, a really big deal because it underscored this fact that color is this generative, constructive thing that your brain is doing, making all kinds of assumptions, filling in the gaps about lighting, about what you think you’re seeing.
In the case of the dress, it’s such a crappy little photograph, very blurry. It doesn’t give you a lot of context. And your visual system, your own brain, has to make a guess about what the lighting is. And if your brain guesses that the lighting is nice, warm, direct sunlight, then it implicitly subtracts out a little bit of the yellow from the image, and you see it as blue and black. Whereas other people looking at exactly the same pixels on the same monitor who assume that the lighting is cool, indirect, shaded light from blue sky, their brains color-correct the image, subtract out some of the blue, and they see it as white and gold. And so you have these two groups of people whose brains have just made different assumptions.
Why do you think that left people feeling so unnerved? When this happened, people could not possibly believe someone else could look at that dress and see a different color.
It was amazing! And, you know, it’s still, to date, I think, the most viral image in the history of the internet. Right when it came out, my initial reaction too was like, “Huh, that’s weird. I wonder what’s going on there.” And a lot of my colleagues thought, “Well, maybe it’s got to do with proportions of rods and cones, or people are looking at different displays, or maybe people are just silently color blind.”
But I think the idea that your own brain could play such a fundamental role in determining what the pattern of wavelengths means, even for vision scientists, wasn’t sitting front of mind.
I think the reason that it played so deeply, if I could wax poetic, it’s that our contemporary society depends on a shared experience, right? Our laws depend on a common idea of what’s right and wrong.
Yeah, like whether my red is your red; we still need to be able to point at something and agree that it’s red.
Yes, and here was an example where it was like: “That isn’t white and gold, that’s blue and black, clearly. Do we live in a shared reality?”
And if you can’t trust your eyes, what can you trust? I think people genuinely felt like, “Is this the beginning of the end?” Like, “Is our whole society collapsing?” I mean, look at Twitter, there were all sorts of expletives flying around.
Have you ever gotten into an argument about a color? I once got into an argument about tennis balls and what color they were.
Yeah, what color are they? I’m curious.
I couldn’t believe anyone thought they were yellow! I always thought they were green.
They’re totally yellow. I mean, we can get into one now. You’re wrong. It’s so funny — I really thought that they were definitionally yellow.
So what is going on with tennis balls?
Tennis balls are funny. I mean, if you ask people to pick their best example of green and blue and red and orange and yellow and so on, there’s a lot of variability. Green and blue is the most variable. Some people’s best example of green is another person’s best example of blue.
Meaning, you could ask me to pick a color that would be perfectly green, and then someone else would be like, “No, that’s blue.”
Yeah, exactly. And this isn’t language-based. This is true across all cultures.
We just perceive blues and greens kinda badly or vaguely?
Yeah, and one of the ideas that we have about that is that blues and greens aren’t really the colors that are tied to objects.
So if I ask you what colors are objects, it’s a weird question! It’s like, objects can be any colors. But it turns out, if you actually go and measure, you know, the colors of things that you choose to label in the world, most of them are, like, yellow, brown, red, pink, some purples, not many.
Yeah, I guess green and blue is the background. Like green’s the forest, and blue is the sky.
Yeah, exactly. And, and even in nature, there are very few natural blue objects, and that’s partly what made blue as a pigment so desirable. So what’s weird about yellow is that yellow, if you just ask people in the rainbow to pick where yellow is, people are incredibly consistent.
So people really know yellow.
They really know yellow. And I think what’s going on with the tennis ball is that it is a little bit fluorescent. It’s actually emitting a little bit more light than it’s taking in because it’s reprocessing it, short-wavelength light in the visible spectrum.
So they’ve picked this bright yellow, which is right at the peak of our visual system sensitivity. So the color of the tennis ball is the optimal wavelength that we can detect with our eyes, and it’s right in that range where it’s technically probably closer to green than it is to yellow. But because it’s so bright, and yellow is considered a bright color, the brightest color, people could be persuaded to see it in a yellow direction.
What I hear you saying is that I’m right — and it’s green.
Yeah, yeah. Although, I still like it as yellow.

Samoa leader apologises for Nazi salute after video from 2007 emerges
- Published
Samoa's prime minister has apologised after a video emerged of him giving a Nazi salute while saying "Heil Hitler" at a family gathering.
In the seven-second clip filmed in July 2007, Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt is seen leading about a dozen people in the salute. "Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler!" he says, then thanks the group for responding.
Schmidt has acknowledged that his words and gesture "were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt", adding that the clip was recorded at a private gathering and "not intended for the public".
"I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism," Schmidt said in a statement published on Facebook on Monday.
The footage was first reported by local outlet the Samoa Observer in a news story on Sunday.
It said the video was filmed at a Schmidt family reunion in July 2007, when Schmidt was deputy speaker of parliament and quoted a family member who said he was the master of ceremonies at the gathering.
Samoa, a tiny island nation of about 221,000 people, sits about halfway between New Zealand and Hawaii.
It was under Germany's control in the early 20th century, but the colonisation ended shortly after World War One broke out.
Schmidt, who has Samoan and German heritage, took office as the country's eighth prime minister in September 2025.
He wore a Jewish prayer shawl during his swearing-in ceremony and has made clear his support for Israel during the early days of his premiership, saying that Samoa "stood with Israel".
"If people around the world don't like it, that's up to them, but Samoa stands with the land of God... There is only one God our country believes in, the God of Israel," he had said.

Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in physics for work on high-energy neutrinos from space
STOCKHOLM — Francis Halzen won the Nobel Prize in physics on Tuesday for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and his discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.
"Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument. His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy," Mark Pearce, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics, said in a news release.
Halzen spoke to the committee by phone from Italy on Tuesday.
"It was a great surprise and I obviously didn't expect it," he said.
Halzen said it was predicted before that he would win the Nobel Prize but the announcement still made him feel "strange."
Born in Belgium, the 82-year-old scientist is affiliated with the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the U.S. Efforts by The Associated Press to reach him were not immediately successful.
The IceCube Neutrino Observatory is a research facility located at the South Pole in Antarctica, according to its website, and the University of Wisconsin–Madison is its lead institution.
Neutrinos are tiny cosmic particles with a mind-bogglingly small mass. Yet they are everywhere: they spew from stars like the sun and trillions zip through our bodies every second.
Scientists can't glimpse the mysterious ghost particles zooming around on their own. Instead, they measure what happens when the tiny particles collide with other bits of matter, producing flashes of light or charged particles.
Halzen studied a rare gang of neutrinos that scientists consider messengers from the cosmos, offering clues to how the universe evolved.
His research into capturing neutrinos at the South Pole dates back to the 1980s.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the award in Stockholm.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.
Last year, three scientists won the Nobel Prize in physics for research on the strange behavior of subatomic particles called quantum tunneling that enabled the ultra-sensitive measurements achieved by MRI machines and laid the groundwork for better cellphones and faster computers.
The announcements of this year's prizes began Monday with the Nobel Prize in medicine being awarded to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.
This week's awards continue Wednesday with the chemistry prize and literature on Thursday. After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Monday.

Cornell taps ex-Justice Department official Sally Yates to review school's handling of sexual assault cases
'It is imperative that Cornell be willing to examine itself,' school trustee says
A former high-ranking Department of Justice official will look at how Cornell handles sexual misconduct complaints, university trustees announced Tuesday as they tried to address an outpouring of anger over allegations of a 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house.
Sally Yates, who was a deputy attorney general in the Obama administration, will spearhead the review, the trustees said. The assessment is to include how the Ivy League university investigates reports of sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, campus police responses and more.
"It is imperative that Cornell be willing to examine itself with the same rigor we expect of others," trustee chair Anne Meinig Smalling said in a statement.
The announcement comes after days of outrage and a large demonstration over Cornell's response to a complaint from a woman known publicly only as Jane Doe. She told campus police in November 2024 that she had been sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi fraternity brothers the month before after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs.
No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, and the Ivy League university has said it expelled some students and suspended others.
Yates will look at how the woman's complaint was handled and at the oversight of fraternities, sororities and other campus groups, Cornell said.
The woman sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others last month.
Lawyers for two of the former students denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Court records show that during an investigation Cornell conducted under the federal Title IX law, some of the accused students contended that the sexual activity was consensual.
The lawsuit put a new, countrywide spotlight on the allegations and how the campus police, university and local prosecutor had reacted.
New York's attorney general is now conducting a criminal investigation, and the state's governor called for an independent review of Cornell's handling of the matter — the review that Yates now will lead.
Cornell students, professors and others packed a campus plaza Monday to protest the university's response to the matter and demand more accountability, greater transparency, an overhaul of the disciplinary process and other changes.
Yates had a decades-long career at the Justice Department, serving for years as the top federal prosecutor in Atlanta and later as a deputy attorney general.
She achieved particular prominence in January 2017 when, as acting attorney general in the early days of the Trump administration, she directed Justice Department attorneys not to defend the constitutionality of President Donald Trump's refugee and immigration ban. She was swiftly fired, with Trump accusing her of betrayal and insubordination.
Yates also generated headlines when it emerged that, in a conversation days before her departure, she had expressed alarm to the Trump White House about contacts that Trump's new national security adviser, Michael Flynn, had had with the Russian ambassador during the presidential transition period. Flynn later was fired.
Yates has been in private practice since her departure from the Justice Department. Her practice at the King & Spalding law firm includes conducting independent investigations for outside organizations and companies.
She led a high-profile inquiry into alleged abuse and misconduct, including claims of harassment and coercion, at the National Women's Soccer League. The investigation concluded in 2022 with a finding of systemic abuse .

Kane's rise from childhood keeper to equalling England cap record
- Published
Harry Kane has reached another significant England milestone by equalling Peter Shilton's 36-year-old record as the most-capped Three Lions player.
The Bayern Munich striker made his 125th appearance for the national team against the Czech Republic in the Nations League on Tuesday.
Kane is already his country's record scorer with 89 goals in 124 appearances in a full international career he started by opening his account 79 seconds into his debut.
He may be 33 but remains a key player for club and country. BBC Sport has a look at the origins story of the England captain.
- England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender 
  - Published21 minutes ago
From safe hands to hot-shot striker
When a six-year-old Harry Kane arrived for trials with Ridgeway Rovers in 1999, the youth side - who a generation earlier had produced David Beckham - thought they had found themselves a new goalkeeper.
Dave Bricknell, former Ridgeway Rovers coach: "We're doing a little shooting session, and I ask for a lad who can go in goal.
"This little boy puts his hand up and says: 'I'll go in goal.' We give him some gloves, and he performs heroics - makes some fantastic saves. He's tipping it round the post, tipping a couple over the bar.
"I'm thinking this is great, we've got a goalkeeper. And then this woman came up to me and said he's better on the pitch.
"We put him on pitch and he smacked goals in left, right and centre. So he ends up being our centre forward."
Kane's prolific form for Ridgeway Rovers and his Waltham Forest district side caught the attention of professional scouts. Arsenal initially snapped up the youngster but decided not to keep him, while Watford also passed up the opportunity to sign Kane.
Trevor Bailey, Kane's manager at Waltham Forest: "Harry could have done nothing all game, but if that chance came up it was in the onion bag.
"He was always on the move up front. When he got a chance, guaranteed four out of five he was going to score or set someone up."
Alex Welsh, former academy coach at Arsenal: "I first met Harry in the academy and he was a very competent goalkeeper, but his real desire was to score goals.
"I am absolutely convinced that is the reason why he is such a clinical striker - he intuitively knows what the goalkeeper doesn't like. He shoots early when the goalkeeper's not set."
Bricknell: "I believe he was second top-scorer at Arsenal behind Benik Afobe, and then for some reason they decided at 11 years of age that they didn't want him anymore."
The 'model student' with a Beckham Mohican
Kane attended Larkswood Primary Academy before moving to Chingford Foundation School, where he was inevitably the star of the football team. But, as a dedicated student, Kane impressed his teachers across the board.
Mark Leadon, Kane's PE teacher: "Aged 11, Harry was technically very gifted, with a great first touch, and a very clever player. He always knew where to go, right from an early stage.
"He was also a very good cricketer - he opened the bowling from year seven to 10 and batted at four or five. But he loved football. He was never a prima donna, and he would always put a shift in.
"What came through more than anything else was his determination to succeed. That work ethic was clear."
Luke Robinson, Kane's childhood friend and team-mate: "The only thing on his mind was football.
"We used to have a laugh, a couple of games of Fifa, but he was always driven. He'd always keep himself to himself.
"He loved David Beckham, he came in with the Mohican, everyone was laughing but he loved it. He loved football, 24/7, he lived and breathed football."
'Gold medallist? He wasn't even on the podium'
It was Tottenham Hotspur who offered Kane hope after his earlier disappointments, but the future England captain was by no means the pick of the bunch for his age group.
Kane's desire to learn and improve endeared him to the Tottenham academy staff and he signed scholarship terms with the club on his 16th birthday in July 2009.
Alex Inglethorpe, former Tottenham youth-team coach: "When I joined Spurs as under-18 coach, Harry was 13.
"I'd like to say he was the gold medallist in the group and we'd all spotted he was going to be the fantastic player, but I'd be lying. He probably wasn't even on the podium.
"If there was something that endeared him to you it was that he was very, very low maintenance. It became fairly evident when Harry became a scholar he was someone who could finish.
"He was wonderfully demanding to coach because he always wanted to stay out and do extra. That obsession to improve is undoubtedly his greatest strength.
"It was probably around 16 he started having an impact on the youth team. We trusted him to come off the bench and have an impact - anywhere from right wing, number 10, centre-forward, sometimes in midfield."
Living the loan life
Kane went to League One Leyton Orient - making his professional debut in January 2011 at Rochdale, coming on for veteran striker Scott McGleish. Kane would score five times in nine starts.
McGleish: "Harry was not like other Premier League players, where you feel they're going to come in 'Billy Big Time'. He wanted the experience of learning what I call men's football.
"From the word go he was ready to fight for his place. In training, he was willing to just knuckle down and work hard.
"You could see in training and subsequently the matches he had ability and a desire to go further, but you're still looking like a young 17-year-old: very slight, still needing to physically develop, not the quickest but technically excellent."
After a few first-team games for Spurs, he went on loan to Millwall in January 2012 to Championship strugglers Millwall. Kane's nine goals helped save Kenny Jackett's side from relegation.
Former Millwall defender Alan Dunne: "I've seen a lot of players come to the Den and freeze, because within five minutes they're being called names they've never heard before and they can't cope with that pressure.
"But it didn't faze him - he was a focused lad, he was confident in his ability."
Former Tottenham manager Tim Sherwood: "I used to watch Harry a lot at Millwall, and it was an intimidating atmosphere. I remember overhearing one of our scouts come and talk to Harry Redknapp - who was Spurs manager at the time - and say: 'We need to get Harry Kane out of Millwall, it's no good for him there.'
"I went straight in and said: 'This is the perfect atmosphere for him."
After making his Premier League debut for Tottenham in August 2012, Kane was sent on loan again. The 19-year-old only made three appearances in the top flight for Norwich because of injury, and then had a loan spell at Leicester where he and future England team-mate Jamie Vardy struggled for regular starts.
Off the mark for Tottenham
After four loan spells in three seasons, Kane spent the entire 2013-14 campaign with Tottenham. But it was not until April, after Andre Villas-Boas had been sacked and replaced by Sherwood, that a 20-year-old Kane was handed his first Premier League start for Spurs, scoring his first top-flight goal in the process against Sunderland and also netting in the following two games against West Brom and Fulham.
Sherwood: "It didn't feel a gamble at all to give Harry that start. It was almost overdue to be honest.
"Roberto Soldado was in front of him in the team, and nobody wanted Roberto to do well more than me - but every single day in training Harry was outperforming him. He didn't let me down.
"Harry wanted to get to the top, and nothing was going to stop him achieving that because of the ability, desire and mentality he possesses.
"I was the biggest believer Harry Kane ever had, because I used to think he was a mix between Teddy Sheringham and Alan Shearer."
Kane becomes a Spurs legend
Kane never looked back after scoring 21 top-flight goals the following season - and earning his first England call-up in March 2015.
He ended up as the club's all-time top scorer with 280 goals in 435 appearances - and three Premier League Golden Boots, but no trophies
Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola, who tried to sign him, said in 2023: "What an exceptional player – the numbers and, more than the goals, the quality. Harry Kane remains one of the best strikers I have ever seen in my life."
Former Spurs team-mate Son Heung-min: "Leader, brother, legend.
"Since day one it has been a joy to play by your side. So many memories, amazing games and incredible goals together."
Then Tottenham boss Ange Postecoglou: "Harry was brilliant throughout. You want to work with the best players and he is a hell of a striker and I thought he could help me.
"He has left an indelible mark at this football club, will go down as one of the greats."
Kane keeps banging in goals at Bayern
The only thing missing from Kane's career CV was trophies - and in 2023 he joined German side Bayern Munich, where he has continued to impress.
He has scored 152 goals in 154 games for the club, won the Bundesliga Golden Boot three times and won two German titles and a German Cup.
Former Bayern defender Lothaur Matthaus: "Kane has reinvented the centre-forward game, as Manuel Neuer did with goalkeepers.
"I don't see a better striker in the world right now. Not just because of his goals, but because of his versatility and the positions he plays.
"Kane also demonstrates qualities as a passer, dribbler, and tackler. He is simultaneously a goalscorer, playmaker, box-to-box player, and tackler."
Ex-England striker Shearer, speaking this summer: "To me he looks fitter and stronger than before.
"He's come into this World Cup off the back of a brilliant campaign for Bayern Munich and looks very sharp and very confident - as you would do after scoring 61 goals in one season. Those numbers are just ridiculous."
BBC pundit Chris Sutton: "He has to be in that bracket when you talk about the world's best. Harry Kane has instincts that are simply uncoachable."
Some of these interviews were first published in 2016

A chronic autoimmune skin condition in which the body’s immune system mistakes melanocytes (cells which produce melanin, giving colour to your skin, hair and eyes) as enemies and attacks them. This leads to patches of depigmentation anywhere in your body. This condition is known as vitiligo.
Types of vitiligo
The main types of vitiligo are non-segmental and segmental vitiligo.
Non-segmental vitiligo is the most common form, where colour loss appears symmetrically on both sides of the body, such as both hands or both knees. Segmental vitiligo, on the other hand, often starts at a younger age and affects only one side or a single specific area of the body.
What causes vitiligo?
While the primary reason for vitiligo is not fully understood, it is seen to be caused by various factors, from genetics to immune dysfunction.
Research has shown that vitiligo is primarily a T-cell–mediated autoimmune disease where CD8+ cytotoxic T cells attack and destroy skin pigment cells called melanocytes, leading to white patches on the skin.
Having a family member with vitiligo or other autoimmune diseases is shown to have an increased risk, suggesting shared genetic susceptibility. Environmental factors like oxidative stress, skin trauma, and certain chemicals can sometimes trigger or worsen vitiligo in genetically susceptible people.
Vitiligo is also often associated with other autoimmune conditions, especially autoimmune thyroid disease, so clinicians may screen for these in some patients.
Symptoms of vitiligo
The main symptom of vitiligo is depigmentation and the appearance of patches on your body. This can be anywhere from your face and hands to your knees or feet. Hair in the affected area may also turn white.
There are various ways through which doctors can help you diagnose vitiligo and determine what type of vitiligo you may have. One major examination done is the Wood’s lamp examination, where ultraviolet light is used to distinguish vitiligo from other hypopigmented conditions.
Treatment options
Treatment for vitiligo is mostly connected to re-pigmentation, or slowing progression, depending on the type of vitiligo and patient preference rather than a guaranteed cure.
There are various types of topical treatments (like creams for external use) which can often help with inflammation, as well as medical light treatments like narrowband UVB phototherapy and excimer laser or lamp. Availability of certain treatments also changes from country to country and by the patient’s age group. There are situations where oral medication is also used for the short term. People with stable vitiligo can also consider surgical options if other treatments are not working, and depigmentation therapy if a major part of the person’s natural pigmentation is lost.

Anthony Albanese has been urged to use national cabinet to stop the use of unmarked communal graves to bury impoverished Australians and address failings that are leaving family and friends blindsided.
Guardian Australia’s revelations on Tuesday that unmarked, communal graves were being used, in some cases without notifying the families of the deceased, prompted widespread political condemnation on Tuesday, including from federal Liberal MPs, state Labor ministers, and the Greens.
The New South Wales government committed to an urgent review of the practice.
The health minister, Ryan Park, said he had not been previously aware of the way the graves were being used by his government.
He has tasked his department to explore reforms, including emulating the Victorian model, where individuals are buried with their own plot and marking, a process that costs just $3,000 per funeral.
“I think it’s something that we need to do better,” Park said. “Quite clearly, the dignity of those who have … passed, as well as for their families, is something that we need to take into consideration, and we need to do this better.”
Independent senator David Pocock urged Albanese to raise the issue at national cabinet and seek a uniform agreement across states and territories to ensure dignified burials and a basic standard of notification to families, friends, and others associated with the deceased.
“Being poor in a country as wealthy as Australia should not condemn you to an unmarked communal grave,” he said.
“While I appreciate that this may not be at the top of most people’s list of daily concerns, how we treat our most vulnerable, including in death, goes to our values and who we are as a country.”
Vietnam veterans, rough sleepers, people with gambling addictions and migrants from developing countries have been buried together at Rookwood cemetery in western Sydney, with each plot often holding between four and six unrelated people.
Shadow minister for defence personnel Phillip Thompson described the burials of war veterans as “deeply concerning”.
“I am disappointed to hear Australian veterans are among those being buried in unmarked mass graves,” Thompson said. “These men and women served our nation and deserve dignity, respect in death, regardless of their financial circumstances.”
He said it was the job of the federal government to ensure every veteran is identified and appropriately commemorated.
NSW Greens MP Sue Higginson called on the NSW government to urgently examine whether its model for identifying the friends and family of deceased persons had “the people, resources and safeguards” necessary.
“Matters of grief, death and human dignity cannot be treated as administrative burdens to be processed at the lowest possible cost,” she said. “Nobody should receive a lesser measure of humanity in death simply because they died without money.”
In at least six cases identified by the Guardian, friends, families, homelessness charities and community leaders had not been informed about the process, denying them a chance to intervene and pay for alternative funeral arrangements, a likely breach of NSW Health policy.
‘Unacceptable’
Park has accepted that past failings are “unacceptable” and NSW Health has apologised, acknowledging that it has not always treated those without financial means with the dignity and respect they are entitled to.
“Families and friends who have lost a loved one face many challenges managing arrangements during a time of grief, and all deceased persons should be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their financial circumstances,” a NSW Health Pathology spokesperson said.
“It is clear this has not always occurred with respect to the burials or cremations for deceased people without the financial means to pay for a funeral, and NSW Health apologises for the distress this has caused to those who have lost someone they love.”
NSW Health also said it is “committed to changing the way we work”. That includes reforms to better work with loved ones, funeral service providers and partner agencies to “assess and manage deceased persons without financial means”.
The government has also signalled greater cooperation with community and charity groups to seek funeral funding, after the Guardian revealed at least 18 people known to homelessness services had been buried in unmarked and communal graves without the sector’s knowledge.
The rules require the government to do whatever it can to contact family, friends and others associated with the deceased before burying or cremating them, to check if they want to fund alternative funerals.
Who is responsible?
Responsibility for that process had been shared between NSW Health and police until 2025. Reforms last year gave NSW Health Pathology responsibility for the process when deaths occurred in the community or in cases before the coroner, replacing police.
Park said the changes made since 2025 were significant in establishing a more “person-centred approach to ensure all deceased persons are treated with the respect and compassion they deserve”.
“Losing a loved one is never easy, and everyone should be treated with dignity and respect when they pass, regardless of their financial circumstances,” Park said.
“Previous arrangements have meant that this has not always been the case, and that is unacceptable.”
Independent Sydney MP Alex Greenwich welcomed changes made by NSW Health to address the problem. “Those who are marginalised and vulnerable in our community deserve the opportunity to be farewelled respectfully, honouring the life they lived,” he said.
Guardian Australia’s investigation has identified serious failings in burials that occurred this year, after the 2025 reforms. That includes the case of Peter Giesel, a Sydney man who died in 2024 and was buried in an unmarked communal grave in June without the knowledge of his sister, Nicole, or close friend Elaine Grady.
NSW Health said it had updated its policy to require “the provision of a uniform flat grave marker for people who have been buried”.
Despite this, burials have continued to occur without any marker.
The operator of Rookwood, Metropolitan Memorial Parks, says the state government has not funded it to provide grave markings.

Delhi Capitals announced Sourav Ganguly as its head coach for the IPL 2027 season on Tuesday.
Ganguly will take over from Hemang Badani, who was the head coach for two seasons, in 2025 and 2026. In Badani’s two-year stint, DC failed to qualify for the Playoffs.
The team finished fifth in the 2025 season, before finishing sixth in the 2026 season.
Ganguly’s association with the Capitals’ franchise goes back many years. In 2019, he joined the franchise as an advisor and over the years, has held multiple leadership roles within the ecosystem.
The former India captain oversaw the men’s and women’s teams as DC’s director of cricket between 2023 and 2024, and was the head coach of the Pretoria Capitals in the SA20 for the 2025 season.
Speaking on his appointment, Ganguly said: “I am looking forward to take on the role of Head Coach in the IPL. Delhi Capitals is a franchise very close to my heart, and one that I have shared a strong relationship with over the years. I have worked closely with the owners, management, support staff and players, which makes this an exciting responsibility for me. We have a talented group and have played a good brand of cricket in the recent past. I am looking forward to working with the squad, the new season, and building a strong and fearless team.”
Parth Jindal, Delhi Capitals chairman and co-owner, said: “Dada is and has always been an integral part of the Delhi Capitals family. I am incredibly proud and honoured to announce that one of the greatest Indian captains and administrators is now stepping into coaching by taking over as the head coach of the Delhi Capitals. I am excited to see him take on this role and I’m sure that under his guidance and visionary leadership Delhi Capitals will be best prepared to challenge for the IPL title. I cannot wait for all our players and staff to learn from Dada and am looking forward to seeing DC in action at the earliest.”
