Comedian Sebastian Maniscalco is facing backlash from fellow comics who claim his takeover of SiriusXM’s Raw Comedy channel is harming up-and-coming talent, as reported earlier by Deadline. Many established comics, including Patton Oswalt and Margaret Cho, have posted videos online calling on Maniscalco to carry on Raw Comedy’s legacy by highlighting newer comedians on his channel, instead of mostly focusing on well-known ones.
Sebastian Maniscalco’s SiriusXM channel is hurting up-and-coming talent, comics say
Maniscalco’s channel replaced SiriusXM’s Raw Comedy, which highlighted a wider pool of more than 800 comics.
SiriusXM launched Sebastian Maniscalco’s Comedy Radio in April, which is “curated and headlined by Sebastian himself,” according to the satellite radio provider. The move replaced SiriusXM’s long-running Raw Comedy channel featuring uncensored stand-up comedy shows from a range of talent. Now, the channel airs Maniscalco’s own show, alongside a stream of stand-up content that comedian Dan Soder says features “very famous comics who are dead or who don’t necessarily need the money.”
The widespread criticism comes as Stand Up for Standup, a nonprofit organization that provides resources for comedians in need, published a report about the channel’s shift away from emerging talent, who rely not only on the visibility they receive from appearing on the station, but also on the royalties they earn from SiriusXM. The organization says that since March, the spins on Maniscalco’s channels have decreased from a wider net of more than 800 comics to a much narrower pool of 275 artists, largely skewed toward celebrities.
“We believe this shift, both in the overall quantity of artists enjoying plays on Channel 102, and the change in distribution across all spin-getters favoring the top few, is bad for comedians, and bad for the future of comedy,” Stand Up for Standup says.
“There’s a lot of up-and-coming comedians who are depending on the money and the checks that they get from Sirius,” Oswalt says in an Instagram video. “But 500 of them have been booted off of Sirius… You can easily reverse this decision. Get those young comedians back on the Sirius channel. Let them get those checks.” Many other comedians, including Liz Miele, Kyle Kinane, and Michelle Wolf, have called out Maniscalco as well.
In a statement to Deadline, SiriusXM says Maniscalco’s channel “introduced a new creative direction and a regularly evolving programming mix for the channel,” adding that “SiriusXM continues to invest in comedians more than any other audio platform.” Neither SiriusXM nor representatives for Maniscalco immediately responded to The Verge’s request for comment.

A bill introduced in the US House of Representatives seeks to honour Indian Captain Smit Machchhar for his actions in thwarting an attempted terrorist attack aboard flydubai Flight 1073, while also recognising the crew and passengers who helped secure the aircraft. The resolution, introduced on 05/10 by Congressmen Josh Gottheimer, Don Bacon and Michael McCaul, honours Machchhar and those aboard the flight while condemning the attempted attack. The measure has been referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs. According to the resolution, Flight 1073 departed Dubai International Airport for Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv on 30/09, carrying approximately 174 passengers, including four US citizens and 27 children. Quick answers to key questions Captain Smit Machchhar fought off an attack from the co-pilot, used his remaining strength to unlock the cockpit door, enabling off-duty pilots to land the aircraft safely after it lost over 16,000 feet in altitude. The co-pilot, Hamam al-Hammami, allegedly intended to seize control of the aircraft mid-flight, which was identified by investigators as an attempted terrorist attack aimed at crashing the flight into Ben Gurion Airport. Authorities condemned the attempted attack and the US House of Representatives introduced a bill honoring Captain Machchhar and the crew for their bravery while calling for a full investigation by the UAE and Saudi Arabian governments. Investigators are examining whether co-pilot al-Hammami's possible motivations and intentions indicated a broader terrorist agenda, given he had planned the attack before even joining Flydubai. Captain Smit Machchhar is reported to be making steady progress in his recovery, having improved in mobility and communication after suffering serious injuries during the attack. Midway through the flight, the first officer attacked Captain Machchhar on the flight deck with the aircraft’s emergency crash axe and attempted to seize control of the aircraft. The aircraft lost more than 16,000 feet of altitude in under 30 seconds, the resolution said. Despite suffering grave injuries, Machchhar fought off the attack and used his remaining strength to unlock the cockpit door. This allowed off-duty pilots to enter and land the aircraft, while crew members and passengers restrained the first officer. The aircraft subsequently landed safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia, with all passengers and crew accounted for. The resolution cited an 03/10 announcement by the Attorney General of the United Arab Emirates that an Emirati investigation had determined that the first officer attempted to carry out a terrorist act. The measure honours Machchhar for protecting everyone aboard the aircraft and commends the off-duty pilots, cabin crew and passengers who secured the flight deck and brought the aircraft safely down. It also calls for a full and expeditious investigation by the governments of Saudi Arabia and the UAE, with the United States and Israel to be kept fully informed. The Indian Embassy in the UAE said Captain Smit Machchhar is making steady progress in his recovery and remains in close contact with his family, doctors and local authorities. "Health Update: Capt Smit continues to make steady progress and is regaining his health," the Indian Embassy in the UAE stated, adding that it "remains in close touch with his family, doctors & local authorities, extending all possible assistance." "We thank everyone for their prayers & wish him a speedy recovery," the Embassy added. Earlier, the BAPS Hindu Mandir in Abu Dhabi held special prayers and an abhishek ceremony for Machchhar. Saints, community members and volunteers gathered at the temple to pray for his recovery and support his family. Reports by The Times of Israel said the Omani co-pilot, Hamam al-Hammami, had planned to direct the aircraft towards Ben Gurion Airport and was detained for questioning in the UAE. CBS News reported that Israel scrambled fighter jets and was prepared to intercept the aircraft if it continued towards Tel Aviv. The jets were later withdrawn after the aircraft turned towards Saudi Arabia for an emergency landing. Israeli forces had attempted to contact the cockpit by radio but received no response. A pre-set emergency system was activated, an emergency command centre was formed and Israeli airspace was sealed. US President Donald Trump also said on Monday that he "personally" believed Iran was responsible for the attack. "I do. I personally do," Trump said when asked whether he believed Iran was responsible for the attack on the flydubai flight. The incident has since drawn international attention to Machchhar's actions, as well as the coordinated efforts of the crew and passengers that enabled Flight 1073 to land safely. An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms.
Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days.
On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said.
Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown.
Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”.
“My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?”
The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing.
Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday.
The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts.
More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff.
The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war.
The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human-rights record, but has largely kept the majority of funds flowing.
This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, read a state department memo revealed by Reuters.
While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.”
Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”.
Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed.
Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on Reporters Without Borders Press freedom index. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsada2sh are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS.

These signs are typically placed on private property instead of closer to the road where most official road signs are located in Japan. Considering this, as well as Japanese online stores selling these kinds of products, the signs appear to be largely bought and erected by local residents, rather than government officials.
Throughout 2026, a claim circulated online that people in Japan had put up road signs warning drivers about cats jumping out into traffic. Many posts include numerous photos of yellow, diamond-shaped signs in different locations. All the images feature black silhouettes of cats and text in Japanese.
For example, one Instagram post reads, in part (archived), "In parts of Japan, locals have installed adorable warning signs that alert drivers to the possibility of cats suddenly jumping out into the street."
One sign pictured in that post shows three cats leaping, arms stretched out and wide, across the surface. The accompanying text, translated to English using DeepL, reads, "Beware of Cats Darting Out," or "Watch for Cats Crossing the Road."
Reddit (archived) and TikTok (archived) users shared similar posts. One Instagram user who made the claim (archived) said the designs are put in neighborhoods where outdoor cats hang around residential streets, but did not make a distinction between whether local residents or governments erected them. At least one popular post (archived) was labeled with an artificial intelligence content tag, though it is not clear which part of the images in that post were possibly AI-generated.
Some of the pictured signs do exist along roads in Japan and can be found on Google Maps. Some of the signs are also available to buy online. Therefore, we rate this claim true.
Some posts do, however, appear to feature fictionalized signs or real signs placed in non-existent locations, possibly through the use of AI.
While the available evidence points to most of the documented signs being put up by local residents, Snopes emailed the government of Iwate Prefecture, a province where at least one sign is authentically located, and contacted the National Police Agency of Japan, which handles traffic safety and road signs, to ask for confirmation that a government body did not erect the signs. We will update this article if we receive responses.
Finding the signs
At least three signs could be located on Google Maps. Others were photographed and included in posts by Japanese people or people visiting in Japan, but it was not possible to pinpoint their precise locations on Google Maps.
The sign showing the three leaping cats is in Kitakami, Iwate Prefecture, which is in the northern portion of Japan's largest and most populous island, Honshū Island. Notably, that sign appears to be located where someone's private property meets the sidewalk, whereas other signs along the same road are between the sidewalk and the road itself. This suggests a local resident, rather than government officials, erected the sign, especially considering that a larger warning about cats is placed directly on the wall of another section of that same property.
Another sign can be found in Ino, Kochi Prefecture, which is on the smallest of Japan's four main islands, Shikoku, toward the south of the country. It features a single silhouette of a cat and text that in English reads, "Beware of Animals." This style of sign appears to resemble other Japanese "beware of animals" road signs, such as this one featuring a Japanese raccoon dog.
A third sign appears to be located along a road on Iriomote island, a landmass in Okinawa Prefecture near the southwestern tip of Japan. It features the same "beware of animals" text beneath it.
This sign differs from the first two due to the lack of homes surrounding it and its close proximity to the road. That's because this particular sign warns drivers of the Iriomote cat, a wild cat species that is critically endangered. Road signs put up to help protect the species appear on at least one local travel agency's website. A stock photo of the same style of Iriomote cat warning sign closely resembles the image of the sign shared on social media.
Signs with named locations
Several other images of such signs could be found on social media, with some users specifying their locations. However, it was not possible to independently locate these signs, therefore they may or may not authentically exist. We will update this article if we find any of them at a later date.
For example, an X post from a Japanese-language user included an image of a yellow, square cat warning sign hanging from a tree on Shikine-jima, an island that is part of the Tokyo Metropolis.
A blog post about travel to the community of Bessho Onsen in Japan's Nagano Prefecture includes an image of a cat warning side attached to the side of a building.
One comment under an image on Facebook places another cat warning road sign in Morioka, Iwate Prefecture.
Finally, a blog post by someone biking through neighborhoods west of Tokyo includes two images of a cat warning sign attached to a fence post in an alley. Based on the day's travel described in the blog post, this sign would most likely be in the Wakamatsuchō neighborhood of Fuchū City, Tokyo.
Signs available online
Various cat warning road signs appear on Japanese online retail stores run by Amazon, Yahoo and Rakuten, again supporting the idea that local residents often buy the signs online to place them on private property.
That also means these signs do not necessarily have to appear "only in Japan" like some posts suggest. One of the same signs can be ordered to the U.S. through retailers such as Etsy and in miniature from Amazon's U.S. platform (archived, archived).
There are also many options for signs available through the search "cat warning road sign" on U.S. Amazon.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

'Not again': Arrest of US marine for murder reignites protests in Japan's Okinawa
- Published
For many Okinawa locals, the arrest of a US soldier accused of robbing and killing a woman in a hotel room has reignited decades of frustration over crimes involving US military personnel there.
"Honestly my first reaction was, 'Not again,'" 52-year-old longtime Okinawa resident Ai Sato told the BBC.
"Nothing has changed since I was a child. How many times are we going to repeat the same thing, create more victims, cause their families to suffer, and ultimately, cause the people of Okinawa to grieve?"
Akemi Oshiro, a 62-year-old Ginowan resident shared similar sentiments.
"I know we shouldn't get used to terrible things like this, but because they keep happening, I've stopped being surprised," she told the BBC.
Okinawa hosts the largest US military presence in Japan. It is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops.
US Marine Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was arrested by Japanese police on Sunday. Police say an investigation is underway and that Ballard is in Japanese custody because the alleged crime was unrelated to official military duties.
Whether a US service member is acting in the performance of official duty, external or not can determine which country has primary jurisdiction. When Japan has jurisdiction, but the suspect is under US custody, they can retain custody until Japan brings charges.
Ballard was assigned to III Marine Expeditionary Force and stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan City.
The Okinawa prefectural police say 39-year-old Anna Yagi was found dead early 3 October in a hotel room in Naha.
Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings. Local media citing police have reported that Yagi appeared to have been strangled with a cord.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi registered an official protest with Washington. But residents like Sato feel that's far from enough.
"I am deeply disappointed by the same kinds of government comments we have been hearing for decades -- that they will protest or that they take the matter seriously."
"I want Prime Minister Takaichi to call President Trump directly, someone with whom she has been emphasizing as having a close relationship with, and discuss concrete measures to prevent this from happening yet again," she said.
Following news of the suspected murder, people in Japan have been voicing anger with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice with one user saying: "Enough is enough."
Over the past few years, a number of accidents and crimes have led to growing local opposition to the US presence on the island.
The 2016 rape and murder of a 20-year-old local woman saw tens of thousands of protesters demonstrate against the heavy US presence there. A former US marine subsequently received a life sentence for the crime.
The US currently has about 55,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, with the heaviest concentration based on the tropical island prefecture. Okinawa is one of the country's smallest prefectures by size, but 70% of the land used exclusively by the US military in Japan is located there.
In 1972, Okinawa prefecture was returned to Japanese control after United States forces occupied the islands at the end of the Second World War. Since then, there have been 6,409 arrests for criminal offenses related to US military personnel, according to Okinawa Prefectural Government.
Locals say the significant US presence has stirred resentment over a number of issues from crimes including rapes, assaults, and drunk-driving accidents to local disturbances such as noise and aircraft crashes.
In 1995, three US servicemen abducted, beat, and raped a 12-year-old schoolgirl as she walked home from a stationery store.
In 2025, a US Marine was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a Japanese woman.
"Even 80 yeas after the war, Okinawa where we live is a place that is so unnerving," 48-year-old mother of two boys Hitomi Miyagi told the BBC.
"We will not stop raising our voices hoping for an Okinawa, where we can live in peace."

New Delhi, Oct 6: Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has carried out the successful flight trial of indigenously developed High-Altitude Platform (HAPS). The experimental flight attained an altitude of 21 km above mean sea level (AMSL) and remained at an altitude of 20 km AMSL for more than 30 minutes, before it was commanded to descend back to ground. The system was successfully recovered and flight performance data was analyzed.
Real-time video data and all other vehicle parameters were acquired from the Airborne platform at Ground Control Station during the entire flight, which showed intended flight performance. System carried various instrumentation and control electronic packages like an inertial measurement unit, Global positioning system receiver, onboard cameras, altitude control mechanism besides various other sub-systems. The trial was conducted in coordination with various agencies, namely Indian Air Force, CEMILAC, DGCA, Airports Authority of India (AAI) and other civil authorities.
The High-Altitude Platform, a lighter than air system as a long endurance stratospheric aerial surveillance platform, is being designed and developed by Aerial Delivery Research and Development Establishment (ADRDE), Agra.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh has complimented DRDO, IAF, PSUs and Industry on successful flight trial of High-Altitude Platform and stated that the successful trial is an important milestone in India’s Aatmanirbhar Bharat journey towards realizing a long endurance stratospheric Airship.
Defence Secretary and Secretary, Department of Defence R&D and Chairman, DRDO Rajesh Kumar Singh has congratulated the teams associated with the flight trial of high-altitude airship platform.

London City gelling, Man City flying - takeaways from WSL start
- Published
After five frantic weeks, the Women's Super League takes a two-week break, offering the perfect chance to take stock of a thrilling start to the season.
Here are five key takeaways from the opening weeks.
London City back up pre-season ambitions
For the first time this decade, the established order of the WSL looks under threat.
London City Lionesses and Tottenham have been bullish about climbing the table, while Liverpool also sought to kick on this season.
After five games, London City look the most convincing, with Sunday's statement 6-1 win at Spurs a dazzling example of the talent and depth manager Eder Maestre has at his disposal.
Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas headlined some eye-catching summer signings and she scored twice against Tottenham.
But it was the manner in which the whole team dismantled their previously impressive opponents that was so spectacular, with fellow forwards Kadidiatou Diani and Danielle van de Donk also looking a class above.
"This kind of win can be a game-changer," Maestre said.
No doubt. It is the kind of display that can lead to talk of a title charge.
For Spurs, a humiliating home loss is a reality check after promising early results.
Liverpool acquitted themselves well in narrow losses away to both Manchester clubs but, with key attacking players such as Vivien Endemann missing against United, they lacked creativity.
That points to perhaps the biggest thing both Liverpool and Spurs lack in comparison with London City: squad depth.
Man City remain team to beat
Five wins from five with 16 goals scored, defending champions Manchester City have picked up where they left off.
Sunday's comeback victory over Arsenal made it City's best start to a season since opening the 2017-18 campaign with seven straight victories, cementing their status as the team to beat.
In so doing, City also likely ended the Gunners' title aspirations even this early on.
It helps when their best players are performing. Khadija Shaw's contract renewal in the summer was key and the striker has five league goals already. England winger Lauren Hemp is also in fine form, contributing four goals and two assists.
After some quietly shrewd additions in Beth Mead, Carlotta Wamser and Niamh Charles, City look well set once again.
Their closest rivals are Chelsea, who have responded to an opening-day draw against Aston Villa by winning four straight games without conceding a goal.
While boss Sonia Bompastor wants them to be more clinical, their defensive strength is something they have over City.
As for Arsenal, the gap is 10 points to leaders City, and strong pre-season hopes of a first league title since 2018-19 are vanishing, with manager Renee Slegers conceding on Sunday: "At the moment, we are not in the conversation."
Man Utd finding feet under Olid
Manchester United's summer of upheaval bled into the start of the season, with Eva Olid's arrival from Hearts beginning with convincing defeats by London City and Chelsea.
The message from the club was that this would be a season of transition but recent performances suggest they are getting to grips with her style of play.
Saturday's 1-0 win over Liverpool was United's fourth straight victory in all competitions, with 18 goals scored in the process.
"I am so happy for the players - they deserve it," Olid said. "We have started to click in a lot of things and they fight for each other.
"But there is still a lot to improve. We created chances, but our last pass and our finishing needs to be better."
Summer signing Andrea Medina has been a huge positive on the left wing, with her contribution to the team more pronounced than a single goal suggests.
A trip to bottom side Charlton after the break is a presentable chance for more points before a stern test against Manchester City the following weekend.
Mixed fortunes for promoted clubs following league expansion
This season is the WSL's biggest ever, literally, with the league expanding from 12 to 14 teams and three coming up from WSL 2.
But does bigger mean stronger?
Crystal Palace look the most comfortable of the promoted sides, boasting six points from five games and they moved to eighth in the WSL table by drawing at Aston Villa on Sunday.
But things are more difficult for the other promoted sides, Birmingham and Charlton, who prop up the table.
Despite some promising patches, WSL 2 champions Birmingham have just two points and one of those came against Crystal Palace.
At least France forward Oceane Hurtre looks suited to this level, sitting as joint top scorer in the WSL with five goals from five games.
Hurtre scored against Everton in defeat on Sunday but defender Neve Herron summed things up by saying Blues were "second to everything" after the game.
Meanwhile, it looks bleak for Charlton, bottom of the table with zero points, 15 goals against and only two goals scored.
After their 5-1 loss to Brighton on Sunday, goalkeeper and captain Sophie Whitehouse said: "It just wasn't good enough.
"It's a tough league. The jump up is so big. You can't make any mistakes."
Are attendances falling?
Finally, it is too soon to draw conclusions but attendances at some of the league's biggest matches have been down on previous seasons.
For instance, Chelsea hosted Arsenal on 27 September in a fervent atmosphere, but the game had 36% fewer in Stamford Bridge than in January this year.
Similarly, Liverpool against Everton at Anfield was 19% down on last season, albeit the Merseyside derby was the first game of the 2025-26 season.
Three Saturdays ago, Arsenal kicked off against Manchester United at 17:30 in front of 29,853 fans. Last season, it was a lunchtime fixture that welcomed 37,627.
For balance, it ought to be highlighted that the Manchester City v Arsenal game on Sunday was promoted from the Joie Stadium to Etihad Stadium, and definitely had more than the 4,300 who attended the game last season.
Official figures have yet to be released for it.
Nevertheless, while this is a small sample size, paying customers is a potential trend to monitor as the WSL wrestles with the continued challenge of the schedule.

In my 48 years in public life, I have seen political parties rise and fall. I have seen leaders emerge with great promise and fade away. I have seen governments change, economies transform and technology alter our lives beyond recognition. One lesson has become increasingly clear to me: ultimately, leadership matters.
Comment | In 25 years, has Modi made lasting changes?
In today’s world, technology, knowledge, capital and ideas are freely available. But the true differentiator for nations is leadership — one with vision, integrity, credibility and the ability to execute.
On October 7, 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi completes 25 uninterrupted years in executive office — first as Chief Minister of Gujarat and, since 2014, as the Prime Minister of India. It is a remarkable journey of leadership sustained by public trust. Through changing circumstances, Mr. Modi has remained remarkably consistent in his purpose: the development of India and the empowerment of its people.
The world around us has been turbulent. We have witnessed a global financial crisis, a once-in-a-century pandemic, wars, geopolitical realignments, technological disruption and economic uncertainty. Several democracies have experienced frequent changes of leadership and consequent policy uncertainty. Through all this, India has remained steady at the wheel and an oasis of economic hope.
Leadership built on trust
Such stable leadership cannot sustain itself for 25 years merely through politics. It requires trust. Mr. Modi has earned that trust through an established track record, impeccable personal integrity and tireless self-discipline. In today’s world, public leaders effectively live in glass houses. Every decision and every action can be seen and questioned. To retain the confidence of people over decades under such scrutiny is an achievement in itself.
Mr. Modi brings a unique ability to understand people’s aspirations, translate them into action and communicate those results back to the people.
The results are visible. Over the last decade, India’s National Highway network has expanded from about 91,287 kilometres in 2014 to more than 1,46,000 km. The airport network has grown from 74 airports in 2014 to over 160. Railway electrification has accelerated dramatically. India’s installed renewable-energy capacity has now reached nearly 296 GW, including large hydro, with solar alone crossing 168 GW. Infrastructure today is being conceived not as isolated projects but as an integrated national network through initiatives such as PM Gati Shakti (Prime Minister Gati Shakti — National Master Plan for Multi-Modal Connectivity).
At the same time, India’s welfare architecture has expanded basic security and dignity. Around 80 crore people receive free foodgrains, including five kilograms a person per month for eligible priority households. Tapwater coverage in rural homes has risen from about 17% in 2019 to over 82%. An estimated 24.8 crore Indians moved out of multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23. The significance lies not only in the scale of these programmes, but in their reach. Technology has enabled the State to deliver basic entitlements more directly, transparently and at a scale that was once unimaginable.
Technology in nation-building
Mr. Modi has a deep appreciation of technology and its role in transforming India. He understands emerging technologies, adopts them early and, more importantly, applies them to nation-building. He sees technology as a tool to improve governance, empower people, create opportunities and accelerate development. India’s Digital Public Infrastructure has shown how technology can democratise access to banking, welfare and public services at unprecedented scale. This deep appreciation of technology has enabled him to launch a host of frontier policies aimed at making India take a giant leap and put it in the league of global tech titans. India’s quantum mission, semi-conductor mission, and a host of Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes across electronics and advanced manufacturing are instances of this vision.
India’s space sector is another great example. For decades, India’s extraordinary capabilities in space were centred overwhelmingly around government. By opening the sector to private enterprise and creating an enabling ecosystem, the government has unleashed a new generation of entrepreneurs. Companies such as Skyroot Aerospace, Pixxel, Agnikul, Dhruva and Bellatrix demonstrate what young Indians can achieve when regulation gives way to innovation.
As a Chief Minister first and then a Prime Minister, Mr. Modi has a strong belief in “Team India”. He knows that India cannot be transformed from Delhi alone. Growth needs to be decentralised with States and cities competing. His emphasis on cooperative and competitive federalism has given States a larger role in India’s development journey.
India’s place in the world
In his tenure, India’s stature abroad has also changed profoundly. Today, India’s voice is heard with greater respect on global platforms. India protects its national interest while engaging with different centres of global power, preserves strategic autonomy while building deeper partnerships, and projects its civilisational confidence as a modern, technology-driven nation. India today is among the world’s fastest-growing major economies. But I believe the most consequential phase of our journey is still ahead.
Few countries possess India’s combination of strengths. It has a demographic dividend, an extraordinary entrepreneurial energy, technological capabilities and a young generation that is ambitious, confident and increasingly connected to global opportunity. If we make the right decisions now, the benefits will last for centuries. This is why leadership at this moment assumes historic importance.
Mr. Modi’s 25 years in executive leadership have demonstrated the qualities such a moment demands. The Narendra Modi who became Chief Minister of Gujarat on October 7, 2001, and the Prime Minister leading India today are connected by the same clarity of purpose and unshakeable belief in India’s potential.
Twenty-five years have established his record. The next 20 years can establish India’s place in history. The true significance of these 25 years, however, will be judged by what they enable India to achieve next. Mr. Modi has shifted the country’s development trajectory — from incrementalism to ambition, from hesitation to confidence, and from managing limitations to believing in possibilities. I am confident that the direction he has set and the institutional momentum created during these years will help India realise its ambition of Viksit Bharat 2047 and reclaim its place among the world’s leading nations.
Few leaders are given the opportunity to shape a generation. Rarer still are those who can shape the destiny of a nation. After 25 years of leadership, Mr. Modi’s greatest contribution may ultimately be that he made India believe once again in the scale of its own possibilities — and gave the nation the leadership to turn that belief into reality.
N. Chandrababu Naidu is the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh

On July 19, as Sahida Fakir stepped out of her Navi Mumbai home to buy dinner, she was allegedly picked up and detained by Mumbai police’s Chembur crime branch. Four days later, her husband Jumman Fakir learnt that she was forcibly pushed across the border into Bangladesh on suspicion being an illegal immigrant.
Even as Sahida remains steeped in uncertainty, away from her family in Bangladesh to this day, a writ petition filed in the Supreme Court was heard by a Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana on September 17. The court sought a response from the Centre within four weeks.
A native of Gobindapur village, Swarupnagar block in West Bengal’s North 24 Parganas district, Sahida was not given any opportunity to established her Indian citizenship before being detained, her husband alleged.
Alt News spoke to Sahida Fakir, who narrated to us the harrowing experience of being pushed into no-man’s land at midnight and wading through a marsh to reach the Bangladesh side. According to her, she was picked up by the Mumbai police and kept in a detention centre for four days before being pushed out of India. In this duration, the police didn’t produce her before a magistrate.
“When I was pleading with Mumbai police officials to let me go, they just sneered at me and said we need to fill up the empty seats of the deportation airplane,” she alleged, asking, “How can they be so inhumane? What is my fault? Being a Muslim who speaks Bengali?”
Jumman told Alt News that he reached Chembur crime branch office on July 19 and attempted to prove his wife’s citizenship by furnishing her documents. “The police said that they would need few days to verify her documents and, if necessary, would ask for additional documents. I went to the office again on July 22 with more papers, but the next day, they informed me that she had been pushed into Bangladesh. When I asked how they could do such a thing without giving us any opportunity to prove our citizenship, I was thrown out of the office,” he claimed.
According to Jumman, after almost a week, Sahida called from Bangladesh to inform him that she had allegedly been expelled from India through either the Assam or the Northeast border, and that she was currently living with a family from Satkhira that provided her shelter. “She called me from an unknown number and was crying inconsolably. A family from Bhadiyali village in Kalaroa Upazila of Satkhira was sheltering her, and the Bangladesh police posted two armed guards for her protection outside the residence,” he said. “I get to speak to her occasionally by calling the Bangladeshi family’s number. She is a thyroid patient. Local journalists had arranged some food, clothes and medicines for her, however, that stock is fast depleting.”
The couple has lived in Mumbai for the last 20 years — Jumman works as a car cleaner while Sahida worked as a domestic help. Their elder son Sahin Fakir lives in their native village in Bengal’s North 24 parganas district while 13-year-old Samim Fakir lived with his parents in Mumbai. After Sahida’s pushback, Jumman and Samim left Mumbai and returned to Swarupnagar.

What The Documents Say
According to Sahida’s citizenship documents, including her birth certificate, her Aadhar card, voter card, PAN card, accessed by Alt News, she was born in November 1988. On October 19, 1995, the Bithari-Hakimpur Gram Panchayat, under the Swarupnagar Block, issued her birth certificate (serial number 6382).
Sahida’s father, Aminuddin Gazi, is listed in the 2002 SIR electoral roll (Part 89, Serial 514, Swarupnagar assembly); her grandfather, Badsha Gazi, is also listed in the 1952 electoral roll for Swarupnagar assembly. See below:
On January 29 this year, the Bithari-Hakimpur Gram Panchayat issued a family genealogy stating that Badsha Gazi’s son, Aminuddin Gazi, had 14 children, including Sahida. Sahida’s name also appears in land records accessed by Alt News. Although Jumman’s name appeared in the final SIR list, Sahida was placed in the “under adjudication” category. However, she had appealed against her exclusion.
Following her ‘unofficial deportation’ to Bangladesh in July, Sahida’s family was able to obtain a certificate from Swarupdaha Free Primary School on August 9, which states that she studied there from 1994 to 1998. Her transfer certificate, issued by Jamia Islamia Girls’ High Madrasa located in Swarupnagar block for Class 8 in 2008, is also available.
Sahida’s Account
Speaking to Alt News, Sahida said, “I was kept at the Chembur detention camp for four days. My phone, the money that I was carrying to buy chapatis for my family and my Aadhaar card — everything was snatched away. I begged the police, fell at their feet to let me contact my family, only then did they allow me to make a call for a few seconds. After I informed my husband, he came to the Chembur crime branch office to furnish all the documents to prove my Indian citizenship, but the police didn’t even bother to see or check them,” she alleged.
“After spending four days at the detention centre, they stacked several others and me onto a bus with dark curtains, so we couldn’t see where we were going. If anybody even tried to pull the curtains slightly, the Border Security Force men would beat and abuse them. We later realised that it was the airport. From there we were boarded onto an aircraft, and they took us somewhere on the Assam or Northeast border. I don’t know any of these places, but heard it from other people in our group,” she further alleged.
According to Sahida, she was placed in a group of around 200 people who were also pushed into Bangladesh.
“After we landed, we were taken to a detention centre. From there, we were packed into buses in batches. The bus took us to several other camps. They kept us waiting in some camps for 10 hours, and in some for about 3-4 hours before moving us out. Finally around 1 am, the BSF pushed all of us back into no man’s land,” she claimed.
“We were in a marsh with the muck reaching my neck in some places. I had to wade through the mud on no man’s land to finally reach the Bangladesh side of the border by daybreak,” she added.
The others told Sahida that they could be at the Feni border, near Chattogram of Bangladesh.
Following this, according to the petition submitted in the Supreme Court by her son, Sahin, Sahida somehow managed to reach the Petrapole-Benapole border area after a few days. There, the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) apprehended her, but due to humanitarian reasons, she was provided shelter and was finally able to contact her family on July 31, the petition said.
“A farming family from Bhadiyali village has sheltered me, and despite their financial constraints, they are doing their best to feed me. But do I deserve this hopeless situation? Why do I have to survive on other people’s grace? I have diabetes and thyroid issues. Since July 19, I haven’t had my medicine. My family’s life has been turned upside down. My husband had to flee Mumbai, leaving his meagre employment and my younger son had to leave his studies,” she lamented.
Alt News contacted an officer from Chembur crime branch, who refused to comment on the matter, stating that they are “officially required not to speak on such matters.”
We also reached out to the officer-in-charge of Kolaroa police station in Bangladesh. He refused to comment.
Legal Tangle: Contentious SOP, Loopholes in Govt Order
On August 17, Sahin moved the apex court with a petition challenging his mother’s apprehension, detention and forcible expulsion to Bangladesh, demanding that she be brought back to India. The petition argued that the Mumbai police’s actions directly contradicted the provisions of Article 21 of the Constitution.
The petition also challenged the legality of the Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) dated May 2, 2025, titled ‘Procedure for deportation of illegal Bangladeshi nationals/Rohingyas’, and the ‘Immigration and Foreigners Order, 2025’, insofar as it permits or facilitates removal of persons apprehended within India without the safeguards prescribed by law and the Constitution.
The SOP from May 2025, published by the Union ministry of home affairs (MHA), establishes guidelines for ‘deportation/removal/expulsion’ of Bangladeshi nationals and Rohingyas. According to the SOP: “All State Governments/UT Administrations shall set up a Special Task Force in each District under the police of the State/UT to detect, identify and deport/send-back illegal immigrants from Bangladesh/Myanmar settled in the State/UT concerned.”
“If the suspected Bangladesh/Myanmar national claims Indian citizenship and residence of a place in any other Indian State/UT, the concerned State Government/UT would send to the Home Secretary of the State/UT and District Collector/District Magistrate of the District from where the suspected person claims to hail, the details including name, parentage, residential address, details of near relatives etc. The State Government/ UT/Collector/District Magistrate concerned in turn will ensure that an appropriate report is sent to the deporting State Government/UT after proper verification within a period of 30 days,” the SOP reads.
It is important to note here that the SOP doesn’t mandate an FIR under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, if a suspected Bangladeshi or a Rohingya is apprehended and due investigation, enabling anybody under suspicion of being an illegal immigrant to be simply expelled from India.
A Supreme Court advocate, requesting anonymity, told Alt News that the SOP is inhumane as it empowers the State and the border guarding forces such as the BSF to push back suspected ‘Bangladeshi and Rohingya’ infiltrators into ‘no man’s land’ without any judicial process. The SOP also mandates the handover of suspects to the relevant border guarding forces of Bangladesh and Myanmar, thus enabling the Indian border guarding forces to exercise their powers arbitrarily.
As contention around this SOP rose, the Indian government initiated ‘The Immigration and Foreigners Order, 2025’ — published in the Gazette of India on September 1, 2025, effectively overriding the provisions of the earlier SOP. According to this order, if a suspected foreign national is apprehended without his/her travel document, such as a passport, then that person’s nationality has to be first ascertained by that person’s Nation. After it has been proved beyond doubt that the person is an illegal immigrant, the deportation process will take place.
As per Chapter 3, Article 12(4)(c) of the said Order, it is clearly mentioned: “In the absence of a valid passport or other travel document, the authorities referred to in sub-paragraph (3) may immediately take appropriate steps for getting the nationality verified and for issuance of travel document in favour of the illegal migrant from the Embassy or High Commission of the country concerned in India through the Ministry of External Affairs and necessary steps shall be taken by such authorities to deport the illegal migrant from the country as soon as the travel document is received.”
Based on Sahida’s account of her ‘deportation’, however, it becomes clear that provisions of the Order were not followed. Further, even though certain provisions of the previous SOP were applied, the process, or rather the lack of it, in which she was pushed into Bangladesh, contradicts the rest of it.
In a similar case reported by Scroll.in, 66-year-old Dablu Sheikh and his three sons were picked up from their home in Suti, Murshidabad, under suspicion of being Bangladeshis. They have been missing for over 40 days. Sheikh’s father, Sk Samjani, was also a voter in the Suti Assembly constituency in 1966 and 1995, the report stated, adding that the inspector-in-charge of Suti police station said the four persons were illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators, and thus had been deported to Bangladesh. The officer further said that no FIR was registered against the four men under the Foreigners Act, as they were detained following the Union government circular from May 2025, and directly sent to the Jangipur holding centre. The report suggests that they were deported to Bangladesh from the holding centre.

For a goalkeeper, one mistake can overshadow an otherwise solid performance.
Gurpreet Singh Sandhu knows that better than most. Against Brazil on Saturday, India competed bravely for long periods of the game against the five-time world champion. Gurpreet made two saves from Vinicius Junior, one of the most celebrated stars on the pitch.
But two mistakes followed. So did two goals. And that was that. After half-time, he was replaced. India coach Khalid Jamil has insisted that it was ‘not the end of the road’ for the 34-year-old.
“He is one of the best goalkeepers India has, and we cannot judge him in just two matches, because the next game is coming up. He will be back again,” he said after the match.
On Tuesday, Uruguay awaits – a potential shot at redemption, a chance for a final flourish in this international window.
“Be hard on yourself after that game, which we have lost and look at what we can do better,” Gurpreet told Sportstar in an exclusive interview. “But you can’t stay down forever, because there is a long way ahead . . .”
Learning to lead
Jamil made 11 changes in the squad from the previous international window for the games against Panama, Brazil and Uruguay. Former captain Sandesh Jhingan and veterans like Rahul Bheke and Lallianzuala Chhangte were all excluded. And with Sunil Chhetri retired, Gurpreet became not only the captain but also the most experienced player in the national team dressing room.
“We had the likes of Sunil Bhai and everyone before who were guiding us. The lessons that I have taken from him are about setting examples for the team, on and off the pitch. That’s what I am trying to replicate now as well,” he said.
Leadership has become particularly crucial in Indian football, especially at a time when its wins have dried up, and the FIFA ranking has nosedived.
For Gurpreet, the uncertainty off the field inevitably found its way onto it.
“There is something which will eventually affect everyone, be it the coaching staff, the players, the masseuse, the ball boy, everyone, when you see a lot of uncertainty that was there in Indian football at that point in time,” he said.
India’s men’s top-flight – the Indian Super League (ISL) – was plunged into uncertainty after the 2024-25 season, as it remained on hold for seven months before a truncated 2025-26 campaign began.
ALSO READ | Khalid Jamil backs Gurpreet, demands more from substitutes after India’s loss to Brazil
“I am not trying to make any excuses here, but I am just saying that that was the true reflection of where we were as a nation in Indian football terms,” he added.
“There were no games that were happening for players to stay in shape and have game time, and when you are facing teams who have a setup where they are playing regular football, they will have some (extra) sharpness even if they are a lower-ranked team. That’s something which we were missing in very crucial games.”
But he believes there are signs of better days ahead. The new ISL season begins on October 10 in its old format, while the national team trained for three weeks in Bengaluru before this window.
“I think (this) was the first camp when we had everyone,” Gurpreet said. “Now, we can plan better and see how we want to go (ahead as a team),” Gurpreet added.
A work in progress
Gurpreet has been in the national team for a decade now, and has played under four managers – all from different countries, Jamil being the only Indian tactician among them.
“Coach Khalid is very thorough in his preparation. He does a lot of hard work from morning till evening, in terms of how training has to be set up and how the opponent plays. I’m not going to sit here and compare coaches; I’m just going to talk about what is currently in front of us,” he said.
“I feel like it (team composition) is something which will take time because, since coach Khalid has come, we are trying to find a core group of players we can rely on every single game when we face tougher opposition. Every time, there has been something missing, be it injuries or non-release of players.”
A different test
Brazil gave India and Gurpreet a taste of elite opposition. Today, another former world champion awaits.
“When the news came out, as a player you’re just trying to make sure, checking facts that it is happening or not,” he said. “And then you feel that, okay, it is a great opportunity.”
The two matches so far have provided the Blue Tigers a stage to prove that they have worked on their weaknesses. A 1-1 draw with Panama, ranked 94 places above India, and a pressing game against Brazil earned them praise despite a 0-4 loss.
But for Gurpreet, there will be personal demons to confront — avoiding the mistakes he did against Brazil and staying composed in an era of trolls.
“Fifteen years ago, there was not much involvement of social media, with fans giving their opinions and listening to what is happening around the ecosystem. But now, we have overexposure to everything,” Gurpreet said.
“That is something we, as players, have to learn how to deal with, because now it has become a part of the job. If people are talking good, great. If people are talking bad, no problem. That’s part and parcel of life.”
Gurpreet has been here before. Despite making nine saves against Qatar in 2021, he let in the lone goal that handed India a 0-1 loss.
“When the opposition player comes and tells you that you deserve to be on a different level in terms of the way you play, that is the best compliment that you can receive,” he said.
India did not lose another game in 2021 since, with Gurpreet between the sticks. It won five matches, drew four, while he had four clean sheets and lifted the SAFF Championship title.
Two mistakes and two goals in a friendly can not define a career built over 15 years. And it won’t. Uruguay is next, and for Gurpreet, the only response that has ever mattered is the one he makes with his gloves.

On 02 October 2026, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) held a protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park grounds demanding accountability from the Election Commission of India (ECI) and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Protesters raised concerns over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleged voter deletions, and transparency in the electoral process. Despite Mumbai Police denying permission for the gathering, thousands attended the protest and raised slogans. Police later registered an FIR against the organisers and 400–500 unidentified participants for allegedly violating restrictions on the assembly.
In this context, a video (here & here) is circulating on social media claiming that CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was attacked at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park during this protest. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke was attacked during a protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park on 02 October 2026.
Fact: The video is from 15 June 2026 and shows Abhijeet Dipke being assaulted by unidentified individuals during a youth protest against paper leaks and unemployment in Jaipur, Rajasthan. There are no reports of him being attacked at the Mumbai protest. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video shows that the same video (here & here) has been available online since at least 15 June 2026. These posts describe it as Abhijeet Dipke being attacked in Jaipur, Rajasthan.
According to media reports (here, here & here), on 15 June 2026, Dipke was manhandled and slapped multiple times during a youth protest at Shaheed Smarak in Jaipur, Rajasthan. He had reportedly organised the protest to speak out against paper leaks and unemployment, and to demand the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. As supporters carried Dipke on their shoulders toward the stage, several people emerged from the crowd, pulled him down, and struck his face. This sparked a quick retaliatory scuffle from CJP supporters before the police stepped in and detained the suspects.
Afterwards, Dipke condemned the assault, calling it a sign of fear and cowardice from his opponents. Furthermore, there are no news reports of Dipke being assaulted at the Mumbai Shivaji Park protest
To sum it up, an old video of Abhijeet Dipke being assaulted in Jaipur is falsely shared to claim he was attacked in Mumbai.

A purported screenshot circulated online in fall 2026 of a purported Truth Social post, dated Sept. 22, in which U.S. President Donald Trump wrote that he had "spoken to God" and that "tonight is Armageddon.".
The image spread on multiple platforms, including Instagram, Threads and Facebook. Many commenters appeared to believe Trump actually posted the remarks. The full text of the alleged post read as follows:
I have spoken to God and he has given me a vision of an ocean filled with blood a city of dust a golden throne for me to sit on, eternally!!!, Tonight is Armageddon, the final judgement of good and evil!!!! Lock your doors and do not directly at the flash!!!! God bless us all!!!
President Donald J. Trump
(X user @ZiemowitSzcze11.)
Despite the username matching Trump's real Truth Social username, there's no evidence Trump actually published the post. The earliest version of the image we found appeared on a Polish X account that captioned it (translation via X): "Well, fake, but would you be surprised?" (archived).
We searched Trump's Truth — an online archive of Trump's Truth Social posts — for the word "Armageddon," and none of the three results related to the quote above.
(Trump's Truth)
We also looked all posts Trump actually published on Sept. 22 and found he published four that day. None of the four posts matched the timestamp or content of that in the screenshot.
The fake quote appeared to echo whistleblower reports received by the Military Religious Freedom Foundation that U.S. military commanders told troops their action in Iran was "all part of God's divine plan," allegedly "referring to Armageddon and the imminent return of Jesus Christ."
Trump has echoed similarly apocalyptic language, posting in May 2026, for example, that "a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again" — referring to U.S. attacks on Iran. He's also faced criticism for his posting an image depicting him in the likeness of Jesus Christ.

Seoul – South Korea is preparing a response to force North Korea to apologize for a mine blast in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that seriously wounded two South Korean soldiers, a defense ministry spokesperson said Tuesday.
South Korea is also calling on Pyongyang to come to the table to discuss the misalignment of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL), which bisects the DMZ, the spokesperson said.
The Sept. 21 blast wounded three South Korean troops, two of them seriously.
The spokesperson, Chung Bin-na, did not specify what measures would be taken in response to the blast, which South Korea has said was caused by North Korean mines, citing the results of a joint investigation with the United Nations Command.
Chung said North Korea must remove the mines it planted in the DMZ south of the MDL, but also said there were differences in the exact line that separates the Korean Peninsula as recognized by the two Koreas.
Differing views of the border line are one factor contributing to tension in the area, Chung said.
Some sections of the MDL, which stretches more than 200 kilometers between the east and west coasts with 1,900 markers, have become difficult to identify after decades of limited access inside the DMZ since it was drawn up in 1953 at the end of the Korean War.
North Korea on Friday rejected as “groundless” Seoul’s accusation that North Korean mines seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the DMZ and dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology, state news agency KCNA reported.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of the North’s leader Kim Jong Un, said Pyongyang had not deliberately planted mines in the border zone, KCNA reported.

Author Chetan Bhagat has a new productivity proposal for India's workforce: avoid looking at the clock and the number of hours you are expected to put in at your desk, and instead focus on how much work you can actually get done. He argued that even four hours of dedicated work can be enough for a day, reigniting an old workplace debate over whether longer hours mean greater productivity. Bhagat made these remarks at the 18th edition of the Project Management South Asia Conference (PMSAC) in Bengaluru on 3 October and said, "I work 4 hours a day, and that is enough if you do it with full dedication." "If you genuinely do work for 4 hours in a day, that is enough, good enough. It doesn't mean you have to include meetings, breaks, Wi-Fi issues, and other hunky-dory stuff that the offices often witness. In those 4 hours, you have to prioritise everything you put on the table," he added, according to media reports. However, he also stressed the importance of prioritising everything that an employee puts on the table. According to Bhagat, people should not simply start focusing on putting only four hours a day into their work and consider the rest of their day to be free. Instead, his idea is to encourage people to figure out what deserves their attention the most and complete that task with utmost dedication and discipline. His remarks come at a time when workplaces in India and around the world are grappling with questions over how long employees should work and how their working hours can be used more effectively, even as the rapid rise of artificial intelligence (AI) fuels uncertainty over the future of jobs and how work itself could change. Bhagat's remarks stand in sharp contrast to views expressed by some industry leaders, including Infosys co-founder NR Narayana Murthy, who has advocated a 70-hour workweek for young Indians, linking longer working hours with the need to improve the country's productivity and competitiveness. Murthy later said that he had worked more than 70 hours a week for over four decades and, during the period when India followed a six-day workweek, his weekly working hours often reached 85-90. Commenting on how employees can prioritise work-life balance, Bhagat noted, "No one cares for you unless you are. Do what makes you feel happy; follow 11 rules of life," a reference to his 2024 book, 11 Rules for Life: Secrets to Level Up. His argument attempts to shift the productivity debate away from how many hours an employee spends at work to what they accomplish during those hours. But whether four hours of focused work can really be enough for a day may depend on the nature of the job, workload, and responsibilities.
