A video showing a group of people marching on a road while waving Bangladesh’s national flags is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with claims that it shows illegal migrants raising Bangladeshi flags in Virar, Maharashtra. Some social media users have also linked the video to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, suggesting that the visuals highlight the need for the exercise. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows illegal migrants raising Bangladeshi flags in Virar, Maharashtra.
Fact: The viral video does not show illegal migrants raising Bangladeshi flags in Virar, Maharashtra. It shows participants carrying Bangladeshi flags during a Hero bike advertisement shoot in Virar on 03 October 2026. Prakash Kawale, Senior Police Inspector at Bolinj Police Station, confirmed to Factly that the video was from the shoot. Dinesh Jaiswal, owner of DJ Location, the production house involved, also confirmed this, adding that the shoot was cancelled after a ruckus and that all the participants were Indian. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
Upon closely reviewing the viral video, we noticed several details that raised questions about its authenticity. A mounted camera is visible at the beginning of the video and again around the 12-second mark. A cloth diffuser, typically used to control lighting during a shoot, is also visible. These details indicate that the footage was recorded during a shoot.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple media reports (here, here, and here) featuring similar visuals. According to these reports, a Bangladeshi flag was used during a commercial advertisement shoot in Virar, a suburb in Maharashtra’s Palghar district, which triggered protests from local groups. The reports noted that some locals complained to the police and later burned the Bangladeshi flags used by the production crew. One of the reports also captured the aftermath, showing several youths attempting to burn a Bangladeshi flag.
We contacted Mr Prakash Kawale, Senior Police Inspector at Bolinj Police Station in Virar, regarding the viral video. Speaking to Factly, he confirmed that the video was recorded during an advertisement shoot. According to him, “This was an ad shoot by a Hero Bike company on 03 October 2026.”
We also learnt from the inspector that the shoot was carried out by DJ Location. We also contacted Dinesh Jaiswal, the owner of the production house, who confirmed that the video was recorded during an advertisement shoot for a Hero bike. He said the shoot was cancelled after a ruckus broke out, following which the concept was dropped. He added that all the people involved in the shoot were Indian and clarified that the video was from an advertisement shoot, not a real incident involving illegal migrants.
To sum up, this viral video does not show illegal migrants raising Bangladeshi flags in Virar, Maharashtra; it is from an advertisement shoot.

Relief, frustration among Punggol East Container Park tenants over lease extension offer
Some had already paid deposits and begun renovations at new premises, while others say the one-year extension gives them time to plan their next move.
SINGAPORE: Some businesses at Punggol East Container Park and Tebing Lane were caught off-guard by a one-year lease extension after preparing to close, while others welcomed the extra time to plan.
Founder of Play Pickle Darren Teo told CNA he learnt of the one-year lease extension from his landlord City Sprouts on Saturday evening (Oct 3).
"We were surprised by the news and the abrupt change in circumstances. We had been preparing to vacate Tebing Lane at the end of October and had already begun making operational and business decisions on that basis," he said.
The changes have caused a great deal of uncertainty for the tenants involved, said Mr Teo, noting that businesses need lead time to make decisions about staff, customers, equipment, finances and future locations.
"It has been something of an emotional rollercoaster as well. We had already accepted that we were leaving Tebing Lane, informed our community and started preparing to say goodbye."
Punggol GRC Member of Parliament Yeo Wan Ling announced on Saturday that the four master tenants at Punggol East and Tebing Lane, including social enterprise City Sprouts, had been offered lease extensions of up to a year. This could allow businesses to stay on until the end of 2027.
The tenancies were due to expire on Dec 31, when the land would be returned to the Singapore Land Authority (SLA). City Sprouts had told its subtenants, including those at the container park, to cease operations by Oct 31. In September, more than 50 tenants were preparing to leave, CNA reported.
PLANS ALREADY IN MOTION
Some food and beverage operators told CNA they had committed to new locations, and the extension came too late.
Smok Hous owner Isrudy Shaik first learnt of the extension on social media, before he was contacted a few days later and asked if he wanted to stay on.
"It was a bit too late because I had already put down a deposit and started renovations," the 48-year-old said.
Tenants should have been given a clear timeline from the start, Mr Isrudy said, adding that the initial deadline and subsequent extension had created "a lot of uncertainty".
He worried that repeated changes would cause businesses to lose customers. "People will feel like, 'Oh, this is just a roti prata game – sometimes they close, sometimes they don't.'"
Chickyfish owner Alvin Chua said he had planned to close at the container park regardless of the extension, as business had dropped by more than 50 per cent in the past few years.
"Only recently when they announced about the closing, more people came. But we already cut down on manpower … so we already preplanned this whole thing," he added.
At 6 Tebing Lane, bouldering and strongman gym Ark Bloc had already made arrangements to restore the site for return, said Mr Jeremy Ko, a co-founder of Arkkies, the company behind the gym.
"Honestly, the news (of the extension) ruined my morning," he said.
The company had paid a non-refundable deposit to a demolition contractor and sold about 60 per cent of its equipment, said Mr Ko. Demolition costs will run S$35,000 to S$40,000.
"What frustrates us is that the position previously conveyed through our master tenant was definitive: there was no possibility of an extension. By the time we heard otherwise, we had already made substantial closure arrangements," he added.
The gym announced at the end of August that it would close from Nov 15, after Sports Hub @ Punggol indicated that an extension was off the table. This gave members enough time to use up or refund their passes.
Staff told members to sign up with other gyms, and revenue fell by 20 to 30 per cent in September. Mr Ko expects a further drop in October and November.
"Offering us another year now would not automatically bring them (members) back," said Mr Ko.
Arkkies, which runs 25 gyms in Singapore, will not extend Ark Bloc's tenancy in Punggol and has no confirmed relocation plan. Sports Hub @ Punggol management offered to lower the rent, but a slight rebate cannot cover a 30 per cent revenue dip, said Mr Ko.
CITY SPROUTS RESPONDS
City Sprouts told CNA it was informed of the proposed extension on Oct 3, the same day it was announced publicly.
The social enterprise intends to take up the extension, and its tenancy would run until Dec 31, 2027. Subtenancies would last until about November 2027, leaving time for handover works before the site is returned.
"We recognise that some tenants may already have secured alternative premises or committed resources towards relocation. We do not expect or require every tenant to reverse those plans," said its spokesperson.
Tenants who want to stay will be "given priority" in discussions, said City Sprouts, adding that it will respect decisions to proceed with relocation. "Where tenants would like to remain or require additional time, we are equally happy to work with them on the appropriate arrangements."
City Sprouts is the master tenant at 50 Punggol East Road, where Punggol East Container Park and other green spaces are located. The state properties at 32 Punggol East, 6 Tebing Lane and 10 Tebing Lane are tenanted respectively to Sing See Soon Floral & Landscape, Sports Hub @ Punggol and AT Punggol.
Sports Hub @ Punggol declined to comment, while Sing See Soon Floral & Landscape did not respond to queries. CNA could not reach AT Punggol.
CNA has also asked SLA whether all four master tenants have confirmed they will extend their leases, and why the extensions were announced shortly after subtenants were told to cease operations.
GOOD NEWS FOR SOME
Still, some businesses were glad to hear about the lease extension, saying the extra year has given them some "breathing room".
At Uncle Leong Seafood, shop manager Gary Ong said the business had been scrambling to find a new location after learning on Sep 1 that it had three months to move out.
"We feel quite relieved about the extension," said Mr Ong, who has worked there for 12 years. "We will use maybe six months to start looking for a new shop … we can slow down the pace a little."
Despite the reprieve, the extension only delays an eventual departure from the site the restaurant has occupied for 15 years. Regulars have been dropping by since news broke of the impending closure, he added.
"When we came here, there was no HDB (nearby), just the waterfront," said Mr Ong. "All these years, we watched everything come up."
The site is also frequented by recreational users such as Mr Dickson Len and Mr Brian Lim, who play pickleball there about once every two weeks. The location is convenient for their group and courts are easier to book in the mornings, they said.
Among the long-time patrons is Mr Satesh Raj, 36, who has been visiting the area since he was 19.
"I feel very sad. I literally grew up here. I'm not sure where else there's a place like this in Punggol," he said.

Calm in real life but demons on court - Medvedev runs out of chances
- Published
Daniil Medvedev once said you would need to knock on his hotel door at 6am for seven days in a row to make him angry.
On court, though, he is a far more combustible character who finally ran out of chances when he was disqualified from Monday's China Open semi-final against Novak Djokovic.
Djokovic was serving for a place in the final when the ball ricocheted off the back of the court. Medvedev swiped it into the stands, where it hit a spectator in the face.
A few minutes later the Russian was defaulted, as he had to be, under rules that bar a player from "hitting a ball dangerously or recklessly, or with negligent disregard of the consequences."
Players have got away with worse. There is sometimes anger in their actions, but it is rarely of the bulging-neck-vein variety.
It is more often a sign of irritation and petulance, with frustrations taken out on the ball with little care for the safety of officials, ball kids and the spectators who line the court.
"I can only say I'm a really calm person in life - I actually have no idea why the demons go out when I play tennis," Medvedev said at the 2019 US Open, where he was fined for snatching a towel from a ball person and making an offensive gesture to fans inside the Arthur Ashe Stadium.
"Especially when I was a junior, I had a lot of problems with my attitude.
"I was not getting defaulted, but to have a game penalty was easy."
Returning to the theme at that year's end-of-season ATP Finals, Medvedev said any bad blood soon disappears after leaving the court.
"All my temper goes away after I leave the tennis court. If I'm not happy with my practice, I step out of the court and five minutes later, I'm OK," he said.
It is hard - and probably unwise - to take your eyes off Medvedev's matches, and he is very popular with the media for his engaging, reflective and humorous interviews once the dust has settled.
But he has gone too far on court on many occasions, with much of his aggression directed at umpires.
At Wimbledon in 2017, a 21-year-old Medvedev was so incensed about some of the decisions made by umpire Mariana Alves in his second-round match that he sprinkled coins at her feet as she climbed down from the chair.
He later apologised and denied he was accusing her of bias.
Two years ago, again at Wimbledon, it appeared officials were considering defaulting Medvedev for an outburst towards umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore.
Medvedev claimed he said something in Russian which was "not pleasant, but not over the line" - and, after a discussion between the umpire, supervisor and tournament referee, he escaped with a code violation for unsportsmanlike conduct.
He was fined more than £60,000 for his behaviour at the 2025 Australian Open, which included trying to destroy a net camera, and had an infamous meltdown later that year at the US Open.
On a rowdy New York night, Benjamin Bonzi had match point for a straight-set win against Medvedev in the first round when a photographer inexplicably walked on to court between his first and second serves.
Umpire Greg Allensworth awarded the Frenchman another first serve because of the delay, sparking fury from Medvedev.
Medvedev accused Allensworth of hoping to engineer a quick finish - as he gets paid by the match, rather than the hour - and there was a pause of over five minutes as he whipped up the crowd.
He did save the match point, but went on to lose in five sets before obliterating his racquet by smashing it repeatedly against the table next to his chair.
Medvedev will lose all the prize money and ranking points he earned from his run to the semi-finals in Beijing. He remains in the eighth and final qualifying spot for November's ATP Finals, but the loss of 200 points could yet prove crucial.
The 30-year-old has apologised for his actions and said he hopes to say sorry to the spectator in person.
In New York a month ago, Medvedev reflected on the role of genetics when explaining how his eldest daughter has "my personality on the court".
"She plays a bit. She enjoys it. Maybe it's a bit of a genetic somewhere there," Medvedev added.
"I took her to practice once. She's happy, so she throws the racquet through the whole court.
"The coach looks at me and says: 'I don't know where she got this from...'
"All the people that talk about that I should control myself more - she's three years old. It's not like we taught her to do the things she's doing on the court."

Separatist party projected to win Quebec election, adding new test to Canada's unity
- Published
Canadian media projects the sovereigntist Parti Québécois (PQ) will secure a minority win in Monday's provincial election in Quebec, making Paul St-Pierre Plamondon the incoming premier.
It marks the first time the PQ has been in power since 2014. It could prove to be a test for Prime Minister Mark Carney, setting up confrontations with Quebec over issues like immigration and the monarchy.
The party has also pledged to hold a referendum on Quebec's independence, similar to an upcoming vote in province of Alberta later this month.
The majority French-speaking province has held other votes on this, in 1980 and 1995. Polls indicate only 30% of Quebecers back such a move.
Plamondon has said that vote would occur after US President Donald Trump is out of office.
Carney may find himself managing dual unity crises in different parts of the country, depending on the outcome of the separation vote in Alberta. Trump is due to leave office in roughly two years, meaning that if Plamondon keeps his pledge, a third plebiscite on independence would likely be scheduled for 2029 or 2030.
Separate from sovereignty, Plamondon has made it clear he is willing to fight Ottawa if it is seen as overstepping matters of provincial interest.
He suggested during the campaign that he was going to pressure Ottawa, external on issues like immigration, vowing to fight any increases mandated by the Carney government.
He also pledged to "abolish the monarchy in Quebec" and reroute money spent on its institutions to social services instead.
"We are going to do what we have to do to get the monarchy out of Quebec, repatriate those funds, and send them to social causes," he told reporters in late September.
For example, Plamondon suggested defunding Quebec's lieutenant-governor's office - responsible for representing King Charles III in the province - saying he would instead spend that money to tackle homelessness.
Plamondon was among the Quebec lawmakers who refused to pledge allegiance to the King in 2022, paving the way for a provincial law that now makes the oath of allegiance optional.
His plan to withdraw financial support for the lieutenant-governor's office is likely to face significant legal challenges, given the monarchy's central role in Canada's constitution.
Such a move would also put future Quebec laws in doubt, as one of the key roles of the lieutenant-governor is to give royal assent to new legislation.
Pressed about these hurdles, Plamondon has told reporters that he is ready for a legal battle with the federal government.
The success of the Parti Québécois on Monday is in part due to public fatigue with the previous Coalition Avenir Québec government.
Coalition Avenir Québec made safeguarding Quebec's identity and language central to its eight years in office, but its longtime leader, François Legault, eventually lost significant support among voters.
Efforts to revive the party by replacing Legault with a new leader, outgoing Premier Christine Fréchette, were unsuccessful.
Fréchette conceded her own re-election race in Trois-Rivières shortly before 22:00 local time. She said in a speech that she would work with St-Pierre Plamondon on the transition.
"Governing Quebec is the greatest honour I have ever had," she said. "I have Quebec tattooed on my heart."
The Quebec Liberal Party secured the second-most seats, while the Quebec Conservative Party gained seats.
Prime Minister Carney, who leads the federal Liberal party, remains popular in Quebec, though support for him had recently dipped, external as US President Donald Trump imposed new tariffs on Canada in August, following a breakdown in trade talks.
Quebec is among the hardest hit by the latest US tariffs, with experts at global forecasting firm Oxford Economics projecting a C$2bn blow for the province.
Carney congratulated Plamondon on his victory late on Monday and vowed to work together with the party.
"Building a stronger Québec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada," he said in a post on social media. "I look forward to working with you to support Québec's businesses and workers impacted by tariffs, create more good jobs, work to end homelessness, and get more homes built across Québec."

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is among the most widespread of human viruses. More than 90% of adults are estimated to have been infected during their lifetime. Most people acquire the infection during childhood without developing symptoms. In some, particularly those infected during adolescence or adulthood, it can cause infectious mononucleosis. The virus then remains in the body for life.
A new analysis by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the cancer agency of the World Health Organization (WHO), estimates that about 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024 were attributable to infections. The analysis incorporates recent evidence linking EBV with gastric cancer and places EBV among the infectious agents responsible for a substantial cancer burden worldwide.
What is Epstein-Barr virus?
EBV, also known as human herpesvirus 4, belongs to the herpesvirus family. It spreads mainly through saliva, including through kissing or sharing drinks, food, eating utensils and toothbrushes.
According to WHO, many people infected with EBV have no symptoms. When illness occurs, symptoms can include fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes and marked fatigue. Infectious mononucleosis generally improves within a few weeks, although fatigue can last longer.
After the initial infection, EBV remains in the body in a dormant state. In most healthy people, the immune system keeps the infection under control.
EBV is classified by IARC as a Group 1 carcinogen. It has established causal links with several cancers, including nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt lymphoma and Hodgkin lymphoma. The latest IARC analysis also incorporates evidence linking EBV with gastric cancer.
Who is at risk?
Most people infected with EBV do not develop cancer. The infection is therefore not, by itself, an indication that a person will develop cancer.
People with weakened immune systems are at greater risk of serious EBV-related disease. This includes some people who have undergone organ or stem-cell transplantation and those receiving treatments that suppress the immune system.
The cancers associated with EBV also vary geographically. Nasopharyngeal cancer, for instance, is particularly prevalent in parts of eastern and southeastern Asia. The development of EBV-associated cancer is thought to involve factors beyond the infection itself.
How is it diagnosed?
A person does not normally need to be tested simply because EBV is common.
When infectious mononucleosis is suspected, doctors may make a diagnosis based on the symptoms and clinical examination. Blood tests can provide supporting evidence. These include tests for heterophile antibodies and EBV-specific antibodies, which can help determine whether an infection is recent or occurred in the past.
In suspected EBV-related cancers or serious disease in people with compromised immunity, more specialised tests may be needed. These can include testing for EBV genetic material in blood or other samples and examination of tumour tissue for the presence of the virus.
A positive EBV antibody test does not mean that a person has cancer. Since infection is so common, evidence of past infection is expected in most adults.
What are the treatment options?
There is no treatment that removes latent EBV from the body and there is currently no vaccine against the virus.
According to WHO, treatment for uncomplicated infectious mononucleosis is mainly supportive. Rest, adequate fluids and medicines to control fever and pain may be advised. Antibiotics do not treat EBV because it is a virus.
People with mononucleosis may also be advised to avoid strenuous activity and contact sports for a period, particularly if the spleen is enlarged, because of the risk of splenic injury.
When EBV is associated with cancer, treatment depends on the type and stage of cancer and may include chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted treatment or a combination of these.
Can EBV be prevented?
There is currently no vaccine against EBV. Preventing transmission can also be difficult because infected people may spread the virus without knowing that they have it.
WHO advises avoiding the sharing of drinks, utensils, toothbrushes and other items that come into contact with saliva.
The development of an EBV vaccine is an important area of research. The latest IARC analysis adds to the evidence on the virus’s contribution to cancer and highlights the need for continued research into prevention.

What are emotions, really? And why do we have them?
Simply put, emotions are intangible responses to what we see happening around us. They arise spontaneously, without conscious thought.
Emotions allowed early humans to efficiently dodge dangers as they explored the world around them. While the world and our lives in it are very different today than the way they were for our ancestors, our emotions haven’t changed.
Despite being so fundamental to our survival as a species, however, scientists are still piecing together how emotions arise in our brains. In a study recently published in Science, in fact, scientists have just reported mapping the brain-wide activity patterns that trigger emotions.
The team found that once an emotion was set off, it outlasted the trigger that sparked it in the first place. If this sounds familiar, it’s because this is what you feel when you accidentally stub your toe, burn your hand, and even when you enjoy your favourite flavour of ice cream.
In all these examples, there is incoming sensory information that prompts an emotional response while the good or bad feeling lasts even after the body part has been reflexively pulled back or after the ice cream is finished.
Stories hidden in blinks
In the new study, scientists led by Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University examined how emotions emerged in response to unpleasant (but not painful) sensory stimuli.
The participants were subjected to an eye puff assay: a machine called a tonometer blew light puffs of air into their left eye in specific sequences. Each puff lasted about 60 ms, the gap between puffs was 3-8 s long, and the entire session lasted 5 minutes. The scientists varied the gap between puffs so that participants didn’t reflexively tense up for the next puff they knew was coming.
Also read: Making the brain transparent
During the entire duration, a high-speed camera recorded the way participants closed their eyes and their behavioral and subjective responses.
As expected, repeated puffs of air to the eye elicited reflexive blinking as participants instinctively pulled back from the tonometer. They also kept the eye closed for certain durations or squinted or blinked rapidly during the gaps. As part of their subjective reports, the participants said this experience was “unpleasant” and “annoying”.
The scientists recruited a separate group of participants who were, at the time of the study, inpatients at the Stanford university hospital and had electrodes planted in their brains to check for epileptic seizures. Members of this group who consented to participate underwent the same eyepuff assay. The scientists found that these participants’ behavioural responses were consistent with those of the previous group. They also blinked reflexively and kept their eyes closed for (relatively) long periods.
The real story emerged in the brain activity patterns.
Enter: ketamine
Each puff causes a signal to be broadcast throughout the brain, like a “breaking news” alert, followed by a slower, more persistent signal. In this second phase, based on data from the electrodes in the brains of participants, scientists found that specific circuits in the brain were activated, which were linked to the generation of an emotional response in the individual.
To confirm this possibility, the scientists administered ketamine to some of these participants and had them redo the eye puff assay. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved ketamine’s use as an anaesthetic and at lower doses as an antidepressant. Ketamine also induces short-term dissociation: i.e. for a brief period, it alters subjective perceptions. By injecting it, the team could separate a person’s reflexive response from the emotional one.
The scientists found that being subjected to air puffs in the eye when a person was on ketamine changed neither the initial reflexive behaviour nor the initial burst of neural activity in the brain. However, it caused the subsequent slower brain response to dissipate much faster, so much so that the volunteers no longer described the experience as annoying but as a “tickling of the eyeball”.
Consistent with this ‘weaker’ subjective experience from ketamine, the participants’ behaviour also changed. They didn’t blink or close their eyes between consecutive air puffs. Instead, they held their eyes open even though they knew more puffs were in the offing.
Ketamine is known to block a sensor in the brain whose job it is to integrate signals coming from different corners. This means in the participants injected with ketamine, the brain may not have integrated the various signals into a coherent emotional response.
Of mice and men
Even though vertebrates have brains of vastly different sizes and complexity, the overall ‘brain plan’ is highly conserved. (The brain plan is akin to the building plan of a house or apartment.) To zero in on those systems responsible for emotions and which have survived evolution, Deisseroth’s team repeated their experiments with lab mice. The mice went through the eyepuff assay, had their brain activity measured with surgically planted electrodes, and had ketamine injected.
The team noticed the same patterns in mice as they had in humans. Injecting ketamine substantially changed the spiking activity in some neurons but not others. Only those neurons (or brain regions) coordinating the second phase — the slower response after the burst — were affected by ketamine. The initial burst didn’t change in any way, just as with the human participants.
The scientists could also study the neural activity following a puff in greater detail in the mouse model. They found that the fast/reflexive responses corresponded with a sharp rise in activity in some of the midbrain regions. This included the thalamus, where incoming sensory signals converge before being relayed onward, and the periaqueductal grey, which is involved in emotional behaviours.
They also found that the second phase of neural activity corresponded with activity in the brain’s emotional centres (described by the umbrella term ‘limbic regions’) and the frontal cortex. Again, as expected.
Then they dissected the brain activity patterns by stages, focusing on how quickly activity in brain regions shot up after the eyepuff and how long it took to fade away. They noticed that activity patterns in most of the pertinent regions increased at an explosive pace right after the eyepuff — but the rate of decrease was more interesting.
A pattern appears
The patterns in different regions slowed at different rates, fading first in the midbrain regions and last in the frontal cortex. The thalamus was active both in the first and the second phase. Considering the thalamus is the brain’s coordinating centre for all sensory signals, it makes sense that it would be active in the first phase. Incoming sensory signals go on to higher brain regions from the cortex. So it also served the role of handing off the baton, so to speak, and thus essayed a sort of bridging role across timescales.
The new study is the first to report this sort of differential pattern across different parts of the brain vis-à-vis emotions. At this point, it is not possible to say with any certainty what the implications are for the brain’s cortical and mid-brain areas.
With computational models of neuron firing activity in the mouse and the mouse’s behaviour following the eye puff assay, the team found that the timescale of neural activity was an important factor that shaped the emotional response.
Indeed, if the sensory signals dissipate before the brain has a chance to integrate the information, the person won’t be able to learn the lesson: “protect yourself from that obnoxious thing”. On the other hand, if brain activity is more strongly coupled to the fast and slow phases that Deisseroth & co. observed, such activity also lasts longer than normal, causing its own problems. Over-stabilised brain states have been correlated with depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder, all of which cause people to experience uninterrupted or mistimed thoughts and emotions.
Beyond the binary of health and disease, the fast and slow phases of brain activity highlighted in the study could reveal the fundamentals of information processing in the brain. People differ in how their brains process information about their environment — in turn a product of their genetic makeup and their upbringing in their formative years.
First steps
Why do we have emotions? For now it may be more gainful to flip the question: what would happen if we didn’t have them?
In the absence of an instinctive reaction that our emotions afford us, the brain’s response would be based entirely on risk-benefit analyses, which can be very time consuming. Over time we’d struggle to make decisions both big and small. What should I wear today? What should I make for dinner tonight? What should I study? Whom should I marry? Purely rational thought would turn such questions into never-ending decision-making exercises with no final answer.
The new study has revealed what happens in the brain in the first seconds when an emotion takes root. One hopes future studies will reveal the specific information encoded by this primal circuitry, how they encode different emotions, and how they evolve with time.
Dr. Reeteka Sud is a neuroscientist by training and senior scientist at the Center for Brain and Mind, Department of Psychiatry, NIMHANS, Bengaluru.

You can get Microsoft 365 for free through an eligible Education plan, free web and mobile versions of Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and other apps, or a 30-day Microsoft 365 trial with full desktop apps and 1 TB of OneDrive storage.
Microsoft 365 (formerly Office 365) is a subscription service that gives you access to various Microsoft products. This includes productivity apps like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and OneNote; 1 TB of OneDrive cloud storage; and tools like Teams, Forms, and Loop.
As of writing, a paid subscription starts at $1.99 a month or $19.99 a year for Microsoft 365 Basic and goes up to $19.99 a month or $199.99 a year for Microsoft 365 Premium. Whether getting a subscription is justified depends on which of the included apps and services you use and how much.
If you’re not too sure about that and don’t want to buy a subscription right away, you can get Microsoft 365 for free using the following methods. Which method to pick depends on whether you’re a student/educator and your requirements.
Get the Microsoft 365 Education Plan
Microsoft 365 Education is a special plan for students and educators that provides free access to Microsoft 365 apps and services. You need a valid school, college, or university email address to be eligible. You’d have one if you’re a student or educator at an accredited institution with a Microsoft Education license.
To check if you qualify, visit the Microsoft 365 Education portal, type your institution-issued email address, and hit Next. If you’re eligible, you’ll be prompted to log in with the same email address. Or you may receive a verification link in your inbox. Subsequently, you’ll be able to use the Microsoft 365 apps within the browser or download them to your devices, based on the plan your institute offers.
Microsoft 365 Education is currently available in three plans: A1, A3, and A5. Your institute will most likely offer an A1 plan since it’s free, though some may offer an A3. The major difference between them is that A1 is web-only, whereas A3 supports downloads, so you can use the apps even when you’re offline.
If you don’t have an institute-provided email address or it isn’t eligible for the Education plan, you can get Microsoft 365 for free using the next method.

Use Microsoft 365 for the Web or Native Mobile Apps
Unless you have advanced needs — creating and running macros (VBA) in Excel, multi-device installation rights, or fully offline mode — you don’t really need a Microsoft 365 subscription. The online version of Microsoft 365, which offers access to basic versions of its apps, along with 5GB of free cloud storage, should serve your needs just as well.
All you need for this method is a Microsoft account and a web browser. In your preferred browser, visit the Microsoft 365 online portal and sign in with your Microsoft account. Create a new Microsoft account if you don’t have one.
Next, click the app launcher icon in your dashboard and select the app you want to use. This will open the app in a new browser tab, where you can create a new document or work on an existing one in your OneDrive storage. Any changes you make to the document are automatically saved to the cloud. Keep in mind, though, that the app’s functionality halts completely when you lose the internet connection.
Just like Microsoft 365 for the web, Microsoft also offers mobile apps for many of its productivity apps. So, if you just want to work on a Word, Excel, or PowerPoint document, you can download their mobile apps on your phone or tablet and use them. Just note that these apps offer limited functionality, similar to the web version. However, unlike their web versions, mobile apps support some offline functionality, allowing you to view a cached version of the document or edit local documents, even without an active internet connection.
Get the Microsoft 365 Free Trial
Microsoft offers a 30-day free trial to Microsoft 365. This trial gives you full, unrestricted access to the service, including complete offline capabilities and the ability to download desktop apps to your PC or Mac. You also get 1 TB of OneDrive cloud storage.
A free trial is great for someone who wants full-blown access to Microsoft’s productivity suite for a brief period. It also makes sense for those who want the Microsoft 365 service without committing to an upfront payment.
To subscribe to a 30-day Microsoft 365 free trial, you need a Microsoft account and a valid payment method. Open a browser and go to the official Microsoft 365 free trial page. Click the Start Free Trial button, and log in with your Microsoft account when prompted. If you haven’t taken a free trial with this account previously, you’ll be asked to add a valid payment method. Complete the checkout process. You now have complete access to Microsoft 365.
Set a reminder to cancel the subscription before the 30 days are up. If you forget, Microsoft will convert the trial to a monthly or annual subscription and charge you for the same on your added payment method.
Identify Your Use Case to Find the Right Method
You can use any of the above methods to get Microsoft 365 for free. However, not all of them offer the same level of access. As such, it’s important to identify your use case before choosing a method.
For example, if you want a full-blown Excel experience for a few weeks, the free 30-day trial makes more sense. Meanwhile, you might want to subscribe to the Microsoft 365 Education plan if you’re a student or educator and want desktop access to productivity apps for a longer period. Or use their mobile apps on your phone or tablet if you only need to view or maintain a few Excel sheets.

'I've lost my peace' - Cape Verde hero Vozinha on newfound fame
- Published
Cape Verde's heroic World Cup goalkeeper Vozinha says he craves the "peace and tranquillity" of the life he led before he shot to fame.
The 40-year-old shot to global prominence in June when he almost single-handedly kept Spain at bay as Cape Verde drew 0-0 with the European champions on their World Cup debut.
Vozinha's follower count on social media sky-rocketed over the course of the game, from about 50,000 to more than one million.
But his fame shot up even further when Argentina needed extra time to beat Cape Verde in the round of 32.
Vozinha says his life was easier before his World Cup heroics.
"I've lost my peace and tranquillity," he told the Observer., external
"I no longer have any privacy, or at least much less than I used to.
"Now I go out, I go to a restaurant, and there's always someone who wants to take a photo with me or asks me for an autograph. Or, worse, someone is filming me.
"That's what has changed most in my life, and I don't think there's anything I can do about it."
Vozinha's mother became part of the fairytale too. After he revealed that she had could not afford a visa to watch his World Cup debut, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries announced that the visa fee had been waived.
Now Vozinha has revealed that his mother is visited on a daily basis by fans wanting to talk or to take photographs with him.
"A lot of people want to be famous and have a public profile, but they only see the positive side of that reality," said Vozinha.
"To be honest, if I were offered the life I have today or the life I had before, I'd choose the one I had before."
His World Cup performances for Cape Verde, a West African island nation with a population of 525,000, earned Vozinha a nomination for men's goalkeeper of the year at the Ballon d'Or awards.
"It's nice to feel like a kind of ambassador, but I want to make it clear that what we achieved was a collective effort," Vozinha said.
"We made history and the best news would be if we could harness that momentum to develop our country and improve the living conditions of our people."

Argentina’s foreign minister has told an audience that included the British ambassador that his government would stop the Falkland Islands from exploiting its offshore oilfields as part of a strategy to take sovereignty.
During a speech at a thinktank event in the Argentinian capital, Pablo Quirno condemned the British government for failing to open negotiations over the islands and facilitating a significant offshore oil project in its waters.
Among those in the audience was David Cairns, the UK’s ambassador to Argentina. Cairns, who was photographed listening to Quirno, left the event shortly after the foreign minister returned to his seat.
Quirno told the audience at the event organised by the Argentine Council for International Relations that his country’s president, Javier Milei, had a strategy for the “peaceful” assertion of Argentinian sovereignty.
He said: “The British government not only refuses to enter into negotiations to resolve the sovereignty dispute, but is also taking unilateral measures regarding the exploitation of natural resources in the maritime areas that are part of the controversy.
“Preventing the exploitation of our resources from consolidating the British occupation is part of a strategy to recover, through peaceful means, the full exercise of our sovereignty.”
Last month, Milei told the UN general assembly in New York that the international organisation had failed his country as he condemned the Sea Lion project, an oil development in the North Falkland Basin, as an “unlawful act”.
Argentina has accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands.
On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline stop the oil project or face arbitration and a binding decision under annex VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (UNCLOS) at the international tribunal for the law of the sea.
The UN does not officially recognise British or Argentinian sovereignty and maintains that the archipelago’s status remains a disputed matter that must be resolved through bilateral negotiations. It has repeatedly invited both governments to find a peaceful solution to the dispute that erupted into conflict in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces.
The 74-day war ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentinian military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders.
The UK government has said that the islands, known as Las Malvinas in Argentina and which are home to approximately 3,600 people, will remain a British overseas territory for as long as it is the wish of those who live there. In a referendum in 2013, on a turnout of 92%, 99.8% voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.
In a statement issued last week, the Argentinian government rejected “the manipulation of the principle of self-determination of peoples that the United Kingdom seeks to impose upon it”.
In his speech on Monday night, Quirno also warned third parties that they should not assist Falkland islanders in the exploitation of the natural resources.
A new shipping link is due to be opened between Chile and the Falkland Islands by the end of the year.
Quirno said: “Whoever contributes, directly or indirectly, to the illegitimate exploration or exploitation of resources that belong to all Argentinians will hardly be able to aspire to share in the benefits of our country’s growth.”

'We could all hear her breathing': Witnessing the failed execution of Christa Pike
Last week, I was one of the seven media witnesses who observed Tennessee fail to execute convicted murderer Christa Pike, the first woman to face the death penalty in the state in almost 200 years.
From our previous reporting, each of us had an inkling that the lethal injection process might not go according to plan.
Pike's attorneys had asked the Tennessee Supreme Court to allow her to be hanged instead, citing concerns that a platelet disorder and small veins would make the actual injection not only painful but ineffective.
And Tennessee had already botched an execution attempt in May, when healthcare workers failed to establish complete IV access into Tony Carruthers, who was sentenced to death after being convicted for his involvement in the kidnapping and murders of three people in 1994.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said after the failed execution of Carruthers, who has maintained he is innocent, the state wouldn't try again to kill him for at least a year. After Pike left the execution chamber in an ambulance on Sept. 30, Lee announced he would suspend lethal injections for the rest of the year.
The morning of Pike's scheduled execution, I and the other media witnesses arrived at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville by 8:30 a.m. and waited to be ushered into the prison with nothing but our driver's licenses in hand. The plan was to wait inside until Pike began her journey to the death chamber at 10 a.m.
But we didn't make it that far.
Before the Department of Correction's staffers began moving us away from the outdoor media tent and our belongings, the reporters' phones all went off. A federal circuit court had stayed the execution. This was my fifth stint as a media witness to an execution, and I'd never seen a stay issued. We didn't know what that would mean.
It turned out to mean waiting for nine hours at the prison, barred from leaving the grounds. We spent most of it in the boardroom where parole hearings take place.
Hours of waiting. Then, 'It's a go.'
Throughout the wait, the victim's family often came up in conversation. In 1995, Pike, then 18 years old, killed Colleen Slemmer, who was 19. Slemmer's family lives in Florida and traveled to Tennessee for the execution with money raised through crowdfunding. It's unclear where they waited while the last-minute legal wrangling played out.
Sometime around 6 p.m., the prison system's communications director, Dorinda Carter, told us: "It's a go."
Tennessee had asked the U.S. Supreme Court to lift the stay, and it did. Carter read the ruling aloud to us.
For unknown reasons, it took another hour or so for the security team to usher us into the witness bay, an all-white cinderblock room with black pleather chairs in two rows and a big window overlooking the death chamber. A loudspeaker pipes sound into the room from the chamber when the microphones are on.
A black curtain hangs in front of the window inside the death chamber. Department of Correction workers open it once IV lines are inserted into the condemned prisoner.
The curtain is there to obscure the workers who place the IVs, in order to shield their identities as required by state law. That process is enshrined in the "Lethal Injection Execution Protocol," which is the guidebook the Department of Correction writes for itself. There is no other regulation over executions in the state.
My employer, the Nashville public radio station WPLN, is a party in a lawsuit challenging the state's concealment of the IV insertion. When executions are botched, it's often due to something going wrong while IVs are placed — or with the subsequent step if IVs fail, placing a central line in a deeper vein through the chest, neck, or groin.
A lower court ruled in favor of WPLN and other media plaintiffs in January, but the state appealed the order, and it has been halted while higher courts consider the case.
The death chamber
The American Medical Association officially bars doctors from participating in executions, and many other health professionals also consider assisting an execution to be unethical.
Outside of prison staffers and the execution team, only the prisoner's spiritual adviser and attorney are allowed in the room with the prisoner while the IVs are inserted. So generally, attorneys' descriptions are the only account of the procedure.
Under normal circumstances, witnesses sit in the bay for 10 or 15 minutes with the curtain closed. That's how long it tends to take for the IV team to place a line and start running saline, to prepare for the 5 grams of the sedative pentobarbital that will be pumped in to kill the prisoner.
Once the lines are set, the execution team enters an adjacent, concealed room. The IV lines run through the wall into that hidden chamber, from which the drugs are administered.
But at Pike's execution, we sat in the bay for 45 minutes with the curtain closed and the microphone turned off.
Until Carruthers' failed execution, the Department of Correction kept the lights off in the witness bay during the wait. Witnesses at his execution said they sat in a dark room for an hour and a half as the execution team tried and failed to place an IV line. This time, the prison kept the lights on.
The clock we use to give a minute-by-minute account is in the death chamber, so we can't see it with the curtain closed. John North, a reporter with the television station WBIR in Knoxville, was the only witness wearing a watch. The rest of us asked him over and over what time it was.
After half an hour, it was clear the IV team must have been struggling.
We wondered whether Pike's execution would unfold similarly to Carruthers'. That time, the governor called and ordered the execution halted before the curtain ever opened.
But at 7:27 p.m., we heard the curtain being drawn away.
We saw Pike in profile, lying on the gurney, facing the window for the other bay, where the victim's family and prosecutors sit.
We saw Pike's spiritual adviser, Mikey Noechel, who wore a wine-red sash over his suit. Together, they sang and talked about Buddhist teachings.
Under the state's protocol, the spiritual adviser is allowed in the death chamber as the pentobarbital flow begins, though the attorneys are not.
There is no signal when the lethal drugs start flowing, but it's assumed to begin after the prisoner delivers her final words. It's typical for the spiritual adviser to offer prayers and other support, and for there to be a back-and-forth between the two.
Pike spoke.
"I just want to say that I'm going to leave this world the way I've spent most of my life, and that is with love," she said.
She said that she had love for those who hate her, and that she was at peace with her death.
Moments later, Pike told Noechel her arm was burning. She said it was in one specific spot and asked corrections staff in the room whether that was normal.
Pentobarbital is alkaline, so it burns like drain cleaner if it touches skin. If the IV is administered correctly, that is unlikely to happen.
But Pike and Noechel chatted for what seemed a shocking amount of time. Prisoners tend to show signs of being sedated a few minutes in. Pike didn't.
Something is wrong
The Tennessee Department of Correction uses an odd practice to announce the drugs have been fully administered. There's a small, hinged door built into the wall between the concealed drug management room and the death chamber, with a platform beneath it.
Once the drugs have completely flowed through the IV, the staff open the door and place a rock on the platform. That initiates a five-minute waiting period, after which the curtain closes again to obscure a doctor, who enters the death chamber, checks the prisoner's pulse, and certifies the death.
In each of the executions I've witnessed, the prisoners look unconscious long before the rock comes out, and in the minutes following they're presumed dead.
The rock came out at 7:41 p.m. At 7:44 p.m., Pike was still speaking quietly to Noechel.
My jaw dropped. It was clear to me then that something was very wrong.
Once the five minutes are up and the curtain closes to conceal the doctor, who confirms the time of death, the spiritual adviser moves into the witness bay and stays there until everyone leaves the facility.
But after Noechel entered the witness bay, staff came in and ordered him back into the death chamber. There was only one reason to do so: They were trying again.
The curtain re-opened.
The state's protocol dictates that, as a backup plan, prison staff can run a second round of pentobarbital. According to a statement from the Death Penalty Information Center, which tracks execution attempts and their outcomes, Pike is "the first person to survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs."
Eventually, Pike stopped talking. She started snoring.
She continued to snore after the rock was put out the second time and the curtain closed again. We continued to hear her snore over the loudspeaker.
The state's protocol does not contemplate a second round of drugs failing to kill the prisoner, so there are essentially no rules for the situation the Department of Correction found itself in with Pike.
It's unclear what was happening behind the curtain. Her lawyers later said they weren't allowed in the death chamber.
The curtain closed at 8:16 p.m., and we listened to Pike's snoring for nearly 40 minutes.
Tensions rose between the media witnesses and Carter, the Department of Correction's communications director. I asked her: "Do they do a third round? Are you going to resuscitate her?" Carter didn't have an answer. Another witness, Steven Hale of the Nashville Banner, asked why the curtain was closed. The doctor wasn't certifying Pike's death. We could all hear her breathing.
At 8:53 p.m., the prison warden, Kenneth Nelsen, came over the loudspeaker and said, "Media witnesses, please exit the area."
'Intubated, on a ventilator'
We went out to the news conference, which the Department of Correction usually requires media witnesses to participate in. While one of us was speaking, several emergency vehicles arrived. We saw the caravan leave with its sirens on. That was our only insight into whether Pike was alive.
Pike's attorneys later confirmed she was hospitalized. As of Oct. 1 she remained in critical condition at an undisclosed Nashville hospital, according to her attorneys.
Her lawyers, in an emergency filing with the Davidson County Chancery Court on Oct. 2, alleged that the execution team apparently didn't "realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown" and that pentobarbital had "in whole or in part" entered her body instead of her veins.
Pike arrived at the hospital with both of her arms "swollen, burned, and blistered," they wrote. "She is intubated, on a ventilator, and remains unconscious."
Pike's future, as well as that of lethal injection in Tennessee, is uncertain.
Lee, the Republican governor who has paused executions for the rest of the year, leaves office in January. The front-runner in the Nov. 3 election to replace him, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, has been a vocal supporter of the death penalty. After Pike's failed execution, the Republican candidate posted her solution to X.
"Bring back the electric chair and deliver justice for these victims swiftly," she wrote. "As your governor, I will do just that."
The electric chair was last used in the United States in Nashville when Tennessee executed Nicholas Sutton in 2020. He was one of five prisoners who chose the electric chair over lethal injection in the state from 2018 to 2020.
This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with Nashville Public Radio and KFF Health News.

The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.
The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.
Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial.
The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17.
On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings. In the end, he was released in the late afternoon wearing a red T-shirt to be greeted by friends, family and flowers.
Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered.
His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”.
The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.”
Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture.
The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly.
The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member.
His Dumbarton-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “There have been so many setbacks and disappointments in the last nine years that I didn’t dare to believe it until I saw Jagtar walking out of the prison gates with my own eyes. The last two weeks have been torture – knowing that Jagtar had been granted bail, but the authorities were refusing to let him out. I’ll sleep well tonight, knowing that he’s not behind bars.
“Tomorrow morning, the fight continues, because he’s still on trial and facing the death penalty for something he didn’t do, trapped in a sham legal process designed to punish him for standing up for human rights”.
Reprieve’s deputy executive director, Dan Dolan, said: “While tonight is the first night in almost nine years that Jagtar Singh Johal is not caged in a prison cell, he still has the threat of a death sentence hanging over him. It should also be noted that, despite bail being ordered, the prison refused to release Jagtar until his family brought a habeas corpus petition and a judge warned the jail they’d be found in contempt of court”.
The UK Foreign Office is understood to have been supporting recent calls for his release on bail after last week’s court order, as have two campaign groups in the UK Redress and Reprieve.

Prem* is a young mathematics graduate from a village in Jharkhand. He was known as an energetic and supportive young person. Children from the village often approached him when they had difficulties with mathematics. When he was selected for a job with the Indian Railways, it was expected to be a moment of happiness. But the thought of leaving his parents, friends, village and the life he shared with them was difficult for him.
In the weeks following the job offer, Prem began having sleepless nights, worrying about how he would cope with a new life and new responsibilities. Gradually, he stopped talking to his family. He began to feel helpless and worthless, lost interest in everyday life and reached a point where he attempted to end his life.
What helped was having people around him who could understand not only what he was going through, but also the world he was coming from. A neighbourhood facilitator working in a community-based organisation was able to sit with him, listen to his worries and share his dukh-sukh. They understood why leaving his parents, friends and village felt so difficult and gave him space to talk about the fears he was carrying.
The support was not about asking him simply to adjust or move on. It helped him think about what mattered to him, what he wanted for his future and how he could remain connected to the people and place that were important to him while taking up the new opportunity. He eventually wrote to the department asking for another opportunity to join. He was invited again and went to work, while continuing to receive support.
Prem’s experience highlights that what looks like a positive life event from the outside can sometimes become overwhelming. A suicidal act can often happen suddenly, during a moment of intense crisis. But the distress behind that moment may have been building for much longer.
For Adivasi communities, distress can be shaped by circumstances that may never appear in a psychiatric consultation.
When distress is accumulates
A recent study in Jharkhand examined psychosocial distress and help-seeking among Adivasi Ho adolescents. It found that distress was often linked to family conflict, pressure around education and work, financial hardship, violence, separation and loss, and difficulties in relationships. Some adolescents withdrew and stopped sharing what they were going through; for some, this included thoughts of self-harm or suicide
These accounts do not offer a single explanation for suicide among Adivasi communities. They show how distress can accumulate across everyday life — in family conflict, having to leave school temporarily or reduce schooling to help with agricultural or household work, substance use, untreated illness, violence, displacement, loss of livelihood, lack of mentorship, identity-related stigma and self-doubt, or the erosion of community and belonging.
When communities are disrupted
Belonging is an important part of suicide prevention. Stereotypes, exclusion, humiliation, discrimination and pressure to hide one’s identity can affect how people see themselves and how connected they feel to society. Historically, Adivasi communities stayed together. But modern development, alongside education and employment opportunities, have in some cases, uprooted Adivasi people from their culture. Mainstream schools do not teach Adivasi children in their own mother tongue; their history is woefully under-represented in the school curricula.
Sandip Sing, a radiologist from the Munda community practising in rural West Bengal and a first-generation learner, says, “There is a rapid transition in accessing and navigating educational and professional spaces, often amid gaps in resources, networks, and institutional familiarity. Bridging these gaps can be challenging, particularly with unfamiliar systems.”
Many educated Adivasis may also have had fewer opportunities to engage with their community’s history, culture, language and traditions, and may have complex or evolving relationships with their Adivasi identities. This matters for mental health because belonging itself is a source of strength. When people are uprooted without finding a new sense of belonging, distress can deepen.
This does not mean that development itself causes mental illness or suicide. The concern is what happens when rapid social change is accompanied by displacement, loss of livelihood, cultural disconnection and weakening social support.
Collective strength, mentoring
The strength of Adivasi life also lies in ways of expressing emotions and sharing knowledge. Songs and dances are not simply cultural performances; they are ways of expressing emotions, maintaining connection and making sense of life. The Adivasi dance itself is a powerful metaphor. People dance in a chain, holding one another. The village headman, Majhi Baba, dances alongside everyone else. An 80-year-old and an eight-year-old can dance together. There is no hierarchy; the strength is in the circle. For suicide prevention, this collective strength matters.
Young people also need places where they can be themselves without constantly having to explain or defend who they are. Lilibiti Saren, a medical officer from the Santhal community working in tribal areas of Bankura, West Bengal, notes that she often finds young people in these communities lacking direction. “There is a need for proper mentorship,” she says.
Locally organised Adivasi youth spaces can help. Such spaces can offer young people opportunities to speak in their own language, share experiences, learn from peers and elders and explore what Adivasiyat — identity, history, relationships and belonging — means to them.
Access and pathways in care
Clinical care remains essential. A person experiencing suicidal thoughts may need assessment for depression, substance use, trauma, psychosis, previous attempts, suicidal intent, access to means and immediate safety. Treatment and follow-up can save lives.
But access to mental health care is itself a major challenge in many Adivasi areas. Services are often limited, distant and unevenly available.
And even when services are available, the pathways into care may not be optimal. An Adivasi person with lived experience of mental healthcare says: “I felt like the psychiatrists and the psychologists were not speaking to me. They were judging me for what I had done and they were trying to find symptoms instead of trying to understand me, my pain and my situation.”
This raises an important question: are our mental health systems listening as carefully as they are diagnosing?
When formal services are scarce, difficult to reach, or experienced as unfamiliar or judgmental, people may seek support elsewhere—including from family, community networks, faith healers or indigenous systems. These spaces may offer something that the formal system does not: familiar language, relationships, cultural understanding and a sense of belonging.
Adivasi mental health therefore cannot be treated simply as another category within rural health. Representation matters — from schools to healthcare institutions and policy making.
Models that could work
In Adivasi communities of Jharkhand, particularly among the Ho, Munda and Santhal communities, Madait refers to a tradition of voluntary help and collective support for someone who needs it or is in distress. It reflects an understanding that some difficulties are too large for one household to manage alone.
This may be a useful way to think about mental healthcare too. The question is not simply how services can be delivered to Adivasi communities, but how communities themselves can shape, participate in and lead the care they need.
The same principle can be seen in Dukhu-Sukhu Baithaki — community support group meetings where people experiencing mental health difficulties and their families can meet, share experiences and support one another. This model works in West Singhbhum, Jharkhand, where people living with mental health conditions come together each month. These spaces do not replace professional care. They bring community knowledge, relationships and mutual support into the process of recovery.
Education without a knowledge of one’s roots; development that comes with displacement and mental healthcare that does not see or hear the people who need help is no longer enough. For suicide prevention, we must ask not only, “What is wrong with the individual?”, but also, “ Where is the community support? Where is the system that understands them?”
Perhaps suicide prevention in Adivasi communities must begin there — not by doing things for Adivasis, but by doing them with Adivasis.

CEC Gyanesh Kumar row LIVE: Congress MPs Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi, KC Venugopal, Pawan Khera and others were briefly detained at Delhi's Akashvani Bhavan as they staged a sit-in seeking CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation on Tuesday. However, they were released after being taken to a police station at the city's Kingsway Camp....Read More
The march by Opposition parties is against the alleged irregularities in poll body decisions, particularly the Special Intensive Revision exercise or the clean-up drive of electoral rolls. The last march from Parliament building to ECI was on August 11, 2025, against SIR.
The protests began on October 2, with Opposition parties and civil society groups giving a call to gather over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
ECI says no meeting sought till 4pm
As Opposition MPs staged a sit-in at Akashvani Bhavan, the ECI issued a statement, clarifying that no party sought a meeting before 4pm. It also objected to the requested venue for the meeting - Parliament House Annexe, saying all meetings should ideally take place at the Election Commission.
"While the Election Commission was considering the aforementioned meeting request from the Hon'ble MPs after 4pm, the Delhi Police DCP informed the Commission that the requested meeting was to involve a group of 240 MPs and was proposed to be held at the Parliament House Annexe. The Election Commission deemed this request unusual and unacceptable, as protocol dictates that such meetings take place within the premises of the Election Commission of India," a part of the statement read.
What we know about the INDIA bloc protest
-Several opposition leaders, including Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra were briefly detained during their march to the Election Commission office. Later in the day, they were again detained at Akashvani Bhavan, where they were staging a sit-in.
-The BJP has dismissed the march, with Union minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan calling the protest another attempt to “relaunch Rahul Gandhi.” The former MP CM also accused the Congress of wanting to “spread anarchy” across the country.
What Delhi Police said
The Delhi Police also issued a statement on Tuesday night, saying they got to know through social media that Opposition MPs were planning a march from the Parliament at 10:30am today, and that no application for permission was made.
“The protesters broke through the first barricade put up by the police and advanced to the second barricade near NITI Aayog. Police repeatedly made announcements informing the protesters of the restrictions in force under Section 163 BNSS and appealed to them to disperse peacefully. Despite this, the protesters did not comply with police instructions and stayed on,” the statement read.
