- A rumor spread online in fall 2026 that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration had formally denied protections for monarch butterflies under the Endangered Species Act until 2030.
- This rumor originates from a September 2026 settlement between conservation groups and the Fish and Wildlife Service over the federal agency's failure to finalize a policy proposal that would have protected monarch butterflies under the act.
- In December 2024, under then-President Joe Biden's administration, Fish and Wildlife formally proposed such a rule. Under the act, proposed rules must be finalized within one year. Thus, Trump's administration was supposed to make a decision by December 2025. It did not, which resulted in the lawsuit.
- The settlement specifies that the Trump administration must finalize the proposal to protect monarch butterflies by June 2030, meaning the administration could technically issue a decision anytime before 2030. However, the Center for Biological Diversity, one of the plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said Fish and Wildlife "asserted that they do not have the resources to issue the final listing before the agreed upon date because of budget and workload."
- Given that we cannot predict the future, we have rated this claim as a mixture of truth and undetermined information.
In fall 2026, a rumor spread online that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration had formally denied protections for monarch butterflies under the Endangered Species Act until 2030.
In other words, posts claimed that the government had refused to designate monarch butterflies as an at-risk species deserving of specific protections under federal law — and that the government would not consider the issue again until 2030.
The claim circulated on Facebook (screenshot) and X.
The claim is largely true, although it omits a few details. On Sept. 30, 2026, the Fish and Wildlife Service reached a settlement with conservation groups, including the Center for Biological Diversity, over a delay on the federal agency's decision as to whether monarch butterflies should be protected under the Endangered Species Act.
The settlement requires Fish and Wildlife to issue a final decision by June 6, 2030. Technically, that means Fish and Wildlife could issue a decision anytime before that deadline. However, Center for Biological Diversity spokesperson Tierra Curry said Fish and Wildlife "asserted that they do not have the resources to issue the final listing before the agreed upon date because of budget and workload."
We reached out to Fish and Wildlife to confirm whether this is true and await a response.
It's also worth noting that Trump is due to leave office in January 2029, so it's possible that a future administration may prioritize making a decision on monarch butterfly protections before 2030.
Because we can't predict what the future holds, we have rated this claim as a mixture of truth and undetermined information.
Monarch butterfly conservation
Fish and Wildlife estimates that, by 2080, the probability of extinction for eastern monarchs ranges from 56% to 74% and for western monarchs the probability for extinction is greater than 95%. Threats to the species include loss of habitat, exposure to insecticides and the effects of climate change, the agency said on its monarch butterfly conservation page.
The Endangered Species Act allows the federal government to designate imperiled species as threatened or endangered. Each designation comes with its own protections and resources for conservation.
For more on the Trump administration's changes to the Endangered Species Act, see our explainer.
Background on conservation efforts
Conservation groups have fought to bring monarch butterflies and their habitats under Endangered Species Act protections since at least 2014, when three groups and a monarch scientist named Lincoln Brower filed a formal petition with the Fish and Wildlife Service. 
In December 2020, under the first Trump administration, Fish and Wildlife announced that protection for monarch butterflies was "warranted but precluded by work on higher-priority listing actions."
Fish and Wildlife's news release on the decision said 161 species were listed as higher priorities for formal protections under the Endangered Species Act ahead of the monarch butterfly.
"With this decision, the monarch becomes a candidate for listing under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), and its status will be reviewed each year until it is no longer a candidate," then news release said.
Under former President Joe Biden's administration in December 2024, Fish and Wildlife proposed an official rule that would have designated the monarch butterfly as a protected species under the Endangered Species Act:
We, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service), propose to list the monarch butterfly (Danaus plexippus), the iconic orange and black butterfly, as a threatened species and designate critical habitat under the Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended (Act). We propose to list the monarch butterfly as a threatened species with protective regulations.
Under the Endangered Species Act, Fish and Wildlife is supposed to publish its final decision within one year of publication of a proposed rule, which would put the rule into effect and thus, in this case, officially list the monarch butterfly as an endangered species worthy of protection.
Trump took office January 2025. His administration did not meet that one-year deadline, which prompted the lawsuit from the Center for Biological Diversity and the Center for Food Safety.
What the settlement says
The settlement does not prevent the Trump administration from making a decision before 2030. Here's what it says on Page 2:
On or before June 6, 2030, the Service shall submit to the Office of the Federal Register for publication a final listing determination for the Monarch Butterfly, pursuant to the ESA, 16 U.S.C. § 1533(b)(6).
Curry, the Center for Biological Diversity spokesperson, said in an email that, in effect, the settlement meant the denial of current protections would end in 2030 with a final listing. The Center for Biological Diversity's news release about the settlement called it a "bittersweet move for conservation groups."
In other words, it's not as if the Trump administration withdrew the proposal to protect monarch butterflies — rather, the settlement means Fish and Wildlife has until 2030 to make a decision on whether to finalize protections for the species.
There are also additional ways, per the settlement, that the deadline to make a decision could be extended. For example, if the government were to shut down due to a lapse in funding before 2030, the deadline would be extended for the number of days the shutdown occurred (see Page 2).

End of an era as Messi prepares to hang up Argentina boots
Lionel Messi is set to play his final match for Argentina against Benin on Tuesday (Oct 6), ending his 21-year international career.
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina: Lionel Messi will pull on Argentina's sky blue-and-white jersey for the last time on Tuesday (Oct 6) and enjoy an emotional farewell in front of his adoring fans in a stadium with a name to match his legacy: Monumental.
Some 85,000 spectators will be present to watch the 39-year-old idol perform his wizardry in a friendly against Benin that brings down the curtain on his 21-year international career.
Millions more will follow the action in South America's largest stadium, Buenos Aires' Estadio Monumental, on TV.
The most-capped player in Argentine history is hanging up his boots two-and-a-half months after losing the World Cup final to Spain.
"I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance," Messi wrote when announcing his international retirement in August.
On Monday, he took part in his last training session with the team at the complex that bears his name in the Buenos Aires suburb of Ezeiza.
Fans gathered to watch there too.
"I believe Messi gave everything, absolutely everything, so it doesn't bother me at all that he's leaving. He has more than earned it, let him enjoy himself, let him rest," Cecilia Adriano, 52, told AFP.
Before the match, the University of Buenos Aires will award Messi an honorary doctorate.
Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028, although following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated.
FILLING THE VOID
No effort has been spared for the sendoff of a player considered one of the game's greatest ever.
Several of the teammates with whom he won the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, and who will form the backbone of the post-Messi team, will play in the game, including defender Cristian Romero, midfielders Alexis Mac Allister and Enzo Fernandez and forwards Julian Alvarez and Lautaro Martinez.
After the game the captain's armband will pass to Romero.
Coach Lionel Scaloni has vowed to try to fill the "void" left by his talismanic captain and the signs from the next generation, some of whom weren't even alive when Messi debuted with the team in 2005, are promising.
In their first games since the World Cup final last week, minus Messi, Argentina thrashed Bolivia 4-0 in a friendly in Cordoba on Wednesday before running rings around Burkina Faso on Saturday at Monumental stadium.
Franco Mastantuono and Gianluca Prestianni, two of Argentina's brightest new hopes, both scored their first international goals in the 7-0 romp against Burkina Faso.
The results have begun the process of lifting the gloom of the defeat in the World Cup final when Argentina and a visibly tired Messi were outplayed by Spain in New Jersey.
Several of Messi's teammates resorted to thuggish tactics which were punished with bans and fines.
RIGHTFUL HEIR TO MARADONA
Messi is not only Argentina's most capped player but also its leading scorer with 125 goals in 207 games, as well as a record 68 assists.
"La Pulga" (The Flea) won the eternal gratitude of Argentines - and sealed his place as the rightful heir to Diego Maradona - in 2022 when he ended their 36-year World Cup drought in Qatar.
During his time with the Albiceleste, Argentina were also crowned 2005 world youth champions, 2008 Olympic champions and they won the Copa America in 2021 and 2024. They also won the 2022 Finalissima, a match between the champions of South America and Europe.
But there were tears along the way too, notably after Argentina's defeat by Germany in the 2014 World Cup final in Brazil, their 1-0 loss to Spain in this year's final and their shock defeat on penalties to Chile in the 2016 Copa America final.
One detail remains unclear, however: who will inherit Messi's coveted number 10 jersey?
"Until Leo's game, we won't give the number 10 to anyone," said Scaloni. "After that, we'll see."
    Source: AFP/fs

Each fall, travelers fill trains to catch some of the US' best foliage views.
But whether you're taking a scenic ride or a regular rail journey, inconsiderate passengers can quickly spoil the experience.
To make sure you're not one of them, Business Insider previously spoke with British etiquette coach William Hanson to learn some of travelers' biggest etiquette faux pas on trains.
From placing bags on empty seats to blasting music, here are seven things travelers should avoid doing.
Don't talk on speakerphone.
Hanson said he understands not wanting to keep your phone pressed to your face for long periods of time, but that it doesn't excuse talking on speakerphone.
"It explains it, but it doesn't excuse it," he told Business Insider in a 2024 interview through his partnership with Trainline, a European train booking app.
Hanson added, "If we were all doing that, let's think we were all on our phones, on the speakerphone making calls in a carriage, it would be a cacophony. You wouldn't be able to hear anything."
Although Trainline said its research found that only one in 10 people reported feeling bothered by others on their phones, it's more polite to just wait until you disembark to catch up on your calls.
Please, don't place your feet on the seats.
And no, it's not better if you take your shoes off.
"Your socks — or heaven forbid you're not even wearing socks — your feet still have germs," Hanson told Business Insider. "And it is not your own personal seat. It is a seat that is shared by numerous passengers on numerous rail journeys."
Bags don't belong on seats, either.
Trainline reported that over a third of people think spreading out over multiple seats is the most annoying behavior from fellow passengers.
Hanson recommends keeping your purses or small bags in your lap, on the floor in front of your seat, or in designated luggage areas.
"The only time you can have a bag on the seat next to you is if you're basically on an absolutely deserted carriage and there are clearly numerous seats for people to go and sit on," he said.
If you do come across another passenger's bag occupying your designated seat, Hanson recommends keeping the conversation reasonable.
"If you are reasonable, they will be able to move their bag," he said.
Try to avoid eating overly fragrant foods, like oranges.
Eating on a train is perfectly fine, especially during long journeys, but Hanson recommends being mindful about your snack choices, especially ones that are particularly fragrant or might be loud.
One option he discourages people from bringing is oranges.
"However delicious an orange is and full of vitamin D, it can actually be quite objectionable as a smell if you are not the one eating it," he said.
Instead, try to stick to options like sandwiches, sweets, nuts, dried fruit, or other fresh fruit, such as grapes.
Be careful not to play your music too loudly in your headphones.
"Some headphones leak when they're too loud, making your favorite playlist a public nuisance," Hanson wrote for Trainline's "Mind the Manners" guide to train etiquette. "I hate to say it but not everyone will be a fan of your audio tastes."
Trainline reported that loud music is the most uncomfortable train issue for travelers.
If you're traveling with a pet, don't expect everyone to be comfortable.
Most trains in the US permit pets on board, although it depends on factors including the company, the size of your pet, and the length of your journey.
If you are able to take your pet on board, the important thing to remember is that others may not love your furry friend as much as you do. Trainline research found that 25% of people are uncomfortable sitting next to a dog.
Hanson recommends that those traveling with their dogs be proactive in opening the lines of communication and asking fellow passengers about their comfort levels.
"If you do see some hesitancy and there are many other empty seats to go and sit in that are not reserved, you're going to move," he said.
He added that context in these situations is important, too. If the dog owner is the second to arrive, it would be their responsibility to move; but if the dog owner is already seated and someone new comes along, it would be their choice to sit or go elsewhere.
The simplest advice? "Talk and be reasonable," Hanson said. "We as humans, we mood match. So, if you go in all guns blazing, then you're going to get a similar reaction back."
And finally, try to let people off the train before you board.
This tip doesn't need much explanation, and yet it remains a common nuisance for travelers, commuters, and locals alike.
"There will be more room for people when you get on if the people have come off the train first," Hanson said.
He added, "If you're standing by the doors anyway, you can get on, and there's often a beep or a signal before those doors close. So everyone just needs to just remember: It will be fine."
Editor's note: This story was originally published in September 2024, and most recently updated in October 2026.

New Delhi, Oct 06: Indian women's cricket team's long-serving captain Harmanpreet Kaur on Tuesday stepped down from her position in all three formats, saying that she has done her duty as leader and is now "ready to play for the love of the game again."
Harmanpreet's announcement came after a BCCI review meeting in Guwahati to evaluate the team's trajectory in the past few months. Chaired by BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia, the meeting was attended by Harmanpreet, vice-captain Smriti Mandhana and head coach Amol Muzumdar.
The 37-year-old led the Indian T20 side for a decade, taking over the position in 2016, and was elevated to ODI captaincy in 2022 before becoming the all-format leader in 2023.
"Today, I step down as captain of the Indian Women's Cricket Team across all formats," she posted on her instagram account.
"This is not an easy decision. It carries years of memories, emotions, sacrifices, and moments that will stay with me for the rest of my life," Harmanpreet said in a lengthy statement.
"Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again. Captaincy ends. The journey continues," she added.
Harmanpreet, under whom India won its maiden ODI World Cup in November last year and recently picked up a second successive Asian Games gold in the T20 format, said she is leaving the captaincy "with a heart full of emotions, but also with peace."
"Because I genuinely believe my team is in a good place," she said.

The institute, located in the city of Incheon, is fully subsidised by the state and still houses some 33 residents, although it has been asked to close down in light of this case.
According to Seo, the abuse began shortly after she began living there, with Kim visiting her at night or in the early hours of the morning to rape her.
Speaking through her lawyer Ko Eun-young, Seo said there was no adult at the facility she could speak to about the abuse, adding that she felt that other staff members would not help her. The care home has not responded to this allegation.
That was her life for almost 10 years, until the case came to light in February 2025, when Seo suffered a head injury.
She said it happened one of the times Kim tried to sexually assault her. She had blocked him with her hands, causing him to throw a glass at her.
Her lawyer told the court that the care home took Seo to hospital and informed her mother about the incident only after the wound on her head had been stitched up.
According to Seo's lawyer, Seo's mother had asked to see CCTV footage to establish how her daughter had been injured, but the facility refused, saying they were not authorised to release it.
As a result, her mother brought her home and decided to withdraw her from the facility. It was only after Seo was told that she would not have to return to the home that she disclosed the sexual abuse to her mum, who then reported it to the police.
"I thought it was safe to speak because I was told I didn't have to go back to Saekdongwon," Seo told the BBC via her lawyer.
When asked how she had managed on her own for so many years, she said: "I just endured it."
A police investigation into Seo's account was then widened to other residents.
They found at least two other alleged victims, including Lee Mi-Na, who said that she was also raped by Kim.
Earlier this month, a judge found all three victims' testimony credible.
He was sentenced to 15 years in jail for raping Lee and Seo, five years less than the original sentence prosecutors were asking for. He has denied all allegations and has since appealed the ruling.
For the third victim, Kim was found guilty of a lesser charge of sexual violence, with the judge saying the charge of rape against her was dropped as they could not find conclusive evidence that "force or threats [were used] that rendered the victim unable to resist".
A joint response committee made up of disability rights and other civic groups have criticsed this ruling, saying a victim's ability to resist an assault should not impact the verdict they receive.
The committee has also criticised the investigation process, saying there was a failure to identify more potential victims.
In November last year, following the initial allegations of abuse, local authorities from Ganghwa County had commissioned a team from Woosuk University to conduct an in-depth assessment of Saekdongwon's residents.
The report, which was submitted to the court as evidence, found indications that many more residents - at least 10 - could have been sexually assaulted by Kim.
But during the trial, the court did not address this finding.
According to local media reports, police had struggled to establish details of alleged abuse when interviewing residents, because most of them had severe disabilities and faced difficulties communicating. Some residents reportedly gave answers unrelated to the questions or did not respond at all.
Kim has not responded to allegations that he may have abused more residents.
Jeon Ji-su, the professor who led the Woosuk research team, told the BBC that investigators had accepted "only the accounts of people who could describe the abuse in complete sentences".
But activists said that this reliance on verbal testimony meant the police failed to recognise residents with greater communication difficulties as victims.
"If victims express their experiences differently from the way we expect, shouldn't the state make a greater effort to hear their voices?" said Baek In-seong, of Hansahoe, a counselling centre for survivors of sexual violence with disabilities.
Police have said that "while there may have been shortcomings in individual instances, these should not be taken as representative of the investigation as a whole".
Rights groups have also criticised others who have sought leniency for Kim.
Ahead of the verdict, a total of 13 petitions seeking leniency were said to have been submitted to the court. One of them, from a social welfare organisation, asked the court to take into account the defendant's "contribution to the welfare sector".
Welfare advocacy group Gyeol condemned the petitioning organisations, saying: "Past service in the welfare sector does not exempt anyone from accountability."
The judge's ruling on Kim's conviction stated that his offence was "particularly reprehensible" because "despite his professional duty to protect and support [the victims'] rights and interests and prevent abuse, he exploited the imbalance of power" with his victims to "gratify his own sexual desires".
Public scrutiny and protests
The case has shocked many in South Korea and raised questions about why the abuse was not prevented in the first place. More shocking is that it happened despite a move in 2011 to strengthen laws to protect people with disabilities from sexual assault.
That was the year a fictional film called Dogani, based on a true story of sexual abuse at a school for deaf children, premiered. Amid intense public scrutiny and protests, the school in question was shut and tougher laws were passed as a result.
These included more specific categories of sexual offences against disabled people, harsher penalties for offences committed by facility directors and employees, and the removal of the statute of limitations for some rape offences involving disabled victims.
But in the case of Saekdongwon, the abuse persisted despite regular regular inspections by Ganghwa County, the local authority responsible for overseeing the facility.
A county official told the BBC that such inspections focused largely on paperwork, and that residents were interviewed only when specific issues arose.
The official said there had also been an external monitoring team but it had received no reports from staff, and expressed regret that the authorities had not examined the situation more closely.
Jo Ha, a representative from the national council of a counselling centre who has supported some Saekdongwon victims, said some families she had spoken to had suspected there was abuse but felt unable to raise their concerns.
Leaving a facility would mean the family has to take on all care responsibilities, as finding alternative placements is difficult.
One survey conducted through a national association of parents of people living in residential facilities for those with disabilities found that around six in 10 people who secured a place in a residential facility had waited at least three years, highlighting the difficulty of accessing appropriate care.
Professor Kim Yoon-tae, the head of Woosuk University's Institute of Cognitive Science, points out that such facilities exercise great control over residents' actions, from what they eat to where they sleep in addition to their access to healthcare and even whether or not to grant they could go outside.
And while Saekdongwon is "a landmark case" because of the scale and duration of the abuse, it is also not an isolated incident, added Jo.
In 2023, an appeals court upheld an eight-year prison sentence for a worker who raped or sexually assaulted two women with intellectual disabilities at a facility in Yeongcheon the previous year.
In a separate case in Anseong, a care home worker was recently sentenced to six years in prison for repeatedly raping a female resident with a disability in 2022.
"The violence women with disabilities experience is not an individual problem," Jo said. "It is structural violence, shaped by overlapping layers of gender, disability, institutionalisation, poverty and social isolation."
- South Korea jails care home head for sexually assaulting disabled residents 
  - Published2 September
'We want to live in peace'
Since the case came to light, South Korea's prime minister has ordered the formation of a cross-government response team, calling the incident "a grave matter that calls into question the very reason for the state's existence".
In April, the government said it had inspected 1,507 residential facilities for disabled people nationwide and identified 33 suspected cases of abuse. So far investigations have been opened into eight of them.
The government also said it would strengthen targeted inspections based on risk factors, as well as joint inspections involving local authorities, police and disability rights advocacy agencies.
Ganghwa County has ordered Saekdongwon to close and the local government has revoked the licence of the foundation that operated it.
However, the closure has been deferred until the remaining residents have been relocated and arrangements for independent living have been completed.
The local government has said it will draw up individual independent-living support plans for all 33 Saekdongwon residents. That process is still under way.
Saekdongwon has filed an administrative lawsuit challenging the revocation of its licence. It has yet to comment on Kim's conviction.
Asked what had changed most since leaving Saekdongwon, Seo said: "I just feel at peace. I'm happy every day."
She also said the best thing was being able to eat and sleep when she wanted.
What she wanted most now was "to cut ties with the director completely and never have anything to do with him again".
But, Seo added, people with disabilities still need somewhere they could feel safe.
"I hope there can be a facility without sexual violence, where disabled people like us can live in peace."

Congo’s Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday (October 1, 2026). They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases, making up for nearly half of the confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.
A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation’s 17th Ebola outbreak.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country’s government for reasons ranging from how it’s managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

Expect lots of tears when Lionel Messi plays a farewell game for Argentina on Tuesday.

The 39-year-old soccer icon announced his international retirement in the weeks following the World Cup final loss to Spain, saying, “The time has come.”
The Argentine Football Association tempted him to make one last appearance for “the farewell he deserves” and thousands of fans are expected to show their appreciation at Estadio Monumental.

“Special moments I know I will miss,” he wrote.
Messi just fell short of winning back-to-back World Cups when defending champion Argentina was beaten by Spain 1-0 in the final in July in New Jersey.
He achieved his ultimate ambition of leading his country to victory four years earlier in Qatar — emulating fellow Argentine great Diego Maradona.
Messi has played 207 games for Argentina and finishes as its all-time leading scorer with 125 goals, 21 of them in World Cups. He appeared in a record-tying six World Cups along with his great rival Cristiano Ronaldo.
He briefly retired from Argentina duty in 2016 then enjoyed his most successful period with the national team, winning Copa Américas in 2021 and ’24, as well as the '22 World Cup.
He's continuing at club level with Inter Miami, and recently won the Campeones Cup, his fourth trophy with the team.

Trump backs down on taxpayer funded ads and now says his PAC will pay for them
More than $10 million in federal funds from a $20 million Homeland Security contract has already been spent on the national broadcast campaign since September

President Donald Trump announced Monday that his political action committee will take over funding for a series of national television advertisements that had previously been paid for with government funds.
The decision follows growing criticism over the spots, which were financed through a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract awarded on September 20 to LMD Agency. According to public records first reported by The Washington Sun, the White House Office of Management and Budget had transferred $20 million to Customs and Border Protection for “OBBB Commemorative Events” a day prior.
Data from ad-tracking firm AdImpact shows that more than $10 million in taxpayer money has been spent on the campaign since September, with ads appearing across both cable and broadcast networks bearing the disclaimer “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
The broadcasts spanned multiple themes, CBS News reported, including one spot featuring Trump stating, “We will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America,” over flashing photos of the president, and another recounting the U.S. capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
Another made the declaration: “God made Trump.”
Critics from both parties raised concerns that the campaign violated federal restrictions against using public funds for propaganda or promotional purposes. Observers noted that at least one spot included video clips previously featured in a 2024 Trump campaign advertisement.
In a letter last month, a group of Senate Democrats condemned the effort, writing: “This is the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars.”
Republicans also voiced concern.
“I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves,” GOP Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana said on “Face the Nation.”
The White House repeatedly defended the campaign, insisting the spots were public service announcements rather than political promotion.
A White House official stated last month that the spots “are clearly not political,” adding: “The President is not on the ballot and the ads don’t have a call to action.”
A White House spokesperson further described the anti-communism ad as “educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country.”
Trump acknowledged the criticism surrounding the campaign Monday on Truth Social.
“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” he wrote. “This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”
The move marks a shift from comments made just days prior.
Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, Trump defended the original funding source, arguing that the broadcasts were intended to promote the nation rather than a candidate, as reported by The New York Times. During those remarks, however, he noted that he would gladly cover the expenses if the arrangement was deemed improper.
Over the weekend, The New York Times reported that Trump had directly instructed his budget director to allocate public funds for the television spots.
The super PAC financing the transition possesses substantial capital to absorb the costs. According to AdImpact, MAGA Inc. entered September with roughly $415 million on hand and, together with two affiliated super PACs, has reserved approximately $194 million for upcoming advertising.
However, diverting super PAC funds to cover the ads uses money Republican strategists had hoped to direct toward key midterm contests, such as the Texas Senate race.
Trump previously said that he is “going to spend whatever amount of money necessary to try and help us.”

Christine Fréchette stepping down as CAQ leader after searing election defeat
The Coalition Avenir Québec failed to win a single seat on Monday night
Christine Fréchette, Quebec’s outgoing premier, announced Tuesday that she will be stepping down as leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec party.
She walked out in the foyer of the National Assembly and was greeted by applause, but got straight to the point in her address to Quebecers.
“Last night, you made your position clear,” she said in French. “You chose to entrust the government to another team. I accept that choice, and as leader, I take responsibility for it.”
“So today, I have submitted my resignation as leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec.”
The announcement comes one day after the party’s crushing defeat in the provincial election that saw it go from a massive majority just four years ago to being wiped off the electoral map.
The party failed to win a single seat on Monday.
Just a few days ago, Fréchette said she would stay on as leader even if she didn’t win in her hometown riding of Trois-Rivières.
She took over as premier following François Legault’s resignation earlier this year, after winning the party's leadership race against Bernard Drainville.
Legault, who co-founded the party in 2011, stayed quiet throughout the campaign.
But he took to social media Tuesday shortly after Fréchette's resignation to thank her for her political commitment.
“Christine was a capable minister. Her speech last night was dignified and exemplary,” he wrote in French.
“She showed great courage during this election campaign.”
He also added she wasn’t responsible for the "wear and tear of power" that "affects all governments.”
He signed off by wishing her the best of luck in her future endeavours.

Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians.

Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides.

Francis Halzen, a physicist at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.” Halzen spearheaded the development and construction of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, enabling physicists to capture high-energy neutrinos created in the distant universe.
“It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn’t expect it,” Halzen said during a news conference in Stockholm, Sweden, speaking by phone from Italy. While the Nobel was awarded to Halzen, he emphasized that his work was the result of a “large collaboration” with other researchers.
“This reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in this project when really no respectable conservative physicist would have joined me. But many talented people did, and that’s why I’m here,” he said.
“I am shocked and absolutely delighted that Francis was awarded the Nobel this year,” said particle physicist Danielle Norcini of Johns Hopkins University in a statement. “He is the scientific visionary and driving force behind [IceCube]. It has transformed our understanding of the universe by detecting the first high-energy neutrinos from beyond our galaxy, opening an entirely new field of neutrino astronomy. The experiment is the extraordinary achievement of hundreds of scientists, engineers, and collaborators, but Francis was the person who dreamed big enough to imagine an experiment of this scale and then relentlessly pushed to make it a reality.”
Ghost particles
As previously reported, neutrinos travel near the speed of light. John Updike’s 1960 poem, “Cosmic Gall,” pays tribute to the two most defining features of neutrinos: They have no charge, and for decades, physicists believed they had no mass (they actually have a teeny bit of mass). Neutrinos are the most abundant subatomic particle in the universe, but they very rarely interact with any type of matter. We are constantly being bombarded every second by millions of these tiny particles, yet they pass right through us without our even noticing. That’s why Isaac Asimov dubbed them “ghost particles.”
That low rate of interaction makes neutrinos extremely difficult to detect, but because they are so light, they can escape unimpeded (and thus largely unchanged) by collisions with other particles of matter. This means they can provide valuable clues to astronomers about distant systems, further augmented by what can be learned with telescopes across the electromagnetic spectrum, as well as gravitational waves. Together, these different sources of information have been dubbed “multimessenger” astronomy.
Neutrinos were first proposed by Wolfgang Pauli in a 1930 letter to colleagues. He was trying to explain some baffling experimental results on radioactive beta decay in atomic nuclei, where energy appeared to be missing—something he deemed (correctly) to be impossible. He thought a new kind of subatomic particle with no charge and no mass may have carried away the missing energy; it was Enrico Fermi who later dubbed it a neutrino.
Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines first observed these ghostly particles in 1956, thanks to fusion reactions in nuclear power plants that proliferated after World War II. Ten years later, physicists detected the first solar neutrinos. This snagged Ray Davis Jr. and Masatoshi Koshiba a Nobel Prize in 2002, shared with Riccardo Giacconi (who was honored “for pioneering contributions to astrophysics, which have led to the discovery of cosmic X-ray sources”).

Inside Chief Justice John Roberts are two wolves.
The Supreme Court is looking for a way to kill climate lawsuits
They just can’t come up with a legal argument that would allow them to do so.
The first wolf is a staunch conservative who spent much of his career litigating on behalf of corporate interests. This wolf looks at a series of climate change lawsuits that could potentially cost the oil industry billions of dollars or more, and recoils in horror.
The second wolf is a judge tasked with following the law wherever it leads. And that wolf seemed baffled by the oil industry’s arguments in Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, a Supreme Court case where two oil companies are asking the justices to shut down dozens of climate change lawsuits.
The Court’s decision in Suncor is likely to shape the future of climate litigation in the United States. If the oil industry prevails, that will probably shut down climate change-related suits in state courts — and it may shut them down entirely because it is unclear whether federal law allows these suits to proceed in federal court. If the oil industry loses, by contrast, it could face dozens of suits in state courts across the country seeking billions of dollars or more.
And the outcome in Suncor is likely to turn on which wolf shows up to the justices’ conference on how to decide the case. Roberts, who asked the most ambiguous questions at Monday’s oral argument in Suncor, clearly wants these lawsuits to disappear. But he also appeared doubtful that the oil companies’ weak legal arguments will allow him to make that disappearing act happen.
Notably, Justice Samuel Alito, who owns stock in oil and gas companies, is recused from hearing the case. So, in the likely event that all three of the Court’s Democrats hold together against the oil companies, Roberts would split the Court 4-4 if he decides to join them. That would leave the Court unable to render a decision, and a lower court opinion, which rejected the oil companies’ bid for lawsuit immunity, would remain in effect.
That said, at least two other justices asked questions suggesting that their votes may potentially be in play. Justice Clarence Thomas, who otherwise appeared sympathetic to the oil companies, repeatedly asked whether his Court has jurisdiction to hear Suncor in the first place. Meanwhile, while most of Democratic Justice Elena Kagan’s questions seemed to favor allowing the climate change lawsuits to proceed, she did ask some questions at the end that indicated that she may be looking for a narrow reason to hand the oil companies a win.
The bottom line is that it is difficult to predict how this case will turn out, as more than one justice asked questions that suggest that their vote is, at least, in play. But the outcome is likely to hinge upon the tension within Roberts — who both signaled that he wants the oil companies to win, but who also expressed deep skepticism of their primary legal argument.
So what is Suncor actually about?
Suncor is one of many lawsuits brought by state or local governments (in this case, the plaintiff is Boulder, Colorado) who’ve sued oil companies claiming that those companies should be liable for the harms caused by climate change within those governments’ jurisdictions. In this particular case, the defendants are Exxon Mobil and Suncor, a company that operates two oil refineries in Colorado.
The lawyer for these two companies, Kannon Shanmugam, told the justices that there are about 60 similar cases brought by municipal governments throughout the country. And, in one of his more pro-oil moments during Monday’s oral argument, Roberts predicted that if Boulder wins in the Supreme Court, there will be numerous other copycat lawsuits filed by other municipalities.
The question in Suncor is whether state courts, including Colorado’s own courts, are forbidden from hearing these sorts of climate change lawsuits.
As Roberts pointed out in one of his less pro-oil moments during Monday’s argument, “there are a lot of familiar situations where conduct outside of a state has broad effects on other states…and yet we allow the state courts in a particular state to bring litigation.” He pointed to “mass tort” suits and “complaints about operations of the internet” as two examples where state courts hear lawsuits involving harms that arise across state borders.
The oil companies’ primary argument is that suits involving air and water pollution are special. But their evidence supporting this argument is confusing and difficult to parse.
Briefly, the oil companies point to several cases, many of which were decided more than a century ago. These cases held that, before Congress enacted the Clean Air Act in 1963, states could sometimes sue other states for cross-border pollution, even though no federal law forbade such pollution. The Supreme Court created “federal common law” permitting these suits, and the oil companies claim that this federal common law preempted any state lawsuits that covered a similar subject matter.
This federal common law, they now argue, has itself been displaced by the Clear Air Act and its partner statute, the Clean Water Act, but the principle that state suits involving air and water pollution are preempted is somehow still in effect. Although there is no provision in the text of the Constitution that supports this argument by the oil companies, those companies claim that their argument is implicit in the “structure of the Constitution.”
The oil companies’ primary legal argument is difficult to understand
If you are confused by all the arcane history and logical leaps contained in the oil companies’ argument, don’t worry. So were most of the justices. Only Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who repeatedly claimed that his Court’s precedents bar Boulder’s lawsuit, seemed to buy what the oil companies are saying without reservation. Most of the other justices expressed at least some reservations.
Justice Amy Coney Barrett, for example, argued that even under the older “federal common law” regime, states still retained some authority over environmental lawsuits, although she noted that the Court’s previous decisions do not really define the scope of that authority. Kagan pointed out that the many suits challenging climate change are similar to past litigation against tobacco and opioid manufacturers. But those suits were heard by state courts.
Many of the justices appear bothered that these lawsuits exist, but the most skeptical justices couldn’t agree on a legal theory they could use to shut them down.
It seems unlikely, in other words, that there are five votes for the oil companies’ convoluted claim that the “structure of the Constitution” somehow bars state courts from hearing climate change lawsuits. But several of the justices did appear troubled by what could happen if dozens of state courts reach conflicting judgments on who is responsible for climate change and who should receive compensation because of it. And some of these justices floated alternative theories for how to hand the oil companies a win.
At one point, for example, Barrett floated the possibility that, if the plaintiffs lose in Suncor, they might file a new suit under the now-defunct federal common law that existed prior to the Clean Air Act. Kagan, meanwhile, suggested that perhaps the Clean Air Act could be read to preempt these suits like Suncor. According to Kagan, that law “sets up an extremely complicated scheme about how regulations of emissions should operate,” and allowing states to hear lawsuits like Suncor would “get in the way of how Congress decided to regulate greenhouse gases.”
And Roberts didn’t so much offer a legal argument in favor of the oil companies’ position as express incredulity of what would happen if those companies lose. “Presumably if you prevail,” before the Supreme Court, Roberts told Kevin Russell, the lawyer for Boulder, “the next day a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit, copy your pleadings, and then there will be at least 50…how do you think that will work out on the ground?”
All of which is a long way of saying that the outcome in Suncor is uncertain. The oil companies led with a weak legal argument, and only Kavanaugh seemed to fully embrace that argument. Many of the justices appear bothered that these lawsuits exist, but the most skeptical justices couldn’t agree on a legal theory they could use to shut them down.
For what it is worth, the oil companies actually do make a strong policy argument that it is a bad idea to allow state courts to do so. As they argue, climate change is a global problem caused by many polluters (and companies like Exxon that supply the oil burned by polluters) throughout the world. It could be impossible to determine which specific companies caused the specific problems caused by climate change in Boulder, Colorado. And even if this obstacle can be overcome, there are many thorny questions about which state’s law should apply when pollution from one state crosses over into another, not to mention the difficult diplomatic issues that could arise if a state court orders a foreign company to pay a large sum of money.
But under our Constitution, the proper solution if the oil companies want federal law to preempt state court suits like Suncor is that they can lobby Congress, and Congress could then draft a statute that balances these companies’ interest in avoiding many conflicting legal decisions with the interests of plaintiffs like Boulder who say they are experiencing real harms from climate change. Congress has the power, for example, to combine all of these state lawsuits into one grand federal lawsuit, where a single proceeding could determine how to portion out the costs of climate change to various energy companies, and how to divide whatever these companies are ordered to pay among the various plaintiffs.
But that solution would undoubtedly require compromises that companies like Exxon will not like. So, instead, they’ve asked the Supreme Court to give them the legal regime that they want, despite the fact that they could not articulate a persuasive legal argument for that outcome. It remains to be seen whether this Court will give the oil companies a win anyway.

NFL suspends two officials for player incidents
- Published
The NFL has suspended two officials for instances of unprofessional conduct towards a player.
Line judge Jeff Seeman has been suspended for two games and referee Adrian Hill for one fixture following the incidents on Sunday.
Seeman was caught on camera seeming to curse at Arizona Cardinals tight end Trey McBride, whose side lost 36-24 away to the New York Giants.
McBride felt he had been interfered with by Giants cornerback Dru Phillips from a pass from Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett that fell incomplete.
Having been hit, McBride complained to Seeman, who appeared to yell a profanity at McBride.
"It's a tough one for me. You hate to see it for obvious reasons. I don't need to go further than that, but I do want to give the man a little bit of grace too," Cardinals coach Mike LaFleur said Monday.
"I know Jeff. He's a good man. It's unfortunate it happened. It can't happen obviously and I'll leave it at that."
Hill's incident involved linebacker Eric Wilson, who featured for Minnesota Vikings as they defeated the visiting Miami Dolphins 15-10.
Wilson was pushed into Hill by Dolphins running back Ollie Gordon II midway through the first quarter after a play was whistled dead because of a Minnesota penalty.

TASHKENT, Uzbekistan – When Nika Kurdiani began to plot London-listed Georgian lender TBC Bank’s expansion into Uzbekistan around 2018, he had to bring plastic bags full of banknotes to pay restaurant bills.
The country of nearly 40 million people — Central Asia’s most populous — had long been largely closed to foreign investment by strict capital controls. Its currency, the sum, was artificially overvalued and credit cards rarely accepted, forcing consumers to carry wads of cash for everyday purchases.
But after almost a decade of economic reform that has helped growth outpace that of most ex-Soviet peers, digital payments are ubiquitous. TBC Uzbekistan, one of few foreign lenders operating in a still mostly state-owned banking sector, is considering an initial public offering (IPO) separate from its Georgian parent.

Inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed Tennessee execution attempt
Her attorneys said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital ‘who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her’

Christa Pike, an inmate who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her, is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said Tuesday evening.
“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed,” attorneys for Pike said in a statement.
“Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” the statement continued.
Her attorneys said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital “who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her.”
The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance carried her away from a Nashville prison last Wednesday.
Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as Tennessee officials attempted to put her to death nearly a week ago last Wednesday.
On Sunday, her lawyer, assistant federal defender Stephen Ferrell, told CNN, “She's still in the hospital on a ventilator, critically ill. We don't really know the prognosis yet and may not know for several days.”
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
Asked by CNN if she’d regained consciousness after the execution attempt, Ferrell replied: “Not that I’m aware of”, adding that doctors were still trying to clear the high barbiturate dosage out of her system.
Pike's execution was delayed for more than eight hours Wednesday as the U.S. Supreme Court considered, and ultimately overturned, a federal appeals court ruling to halt her lethal injection so judges could thoroughly review whether the jury that sentenced her to death should have considered sexual abuse she said she suffered as a child.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.

Our skin, hair and nails require adequate protein, energy, vitamins and minerals for growth, repair and normal functioning. When deficiencies are significant or prolonged, some may become visible. But many of these signs also overlap with hormonal disorders, chronic illnesses, dermatological conditions, stress, poor sleep and other factors. So when and how do you know if there is a nutritional deficit?
What the signs can indicate
Iron deficiency, particularly when it progresses to anaemia, can cause pallor of the skin and mucous membranes, and may be associated with diffuse hair shedding. Spoon-shaped nails can also occur with iron deficiency. Vitamin B12 deficiency may cause hyperpigmentation, particularly over the knuckles, as well as changes in the tongue and oral mucosa.
Zinc deficiency can affect skin integrity and hair growth, while inadequate protein intake can affect hair structure and growth and, in severe cases, cause marked changes in the skin and hair. Vitamin C deficiency can result in bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Dry or scaly skin may be associated with inadequate vitamin A, essential fatty acids or zinc.
Cracks at the corners of the mouth can occur with iron, vitamin B12, zinc or riboflavin deficiency. A smooth, red and sore tongue, or glossitis, can be associated with deficiencies of vitamin B12, iron, folate or niacin.
Ramya Subburaj, senior clinical dietitian and head of the department of dietetics, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, said these signs should be viewed as clues rather than proof of a deficiency. “There is considerable overlap between nutritional and non-nutritional causes,” she said, noting that a person with hair loss should not assume that poor nutrition is necessarily responsible.
What ‘ferritin face’ really means
Terms such as ‘iron-deficiency face’ and ‘ferritin face’ circulating on social media are not recognised medical diagnoses. Iron deficiency can cause anaemia and pallor, but there is no specific facial appearance through which low ferritin can be diagnosed.
Ferritin is a protein that stores iron and its level is used to assess the body’s iron stores. Low ferritin can occur before iron-deficiency anaemia develops. However, it does not produce a distinct facial appearance.
Pushpa Gnanaraj, senior consultant, dermatology, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, said pallor associated with anaemia may be visible in the skin, lips, gums or inner eyelids because of reduced haemoglobin. But dullness, dark circles or changes in facial appearance are not specific to low iron stores.
Vinitha Krishnan, chief clinical dietitian, nutrition and dietetics, SIMS Hospital, Chennai, said any changes associated with depleted iron stores are generally subtle and non-specific. Similar features can occur with inadequate sleep, stress, dehydration, allergies, ageing, thyroid disorders or other nutritional deficiencies.
A proper history and clinical examination are therefore important. Depending on the symptoms, investigations may include a complete blood count, ferritin and iron studies, vitamin B12 and vitamin D. Thyroid testing, zinc assessment or other investigations may be considered when clinically indicated. Dermatological conditions such as eczema, psoriasis, fungal infections, autoimmune disorders and pigmentary diseases may also need to be ruled out.
Correcting deficiencies
When a confirmed nutritional deficiency is responsible for a symptom, correcting it can lead to improvement. The timeline, however, depends on the nutrient involved and the severity and duration of the deficiency.
Pallor and some symptoms associated with iron deficiency may begin to improve within weeks of appropriate treatment, while mouth ulcers and glossitis can also improve after the underlying deficiency is corrected. Hair shedding and thinning generally take longer to recover because hair grows slowly; improvement may take several months. Nail changes can similarly take months to grow out.
Reshma Aleem, senior clinical dietician, Rela Hospital, Chennai, said the extent and speed of recovery depend on whether the deficiency is mild, moderate or severe and on how effectively it is corrected.
Fixing the basics
A varied diet remains the foundation. Adequate protein, pulses, whole grains, vegetables, fruits, nuts and seeds, along with eggs, dairy, fish, lean meat or fortified foods according to dietary preference, can provide a range of nutrients.
Experts caution against taking supplements based only on a social-media checklist. Excessive intake of some vitamins and minerals can itself cause adverse effects and may interfere with the absorption or metabolism of other nutrients. More importantly, treating an assumed deficiency can delay the diagnosis of the actual cause.
The appropriate approach is to investigate persistent changes, confirm a deficiency where indicated and then correct it with dietary measures or supplementation under clinical guidance.

Former German spy chief arrested for espionage and treason
- Published
Former German spy chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says.
Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant.
Prosecutors allege that he used classified intelligence to "draft an analysis" for one foreign intelligence service and maintained contact with another foreign spying service. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved.
Police also arrested former BND employee Manfred D, accusing him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents for money.
Manfred D, who was Hanning's bureau chief and remained in the BND until this year, is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
Local media reported Hanning was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near Münster while Manfred D was arrested in Bavaria. Hanning is due in court on Wednesday and Manfred D will appear on Tuesday.
Prosecutors say Manfred D, who also served as the chief of staff for Hanning's successors between 2012 and 2026, used his role to gain access to highly confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning "in exchange for remuneration".
"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement says.
"On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence ... to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service," prosecutors said, noting it was not clear if "the material reached the intended recipient".
Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D, for several years".
Local media say Hanning's alleged possession of intelligence documents came to light during a separate case relating to German steakhouse heiress Christina Block.
Hamburg public prosecutor's office accused Block of orchestrating the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Investigators allege Hanning was involved in an earlier attempted kidnapping of the children, which he denies.
State criminal police officers reportedly discovered an electronic data storage device containing sensitive information including recent BND documents.
It is not the first time the BND has faced similar controversy. A high-ranking German intelligence officer was charged with treason in 2023 for allegedly passing state secrets to Russia.
Prosecutors alleged Carsten L shared intelligence about the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and received roughly €400,000 ($450,000; £340,000). His trial is ongoing.

Hospitals across the State are up against a shortage of drugs for treating non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Several commonly prescribed drugs for blood sugar management (metformin), hypertension (telmasartan), and cholesterol (atorvastatin) are in short supply in hospitals, even as authorities have assured that these will be back in stock within a week.
“It is not as though we are running short on all drugs. But NCD drugs are medicines that people should be taking without fail as a matter of routine and disruptions in its supply can be worrying. We anticipated this shortage last month and moved fast to make local purchases so our patients do not miss the medication,” the medical officer at a family health centre in Thiruvananthapuram said.
“NCD drugs are in short supply but we have not had any issues because our hospital management committee has adequate funds, apart from the substantial resources that our block panchayat sets aside every year for purchasing drugs, for making local purchases. If a substantial amount of drugs has to be purchased, then we float a tender. However, there are also health institutions in smaller panchayats which might be struggling to make local purchase because of insufficient funds,” the superintendent at a taluk hospital in the suburbs said.
Ideally, when a patient registered at the NCD clinic of a particular healthcare institution comes for review, the hospital should have at least 30 days’ stock of the NCD drugs for the patient to take home. In the present situation, many hospitals are not able to ensure that.
Medical officers said this year, the Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) released only the drug supplies of the first quarter and that the second quarter release of June did not happen at all which led to the shortage of some drugs, including NCD drugs.
The KMSCL purchases around ₹700-800 crore worth of medicines every year for supplying to around 8,000 government healthcare institutions. In its last procurement exercise, 180 items reportedly received no bids, while suppliers quoted higher prices for another 171 items. This resulted in re-tendering and delays in placing fresh orders.
According to sources, the supply orders given in January-March, for some 18 non-bidder drugs, were cancelled by the new government because the prices quoted were considered far too high, which triggered the present shortage. However, fresh procurement orders have been placed and the supplies are expected to arrive within a week, it was pointed out.
The fact that the KMSCL owes over ₹2,200 crore to various pharma firms, for drugs purchased for hospitals as well as the drugs purchased by hospitals for patients under the Karunya Arogya Suraksha Padhati, has not helped the situation. The massive delays in payment is one of the reasons why many pharma forms do not respond to tenders floated by the KMSCL.
Health Minister K. Muraleedharan had directed that the procurement procedures for the next financial year begin in October itself and that the entire process be completed by the end of December.
He also directed that middlemen be removed from the tender processes and that agencies dealing directly in imported medicines also be allowed to take part in tenders. He said a comprehensive overhaul was under way at the KMSCL
According to sources, there are also efforts to form a consortium with medical service corporations of other States so that common purchase tenders can be floated, which might likely bring prices further down.

బ్యాంకులకు వారానికి ఐదు రోజుల పని విధానం అమలు చేయాలని బ్యాంకు ఉద్యోగ సంఘాలు చాలా కాలంగా డిమాండ్ చేస్తున్నాయి. ఈ డిమాండ్పై సెప్టెంబర్ 2026లో యునైటెడ్ ఫోరం ఆఫ్ బ్యాంక్ యూనియన్స్ (UFBU) దేశవ్యాప్తంగా నిరసనలు చేపట్టింది. వీటిలో పెన్షన్ ప్రయోజనాలను మెరుగుపరచడం, పాత పెన్షన్ విధానాన్ని (OPS) తిరిగి అమలు చేయడం, పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న వేతన సమస్యలను పరిష్కరించడం వంటి డిమాండ్లు ఉన్నాయి. సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 చివర్లో మూడు రోజుల బ్యాంకు సమ్మెకు పిలుపునిచ్చారు. అయితే, ఇండియన్ బ్యాంక్స్ అసోసియేషన్ ఈ అంశాలపై చర్చించేందుకు అంగీకరించడంతో సమ్మెను వాయిదా వేశారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, ఆర్థిక మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ జారీ చేసినట్లు చెబుతున్న ఒక గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్ సోషల్ మీడియాలో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) వైరల్ అవుతోంది. ఇందులో అన్ని ప్రభుత్వ రంగ బ్యాంకులకు ప్రతి శనివారం సెలవు ఉంటుందని, ఈ నిబంధన వెంటనే అమల్లోకి వస్తుందని కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం ప్రకటించినట్లు పేర్కొన్నారు. ఈ పోస్ట్లో చేసిన వాదనను ఇప్పుడు పరిశీలిద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ప్రభుత్వ రంగ బ్యాంకులకు ప్రతి శనివారం సెలవు ఉంటుందని ఆర్థిక మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ జారీ చేసిన గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్.
ఫాక్ట్: PIB ఫ్యాక్ట్ చెక్ ప్రకారం, ఆర్థిక మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ ఇలాంటి నోటిఫికేషన్ను ఏదీ జారీ చేయలేదు. సోషల్ మీడియాలో వైరల్ అవుతున్న గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్ OpenAI టూల్స్ను ఉపయోగించి AI ద్వారా రూపొందించినది. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్ట్లో చేసిన వాదన తప్పు.
ముందుగా, ఇలాంటి నోటిఫికేషన్ ఏదైనా విడుదలైందా అని తెలుసుకోవడానికి ప్రభుత్వం యొక్క అధికారిక e-Gazette పోర్టల్ను పరిశీలించాము. అయితే, అక్కడ దీనికి సంబంధించిన ఎలాంటి రికార్డు కనిపించలేదు. అలాగే, ఈ విషయంపై భారత ప్రభుత్వం నుంచి ఎలాంటి అధికారిక ప్రకటన కూడా వెలువడలేదు.
తర్వాత, వైరల్గా మారిన గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్ చిత్రాన్ని OpenAI కంటెంట్ డిటెక్షన్ టూల్ను ఉపయోగించి పరిశీలించాము. ఈ పరిశీలనలో, ఈ గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్ OpenAI టూల్స్ను ఉపయోగించి AI ద్వారా రూపొందించినట్లు తేలింది.
అదనంగా, ప్రభుత్వ ప్రెస్ ఇన్ఫర్మేషన్ బ్యూరో (PIB) ఫ్యాక్ట్ చెక్ ఈ విషయంపై స్పష్టత (ఆర్కైవ్) ఇచ్చింది. ప్రభుత్వ రంగ బ్యాంకులకు ప్రతి శనివారం సెలవు ప్రకటిస్తూ ఆర్థిక మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ ఎలాంటి నోటిఫికేషన్ జారీ చేయలేదని సోషల్ మీడియాలో వైరల్ అవుతున్న గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్ నకిలీదని నిర్ధారించింది.
చివరిగా, వైరల్ అవుతున్న గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్ AI ద్వారా రూపొందించబడింది; అన్ని శనివారాలను బ్యాంకులకు సెలవులుగా ప్రభుత్వం ప్రకటించలేదు.

In late September 2026, an image spread online claiming to show a herd of wild bison surrounding a hiker. According to a Facebook post (archived) with the image, the wild bison were protecting the "stranded hiker" from a wildfire:
A wild bison herd formed a tight circle around a stranded hiker during a wildfire, and firefighters say the formation was the only reason she wasn't overtaken by the flames.
Rachel had been hiking a remote section of the reserve when the wind shifted without warning, turning a controlled burn nearly six miles away into a fast-moving wildfire cutting off her only route back to the trailhead. She had no cell signal, no clear path around the advancing smoke, and less than twenty minutes before the fire line would reach her position on an open grassy ridge with nowhere to shelter.
That's when the bison found her.
A herd of nearly thirty animals, moving away from the fire themselves, suddenly changed direction as they passed her position, slowing and gathering into a tight defensive ring around her exact spot on the ridge, facing outward, the way herds typically only form when protecting newborn calves from predators.
Rachel said she didn't understand what was happening at first, terrified she was now trapped between fire and a wall of two-thousand-pound animals. But the herd held its formation as the fire's smoke rolled over them, and she realized, watching the ash fall around the massive bodies surrounding her, that their sheer size and the churned, trampled earth beneath the herd was creating a wide buffer of bare ground the flames couldn't easily cross.
The fire burned around the herd's position rather than through it. When air support finally spotted the unusual circular formation from above and redirected a rescue team, they found Rachel unharmed at the center, the herd only breaking formation and moving on once the helicopter's rotors got close enough to disperse them.
Wildlife officials say bison herds have never been documented forming protective circles around a human being before, only around their own young. They have no explanation for why this herd made the exception.
(Facebook user "Wonder Paws")
The above image is fake, and the story accompanying it is not true. The image contains numerous signs it was generated using artificial intelligence. There also was no available evidence of bison legitimately protecting a hiker in this manner.
The first sign that the image was artificially generated was visible in the top portion showing the circle of bison. Several of them are facing outward but also appear to have heads on both sides of their bodies. The hiker is also not visible in the top portion. Furthermore, the bison in the lower portion of the image, showing the alleged rescue, appear to be copy-and-pasted versions of the same animal. Some bison in the lower portion also appear to have heads on both sides of their bodies.
The post appears to have first ben shared by a Facebook account that has a history of posting AI-generated material.
The "photograph" was allegedly taken in August 2025, according to the timestamp at the top left. We looked for evidence of news coverage around that time about a rescue involving a woman named Rachel and found no reporting from trustworthy outlets such as The Associated Press and Reuters. The story in the post also did not contain information that would be included in legitimate reports about such an incident, such as the specific location of the wildfire.
The image and accompanying story are an example of AI slop: low-quality content that's easy to create thanks to AI tools. Such content overwhelms social media feeds, leaving users unsure of what's real and what's not.

A number of neighbourhoods in the city are not prepared for the onset of the Northeast monsoon owing to incomplete civic infrastructure projects.
At a meeting with Mayor R. Priya on Tuesday, officials pointed to incomplete projects in areas such as Korattur, Ganesapuram, Saidapet, Parangusapuram, and neighbourhoods along Anna Salai and Arcot Road. Deputy Mayor Mu. Magesh Kumaar said alternative arrangements had been proposed in many areas, such as Besant Road, P.S. Sivasamy Salai, Saidapet Govindan Road, Ganesapuram, Perungudi, and Sholinganallur, because of incomplete infrastructure projects.
Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) Commissioner G.S. Sameeran said: “The cut-and-cover drain work from East Avenue to Padi is in full swing. The GCC plans to have a dedicated drain from East Avenue and from Kiran Palace to Imayam Colony for a total length of 2.5 km. As of now, 2.1 km work has been completed. Efforts are on to complete the remaining 400 metres on CTH Road in another 15 days.”
In the event of a delay in completion of the project by October 15, the GCC plans to deploy additional heavy duty pumps to bail out water during the rain. “Two 100-HP pumps will be set up at the junction of Korattur signal and East Avenue Road. These will send the rainwater to the Lucas TVS front gate, where a highway drain is available. From there, the water will be sent to the new drain near Park Road, from where it will reach the zero point of Otteri Nullah,” Dr. Sameeran said.
Debris in Cooum
As residents have also complained about National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) delaying the removal of debris from the Cooum, the GCC has persuaded the authority to expedite work. “We have instructed the NHAI to remove all debris and temporary structures from the Cooum by October 15. Currently, they have removed nearly 70%,” the GCC Commissioner said.
“Regarding the ongoing Metro Rail work, a technical committee, comprising chief engineers of Chennai Metro Rail Limited (CMRL) and officials of the GCC, Highways and Water Resources Departments, has been formed, and its members jointly visited all the work sites of CMRL and suggested mitigation measures such as pump and sump arrangements, temporary earthen channels, and D-wall modifications. The GCC and CMRL have made arrangements accordingly,” he said.
Work was carried out at 60 sites of CMRL as part of monsoon preparedness across the city. “All culverts across 44 canals have been desilted using six robotic excavators, five float excavators, three amphibious excavators, 40 skid steer loaders. End-to-end desilting has been completed in major canals such as the Kodungaiyur, Padikuppam, and Trustpuram canals. Over 85% of the Otteri Nullah has been desilted. Over 80% of the work on Virugambakkam Canal has been completed. The rest of the work is under way,” Dr. Sameeran added.
