Florence Pugh is no stranger to making a fashion statement.
Pugh has worn daring outfits on red carpets for years, favoring bold sets and sheer designs. This year is no exception, with Pugh pushing fashion boundaries while promoting projects like "East of Eden" and "Spider-Man: Brand New Day."
Take a look at everything Pugh has worn in 2026 so far, ranked from least to most daring.
Pugh wore a high-neck dress to a performance of "Dracula" in February.
Pugh wore a black Patou gown to see Cynthia Erivo's "Dracula." It had a high neckline and short sleeves, hugging her figure until it hit the floor.
A subtle horse pattern was printed on the dress, which added a fun flair. Still, the gown was pretty simple overall, especially when compared to other looks Pugh has worn in 2026.
Pugh's dress for the Netflix Upfront in March was understated.
Pugh attended the Netflix event in a white gown designed by Simone Rocha.
The floor-length dress had a subtly scooped neckline and puffy, long sleeves. A flower was printed on the center, lining the length of the gown.
The dress was beautiful, but it wasn't her most daring look of the year.
She looked effortlessly chic in a navy set at the Venice Film Festival in September.
Pugh appeared at the annual film festival in a Max Mara set.
Her tank top had a scooped neckline, while her wide-legged trousers sat high on her waist.
The outfit had a simple color scheme and silhouette, but Pugh made it look more stylish with strappy heels, wide sunglasses, and a clutch.
For a New York engagement in September, she donned a peach blouse.
Pugh made a series of appearances in New York in September to promote Netflix's "East of Eden." For one of them, she wore wide-legged white trousers and a peach blouse from Chloé.
The blouse had ruffle detailing on the bodice and sleeves, and the hems were slightly ruffled as well. The top's texture added a fun pop to the look, as did Pugh's tiny sunglasses and rattan purse.
She chose a dress with sheer detailing for an appearance on "Late Night with Seth Meyers."
Pugh chose a black dress to speak to Seth Meyers during her New York tour. The neckline was covered in tiered ruffles, while the rest of the dress was made of a silky material.
One side of the skirt showed a slit that cut up her leg, while a panel of sheer fabric covered the other. The skirt gave the appearance that it had been ripped, contrasting with the more structured bodice.
Pugh also wore sunglasses with the gown, despite it being nighttime, for a chic touch.
Pugh wore one of her most glamorous looks of the year at the Emmys in March.
Attending the 2026 Emmys as a presenter, Pugh walked the red carpet in a purple Vivienne Westwood gown.
The form-fitting, strapless dress had a sparkly overlay, and rather than traditional sleeves, a bold, modified cape attached to both sides of the bodice.
A train trailed behind Pugh for even more drama.
Pugh selected a voluminous ball gown for a screening of "East of Eden" at BAFTA in September.
Netflix hosted a screening of "East of Eden" at BAFTA in London, and Pugh celebrated the limited series' release in a black Rodarte gown.
The ball gown had a modern gothic vibe, standing out from Pugh's go-to red carpet style, which often consists of simpler silhouettes.
Large, ruffled sleeves sat off her shoulders, while the neckline curved in a point on the bodice. A large skirt flowed out from her waist with tiers of ruched fabric and a bow in the center.
She wore a subtly sheer top at a photo call in September.
Pugh wore another Rodarte ensemble for an "East of Eden" photo call, diving into the brand's archives for the look.
Her white, shiny top was made of semi-sheer, ruched fabric. Tiers of fabric flowed out from the high neckline, creating volume and a funky feel.
She paired the bold top with high-waisted, wide-legged pants and a belt that said "Rodarte" in overlapping letters for another playful touch.
She selected a gown with crystal detailing for an "East of Eden" event in September.
Erdem designed Pugh's dropped-waist gown.
The dress had a V-neckline that dipped low on Pugh's chest, and crystal embellishments adorned the bodice. Fringed fabric lined the hem of the full, asymmetrical skirt, accentuating her Aquazzura shoes.
Pugh wore a lacy romper in New York in September.
Pugh also stepped out in a Chloé romper during her New York visit.
The strapless top had a semi-sheer, white overlay, while the shorts were trimmed with the same lace. Pugh paired the piece with silver Aquazarra heels.
The outfit struck a fun balance between feminine and modern.
Pugh's dress for "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon" made use of ruching.
Pugh stopped by "The Tonight Show" while promoting "East of Eden."
She chatted to host Jimmy Fallon in an off-the-shoulder Vivienne Westwood gown. The form-fitting dress was covered in ruching, creating dimension. The scooped neckline dipped low, and the asymmetrical skirt cut high on her thigh on one side.
Coordinating Aquazarra shoes completed the look.
Pugh went pantless for an "East of Eden" photo call.
Dior designed Pugh's look for the London photo call.
The base of the ensemble was a white blouse, which she buttoned all the way to her neckline. Atop it, Pugh wore a patterned coatdress that cinched at her waist and had an asymmetrical hemline.
It flared around the back, providing coverage, while rising on one side to show the shirt below.
Her gown at the "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" premiere looked as if it defied gravity.
Pugh celebrated the Marvel film in a silver Tamara Ralph gown.
The off-the-shoulder neckline curved around Pugh's arms, creating the illusion that the dress was floating around her.
It dipped into a low V in the center, with tassels of sparkly fabric flowing to her waist in the same shape. The skirt hugged her figure, with more tassels spilling out from the hem.
Pugh rocked a sheer dress to the "East of Eden" premiere after-party.
After attending the New York premiere for the series, Pugh changed into a Rodarte gown to continue celebrating her Netflix project.
Her sheath-style pink dress was completely sheer. It had spaghetti straps with brooch attachments at each side of the gown, and a coordinating scarf completed the ensemble.
The silhouette was simple, but the fabric made the dress bold.
Pugh looked like she was wearing an ultra-low-waisted skirt for one of her most eye-catching looks of the year.
Pugh attended an evening event for "East of Eden" in an Erdem ensemble.
She wore a sparkly crop top with a bra-like bodice, which matched the top of her high-waisted skirt. At her lower hip, the skirt switched to gray pleated fabric that flowed around her ankles, creating the illusion of wearing two separates at the bottom of her ensemble.
A bow sat on one side, and Pugh added a bow to her hair as well to play up the feminine side of the look.
Pugh stepped out in a sheer set for an "East of Eden" screening in California in September.
Pugh wore one of her most daring looks of the year to a California screening of "East of Eden."
Her yellow archival Rodarte set was made of sheer fabric, with subtle polka dots lining the pattern. Her top had a collared neckline with ruffles flowing around it, and a floral pattern curving around her torso.
The skirt had the same floral pattern on the sides, with ruffles flowing out from her waist. Gray shoes completed the look.
Pugh wore one of her most avant-garde looks of the year in New York in September.
During her New York visit, Pugh wore a black top and trousers from Chloé with Aquazurra shoes.
The embroidered top had a modified corset with a peplum and puffy sleeves. Lace trimmed the collar and sleeves.
The top had a vintage feel, while the billowing pants, which cinched at Pugh's ankle with a bow, put a modern spin on the look. Small sunglasses and a purse with fringe detailing brought Pugh's look together.
Pugh wore her most daring dress of the year to the "East of Eden" premiere in New York.
Pugh wore another yellow look to the New York "East of Eden" premiere, arriving in a custom Vivienne Westwood gown.
The gown's corset bodice had a zipper lining the center, framed by silver sparkle embellishments on either side. It had a modern sweetheart neckline, with the center curve dipping low on Pugh's chest.
An off-the-shoulder shrug sat on her shoulders, with its voluminous sleeves contrasting with the modern bodice. The gown's gray skirt hugged Pugh's figure before flowing into a subtle train.

Canada’s long-running Quebec problem is back in focus as separatist politics regain momentum in the French-speaking province, raising fresh questions over the future of the Canadian federation and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s ability to manage competing demands for greater provincial autonomy. The Parti Québécois (PQ), which advocates Quebec sovereignty, is seeking a return to power after more than a decade. A PQ victory could push the question of independence back to the centre of Canadian politics, particularly if party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon follows through on his pledge to hold another referendum on Quebec’s future. The issue comes at a particularly sensitive time for Canada. Alberta has also been debating the possibility of a referendum on separation, potentially leaving Ottawa facing competing challenges to national unity from opposite ends of the country. The debate is further complicated by US President Donald Trump’s repeated remarks about making Canada the “51st state” of the United States, adding external pressure. Quebec occupies a unique position within Canada. It is the country’s only majority French-speaking province and has a distinct political, cultural and historical identity rooted in its French heritage. The province was part of New France before Britain took control of the territory in 1763. Over centuries, Quebec developed its own institutions, traditions and language protections, setting it apart from predominantly English-speaking Canada. For Quebec nationalists, this distinct identity is central to the argument for greater political autonomy. The sovereignty movement argues that Quebec should have complete control over areas such as its laws, economy, immigration and international relations rather than sharing constitutional authority with Ottawa. The Parti Québécois has historically been the main political vehicle for this movement. Quebec has held two referendums on sovereignty. The first, in 1980, resulted in a decisive rejection of independence. The second, in 1995, was dramatically closer. The “No” side won with just 50.58% of the vote, while 49.42% backed sovereignty. The razor-thin result remains one of the defining moments in modern Canadian political history. The Parti Québécois’ resurgence has brought the independence question back into mainstream political debate. Plamondon has pledged to hold another referendum on Quebec sovereignty if his party returns to power, as per BBC. However, he has said the vote would take place only after Trump leaves office. But a PQ victory would not automatically mean Quebec was on the verge of leaving Canada. Polling suggests support for independence remains a minority position, at around 30%, according to CNN. A renewed push for Quebec independence could pose a major challenge for Prime Minister Mark Carney. Plamondon has made clear that he is prepared to challenge the federal government on issues he considers to fall within provincial jurisdiction, including immigration. That could mean repeated clashes with Ottawa over the division of powers, even before the question of sovereignty formally reaches a referendum. Even if Quebec eventually holds another referendum and the independence side wins, that would not automatically result in Quebec becoming an independent country. A vote would be the beginning of a much larger constitutional and political process involving negotiations between Quebec and the federal government, including questions over borders, assets, debt, citizenship, Indigenous rights and the division of powers. The 1995 referendum showed just how close the question could become. However, three decades later, the political landscape is different. Samsung's The Frame TV is at its lowest price ever right now, at 40 percent off—a very appealing deal for one of the most popular art TVs on the market. The discount applies to the 2025 65-inch model, which is still a very capable TV that does its primary function very well. ‘240 MPs at Parliament Annexe unusual and unacceptable': Why ECI rejected meeting with Opposition MPs
The poll body's statement comes after over 300 Opposition MPs of the INDIA bloc began a march from Parliament Complex to the Election Commission office.
The Election Commission of India on Tuesday rejected a meeting proposal with Opposition MPs, citing their demands as “unusual and unacceptable”. The poll body also clarified that it had received no request from any political party for a meeting beforehand, and had intimated about it by the Delhi Police at around 4 pm.
The poll body's statement comes after over 300 Opposition MPs of the INDIA bloc began a march from Parliament Complex to the Election Commission office, in a bid to meet with the Election Commissioners and hand over a formal memorandum to them.
Rejecting the Opposition's request on grounds of “protocol”, the Election Commission said any political party can request a meeting with the poll body at any time through the established procedure. “The Commission may schedule the date and time for such a meeting based on convenience,” ECI said.
Deep Dive

‘2015 protocol, authorised representative’: Why did ECI reject meeting with Opposition?
The Election Commission of India, while declining to meet with Opposition MPs on Tuesday, citing a procedure established in 2015. It said that the poll body had a protocol for such meetings with political parties. “All political parties have been informed of this and adhere to this process,” the ECI said in its statement.
It said that under this process, whenever a delegation from a single political party or a joint delegation of political parties wish to meet the Commission, they must request an appointment through their “duly authorized representative.” The meeting takes place thereafter at a time mutually agreed upon by both parties, the ECI stated.
‘Unusual and unacceptable’: Election Commission response to Opposition demands
In its statement, the ECI said it had initially considered meeting with the Opposition after being informed that the MPs wished to meet the Election Commissioners.
However, it said that the Deputy Commission of Police later informed the poll body that the meeting would involve 240 MPs from the Opposition and was proposed to be held at the Parliament Annexe, a demand deemed by the ECI as “unusual and unacceptable.”
The poll body said that protocol dictates that such meetings take place inside Election Commission premises. The ECI added that while it had also proposed sending its most senior serving official to the meeting venue to receive the Opposition's memorandum, this was rejected by the INDIA bloc MPs. It said that this step “would have been unprecedented in itself.”
“The ECI respects the country's parliamentary and democratic processes, as well as its own protocols and conventions, which are of utmost importance,” the poll body added.

The Trump administration is facing growing questions over its decision to abandon a fraud and bribery case against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani after he promised to invest $10bn in the US.
For the second time this year, two Democratic senators have demanded attorney general Todd Blanche answer questions about the US Department of Justice department’s handling of the case – and raised concerns over its judgment under Donald Trump.
In August, a federal judge in New York agreed to drop the fraud case against Adani, one of the richest people in the world, at the request of prosecutors, despite having concerns about “irregularities” in the “highly unusual” decision. It has become the latest example of judges raising eyebrows at Trump administration prosecutors for pushing to dismiss criminal cases.
Now, more than a month later, senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal are asking Blanche to clarify whether people close to Donald Trump were involved in that decision.
It comes aftera New York Times report revealed that Adani, represented by one of Trump’s personal lawyers, admitted to offering a $10bn investment in the US to resolve the criminal case. The federal judge overseeing the case determined the investment played no role in the DoJ’s decision to abandon the case.
“These fresh details continue to raise concerns about the judgment of the DoJ, and the extent to which the DoJ is willing and able to prosecute white-collar criminals under President Trump,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in a letter sent on Wednesday, and seen by the Guardian.
Adani was indicted in 2024 in New York for allegedly participating in a bribery and fraud scheme in which he paid Indian officials to secure a contract for one of his companies. He denied the allegations.
Prosecutors suddenly moved to dismiss the case against Adani in May after he hired a new legal team, led by Robert Giuffra Jr, and offered to invest $10bn into the US.
Following the news, Warren and Blumenthal sent a letter to Blanche in June requesting information about the fraud case and raising concerns about whether the justice department dismissed the case in exchange for Adani’s investment.
However, the senators did not receive a response. Since then, new details about the case have emerged, including allegations that Boris Epshteyn, a member of Trump’s personal legal team who also served as an informal adviser, helped Adani.
Another report claimed Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, met with Adani in November 2025, before the case was dropped. A spokesperson for Trump Jr said earlier this year that the conversation “had zero to do with DoJ’s actions in this case”.
A spokesperson for Epshteyn denied being involved in Adani’s “arguments, advocacy or efforts” to the Wall Street Journal in June. Epshteyn was never hired by Adani or his company, the Adani Group, nor did he maintain a relationship with Adani, the spokesperson added.
The Guardian has asked Epshteyn for comment.
The Democratic lawmakers are now asking the DoJ for more information about Adani’s alleged investment offer, including a list of employees who were present when the offer was made, the terms of the offer, when the offer was made and where.
They also want to know whether the DoJ employees knew Epshteyn was allegedly working on behalf of Adani, or if Epshteyn had any contact with DoJ employees regarding Adani, among other questions.
“We are also concerned about the involvement of two of President Trump’s personal lawyers in this case, and the extent to which they reveal potential political influence and special treatment for well-connected insiders at the DoJ,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in their letter.
The Democrats also want to know if Trump Jr, or any person working on behalf of Trump Jr., had contact with a DoJ employee regarding Adani.
Warren and Blumenthal requested responses no later than 5 October. The Guardian has asked Blanche’s office for comment.

Daniil Medvedev: Defaulted for hitting a spectator with the ball but was it the right decision or should he have been able to play on?
'Frustration I wouldn't necessarily say is conducive to clarity of mind' - Johanna Konta and Jonathan Overend both admit Daniil Medvedev was "unfortunate" to have been defaulted against Novak Djokovic; you can watch the ATP 1000 Shanghai Masters live on Sky Sports
Tuesday 6 October 2026 17:51, UK
Daniil Medvedev was defaulted for hitting a spectator with the ball during his semi-final with Novak Djokovic at the China Open, but was it the correct decision or should he have been able to continue playing?
Medvedev was trailing Djokovic 7-5 5-3 and had lost a point when he hit the ball coming off the wall.
The spectator, who was sitting in the first row behind Medvedev, clutched his left eye and appeared to be in pain as he walked out of the gallery, assisted by stadium staff.
Medvedev did not protest the umpire's decision to disqualify him.

Speaking to Sky Sports, Jonathan Overend said: "From the first camera angle we saw the ball leaving Medvedev's racket and weren't sure where it had gone, but I later saw a different angle filmed from the stands and it clearly went straight from the racket into the face of this spectator and so from the minute that was obvious, it was an instant default.
"It was absolutely the correct decision. The rulebook is very clear about that and it was unfortunate for Medvedev. We take him at face value when he says he didn't mean to do it, but it did leave his racket with force and it did strike the spectator.
"It appeared to me that umpire Mohamed Lahyani appeared initially to be uncertain about whether or not to default him but it was only when the supervisor got involved and further views were taken into account that it was clear that it did strike the spectator on the full and disqualification was the correct decision and clearly everyone on court felt that regrettably was the right course of action."
Overend described Medvedev as a "curious character" with the former US Open champion mimicking Djokovic being tired or injured on court which he felt "didn't feel appropriate" in such a match and such an opponent.
"For the disqualification to happen a few games later, it was out of character in the sense that I haven't seen him do that before but with Medvedev over the years you expect the unexpected and there is a certain volatility to him so maybe we shouldn't have been too surprised," he said.
'He wouldn't intentionally hit a spectator'
Johanna Konta also feels Medvedev was "unfortunate" to have been defaulted after watching numerous replays of the incident.
The former British No 1 said: "I can almost with certainty say he wouldn't intentionally hit a spectator with a ball. However, we have seen him do other things out of frustration from kicking the microphone, smashing rackets, and mouthing off.
"He's got quite a vocabulary on him, so it's not out of character for him to get frustrated but he obviously misjudged the angle of his racket, he misjudged the height of the backboard, he misjudged his whole surroundings.
"Frustration I wouldn't necessarily say is conducive to clarity of mind, so more than anything if you're feeling angry and frustrated, you won't necessarily be in control of your ability as if you weren't, so he wouldn't have intentionally done that."
Overend claims you have take Medvedev at "face value" with people believing he did not do it intentionally. When reviewing the footage, he said: "I don't think you're saying for certain that he's not doing that deliberately because he hits it at pace.
"He slices it but it is travelling at pace. He's intentionally coming right under the ball to stun it, but then he plays a really bad shot."
Konta said: "Medvedev was caught in between when you slice and you try and hit it back to you against just hitting it flat against the backboard, but I think he realises that the ball kid is there and I think if you're frustrated and you're thinking 'I can't hit the backboard because if it hits the ball kid I'm going to get defaulted' I wonder if he got caught in no-man's land and that's why it looks in between two shots because where he has hit it is right above the ball kid's head.
"I cannot see Medvedev doing it intentionally. I cannot imagine what that felt like in the pit of his stomach."
Do the ATP need to unify the criteria once and for all?
"Where tennis has to be careful here is making sure there isn't a grey area with regards to this rule," explained Overend.
"I think back to the Winston-Salem final of 2024 which was when Alex Michelsen launched a ball like Medvedev into the spectators, very, very close to the court, but then the umpire went over to the spectators to see whether anybody had been hit directly and because it didn't appear to hit anybody directly or injure them, Michelsen, who was absolutely convinced that he was going to get defaulted from that match was effectively let off and he was allowed to continue.
"That to me is a grey area because that is almost saying the severity of the impact dictates whether the player is disqualified or not.
"Tennis has got to be quite careful that if there is a rule in place here, which there is, it's enforced with consistency. In my opinion, launching a ball at pace, into spectators, is an instant disqualification and has to be for the safety of everyone. Players have been defaulted for less, let's put it this way!"

Black Hills plans $1.8 billion investment to power Google's data center
Oct 6 : Black Hills Corp said on Tuesday it signed agreements to power a proposed Google data center in Cheyenne, Wyoming, and plans to spend $1.8 billion from 2027 to 2029 on new generation capacity, as tech firms race to secure electricity for power-hungry AI data centers.
• Black Hills said it will build 564 megawatts (MW) of new generation capacity for the Cheyenne project
• The project is expected to draw on a 2.7-gigawatt (GW) resource mix, including reserve margins, with power deliveries set to begin in late 2027 and peak load expected in 2030
• Black Hills will supply up to 590 MW from the grid, mostly from a new gas plant at its Cheyenne Prairie Generating Station and manage about 2.1 GW of third-party resources in Wyoming through a privately managed microgrid
• The South Dakota-based utility expects the project to add about $150 million to its net income by 2030
• The agreement requires Google to cover the full cost of supplying electricity to the data center, preventing those expenses from being passed on to other utility customers
• Separately, Google also signed a 3.59-GW power contract with Constellation Energy, which will invest more than $4.3 billion in its fleet
• In August last year, Black Hills agreed to merge with NorthWestern Energy in an all-stock deal to create a $15.4 billion regulated electric and natural gas utility

Son of Zambian bishop detained in post-election raid fears for his father's safety
The son of detained Zambian opposition politician Bishop Trevor Mwamba has told the BBC he is concerned for his father's safety after the former Bishop of Botswana was detained along with 10 other opposition figures by authorities.
Eno Mwamba said his father, who is leader of the United National Independence Party, has been charged with treason following President Hakainde Hichilema's disputed election victory.
The opposition politicians have been held since a raid by security forces on 14 August.
Opposition leader Brian Mundubile, head of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), had gone into hiding after disputing the election result, but has since also been detained by the authorities.
The government accuses the opposition of planning an armed insurgency and have charged the detained politicians with treason. They have denied the charges.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

India recorded 3,832 new leprosy cases among children in 2025-26, including 37 who had Grade-2 disability (G2D) at diagnosis — an indicator of delayed detection. The child caseload was 91.6% higher than the National Leprosy Eradication Programme's (NLEP) target of 2,000 cases for the year.
The figures, from the latest NLEP annual report for 2025-26, come even as India pursues the National Strategic Plan for Leprosy 2023-27, which seeks to interrupt transmission at the district level by 2027. Under the roadmap, a district is considered to have interrupted transmission after reporting zero new indigenous child cases for five consecutive years.
The NLEP's programme objectives include zero disability among new child cases and a national G2D rate of less than one case per million population. The roadmap projects 1,000 child cases and a G2D rate of 0.5 per million for 2026-27.
The appearance of children among newly detected cases matters beyond the absolute number. The World Health Organisation (WHO) considers new cases among children below 15 years an indicator of recent transmission, while G2D among newly detected patients indicates delayed diagnosis.
The WHO also says disabilities among newly detected child cases signal both delayed detection and ongoing transmission.
India recorded 63 children with G2D in 2019-20, followed by 35 in 2020-21, 41 in 2021-22, 55 in 2022-23 and 45 in 2023-24. The continued detection of children with G2D contrasts with the NLEP's objective of zero disability among new child cases.
The latest numbers therefore raise a fundamental epidemiological question: if India is working to interrupt transmission by 2027, why are children still developing leprosy, and why are some reaching diagnosis only after visible disability has appeared?
India detected 91,783 new leprosy cases in 2025-26, according to the Union Health Ministry. The prevalence rate was 0.56 per 10,000 population, and 1,945 patients had Grade-2 disability at diagnosis, accounting for 2.12% of all newly detected cases. The national G2D rate was 1.34 per million, above the NLEP's target of less than one case per million.
According to the WHO's latest global update, India reported the world's largest number of newly detected leprosy cases in 2025, with 91,783 cases, followed by Brazil with 22,901 and Indonesia with 16,292. Together, the three countries accounted for 78.3% of all new cases reported globally. The WHO notes that, although the update is for 2025, India reported data for April 2025 to March 2026.
India also reported the world's largest number of new child leprosy cases in the WHO's 2025 global update, with 3,832 cases.
The WHO figures and the NLEP figures refer to the same reporting period for India — April 2025 to March 2026 — although the WHO presents India's data in its 2025 global table. The WHO table records 3,832 child cases and 37 child cases with G2D for India.
Dr. Kabir Sardana, Professor and Head of Dermatology at ABVIMS-Dr. RML Hospital, Delhi, attributed the continuing burden partly to gaps in case detection.
"Data points to the fact that there is poor detection, which is why we are seeing more children with leprosy," he said.
The Health Ministry identifies high-endemic and hard-to-reach areas as priorities for intensified case detection. The NLEP emphasises active case detection, household contact surveys and focused campaigns, along with special plans for hard-to-reach areas. The programme also identifies stigma and discrimination as continuing concerns.
The WHO says prolonged, close contact with untreated cases allows transmission to continue, while the disease's long incubation period makes interruption difficult. New child cases are considered an indicator of recent transmission, although the presence of a child case cannot by itself establish when or where the infection occurred. The WHO notes that symptoms can appear years after infection.
Leprosy, or Hansen's disease, is a chronic bacterial infection caused mainly by Mycobacterium leprae. It primarily affects the skin and peripheral nerves. Transmission occurs mainly through prolonged, close contact with an untreated person. The disease is curable with multidrug therapy, a combination of antibiotics provided free through public-health programmes.
Children and household contacts are particularly important to surveillance because a new child case can indicate ongoing transmission within a community. However, the presence of a child case cannot by itself establish when or where the infection occurred. The average incubation period is about five years and can be considerably longer.
India's child caseload has fallen substantially from a decade ago, but the decline has not been linear. The country detected 11,365 children with leprosy in 2014-15, 11,389 in 2015-16 and 11,770 in 2016-17. The number fell to 10,287 in 2017-18, 9,227 in 2018-19 and 7,859 in 2019-20.
Child detections fell sharply during the COVID-19 period, reaching 3,753 in 2020-21, before rising to 4,107 in 2021-22. They fell again to 2,363 in 2022-23 and 2,335 in 2023-24, before rising to 3,832 in 2025-26. Changes in reported case numbers also reflect the intensity and reach of case detection, making it difficult to interpret the trend as a direct measure of transmission alone.
The Health Ministry has identified high-priority States and districts where the burden remains concentrated. Twenty-three districts in Chhattisgarh, 21 in Jharkhand, 18 each in Maharashtra and Odisha, and 10 in Madhya Pradesh had a prevalence rate above one case per 10,000 population, according to the Ministry.
These figures identify districts with prevalence above the elimination threshold; they should not be read as meaning that these are the only States or districts with continuing transmission.
For a disease that is curable, and for which early detection and treatment can prevent the progression to disability, the continued detection of children — including some already showing Grade-2 disability — highlights the tension between programme targets and what is still being detected in communities.

Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
- Published
Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya.
The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people.
The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics – by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up. He is aiming to get another 2.3 million on board in the next round.
"It was the Gen Z way of doing politics," he tells me. "Fun, trendy, sexy, fashionable. Because of how we created the hype around it, people had the fear of missing out. Everybody wanted to be involved."
Gen Z, the term used to describe people born in the late 1990s and early 2000s, burst onto the scene two years ago with mass protests that forced the government to retreat on a widely unpopular tax bill. But their victory was followed by a police crackdown that killed and injured dozens of demonstrators.
Now many young Kenyans are planning to move from the street to the ballot box, angry with a political establishment they accuse of corruption and police brutality.
And they have the numbers to make a difference - more than 30% of voting-age Kenyans are younger than 35.
Polls suggest President William Ruto is looking vulnerable.
[The youth] just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created"
But can Gen Z convert a decentralized digital-led rebellion into organised political power?
"These youth-led movements are a wild card, in that they are unpredictable," says political analyst Tom Mboya.
"They don't require much in the way of resources and can pop up at any time. The finance bill protests were political in nature, but the movement has not been tested at an overtly political level. So if they decide to support a candidate, then he's likely to do fairly well."
One of the strengths of the digitally savvy Gen Z activists is that they have been able to mobilise outside the party structures and ethnic allegiances that anchor Kenyan politics.
Allans has been careful not to advocate a particular candidate or party – emphasising leadership rather than politicians, marshalling a new force, he says, outside traditional tribal voting blocs.
"There has never been a case where there is a bloc that is not affiliated to any person or any party. They just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created," he says.
"It's more of a swing vote because you cannot tell who we are going to vote for."
Ruto and his United Democratic Alliance (UDA) are facing strong head winds with less than a year to go before the August 2027 vote.
More than three-quarters of respondents to a survey conducted in June felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, with two-thirds saying their personal economic situation had worsened since Ruto was elected in 2022.
But analysts argue that the president does not necessarily have to be popular to win. He is a master political organiser with the resources of the state, they say.
Ruto's political rivals are also fragmented, and it is not yet clear whether they can form a united opposition to take him on.
One man who has captured the attention of many Gen Zs is Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has emerged as the leader of a movement called Linda Mwananchi (Protect the Citizen), which is getting strong support from disaffected young people.
Sifuna first caught their attention when he tried to stop police from shooting at protesters who were storming parliament during the 2024 demonstrations.

  - Published28 April 2025
Now he is championing a "people-led" movement that promotes the protection of human rights and rule of law as enshrined in the constitution.
He has yet to officially declare a run for the presidency, but is already on the road rallying support. The BBC caught up with him on a recent trip to Meru county in central Kenya, a region that voted strongly for Ruto in the last election.
"Young people want us to create an environment where everybody feels that they can compete fairly," he told me before starting out on his raucous road show.
"We need to absolutely dismantle the system so that everybody has a fair chance at life, a fair chance at education, a fair chance at employment, and the opportunities to grow themselves.
"This election in 2027 is when this theory that the young people are advancing will be put to the test," he said. "Our challenge as a leadership is to ensure you have a compelling message that then encourages people to come out, let them see the vision for the new country."
Ruto also had a compelling vision for the country when he came to power in 2022.
He promised to transform the economy from the bottom up, with a focus on lifting the marginalised. His government has since introduced changes including landmark reforms that widen access to public healthcare, but many young people felt betrayed by his austerity measures and tax hikes.
"I'm here to participate in a revolution change that we want a new Kenyan youth leader who knows the common problems that are facing the young people," 23-year-old Brandon Muremi told the BBC.
I found him in a relatively quiet corner of the final stop in a hectic day of a "rolling rally" – Sifuna's convoy visited four locations, sometimes blocking traffic as he and local politicians climbed on top of their vehicles and delivered rousing speeches at ear-splitting volumes.
They promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths"
"We are looking for a leader who sticks to his plans, not just talking the promises that he makes," agreed Conrad Mutangili, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering student who had come out of curiosity.
"We are looking for somebody who can actually accomplish and actually bring to the people what they are talking about," he said. "Because they promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths."
"We want immediate results," said a 22-year-old computer science student, Yvonne Kileme, acknowledging that the results of government projects may be more long-term. "And one thing that we want as youths is employment, employment, employment, employment."
Ruto argues strongly that his government is delivering jobs, and says the high rate of youth unemployment is a problem that predates his presidency.
He has reached out to Gen Z with various programmes that offer grants and loans to small business and youth-led enterprises, technology hubs and digital work opportunities.
The national youth leader of Ruto's UDA, Kariuki Ngunjiri, told the BBC he was confident of winning the election with an overwhelming majority.
"The president is a listening president and he's been able to now come down to the youth, get what their concerns are, give them jobs, and that has absolutely, even for the party, given us a head start," he said.
"We are not worried about the social media buzz because we are people who actually engage the young people on real, actual, tangible development. What you see mostly on sponsored hashtags and sponsored headlines does not really concern us."
He was speaking as a senior sports official promised to expand the stadium-building programme with another venue, at a packed UDA town hall meeting in Kangema, about 100km (60 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi.
Like so many others, 23-year-old Shintah Mutahi was job hunting.
"I came to listen to what they were saying," she said, "maybe find an opportunity for a job. I think they can give me a chance, they should just be given some time to do that."
John Kiragu, a local UDA youth leader, said he understood the grievances that had driven young people to protest.
"There have been challenges," he said, "but now the government is really trying hard to consolidate the youth. The government is implementing programmes that will really uplift their lives."
Kiragu told me he was involved in a programme to deal with youth alcoholism – a real problem in this region. Many of the young men who attended the morning town hall meeting were already drunk on a cheap local liquor.
The captain of the local football team, Calvin Ware, also turned up to hear the stadium announcement. He said he had heard similar promises many times before, especially before elections, and this one was not going to influence his vote.
"We have already made our mind," he said. "The whole government should go home. We want to build a new Kenya, new youth, new people, fresh people from all over the country, and we are not basing on tribal [allegiances] or anything else. We just want a change, a change, and a change. Nothing else."
As we were speaking, we heard a loud cheer – the event had ended and people were lining up to receive cash handouts – 350 Kenyan shillings, about $3 (£2.20).
It is common practice to pay people to attend political meetings in Kenya, and politicians can use much larger sums to try and influence votes.
"More so than many other parts of the world, money talks in an election here," says political analyst Mboya. "The cost of politics is significantly higher than in other parts of the world."
Less than a year to Kenya's election, it does feel like politics might be changing, that the race could be shaped by youth disillusionment with the political establishment. But while the Gen Z movement has rejected the "old politics" based on ethnic group and money, those have been the building blocks that win elections in Kenya.
Nobody yet knows what the energy of Gen Z voters will mean at the ballot box.

On 02 October 2026, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) held a protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park demanding accountability from the Election Commission of India (ECI) and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Protesters raised concerns over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleged voter deletions, and transparency in the electoral process. Despite Mumbai Police denying permission for the gathering, thousands attended the protest and raised slogans. Police later registered an FIR against the organisers and 400–500 unidentified participants for allegedly violating restrictions on the assembly (here, here, and here).
In this context, two videos are circulating on social media (here, here, and here) claiming to show the CJP protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai. Let’s verify the truth behind these videos in this article.
Claim: The videos show the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai on 02 October 2026.
Fact: The videos do not show the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest at Shivaji Park on 02 October 2026. The first video was recorded at CJP’s protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, while the second video shows the Tiranga Vijay Rally jointly organised by Shiv Sena (UBT) and Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) at Shivaji Park on 26 July 2026 . Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
Upon closely reviewing the viral videos, we noticed ‘Delhi Police’ written on the barricades. This indicates that the videos were recorded in Delhi, not Mumbai, as claimed in the viral posts.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to the same video uploaded on the Facebook page ‘Indian Sawarn Samaj News’ on 08 August 2026. The video was uploaded with a caption stating that it shows a CJP protest in Delhi demanding the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan. This confirms that the viral video predates the CJP protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai on 02 October 2026.
We also geolocated the high-rise building visible in the viral video to Jai Singh Marg, Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, Delhi. A comparison of the building in the viral video with its appearance on Google Maps Street View can be seen below.
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) began its protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 06 June 2026, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged irregularities in NEET-UG 2026. The protest continued for several weeks and was called off on 25 July 2026 following Pradhan’s resignation and government assurances on some of the protesters’ demands.
Video 2
We conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to the same video uploaded on the Facebook page ‘Mumbai Explore’ on 26 July 2026. The caption states that Dadar celebrated a memorable victory with grand celebrations. This confirms that the viral video predates the CJP protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai on 02 October 2026.
According to reports, the Tiranga Vijay Rally was held at Shivaji Park on 26 July 2026, one day after Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned. It was jointly organised by Shiv Sena (UBT) and Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS), led by Uddhav Thackeray and Raj Thackeray. The rally was originally planned as a Tiranga Morcha demanding Pradhan’s resignation, but after his resignation on 25 July 2026, it was turned into a victory gathering celebrating the student movement. Thousands of people attended, carrying the national flag and posters (here, here, and here).
We found multiple posts (here, here, and here) on the official Shiv Sena (UBT) social media handle featuring the rally. The stage, banners and other visual elements seen in these posts match those visible in the viral video, confirming that the viral video shows the Tiranga Vijay Rally held at Shivaji Park in July 2026, not the CJP protest held there on 02 October 2026.
To sum up, none of these viral videos shows the CJP protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park on 02 October 2026.

NEW DELHI: High drama unfolded in the heart of Delhi on Tuesday as INDIA bloc MPs marched towards the Election Commission demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.The day-long protest ended after Delhi Police detained Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, KC Venugopal, Amrinder Singh Raja Warring, Charanjit Singh Channi, and several other opposition MPs at Akashvani Bhavan, where they staged a sit-in after being denied a meeting with election officials.The protest was part of the INDIA bloc's wider campaign against the Election Commission over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.Opposition parties have accused the poll panel of disenfranchising eligible voters and have demanded Kumar's resignation. They have also sought the scrapping of the ongoing SIR exercise and the restoration of names they allege were wrongly deleted from electoral rolls.Here are the top developments from the opposition protest:
Rahul leads the march
Rahul Gandhi, along with several opposition leaders, began the march from Parliament towards the Election Commission headquarters, raising slogans of "Vote Chor, Gaddi Chhod" and carrying placards and cutouts of Gyanesh Kumar.
The protest route saw heavy security deployment, with barricades placed across central Delhi and Rapid Action Force personnel deployed around Transport Bhawan ahead of the march. Police stopped the opposition MPs near the NITI Aayog office.Rahul climbed atop heavy iron barricades near the NITI Aayog office and waved the Tricolour as he attempted to advance towards the EC headquarters.Tensions escalated as Delhi Police detained Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Congress general secretary KC Venugopal and several other INDIA bloc leaders near the NITI Aayog office.Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, Trinamool Congress leaders Abhishek Banerjee, Derek O'Brien and Mahua Moitra, and CPM MP John Brittas were among those put into police buses.
Rahul, Priyanka enter Akashvani Bhavan
The protest took an unexpected turn when Rahul and Priyanka walked into the nearby Akashvani Bhavan, shifting the protest away from the heavily secured route.As police began detaining INDIA bloc MPs and putting them into buses, Rahul spoke to his sister, who was seated inside one of the buses, before making his way towards the reception entrance of Akashvani Bhavan, catching several opposition MPs, including some from his own party, by surprise.At the entrance near gate number 3, Akashvani Bhavan staff initially tried to prevent Rahul Gandhi from entering, leading to a tense stand-off. He eventually entered the premises accompanied by his security personnel.Around 12.45 pm, Congress general secretary KC Venugopal and Rajya Sabha MP Pawan Khera reached the gate and sought entry. New Delhi deputy commissioner of police Sachin Sharma also arrived and held talks with the leaders, who were subsequently allowed inside.
Nine-hour sit in
After Rahul and other Congress leaders positioned themselves inside Akashvani Bhavan, mats were laid out and the sit-in began.While Rahul remained mostly seated, Priyanka Gandhi held talks with police officials.Refreshments were brought in for the protesters. Packets of potato chips, bhujiya and chocolates, along with water bottles and soft drinks, arrived from a kiosk outside NITI Aayog. Diet Coke was brought from Patel Chowk, while rolls arrived from Khan Chacha.Later, Srinivas was seen clearing used packets from the area where the leaders had gathered. Mosquito repellent was also brought inside in the evening.The crowd outside Akashvani Bhavan grew as Congress workers gathered and raised slogans in support of Rahul Gandhi.Around 2.30 pm, reporters pushed their microphones through the grille as Rahul spoke to them from inside the premises."I don't care what the BJP says. I am standing here to protect democracy," he said."What has been done to the country is treason. Be it PM Modi, Shah, the RSS chief or Gyanesh Kumar, none will be spared," Gandhi alleged.
BJP hits back
Amid the protest, the BJP held three press conferences and accused Congress and its allies of creating "anarchy" to "relaunch Rahul Gandhi".The BJP also accused Gandhi of being "kaamchor", alleging that he should work on the ground instead of accusing others of being "vote chor".Union minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan accused the INDIA bloc of "venting its frustration" over electoral defeats by making baseless allegations against constitutional bodies and attempting to malign their image.BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi criticised the opposition for what he called "theatrics on the streets" and questioned the Congress over its demand to provide voting rights without verification to those identified as "absent, shifted, dead and duplicate" voters.
Rahul, Priyanka detained
After several hours of protest, Delhi Police cleared the site and detained Rahul and Priyanka along with several opposition MPs, including Pawan Khera, KC Venugopal, Amrinder Singh Raja Warring, Derek O'Brien and Mahua Moitra.According to Delhi Police, around 260 individuals, including 10 Parliamentarirans, were detained and taken to various police stations in Delhi, where necessary legal action is being taken in their regard. The detainees were taken to New Police Lines at Kingsway Camp.Congress hit out at the Modi government, saying the action was a sign of a regime that "knows its exit is imminent"."Method of disenfranchising Indians has just become murder of democracy in India," Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said."The leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi has been dragged away from a peaceful sit-in protest that had a simple and straightforward demand - a meeting with the Election Commission of India," Ramesh said in a post on X."The Delhi Police that is controlled by the co-conspirator of the murder of democracy in India has arrested the leader of opposition in Lok Sabha and others. This is the sign of a regime that knows its exit is imminent," he added.
EC issues clarification
Meanwhile, the Election Commission said no political party had formally sought an appointment for a meeting with it."Earlier today, during the march of certain political parties towards the Election Commission, it was learnt through the media that some Members of Parliament wished to meet the Commission along with their delegation. With regard to today's developments, it is clarified that, till 4.00 PM today, no political party, through its representatives, had sought an appointment for a meeting with the Election Commission," the EC said in a statement.The poll panel said it subsequently learnt through Delhi Police that a delegation of MPs, led by leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, wanted to meet the Commission and submit a memorandum.The EC said its established procedure requires political parties or joint delegations to seek appointments through their authorised representatives. Meetings are then held at a mutually agreed time at the Commission's premises.
The poll panel said that after 4 pm, while it was considering the proposed meeting, Delhi Police informed it that the delegation comprised 240 MPs and wanted to meet at the Parliament House Annexe.The Commission termed the request "unusual" and said it could not be accepted because, under ECI protocol, meetings with political parties are held only at the Commission's premises.The INDIA bloc's protest was part of its wider campaign against the Election Commission over the SIR exercise. Opposition parties have accused the poll panel of disenfranchising eligible voters and have demanded Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.The bloc has also sought the scrapping of the current SIR exercise and restoration of names it alleges were wrongly deleted from electoral rolls.
Rohitashwa Ranjan is a digital journalist with The Times of India, where he decodes Indian politics as a carefully staged production with scripts, subtext and everything behind. His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength.
Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards.
In India, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons.
Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, in Portugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C, smashing many July records from previous decades.

A decade ago, actor Deepika Padukone said in an ad campaign: ‘My body, My choice.’ But, in reality, when it comes to older people, society often wrests that agency from them. Last week, as the world observed both International Day of Older Persons (October 1) and Gandhi Jayanti (October 2), Mumbai-based Sumira Roy’s documentary film Bhangaar (Obsolete), raised the question of dignity in death and the right to die for the elderly.
The yet-to-release Marathi film, which won the National Film Award for Best Non-Feature Film last month, was screened by the Kriti Film Club in Delhi NCR.
Bhangaar trains the lens on Narayan and Iravati Lavate, an octogenarian Maharashtrian childless couple, who petitioned for active euthanasia in 2018. Iravati succumbed to cancer in 2023, Narayan lives in an old-age home. His eyesight and memory, too, have deserted him. After the news of the National Award came in, Roy wanted to share the moment with Narayan. She rang up Prakash Joshi, the brother of Iravati, who also appears in the film. Joshi told her that due to Narayan’s present old-age health and impediments there of, nothing would register with man.
While Nilesh Maniyar and Shonali Bose’s documentary A Fly on the Wall (2024) is also on the same subject and travels with Chika Kapadia to Switzerland for his last days, Roy’s documentary shows how only privilege can afford that right.
Monisha Advani, Bhangaar’s producer and partner, Emmay Entertainment, calls the film personal, “My late mother was a Maharashtrian and while growing up, the frugality of my maternal grandparents’ lives somewhere was mirrored in the Lavates. Sumira has given me the opportunity, in a private way, to pay tribute to my familial pedagogy."
Excerpts from an interview with director Roy:
You are from an advertising background; how, when and why did you transition into filmmaking and documentary films at that?
Since I’ve been a student, I’ve been passionate about films and documentary films and had even sat for the FTII entrance examination. But the women in my family were against me going to Pune and feared the casting couch in the film industry. Years later, when I went to Japan for work, I did a postgraduate course in Japanese cinema, theatre and painting. I was just hooked on when I saw [films by Yasujirō] Ozu and all the greats there. So, I thought, there’s a roundabout way to do films through advertising films. There’s a great amount of discipline in ad films; you shoot minimally and you have only 30-40 seconds to tell your story. Ad films [at Ogilvy and JWT] also gave me a lot of exposure to a lot of things that you need in documentaries. For instance, understanding human behaviour. And then, in documentaries, I learnt how to listen… to people’s stories. I went on foreign location shoots and for post-production. All that’s helped me now. In 2011, I left advertising and started two agencies, mainly for production. I was a little bit jaded and cynical, trying to do these falsehoods to make people buy things they didn’t need.
Did the Central Board of Film Certification raise any objections in Bhangaar?
Only to the title. The censor board didn’t like the word bhangaar [obsolete] and called it insulting. I had to keep going back to explain to them that the word is what Narayan uses [in life and in the film]. It’s his, not mine. After some time, they agreed but asked me to carry a disclaimer in Marathi at the start of the film that this is the character’s interpretation of the title. That was fine by me.
There seems to be a thematic continuity between your documentaries Last DaysLast Shot (2017) and Bhangaar. Tell us about the earlier film.
I have an idea, and then I make a film. I don’t just go and make documentaries, because I’m not an activist or an investigative filmmaker. As Narayan says in the film [Bhangaar], the day you’re born is the beginning of death. He echoes the Myth of Sisyphus when he says there’s no purpose to life; it’s absurd. I am drawn to existentialism, and like diving into the interior of minds.
For my earlier film, I was interested in exploring the philosophy of moksha and nirvana. I went to Banaras [Hindu] University, and walked around in the gullies and ghats. People would pop out from the woods to say, ‘Come listen to my poem.’ There, I found a Bengali poet-artist who had gone to Japan and become famous. He returned to Varanasi with his Japanese wife [they ran the Kumiko Guest House]. By the time I shot him, he looked like Rabindranath Tagore. He was about 80 or 81. He told me his idea of moksha: to dissolve the ego. Then I met a 26-year-old Dom in Harishchandra Ghat cremation ground, who [told me he] hardly got a chance to light the fire, and couldn’t make money with it. So, he bought a camera and started shooting the relatives of the dead. He said from his experience that a good person’s corpse burns faster than a sinner’s.
What drew you to Iravati and Narayan Lavate’s story?
It’s a personal reason. My long-widowed mother was quite active in life. She’d drive, have a social life, her body and mind intact. A year before she passed away, she started saying, ‘I want to die with dignity.’ I was a documentary filmmaker, but I never listened to her nor asked her what she meant. I was petrified of her dying. [After] she passed away, I was stricken with grief and regret. I came across the Lavates’ story in Mid-Day; they asked for the right to die together with dignity. That struck me, and I went to meet them in their 12x12 room in a Mumbai chawl, to get closure for what I hadn’t done with my mother. They taught me so much about Marathi literature and theatre. Narayan looked like Picasso to me. He knew the Constitution by heart. I asked, how could they want to die. He said, ‘It’s time to go.’
They had this fixed spiel they would rattle to the media/news channels. They would do the same during our initial days of shoot. I just told them not to look at the camera and go about their days. I had to be a fly on the wall and filmed them over four years. Afterwards, they forgot there’s a camera. My DOP is brilliant because it was a boot camp for her, with no lights, no space to set up the camera. The aerial shot of them playing cards was shot from atop a washing machine.
In India, the elderly population is growing rapidly even as the birth rate declines. What did your research throw up about ageing and caregiving?
The elderly are growing three times faster than the population of the youth. Palliative care exists only for the rich. There’s no geriatric care and no focus on what is going to happen to the elderly population. All of us are in some stage of caregiving. We are either watching our parents or grandparents.
Gandhi spoke of self-rule. Swaraj is not just political self-rule but also the rule/autonomy over oneself. Does that idea of self-determination versus duty get complicated when it comes to an older person’s choice to die?
Loss of personhood and loss of autonomy, which older people fear, is exactly why they [Irawati and Narayan] asked for it [active euthanasia]. We do not connect with our families. Our conversations revolve around whether they have taken their medicines, if the oxygen tank is running low, if the nurse administered the injection. That’s our only conversation with them. The elderly feel like they are [outdated] machines. We have moved away from joint families to nuclear families. As a society, we have forgotten how to respect someone who has lived longer than expected. We keep talking about Gen Z and loneliness, but loneliness is far worse among the older generations. We hardly talk about it. Even our films don’t.
We’ve read about the Aruna Shanbaug case. This year, the Supreme Court gave its landmark judgment permitting passive euthanasia for Harish Rana who was in a vegetative state for over 13 years. What has been the impact of the Lavates’ petition?
Narayan and Iravati are the pioneers of this, at least in our country, or in South Asia. The courts are getting more and more petitions since. The press doesn’t cover many of these.
Bhangaar (Obsolete) screens on October 1 at the India Habitat Centre, Delhi, and on October 4 at Museo Camera, Gurugram at 4.30 pm.
