Shares in Skydance Media fell 3% on Tuesday, their first day of trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
The stock’s new ticker symbol, SKYD, is an update from PSKY, the one used for Paramount Global shares. Skydance stock finished the day at $9.51 and has pulled back 15% since the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery under the Skydance banner was first proposed last February. Historical comparisons are not exact, as the stock used to trade on the Nasdaq, though the context is considered valid by market watchers.
After an 11th hour delay over the summer due to antitrust lawsuits filed by 12 states and the Writers Guild of America, the $110 billion merger finally closed Tuesday morning before the trading day began. The combined company is starting off with $70 billion in pro-forma annual revenue and assets like CBS, HBO, CNN, Nickelodeon and the Warner and Paramount film and TV studios.
The deal initially saddles the company with $80 billion in debt, and the leverage ratio approaching seven times EBITDA has made some investors nervous. Credit ratings agency Fitch cut Skydance’s rating on Tuesday, citing the debt along with what it called “structural pressure on linear revenues, streaming competition and hit-driven content risk.”
Watch on Deadline
RedBird Capital founder and Skydance board member Gerry Cardinale has acknowledged the scale of the debt but has said he is “all in” on the deal, putting $4 billion into Skydance. He expects that the combined entity’s combination of intellectual property, proven brands and technology-forward strategy will combine to increase revenue despite industry headwinds. Cardinale reminded attendees at a Bloomberg conference in L.A. last week that he is “a growth guy.”
While CEO David Ellison and other executives met with employees on the Warner lot and were scheduled to mingle with the media at a press event across town at Paramount, the management team has not yet made a full pitch to Wall Street. Accordingly, Tuesday’s closing and “Day One” activities did not elicit an immediate wave of reports from analysts, who are poring over SEC filings and adjusting their estimates for the new company.

The director of films once considered too domestic for foreign export, Yasujiro Ozu (1903-1963) now sits high in the world cinematic pantheon. From his signature low camera angles to the “pillow” shots that serve as postcard-like pauses between scenes, his technique has been obsessively analyzed but remains sui generis.
That, however, is not the main subject of the splendid Daniel Raim documentary “The Ozu Diaries.” Drawing from Ozu’s journals and essays as well as other archival materials, it focuses more on the man and artist than his aesthetics.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.

On August 1, 2026, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari claimed that of the 27 lakh people whose names were deleted from the voter list after adjudication due to ‘logical discrepancy’, only seven lakh had filed appeals before the court-appointed appellate tribunals seeking inclusion in the electoral rolls.
Speaking at the launch of the Census self-enumeration exercise in Kolkata, he said, “Out of the 27 lakh people who were given an opportunity to approach the SIR tribunal, around seven lakh had applied. The rest have not submitted any application or appeal so far.”
The figure was reported by multiple media outlets which quoted the chief minister (1, 2, 3). Adhikari went on to link the failure to appeal with questions of citizenship, and citizenship with access to welfare, saying, “Until the entire process was completed, it would not be possible to determine whether those who had not made any claim as voters would later seek recognition as Indian citizens.” He added, “If someone is not a citizen of the country, they will not get benefits of any social scheme.”
Five days later, The Telegraph published the same seven-lakh figure, this time attributing it to an unnamed senior official of the West Bengal government. According to the report, the official said, “It has been found that only about 7 lakh of the 27 lakh voters excluded by the adjudicators for ‘logical discrepancies’ have appealed before the tribunals.” The official said the figure had emerged from a compilation of reports from various districts, and that the state authorities had no idea why the remaining 20 lakh had not appealed before the tribunals.
The Figure was Unverifiable at that Time
In August, the seven-lakh claim could not be independently verified against any official source because the Election Commission’s own disclosure did not provide a separate breakdown of appeals filed against the exclusion of voters. An RTI reply that disclosed the total number of appeals carried a footnote clarifying that the figure included both appeals against the inclusion of names in the electoral roll and appeals against exclusions.
The RTI was obtained by Isha Khan Choudhury, Congress MP from Dakshin Malda in West Bengal, and placed before the Supreme Court on August 24, 2026, during the hearing of a petition filed by Prasenjit Bose of the Congress and Derek O’Brien of the Trinamool Congress against the Election Commission of India.
During the hearing, Justice Joymalya Bagchi observed that the break-up of the appeals mattered since “it was exclusion which was causing an immediate violation of a person’s rights.” The bench consequently directed the ECI to provide a separate account of the appeals, specifying how many were pending before the tribunals and segregating appeals relating to voters who had been excluded or included, as well as cross-appeals.
The ECI submitted this segregation on September 16.
ECI Numbers Refute Adhikari’s Claim
According to the latest affidavit filed by the ECI before the Supreme Court on September 16, 2026, of the more than 38.31 lakh appeals filed, over 22 lakh were filed against exclusion by voters whose names had been excluded or deleted, while more than 16 lakh were filed against inclusion.
Of the more than 38 lakh appeals filed, only 1.26 lakh had been decided by that date. Annexure R/1 to the ECI’s affidavit provides a district-wise break-up of the total appeals submitted to the appellate tribunals and is reproduced below.
It must be noted that the total number of appeals filed, as mentioned in the ECI’s affidavit (38,31,429), does not match the total number of appeals submitted in Annexure R/1 (38,29,926). The discrepancy is 1,503 appeals. Nevertheless, the outcome-wise data provided in the annexure shows that 8,649 appeals resulted in exclusion from the electoral roll, while 1,13,943 resulted in inclusion. In other words, nearly 93% of the appeals that had been decided resulted in the elector being included in the electoral roll.
Did the Claims Accumulate after the CM’s Statement? No
One may argue that the chief minister spoke on August 1, while the Commission filed its figure in the Supreme Court on September 16, leaving enough time for appeals to have accumulated in the intervening period. The available data, however, allows this possibility to be tested directly, because appeal totals are available for both dates. On August 7, 2026, six days after the chief minister’s statement and a day after The Telegraph report, the tribunals already had 38,10,620 appeals, according to an RTI response from the ECI to Isha Khan Choudhury, Congress MP for Dakshin Malda. By September 10, 2026, the figure stood at 38,29,926, according to the district-wise report annexed to the Commission’s affidavit. Thus, the total number of appeals increased by just 19,306 across the entire state during this period.
In the light of the latest revelations made by an Indian Express investigation, which have raised serious questions about the functioning of the Election Commission of India and chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, the seven-lakh claim takes on an even greater significance.
To sum up, Suvendu Adhikari’s claim on August 1 that out of some 27 lakh electors placed under adjudication and subsequently excluded from the electoral roll, only seven lakh had appealed against their exclusion is difficult to reconcile with the data that was already available at the time. The ECI has made it clear that the number is around 22 lakh. The discrepancy assumes greater significance given that Manoj Agarwal, the then chief electoral officer of West Bengal who oversaw the SIR process, is now the Bengal’s chief secretary.

Jagtar Singh Johal, a British Sikh man who was arrested in India in 2017 in connection with alleged terrorism offences, has been granted bail by a Delhi court.
Johal, from Scotland, was arrested for his alleged role in funding the Khalistan Liberation Force, which had carried out targeted killings in India’s Punjab region.
His full trial has been repeatedly deferred by the authorities in the federal court but largely similar conspiracy charges were dismissed by a court in Punjab last year. Throughout his detention the prosecution has failed to produce verifiable evidence, leading to the deferred hearings.
Johal, now 39, travelled to India to marry his fiancee in late 2017. On 4 November, three weeks after the wedding, the couple were shopping with a relative in the Punjab city of Jalandhar when a group of men took Johal from his car, placed a black hood over his head and put him in an unmarked vehicle. He claims he was then denied access to a lawyer and tortured in an attempt to extract a confession. A question remains over whether he was arrested following a tip-off from British intelligence services.
Commenting on Friday’s ruling, Johal’s Scotland-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “The past two years has been an expensive rollercoaster, contesting bails at the supreme court and back to the high court. I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison. We have waited so long and fought so hard for this moment.”
He added of previous hearings: “Whenever the evidence against Jagtar is tested in court, judges find what we’ve said all along, which is that there isn’t any.
“How long will this sick joke of a legal process be allowed to continue? We’re obviously delighted that Jagtar will soon be released, but he won’t be truly free until he is back in Dumbarton, with his wife and family.”
Gurpreet Johal, who also lives in Dumbarton, has lobbied a succession of UK foreign secretaries, who have repeatedly admitted the case has dragged on too long, but have been reluctant to call publicly for his release on the grounds that they should not interfere in the judiciary of another country.
The UK government recently appointed Alistair Burt as a special envoy for complex consular cases and he has met Gurpreet Johal in Scotland to discuss the case.
Dan Dolan, the deputy executive director of Reprieve, one of the organisation’s fighting for Johal’s release, said: “While this judgment is welcome as Jagtar should not be in prison a day longer, we must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way. The conditions attached are likely to be onerous. We must also remember that Jagtar will still be facing the death penalty in eight cases against him, despite these cases essentially duplicating trumped-up charges on which he has already been fully acquitted.”
Chris Esdaile, a senior legal adviser to Redress, another organisaiton representing Johal, said granting bail “can’t undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention”.
He added: “The need for accountability for the allegations of torture and the deeply flawed proceedings against Jagtar remains urgent.”
Johal’s lawyers said they were still awaiting the details of what would happen next in relation to posting bail terms. While the judges’ order was that Jagtar should be released on bail, he remained in custody while judges confirmed his bail conditions, which may be stringent. The court must also confirm the sums of money that must be posted as a bond.

The Keralam government’s announcement that it will make private health care more “affordable” through consultations with the private health sector, and that a Bill in this regard was in the offing, should be seen against the State’s seven-year legal battle before the Kerala High Court upheld the Kerala Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulations) Act 2018, throwing out all objections raised by private hospitals.
The KCE Act was the first ever attempt made in the State to bring the entire health sector, public and private, under a regulatory framework.
But the Act was systematically opposed and its implementation stalled at every turn by the private health sector in the State.
It was in November last year that the Kerala High Court threw out all objections raised by the Kerala Private Hospitals’ Association (KPHA) and the Indian Medical Association (IMA) and upheld the validity of the Act.
Contentious area
Unlike the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 (Central Act 23 of 2010), which attempted to cap the treatment/procedure/diagnostic rates charged by the private health sector by fixing a price range, the KCE Act had not touched this contentious area at all.
The KCE Act just insisted on mandatory registration of all clinical establishments under all systems of medicines (including hospitals, clinics and laboratories) and that every establishment maintain certain minimum standards based on the category in which they fall. It also said that hospitals display their rates for various procedures openly so that there is transparency.
However, the private health sector argued that it violated rights under Article 14 and Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
Appeal in SC
Even after the High Court specifically held that KCE Act’s Section 16 (mandatory registration of clinical establishments), Section 39 (display of fee rates and package rates for services) and Section 47 (obligations concerning life-saving treatment/emergency care and safe transfer of patients) were constitutionally valid and gave directives to the government to implement the Act without delay, KPHA went in appeal to the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court has not stayed the KCE Act, but granted members of the petitioning associations interim protection against coercive action by the government.
Yet to register
Kerala Clinical Establishments Council, which is responsible for the implementation of the Act, maintains that the registration process is continuing and that even now, many clinical establishments are yet to register themselves under the council.
Small hospitals with up to 15 beds have been given some concessions by the council, trimming down the checklist for assessment to just basic and essential points, so that at least the basic registration brings these establishments too within the regulatory framework.
The government’s efforts to draft a new Bill to bring in a regulatory framework that “protects patients’ interests while taking into account the operating costs and practical difficulties of private hospitals” is well-intentioned, but the fact remains that the private health sector is still holding out against the KCE Act at the Supreme Court.
Questions are also being raised whether a new legislation is in order or if the costing regulations can be incorporated into the KCE Act itself.
‘Entirely welcome’
Meanwhile, public health activists like B. Ekbal have stated that any attempt by the government to regulate the treatment expenditure in the private sector and save people from catastrophic health expenditure is entirely welcome.
Dr. Ekbal said that though private hospitals are an essential component of the health system, health care cannot be left entirely to market logic. It is the government’s responsibility to regulate the sector adequately so that patients are not exploited.
In a statement here, Dr. Ekbal said that the Standard Treatment Guidelines (STGs) should be insisted on and that the government initiate a scientific cost evaluation of various medical and diagnostic procedures and treatments so that a rational and transparent rate list suited to the State can be evolved.

Enterprise software major ServiceNow is betting that its next leg of growth in India will come not just from digitisation of IT functions, but from enterprises putting AI to work across business processes, even as the rush to adopt the technology creates a parallel challenge around governance, security and identity. At its World Forum in India on Tuesday, October 6, ServiceNow announced AI Workflow Factory and Autonomous Engineer, two products aimed at helping enterprises identify where AI can improve work and then build, run and extend AI-powered workflows across the organisation. The launches come at a time when Indian enterprises are moving beyond AI experimentation, with CIOs increasingly looking at how to deploy the technology across customer experience, employee operations, software development and business processes. For ServiceNow, that creates an opportunity to move beyond its traditional identity as an IT service management company and position itself as the layer through which enterprises orchestrate AI across their existing technology stack. But the company is also betting that as AI becomes more deeply embedded into enterprises, security and governance will become inseparable from the adoption story. ServiceNow’s India AI Push Moves Beyond Pilots ServiceNow’s India strategy rests on three interconnected opportunities: domestic enterprises, global capability centres (GCCs) and its large technology partner ecosystem, ServiceNow India tech and business centre head Sumeet Mathur said in an interview with Inc42. The company has been expanding beyond its traditional strength in IT service management, with ambitions to become an “enterprise operating system” spanning IT, HR, customer service, finance, supply chain, legal and workplace operations. AI is now becoming the connective tissue across these functions. The company is seeing a growing willingness among Indian CIOs and CISOs to explore disruptive AI use cases rather than simply run small pilots. “The willingness is very high, and once you start to open your mind that I want to use this piece of technology in 10 different ways, then of course the problems are very visible,” Mathur said. That appetite, however, is running ahead of the governance structures needed to deploy AI safely. A ServiceNow AI maturity assessment cited by the company found that only 22% of Indian enterprises have AI testing, auditing and risk-assessment processes in place. Amit Zavery, president, COO and chief product officer at ServiceNow, said on the sidelines of the event that governance cannot become an excuse for delaying AI adoption but needs to be built into the process early. “It just slows you down enough to run faster later. If you’re going to run faster without any kind of brakes around it, it will crash,” Zavery said. The distinction is becoming increasingly important as enterprises move from individual AI experiments to multiple deployments across an organisation. The question is no longer simply whether an AI application works, but whether it can be governed, monitored and scaled without creating new operational or security risks. From IT Workflows To An Enterprise Operating System ServiceNow’s pitch is that enterprises do not need another standalone AI application. They need a layer that can connect AI models, existing applications, data and workflows. AI Workflow Factory is designed to help enterprises identify opportunities where AI can improve workflows and then build and operate those workflows. Autonomous Engineer, meanwhile, brings more autonomous capabilities into software development, including planning, building and testing. The proposition addresses one of the biggest problems emerging as companies scale AI: fragmentation. Enterprises building AI applications often have to stitch together different models, data sources, applications and workflows. They also have to manage changes when models are updated or prompts and underlying systems change. AI Workflow Factory brings more of that lifecycle onto a common platform, including building, deployment, governance and ongoing management. The broader ambition is to make ServiceNow the operating layer through which enterprises can introduce AI into existing business processes without having to rip out their existing technology infrastructure. This is also where ServiceNow believes it can differentiate itself from hyperscalers and model providers. Microsoft, Google and AWS can provide infrastructure and AI models, while companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic provide frontier models. ServiceNow, however, wants to sit one layer above these technologies, connecting them to the enterprise systems where work actually happens. AI Agents Create A New Identity Problem That strategy becomes more complicated as enterprises move from generative AI assistants to autonomous AI agents. Today, many enterprise agents still operate on behalf of a human. But as agents begin interacting directly with email, CRM systems, databases and other enterprise applications, the identity and access problem becomes significantly more complex. An AI agent could initiate another agent, access sensitive data and execute an action without a human manually intervening at every step. “The hardest problem I believe for agentic AI to become a reality is identity,” said Tarun Thakur, cofounder and CEO of identity security startup Veza, which ServiceNow acquired earlier this year. Veza was founded around the problem of understanding not just who an employee is, but what that identity can actually access across an enterprise’s applications and systems. Its Access Graph maps identities, permissions and relationships across enterprise systems, giving security teams visibility into effective permissions rather than simply relying on roles and groups. ServiceNow historically had extensive visibility into enterprise assets through its configuration management database (CMDB), but lacked the same depth of access context. The Veza acquisition brings those two pieces closer together — what an enterprise has and who or what can access it. That becomes particularly important as the definition of an “identity” changes. “Agent identity is ephemeral — it comes and goes,” Thakur said, pointing to a future where enterprises could have large numbers of temporary machine identities being created and removed as AI agents perform specific tasks. ServiceNow has also integrated Veza into its broader security portfolio, while using its AI Control Tower to help enterprises discover and manage AI agents across their technology environment. The company believes AI security could eventually become a significant new cybersecurity category as enterprises move towards more autonomous systems. The India AI Opportunity The AI opportunity also gives ServiceNow a broader opening in India than its traditional IT-service customer base. India is home to more than 2,100 GCCs employing around 2.35 Mn people, according to Mathur. These centres are increasingly responsible for technology, product development, cybersecurity and global technology decisions for their parent companies. For ServiceNow, that means the India opportunity can extend beyond selling to Indian businesses. GCCs can also influence technology decisions made for global organisations. The company’s partner ecosystem further strengthens that position. Mathur said around 30,000 engineers are working on ServiceNow in India across major system integrators including Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG and EY. BFSI remains among the company’s strongest verticals in India, while healthcare and life sciences, consumer and retail and the public sector are also important markets. Interestingly, in July, ServiceNow’s venture arm invested $40 Mn in Delhi NCR-headquartered BUSINESSNEXT, which sells software to banks, insurers and other financial institutions. Betting On The Orchestration Layer The larger strategic question is whether ServiceNow can establish itself as the control and orchestration layer as enterprises adopt AI from multiple vendors. The company is not trying to own the underlying AI models. Instead, it is building an open platform that can work with different frontier, open-weight and domain-specific models. Zavery said customers ultimately care about the outcome rather than which model powers a particular task. ServiceNow therefore tests different models and can route workloads depending on the task, performance and economics. That model-agnostic approach could become increasingly important as enterprises seek to avoid being locked into a single AI provider. ServiceNow is also competing in a market where Microsoft, Google, AWS and Salesforce increasingly position themselves as orchestration or control layers for enterprise AI. According to Mathur, ServiceNow’s advantage comes from its existing position across enterprise workflows. “ServiceNow was always a platform company,” he said, arguing that its role is to coordinate different systems and business processes rather than own every underlying technology. That positioning is increasingly extending into cybersecurity as well. ServiceNow’s security business was already generating more than $1 Bn in annual contract value globally before its recent acquisitions, according to Mathur, and the company is now seeking to build a much larger cybersecurity franchise around identity, vulnerabilities, incident response, OT/IoT and AI security. The Veza acquisition therefore fits into the same broader thesis: as more AI agents enter the enterprise, ServiceNow wants visibility into not just the applications and workflows they interact with, but the identities and permissions behind them. For Indian enterprises, the next phase of AI adoption could therefore shift the question from what AI can do to what AI can do inside their organisation, especially at scale. That is the gap ServiceNow is betting its India strategy can fill.

Kenyan prisoners play chess for fun behind bars and to help with rehabilitation
Kenya’s Department for Correctional Services has introduced chess across the country’s prisons since 2024, in one of the most prominent institutional carceral chess programs in Africa
MURANG'A, Kenya -- The black-and-white stripes of Brian Gatonye’s prison uniform match the pieces staring back at him from the chessboard at Kenya's Maranjau Prison.
The 27-year-old has served about 18 months of a three-year sentence for assault and is due to be released in November 2027.
During a break in the prison yard, he considers his next move: a pawn, perhaps, or a knight. The break isn't long, but if he finishes the game quickly he may have time to face one of the skilled guards.
But it is unwise to rush or act impulsively — in chess as in life, he has learned.
“Chess has taught me a lot,” Gatonye said. “It has taught me (about) being calm, choosing my decisions wisely. Before doing an act, I have to think first of what the repercussions are — and then I move.”
Gatonye is among a growing number of Kenyan prisoners who have taken up chess in recent years. The game has become part of rehabilitation programs in the country’s prisons, where officials and participants say it encourages patience, problem-solving and interaction between prisoners and guards.
At Maranjau, which holds about 450 prisoners according to Superintendent Humphrey Young, some choose chess over resting or playing soccer during their free time. They are drawn by the competition and what they say the game does for their state of mind.
“Chess has become one of our integral programs,” Young said. “Some of the skills chess teaches our offenders as they reintegrate back to society is how they can improve their problem-solving processes, and how they can think around issues that affect them once they’re out.”
Chess programs have operated in some Kenyan prisons since at least 2022. The government has supported the initiative alongside the International Chess Federation, known as FIDE, Chess Kenya and The Gift of Chess, a nonprofit organization that distributes chess sets.
The game is now played in all 134 prisons in Kenya, according to Phylis Ngigi, global outreach director for The Gift of Chess.
Kenya participated for the first time in FIDE’s Intercontinental Online Chess Championship for Prisoners in 2024. Competitions are also held between Kenyan prisons, while some guards have been trained as chess coaches and play alongside prisoners.
At Maranjau, Young said the games create opportunities for prisoners and guards to interact in a less formal setting.
Supporters say chess offers more than recreation. Responsibility and the ability to work with others are important elements of prison rehabilitation, said Monica Njoroge, a project officer at Resources Oriented Development Initiatives.
The Kenyan nonprofit runs farming programs in prisons, where participants tend communal gardens while learning agricultural skills that could help them find work after their release.
Njoroge is not involved in the chess program, but she frequently visits Maranjau and has watched prisoners play.
“It is a game that trains patience and also having a clear mind in making decisions, being keen on what your next move is and the consequences that will come,” she said.
Kenya’s prison chess program has not been independently studied, and its long-term effects on behavior or reoffending are unknown.
For the prisoners gathered around the boards at Maranjau, there is a simpler attraction: They enjoy the game.
“It is a social game,” said Edwin Raj Walukaya, a 31-year-old prisoner. “It gives us friends and occupies our minds.”
For Gatonye, chess has become something he hopes to carry with him beyond prison.
“After being released, I hope to continue playing chess,” he said. “It brings peace inside my mind and heart.”

Can You Use Lobby Hacks to Get the Crystal Candy Axe in Fortnite for Free?
No, there’s no Fortnite Lobby Hack available at the moment that you can redeem to get the Crystallized Punisher Pickaxe or Crystal Candy Axe in Fortnite.

A ‘Wall of Hope’, a youth-led initiative by the Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF) and its Department of Youth Mental Health, was unveiled at the IIT-Madras Research Park in Taramani on Saturday, a press release said.
With young people facing increasing mental health challenges and suicide remaining concern, creating spaces for expression, connection, resilience, and help-seeking is vital.
The mental health campaign, which began on October 10, 2025, encourages young people aged 10-25 to express, share, and reflect upon their personal reasons for living, through brief messages of hope.
Adolescents and young adults across the country were invited to write the purpose of life on colourful post-it notes.
The activity is completely youth-led through peer leaders and trainer modules, where young people played a central role in leading and facilitating the campaign.
More than 20,000 responses from across six States have been collected.
Additionally, 400 volunteers have been trained to conduct this activity, which is voluntary and anonymous, to initiate and foster conversations around mental health.
Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, Madras High Court judge, and Lakshmi Vijayakumar, founder of suicide prevention organisation SNEHA, participated in the event, besides SCARF vice-chairperson R. Thara and director Sridhar Vaitheswaran.
(Assistance for overcoming suicidal thoughts is available on the State’s health helpline 104, Tele-MANAS 14416, and Sneha’s suicide prevention helpline 044-24640050)

The Diabetic Foot Society of India (DFSI), under the aegis of its national president V.B. Narayanamurthy, has written to Zulfiqarali G. Abbas, president of the Pan-African Diabetic Foot Study Group (PADFSG), proposing the formation of a global alliance on diabetic foot survival and limb preservation.
The letter, a copy of which was shared with The Hindu, notes that diabetic foot ulceration is an under-recognised cause of premature death, major amputation, recurrent illness, disability, and social exclusion. Available evidence shows that its five-year mortality is comparable to that of some cancers. And yet, global investment, policy attention, organised pathways, and post-amputation support remain substantially below the scale of the problem, the letter notes.
The DFSI, therefore, has proposed that institutions, including itself, King’s College London, International Association of Diabetic Foot Surgeons, D-Foot International, American Limb Preservation Society, Federation of International Podiatrists, and PADFSG, come together to form a Global Alliance for Diabetic Foot Survival and Limb Preservation, to create a sustained, scientific, and policy platform for prevention, limb preservation, improved survival, rehabilitation, surveillance, research, and engagement with governments and the World Health Organization (WHO).
The letter further stated that DFSI would announce the shared intention to form the Alliance at its next national conference, slated to be held on October 2, 2026. This, it said, would be an announcement of intent rather than a representation that the Alliance had been legally constituted or that any institution had accepted a financial or contractual obligation.
The letter urged the PADFSG to provide in-principle concurrence with the formation of the Alliance and the proposed conference announcement.
Apart from the proposal for the alliance, the letter also contained a draft Joint Global Declaration for joint consultation and unveiling, and asked for comments on the proposal and draft declaration from the PADFSG.
The DAFSI also stated that subject to the PADFSG’s concurrence, it proposed to convene the first founding meeting of the Alliance within 30 days of its conference.
The proposal
The proposal noted that the Alliance would provide a common platform for scientific leadership, policy advocacy, regional demonstration programmes, and responsible resource mobilisation. Its objectives would include advocacy with the WHO and national governments to secure explicit recognition of diabetic foot disease as an important medical condition; to improve survival and quality of life through multi-disciplinary care and patient-centred research; to promote prevention, early detection, and rapid referral; to advance surveillance and support the development of registries; to strengthen post-amputation rehabilitation; to promote research and training programmes; and to ensure the meaningful participation of people living with diabetes in governance and programme design.
The proposal also detailed membership and governance, standing bodies, the Secretariat, proposed activities of the Alliance, donor engagement, and financial management, as well as a performance framework and a risks safeguard.
The declaration
The draft declaration called for diabetic foot disease to be recognised as a major cause of premature death, disability, and exclusion. It called upon the WHO Director-General, regional directors, and member states to make diabetic foot prevention, limb preservation and survival a visible part of diabetes policy, establish common indicators and baseline registries, and support flagship programmes in at least two WHO regions.
It also proposed a goal to reduce risk-adjusted five-year mortality after a new diabetic foot ulcer by 30%, and potentially avoidable major amputations by 50% by 2030.
The draft declaration called for coordinated action that keeps people alive, mobile, included, and able to live with dignity.

White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
- Published
Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego has sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly worded rebuttal from the White House.
California Governor Gavin Newsom condemned the comment - made by Trump at a campaign rally in Nebraska - as "deranged and dangerous," while LA Mayor Karen Bass described them as threats and an attempt to "encourage attacks on American lives".
According to the White House, however, Trump was saying that American cities would have been threatened by Iran had he not launched a war there earlier this year.
Both LA and San Diego house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.
Trump, while speaking on Monday in Nebraska about the Iran conflict, said: "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego."
There were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made.
The morning after Trump's statement, Governor Newsom announced that the "dangerous - if not treasonous" statement had prompted him to direct California's State Threat Assessment Center to "monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the remarks as an invitation" to target California.
The agency is designed to detect and prevent security threats in the state.
San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote that the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his "reckless war talk".
Trump is yet to respond to the statements made by California's leaders.
In a post on X, White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung described the "media freakout" over Trump's comments as "not rooted in reality".
"He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung wrote. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money".
The president and other administration officials often claim that disrupting Iran's nuclear programme was essential for US national security, and that any issues that have stemmed from the conflict were necessary.
A separate X post, from the official White House rapid response account, described journalists from the Los Angeles Times reporting on the comments as "buffoons" and again pushed back on the characterisation of the comments by Newsom and others.
"He was saying the US is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance," the account added.
San Diego, located 17 miles (27km) from the border with Mexico, is the eighth largest city in the US and is home to Naval Base San Diego, the home port of the US Navy's Pacific Fleet, and Naval Amphibious Base Coronado - the main training centre Navy Seals on the West Coast.
It is also where Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton is located, a base which 70,000 service members and civilians work at.
Located approximately 120 miles (193 KM) north of San Diego, Los Angeles is the second most populous city in the US.
It is home to the space system command headquarters of the US Space Force, as well as the Los Angeles Air Force Base.
This not the first time the US president and California governor, who may run for president in 2028, have publicly clashed.
Last year Trump described him as incompetent, saying he had failed to adequately respond after some of the Los Angeles anti-immigration enforcement protests turned violent.
Newsom accused Trump of a "brazen abuse of power" after military personnel were deployed to secure federal buildings during those protests.
Earlier this year, Trump mocked Newsom's dyslexia, saying presidents should not have learning disabilities, which led to criticism from dyslexia charities.

In October 2026, a screenshot of an alleged post from U.S. President Donald Trump's Truth Social account spread online, showing Trump seemingly thanking billionaire Elon Musk for artificially increasing Republican votes ahead of the November 2026 midterms.
The purported post (archived) stated:
Republicans must WIN the 2026 Midterm Elections, and we must use every appropriate tool—Whether you vote early, absentee, by mail, or in-person, we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dummods with massive turnout! THANKS TO THE GREAT ELON MUSK EVERY REPUBLICAN VOTE COUNTS AS 3 VOTES! SO IMPORTANT - PLEASE GET OUT AND VOTE, AND MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! President Donald J. Trump
(@realDonaldTrump on Truth Social)
The above post is a doctored version of a real Truth Social post from Trump's account. The yellow highlighted line about Musk was edited into the post. As such, we rate this image as fake.
On Oct. 3, 2026, Trump wrote (archived) the following post on Truth Social. The fake highlighted line about Musk was added after "we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dumocrats with massive turnout!":
Republicans must WIN the 2026 Midterm Elections, and we must use every appropriate tool — Whether you vote early, absentee, by mail, or in-person, we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dumocrats with massive turnout! SO IMPORTANT — PLEASE GET OUT AND VOTE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP
swampthevoteusa.com/
(@realDonaldTrump on Truth Social)
The post in the screenshot is clearly edited, based on the nonsense phrase "Dummods" which appears to be a garbled version of "Dumocrats."
Snopes also looked up variations of the phrase on Trump's Truth, a website that archives his posts "every few minutes" and makes it easier to find them — including deleted posts. There was no evidence of Trump thanking Musk on Truth Social for making "every Republican vote" count as three votes.
Trump has been speaking at campaign rallies nationwide, trying to drum up support for Republican candidates ahead of the November 2026 midterm elections.

Keralam Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan’s statement at a recent function about avoiding unnecessary angioplasty seems to have stirred a hornets’ nest with many doctors objecting to the “generalised statement,” while some lone voices pointed out that Mr. Satheesan was 100% right and that unnecessary procedures had become the norm.
In a Facebook post, Rajesh Gopalan Nair, Professor and Head of Cardiology at the Government Medical College Hospital, Kozhikode, had appreciated Mr. Satheesan “for pointing out a truth.” But it set off an avalanche of comments from the doctors and public, with the latter narrating their harrowing experiences in hospitals and appreciating Dr. Rajesh for calling a spade a spade, while many doctors expressed disappointment at Dr. Rajesh’s stand.
Dr. Rajesh, however, made it clear in his post that a person coming into the emergency with a suspected heart attack should in no way distrust the doctor, for the situation may call for an immediate angioplasty.
Second opinion
He also explained clearly the situations when one could afford to wait and seek a second opinion, if angioplasty was suggested to a patient. He also cautioned the public against looking at every doctor or hospital with suspicion. Angioplasty should definitely be done when it is clinically indicated and these situations are clearly documented, he said.
Even though much of the medical fraternity expressed their displeasure at the “unsubstantiated” statement of the Chief Minister and the support that unexpectedly seemed to have come from one of their own, Dr. Rajesh refused to be cowed down. He maintained that he stood by his position that some of the angioplasty procedures done in hospitals were indeed not warranted.
On Monday, the Interventional Cardiology Council of Kerala (ICCK) said in a statement here that public’s apprehension over “unnecessary” medical procedures should not delay life-saving treatment during a heart attack emergency.
Responding to the Chief Minister’s remarks on avoiding unnecessary investigations and angioplasty, the council said it supported evidence-based and ethical medical practice and the principle that every intervention must have a clear clinical indication.
ICCK president Rajesh T. said that public discussion on angioplasty should clearly differentiate between elective intervention in stable patients and primary angioplasty during an acute heart attack, where treatment is highly time-sensitive.
What the data show
According to Statewide ICCK registry data presented at the council’s last annual conference, more than 70% of angioplasties performed in Kerala involved acute and emergency clinical situations.
He said the council welcomed any discussion aimed at strengthening evidence-based care, transparency and public confidence in the health-care system. “In stable patients, there is usually greater scope for detailed evaluation and for deciding whether medicines, further assessment or intervention would offer the greatest benefit. In an acute heart attack, however, delay can have serious consequences,” ICCK said.
However, the council cautioned that a general atmosphere of mistrust surrounding cardiac procedures could have unintended consequences, particularly when a patient develops severe chest pain or other symptoms suggestive of a heart attack.

Rival clubs want range of punishments for Man City
- Published
A number of Premier League clubs want Manchester City to be hit with both "retrospective punishments" and sanctions for the future for their mass financial rule-breaking, sources have told BBC Sport.
An independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.
City have appealed against the verdict.
However, there is said to be a consensus among a group of top-flight club executives that if City's appeal is unsuccessful, the sanctions should make reparations for the period when they broke the rules, while also limiting their powers in future.
There is also a feeling from at least four Premier League boardrooms that a "one-hit" points deduction resulting in relegation to the Championship would be an insufficient punishment given the severity of City's wrongdoing.
There is understood to be nuance in exactly what clubs consider a fitting penalty for the eight-time Premier League champions, who were found guilty of all serious financial rule breaches in a damning verdict by an independent commission.
One senior club source said City should be stripped of their titles, and added there was "no great rush" among clubs to push for the redistribution of trophies, but rather to take honours away and leave them vacant.
The source warned the credibility of the Premier League would be lost if City were allowed to keep the eight major trophies they won during the period they have been found guilty.
However, in a sign of a range of opinions across the league, BBC Sport was previously told there was little appetite among other clubs for City to be stripped of titles.
Regarding the timescale for sanctions in the future, there is a concern among club executives that a sanction applied just to one season would merely provide City with a "bump in the road" given the likelihood of them returning to the Premier League at the first time of asking.
A number of Premier League figures therefore believe any points deduction should be split over multiple seasons, while there is also a sense that transfer bans that stretch over a number of windows would also significantly hinder City's ability to regain their top-flight status as quickly as possible.

One club source also said it would be "bizarre, almost obtuse" if City were able to trade in the upcoming January transfer window, if this process is ongoing and sanctions have not been applied.
Some clubs cited feeling "in the dark" regards the Premier League, including around the chronology and timescales of the appeal and the sanctions hearing.
However, sources said there was "empathy" and "understanding" about the difficult position the Premier League is in, given the gravity of this situation and the ongoing legal process.
Regarding financial reparations, one idea that has been mooted - and which a club source found "merit" in - was to apply a "tariff-based system", whereby City's past league finishing positions would be altered via a points deduction.
Rival clubs could then be paid compensation by City based on where they would have finished versus where they did finish.
BBC Sport understands Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca will speak to players collectively after they arrive back from international duty on Thursday, before their Premier League match against Liverpool on Sunday (16:30 BST).
The trip to Anfield is their first game since news of the verdict broke.
Merseyside Police says it has received queries in relation to the match, and when asked by BBC Sport if any special measures would be put in place the force said it will have "an appropriate policing operation in place on the day".
Sources at Liverpool have told BBC Sport it is a case of "business as usual" and there are no extra measures being put in place. Conversations and meetings between the club, supporters and relevant authorities take place before every home game.
One source said while everyone "has the right to express their feelings" they hoped supporters would not overstep the mark.

A video showing Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that he said Major Rajendra Pratap drank cow urine for 40 days to quench his thirst during the 1965 India-Pakistan war and urged modern soldiers to continue the practice. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth stated that Major Rajendra Pratap drank cow urine for 40 days to quench his thirst during the 1965 India-Pakistan war and urged modern soldiers to continue the practice.
Fact: The viral video has been digitally altered. The original footage shows COAS General Dhiraj Seth visiting a mega cataract surgery camp in Tangdhar, Kupwara district, where he interacted with patients and army veterans. The audio promoting the consumption of cow urine was not part of the original video and has been falsely attributed to him. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led to reports from several media outlets with similar visuals (here, here, here, here). According to the descriptions, the video shows Chief of the Army Staff (COAS) General Dhiraj Seth visiting a mega cataract surgery camp organised by the Indian Army in Tangdhar, Kupwara district. He is also seen interacting with patients and army veterans.
After verifying these reports, we could not find any mention of General Dhiraj Seth talking about cow urine during his interaction with patients or army veterans.
Further, we analysed the audio using AI detection tools Hiya and Resemble AI, which indicated that the audio is likely AI-generated and may involve voice impersonation.
We also found that on 27 September 2026, the Indian Army’s official Fact Check handle clarified that the video had been digitally altered. It stated that genuine footage of the Army Chief had been manipulated and falsely attributed to fictitious statements that were unrelated to the original event.
To sum up, this video showing COAS General Dhiraj Seth promoting the consumption of cow urine has been digitally manipulated.

Torrential rain and potentially damaging flooding are forecast in eastern Spain over the coming days, as cold upper air moves over the warm, humid surface air of the Mediterranean Sea, fuelling violent, slow-moving thunderstorms near Spain’s east coast. The weather pattern, known as a Dana, occurs most often in autumn.
Models show more than 100mm of rain could fall across the region on Friday, with 200-300mm possible in some areas. Cities including Valencia and Castelló de la Plana, are most at risk. Valencia has experienced several damaging floods in recent years. Catalonia has now put three towns under lockdown and Valencia has shut schools for nearly half a million children.
Meanwhile, heavy rainfall in Nepal last week resulted in 542 disaster incidents and left 27 people dead between 24 and 27 September, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Of the recorded incidents, 304 were related to landslides while 87 were linked to flooding.
During this extremely wet period, 186 meteorological sites recorded more than 100mm of rainfall, with Dedhgaun, in Lumbini province, recording 544.2mm. Nearly a million people received SMS flood warnings, and 2,000 people living in high-risk areas were relocated.
This heavy rainfall also affected the Gandak River in Bihar, north-east India, which reached a record water level of 91.25 metres on Tuesday, 0.35m metres above the previous record, set only in 2024, according to the water resources department. So far, 169 seepage points along the embankments have been repaired, with teams deployed across several sites along the river as the embankments continue to face heavy water pressure.
Strong winds, heavy rainfall and coastal flooding have hit the north-east US as a very deep area of low pressure developed into a nor’easter on Saturday. Such storms are named due to the north-easterly winds typically affecting coastal areas. This was the first nor’easter of the autumn and winter season, bringing gusts of up to 74mph (119km/h) and waves rising to 3 metres.
The storm left approximately 200,000 people without power, inundated the streets of New York City and killed one person when a tree fell in Brooklyn. However, the storm also uncovered a piece of history as the wreckage from the Warren Sawyer, a three-masted ship destroyed in 1884, washed ashore on Nantucket, off Cape Cod in Massachusetts.

Netflix’s Chumbak has been receiving attention for its quirky characters, situational humour and distinct storytelling. Among the ensemble, Sandeepa Dhar’s Kiran brings a grounded perspective to the otherwise chaotic world of the show. Reflecting on how she came on board and the challenge of playing Kiran, Sandeepa credited creator and director Aatish Kapadia for helping her explore comedy.
Sandeepa Dhar credits Aatish Kapadia for helping her discover comedy with Chumbak: “I found it interesting because I had never really done comedy before”
Sandeepa revealed that her association with Chumbak began with an unexpected call. She said, “It happened on a random Thursday when I got a call from the director of Chumbak. He told me that Netflix and JD–Aatish were doing a show together and wanted to test me for it. I was like, ‘Me? Comedy?’ I found it interesting because I had never really done comedy before. Then I read the scene they sent me, and it was hilarious.”
The actor said meeting Aatish Kapadia further convinced her to take up the project. Recalling his narration of the show, she added, “The deciding factor was meeting Aatish Kapadia. He narrated the show to me and played all the characters himself while narrating the scenes. It was almost like watching a play. He is such a brilliant actor apart from being a director. I immediately felt that I had to be part of the show.”
Sandeepa also spoke about the challenge of portraying Kiran, who is among the more sensible characters in the series. She explained, “It was difficult because Kiran is probably the only character who is relatively sane. She reacts to situations in the way most viewers would be like, ‘What the hell is happening?’ While doing comedy, you have to create humour through your reactions.”
According to the actor, maintaining the right balance was important while performing the character. She said, “At the same time, you cannot overdo the reactions because then they can become gimmicky. I discussed that with Aatish because there is a reason he has written Kiran as the sane person in this madhouse.”
Sandeepa’s comments offer a look at the process behind developing Kiran and finding the right tone for her performance. While the show’s eccentric characters contribute to its humour, Kiran’s relatively grounded reactions provide a different perspective on the situations unfolding around her.
Her experience also highlights the role Aatish Kapadia played in bringing her into the project. His approach to narrating the show and portraying its different characters gave Sandeepa a sense of its comic world and encouraged her to take on a genre she had not explored before.

‘UN is gridlocked’: Jaishankar says global body ‘largely irrelevant’ in decision-making
Jaishankar made the remarks while responding to a question during an interactive session at the 5th Kautilya Economic Conclave in Delhi.
External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Monday said the United Nations needs urgent reform, arguing that the global body has increasingly failed to play a meaningful role in decisions on major international crises, including conflicts in Ukraine and the Gulf.
Jaishankar made the remarks while responding to a question during an interactive session at the 5th Kautilya Economic Conclave in Delhi, news agency PTI reported.
Also Read | The UN can still work towards restoring trust
'UN has been largely irrelevant to decision-making'
He was asked about the future of the UN and multilateral institutions amid growing questions over their effectiveness in addressing global challenges.
"Where the UN is concerned, I think it's obvious to everybody by now that the UN is gridlocked. If you look at the big issues of the day, whether you look at the conflict in the Gulf, whether you look at the conflict in Ukraine, whether you look at other issues in Africa, whether you look at Covid, actually, the United Nations has been largely irrelevant to the decision-making," Jaishankar said.
"I think, again there's a widely held view that a lot of it is because the (UN) Security Council is gridlocked, that the Security Council no longer represents the entirety of the global interest," he said.
Also Read | ‘World on edge of abyss today, seeing weaponisation of everything’: Jaishankar at UN
'UN remains a prisoner of the past'
Jaishankar has previously criticised the functioning of the UN at international forums.
"The world has evolved into a smart, interconnected and multipolar arena and its members have increased fourfold since the UN's inception. Yet the UN remains a prisoner of the past," he had said at the 2nd Foreign Ministers meeting of G20 Brazil 2024.
Speaking at the conclave, Jaishankar pointed out that the UN was established with 51 members and now has nearly four times as many.
"So, if you have grown four times, and you want to keep the old board of management, it's not going to work. I mean, it's common sense," he said.
Also Read | India has 'gone beyond advocacy', held talks with both Russia and Ukraine to end war: Jaishankar
'Few countries' resisting UN reform
Without naming any country, Jaishankar said some nations were opposing changes to the UN while invoking Africa's interests to justify their position.
"few players, a few countries who are resistant to the reform of the UN, and, they are using the name of Africa, they are using Africa's interest as an argument to block the reform of UN".
He said African countries themselves have clearly articulated their position on the issue.
"And the irony is Africa actually now has a clear position. Africa has actually come to the intergovernmental negotiations and indicated what they would like to see. They've laid out their position," he added.
'We need the UN'
Jaishankar said the focus should be on strengthening the UN rather than bypassing it.
"So, I think we need to see whether, we will continue to watch, in a sense, the irrelevance, or I would say ineffectiveness, a better word, of the UN. And it's an important question, because we need the UN. The UN has done a big service to the international community," he said.
He argued that our job must be to "fix the UN, not to work around the UN", adding the UN itself has to help with that process.
The flagship event was held under the theme 'Resilience in an Age of Flux'.
Jaishankar shared the stage with former Singapore foreign minister George Yong Boon Yeo during the closing session of the three-day conclave.
Also Read | 'US has deliberately become a lonelier power': Jaishankar highlights shifting world order
'System is broken': Jaishankar on global trade
On the international financial architecture, Jaishankar said the concerns extend beyond the financial system to global trade.
"I do think, not just the financial system, but more important the trade system...There's a widespread feeling in the world that the system is broken. That at the heart of the issue is we created a system for market which is based on market principles."
"And we today have very substantial non-market practices which have not been called out. And the non-market practices today have distorted the international economy. So, this struggle between a market norm and the non-market reality, I think is at the heart," he added.

Swyer syndrome is a rare condition in which a person is born with XY chromosomes, the combination usually associated with males, but their reproductive organs develop along a typically female pattern. The person typically has female external anatomy and a uterus and fallopian tubes.
The condition often goes unnoticed during childhood and comes to light during adolescence, when puberty does not progress normally or menstruation does not begin. It can also be diagnosed later during investigations for infertility. Here’s all you need to know about Swyer syndrome.
What is Swyer syndrome?
Swyer syndrome is a rare difference of sex development, medically known as 46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis. According to the US’ Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center, a person with the condition has a 46,XY chromosome pattern, but the gonads do not develop into functioning testes. Instead, they remain as small, non-functioning structures called “streak gonads”. The person generally develops female external genitalia, while the uterus and fallopian tubes are usually present. The condition is estimated to occur in about one in 80,000 people,
Swyer syndrome results from disruption of the genetic pathway involved in testicular development during early embryonic development. The SRY gene, located on the Y chromosome, plays an important role in initiating this process. However, an SRY mutation is not found in every person with Swyer syndrome.
What are the symptoms?
Swyer syndrome may not be apparent during childhood and often comes to light during adolescence, when puberty does not progress normally. One of the most characteristic signs is primary amenorrhoea, meaning that menstruation does not begin.
Delayed or incomplete development of secondary sexual characteristics can also prompt investigation. Because the streak gonads do not produce sufficient sex hormones, spontaneous breast development may be limited. The condition can sometimes remain undiagnosed even when a person reaches adulthood.
How is Swyer syndrome diagnosed?
Diagnosis usually involves looking at the person’s chromosomes, hormone levels and reproductive anatomy. Karyotyping, a test that examines the number and structure of chromosomes, typically shows a 46,XY pattern in Swyer syndrome. Blood tests generally show evidence of gonadal failure, including low levels of sex hormones and elevated levels of hormones such as follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinising hormone. Ultrasound or MRI can be used to examine the uterus and the gonads.
Genetic testing can be used to investigate the underlying cause, including variants in SRY and other genes involved in gonadal development. However, not finding an SRY mutation does not exclude Swyer syndrome. In some patients, even more extensive genetic testing may not identify the precise molecular cause.
Can Swyer syndrome be treated?
There is currently no treatment that can change the 46,XY chromosome pattern or turn the streak gonads into functioning ovaries. However, the effects of Swyer syndrome can be effectively managed. Hormone replacement therapy, usually involving oestrogen and subsequently an appropriate progestogen regimen when indicated, is used to induce and maintain puberty, support development of secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone health.
The streak gonads also need to be assessed because they carry an increased risk of gonadoblastoma, a type of germ-cell tumour. Decisions about gonadectomy and its timing are now generally individualised according to the underlying diagnosis and tumour risk.
Fertility is another important consideration. Because the streak gonads cannot produce eggs, people with Swyer syndrome cannot conceive using their own eggs. However, if the uterus is present and sufficiently developed, pregnancy can be possible through IVF using a donated egg or embryo. Research shows that patients with Swyer syndrome can have successful pregnancies following endometrial preparation with hormones and IVF using donated eggs. Following pregnancy and delivery, continued hormone replacement is important for maintaining bone health.
In other words, Swyer syndrome itself cannot currently be reversed, but its effects can be managed. Hormone replacement can address the absence of normal gonadal hormones, removal of the streak gonads can reduce the risk of tumours, and assisted reproductive techniques can make pregnancy possible for some patients.

Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?
- Published
The pilot who was stabbed on an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday has been identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar.
Capt Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, forcing the plane to divert to Saudi Arabia.
The captain, who has been hailed as a "true hero" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was taken to a hospital in Tubak City, north-western Saudi Arabia, where he remains in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Riyadh.
Writing on X, Netanyahu said Capt Machchhar "saved the lives of 174 people" and prevented "a catastrophic mid-air disaster".
What do we know about Capt Machchhar?
Capt Machchhar joined Flydubai in 2022 - he was an experienced pilot by then, having worked at Indian airline SpiceJet since 2011.
He has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.
His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives".
Last year, Capt Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter.
Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work with his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]," he added.
Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family.
"Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised.
He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely.
"In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations.
At the time of the conversation, Capt Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had had to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues causing delays.
He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want."
Indian social media has been awash with praise for Capt Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral.
What happened on the Flydubai flight?
Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time) en route to Ben Gurion Airport in Israel.
The flight was carrying at least 150 people, with Netanyahu saying "almost all" passengers were Israeli.
Data from flight tracking website Flightradar24 shows the plane made a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia around two and a half hours after take-off, dropping more than 17,000ft (5,000m) in less than two minutes at around 05:21.
Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code, which indicates a hijacking.
At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.
Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.
Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.
But speaking on Wednesday after the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.
He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".
The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in north-eastern Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.
The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Capt Machchhar.
Modi and Trump praise Capt Machchhar
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Machchhar "showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others" despite being seriously injured.
"His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," he wrote in a post on X, adding that he hoped for the pilot's speedy recovery.
Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar praised the pilot's "extraordinary courage and remarkable presence of mind, even in the face of grave danger".
Speaking to reporters at the White House, US President Donald Trump said that "the pilot was in very bad shape" but had the sense to open the cockpit door during the attack.
"Amazing, in a way he was a hero, to open the door. He was able to fall back and get the door open."

India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.
The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.
Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.
Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.
The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said, at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”
Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.
“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”
Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said that the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.
“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.
The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.
Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try and stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.
Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.
Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election commission office in Delhi next week.

Remember MapQuest? You can now use it with Android Auto
If you use Android Auto, you can try out the beta mapping service today.
Launched in 1996, MapQuest, the world's oldest commercially available web mapping service, recently introduced Android Auto support, making it an alternative to Google and Apple Maps with the added distinction of calling a certain body of water in North America Lake Ontario, despite pressure from President Donald Trump.
The decision to retain the lake's 380-year-old name drew a lot of attention. While both Apple and Google bowed to that pressure and changed how the name appears to map users in the US, MapQuest did not. This refusal prompted a huge spike in interest in its service, the company said. Usage grew to 50 times its normal rate, and the apps it offers generated over 1.5 million downloads. MapQuest quickly became the No. 1 mapping app on Apple's App Store. "Hundreds of thousands of people signaled to us this weekend that we got it right, by downloading our app," said Doug Berger, general manager of MapQuest in a statement.
The company is feeding this interest with the introduction of beta support for Android Auto on Google Play.
How to install MapQuest with Android Auto
Using MapQuest with Android Auto is simple:
- Open Google Play on your Android smartphone, find MapQuest, download and install the app, or update it to the latest version if already installed.
- Scroll down the MapQuest page in Google Play, join the beta program and update the app.
- Connect your smartphone to your car in the usual way, using Bluetooth or a compatible USB cable. The MapQuest icon should appear on your dashboard alongside any other mapping services you have installed, such as Google Maps and Waze.
- If it does not, open Settings on your smartphone and go to Connected devices > Android Auto > Customize launcher and ensure the MapQuest checkbox is actually checked.
Once these steps are complete — including joining the beta program — you should find MapQuest available to you in your vehicle.
Using MapQuest on Android Auto
Initial user feedback on MapQuest's Android Auto beta suggests the application remains a little rough around the edges in comparison to Google or Apple Maps. Various reports claim there have been complaints of app crashes, delayed response times and voice navigation prompts that cut off in the middle of sentences. Interface quirks have been identified, and there may be some frustration that some real-time features are limited to North America (US and Canada).
To be fair, this is beta software; flaws and foibles are to be expected, and the company's social media feeds suggest its developers are actively working to improve the app, including regular software patches.
What features does MapQuest on Android Auto provide?
MapQuest's Android Auto solution currently provides:
- Turn-by-turn navigation
- Real-time traffic updates
- Route optimization
- Search for locations, such as gas stations or EV chargers
- Favorites and saved locations
- Voice search
- Speedometer display to show current speed against the speed limit
- Crowdsourced incident reporting
While the software moves through the beta process, drivers seeking immediate alternatives for Android Auto or Apple's CarPlay may also want to try and download Waze, Sygic or TomTom Go.
