On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.
Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.
Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.
Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.
After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.
Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.
“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.
“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”
On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.
“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”
Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.
When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”
The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.
In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.
“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”
With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.
She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.
“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”

In September 2026, a lawsuit brought against Cornell University and seven of its male students alleged the men drugged and raped a 20-year-old female student in October 2024. The story spread online along with claims that the accused students faced little or no consequences, though some allegedly lost their jobs or were expelled.
As Snopes previously reported, the lawsuit named seven male students as defendants: Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar. According to Doe's lawsuit, Cornell temporarily suspended the accused students on Nov. 8, 2024, (Page 29) but they were given the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by writing an essay to the university. Cornell has denied that the students only had to write essays as a disciplinary measure.
Posts on X, Facebook and Instagram claimed two of the accused students, Sarabia and Ingalls, lost their jobs at Wells Fargo and Data Annotation Tech, respectively. Jane Doe's attorney also reportedly claimed two of the students were expelled from the university, without naming them.
Snopes emailed a spokesperson for Cornell University to determine the enrollment status of each of the accused students. The university declined to respond to specific questions about the accused, directing us to its official statement. The statement says that students were expelled and/or suspended but would not identify which students:
Temporary suspensions and other restrictive measures were issued when the conduct was reported. Chi Phi, Xi Chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus. Following the university's Title IX investigation, sanctions including expulsions and suspensions were issued by a hearing panel comprising trained faculty and staff. Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students, and the university is therefore unable to make a public statement regarding any other disciplinary response.
Below we break down everything we know about the education and employment status of each of the seven accused students. We will update this story as we learn more.
Diego Sarabia
Student newspaper The Cornell Daily Sun and Cornell's online directory say Sarabia is an alumnus from the class of 2025.

- The claim that a Russian oligarch close to President Vladimir Putin paid for Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding in May 2026 is still under investigation.
- The investigative newsroom ProPublica reported on Sept. 14 that Umar Kremlev, a Russian boxing and sports betting mogul, "bankrolled" the wedding of the U.S. president's son with an undetermined six-figure sum.
- Trump and his wife, Bettina Anderson, said on Instagram that Kremlev had paid for two days of celebrations after the couple's private May 22 wedding. The couple described the post-wedding festivities as "an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend" that was "never intended to be our wedding weekend."
- ProPublica's reporting raised questions about a potential political conflict of interest because Kremlev has previously benefited from Russian government contracts to his companies and Trump has previously advised his father on political appointments.
- Days after ProPublica's reporting, President Donald Trump said his son had paid back Kremlev. This claim remains unproven as of this writing.
- Snopes could not independently view and verify sources that substantiated either ProPublica's or Anderson and Donald Trump Jr.'s claims about what exactly Kremlev paid for in relation to their wedding. Therefore, we leave this claim unrated.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have contacted the Trump family, the White House and Kremlev's press office for further comment on ProPublica's reporting and are waiting for responses.
In September 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that a Russian oligarch close to President Vladimir Putin paid for Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding that May.
Trump, U.S. President Donald Trump's oldest son, married the socialite and model Bettina Anderson in the Bahamas on May 22, followed by two days of festivities.
One Threads user who shared the claim about the funding of Trump's wedding wrote:
A Russian oligarch who is close to Putin paid for a good portion of the wedding between Donald Trump Jr. and Bettina Trump. Let's say it again for the people in the back of the class: THERE. IS. A. RUSSIAN. ASSET. SITTING. IN. THE. WHITE. HOUSE.
Similar claims circulated on X (archived), Facebook (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers also contacted us about the rumor.
The claim circulated after the independent newsroom ProPublica published an investigation that found Umar Kremlev, a prominent figure in the Russian boxing and sports betting scenes, paid an undetermined six-figure sum for a lavish island party in connection with Anderson and Trump's wedding. The couple appeared to confirm this payment from Kremlev as "an extraordinarily generous wedding gift" in a statement on Instagram (archived).
However, while the newlyweds appeared to confirm that Kremlev had paid for celebrations that took place directly after their Bahamas wedding, they did not appear to accept ProPublica's claim that Kremlev had "bankrolled" the wedding either in whole or in part.
Kremlev's payment presented a potential conflict of interest, ProPublica's reporting claimed, because of the Russian's reported proximity to Putin and Trump's position as a "political power center" as an adviser to his father. It was unclear at the time of this writing exactly how close Kremlev was to Putin, though Russian reporting found his businesses had benefited from government contracts.
After ProPublica's reporting, the U.S. president claimed (archived) that his son paid back Kremlev for the celebrations. This claim is unproven.
ProPublica's investigation was based on interviews with at least three people "familiar with the event" and records reviewed by the outlet.
We contacted ProPublica to independently verify the sources that formed the basis of their investigation. A spokesperson said, "ProPublica doesn't comment on sourcing beyond what we put in our stories, but we do want to flag that Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Anderson, have since confirmed the payments."
Because Snopes could not independently view and verify sources that proved either ProPublica's or Anderson and Trump's claims about what Kremlev paid for in relation to their wedding, we leave this claim unrated.
We contacted The Trump Organization and Kremlev to verify statements given to ProPublica and seek further comment on the outlet's reporting. We await replies to our queries.
The statement
Anderson and Trump wrote on Instagram on Sept. 14, 2026:
Don and I got married privately on Friday, surrounded ONLY by our family. It was intimate, deeply personal and one of the most beautiful days of our lives.
The weekend that followed had actually been planned well in advance as a fun weekend with friends. It was never intended to be our wedding weekend. When our original wedding plans changed, we simply decided to get married before it and arrived at an already planned weekend as newlyweds.
Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding. It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful.
It's unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn't require a political motive. Generosity doesn't automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift.
While the statement (signed: "With love and gratitude, Don & Bettina") did confirm Kremlev had paid for a "fun weekend with friends," the couple appeared to distinguish between the wedding itself and Kremlev's reported gift of a preplanned event that was "never intended to be our wedding weekend."
According to ProPublica's reporting, Kremlev was not present at the couple's wedding ceremony, but they had their first dance on the island he allegedly rented "for around $100,000 a night." It was unclear how that detail aligned with Anderson and Trump's statement that claimed the celebrations paid for by Kremlev were unrelated to the wedding.
Uncertainties remain over Trump-Kremlev friendship
Though Anderson and Trump described Kremlev as a "dear friend," ProPublica reported that the men "appeared to have met only recently." Kremlev's press office reportedly told ProPublica they met "a couple of years ago." In 2025, Trump spoke at an event hosted by the International Boxing Association, of which Kremlev has been the president since 2020.
A spokesperson for Trump reportedly told ProPublica that he and Kremlev bonded over a love of boxing and the outdoors and that Kremlev did not talk about "political matters" with his American friends.
That could well be true, given that ProPublica reported that Kremlev spoke "limited English."
Though it was unclear exactly how close Kremlev was to the Russian president, reporting by the Russian independent newsroom Proekt found that Kremlev rose through the Russian boxing and sports betting worlds in large part due to being awarded government contracts for his businesses. Kremlev said in a February 2024 interview that he would not describe himself as a friend of Putin's but praised the president's work ethic.
Kremlev received a government award from Putin in April 2026 for his services to sport.
The next month, Kremlev's Telegram account (archived) showed he visited China at the same time as Putin, days before Anderson and Trump's wedding, though Kremlev's press office said he was not part of Putin's official delegation on the trip.
Trump family had 'no clue' about 'dear friend' Kremlev
Though Anderson and Trump described Kremlev as a "dear friend," two other members of the Trump family did not appear to know who the generous gift-giver was.
A spokesperson for Eric Trump reportedly told ProPublica that he had "absolutely no clue" who Kremlev was.
Donald Trump reportedly told The New York Times on Sept. 14 that he, too, did not know who the Russian benefactor was.
Four days after ProPublica published its reporting, on Sept. 18, the president told reporters at the White House that he had "heard" that his son paid back Kremlev for what the newlywed couple initially described as a wedding gift. He did not say whether paying back Kremlev had always been the plan or whether it was sparked by ProPublica's reporting.
At the time of this writing, neither the White House nor Donald Trump Jr. has publicly proved Kremlev's money was repaid, nor have they returned queries from Snopes about the alleged payment.
During the same news conference, the president appeared to play down the significance of Kremlev being Russian and but also appeared to muddle Anderson and Donald Trump Jr.'s distinction that Kremlev's celebrations were not part of their wedding.
Donald Trump called Kremlev's celebrations a "wedding party" and suggested that it was a normal thing to give to newlyweds. He said, "I've given, well, I don't know, maybe he didn't do a background check, but I've given, I've given wedding parties for numerous people."
The president later repeated, "I have to say, though, you know, giving a wedding party is pretty common."
Reporting sparks bipartisan calls for investigation
ProPublica's investigation into Kremlev's alleged payments raised immediate concerns on both sides of the political divide.
Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the lead Democrat on the House Committee on Oversight and Reform, wrote in a Sept. 14 letter to Donald Trump Jr. that the committee was investigating the "numerous ways in which you have sought to enrich yourself and your family on the basis of your proximity to President Donald Trump."
Garcia wrote that, to this end, "your ties to your self-described 'dear friend' Mr. Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch responsible for bankrolling your May 24, 2026, wedding celebrations in the Bahamas, may be the most serious allegation against you to date."
Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, wrote to the Senate Judiciary Committee on Sept. 21, asking it to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. in connection with an investigation "into the use of presidential family relationships for private financial benefit, preferential treatment, or access by domestic and foreign interests."
It was unclear what the outcome of any such investigation in the House or Senate would be, especially if Trump had indeed paid back Kremlev for the alleged gift.

Eradicating Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection early could become an important strategy for preventing gastric cancer, Nobel laureate and gastroenterologist Dr. Barry Marshall said, stressing the need for wider testing, appropriate treatment and confirmation that the infection has been cleared.
Dr. Marshall, who shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Robin Warren for their discovery of H. pylori and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, said the bacterium should no longer be regarded only as a cause of ulcers.
“H. pylori is much more than an ulcer organism. If the infection persists for many years, it can cause chronic inflammation in the stomach and increase the risk of gastric cancer. That gives us an opportunity because this is a potentially preventable cause of cancer," Dr. Marshall told PTI.
Dr. Marshall was in India to attend the World Congress of Gastroenterology (WCOG 2026) in the national capital.
Held in India for the first time, the four-day event, which concluded on October 3, brought together around 3,000 delegates from 61 countries to discuss the changing global burden of gastrointestinal and liver diseases, including H. pylori infection, gastric cancer prevention, early diagnosis and treatment.
His comments come amid renewed global focus on population-based H. pylori "screen-and-treat" programmes for gastric cancer prevention.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) working group has recommended such programmes in populations where the benefits are expected to outweigh potential harms.
Dr. Marshall said the priority should be to identify infected individuals and ensure they receive effective eradication therapy.
"If we can find the infection before there has been extensive damage to the stomach, we have a much better chance of preventing the chain of events that can eventually lead to cancer," he said.
However, rising antibiotic resistance is emerging as a major challenge to this approach, he highlighted.
A 2026 review in Gastroenterology noted that increasing antimicrobial resistance is threatening the success of established H. pylori treatment regimens, while concerns also remain about the effects of repeated antibiotic exposure on the microbiome.
"We cannot simply keep giving the same antibiotics and expect the same results. Resistance varies between countries and even between regions, so treatment needs to take local resistance patterns into account," Dr. Marshall said.
The IARC guidance similarly emphasises antibiotic stewardship, treatment based on local resistance patterns and follow-up testing to determine whether eradication has been successful.
Dr. Marshall said India, where H. pylori infection is common, has an important role to play in generating evidence on local bacterial strains and antibiotic resistance.
"India has a very large population with H. pylori, so it is an important setting for research. We need to understand which strains are circulating, what antibiotics are still effective and how we can make testing and treatment accessible," he said.
According to the IARC guidance, Indian recommendations have included bismuth-containing quadruple therapy in areas with high clarithromycin resistance, highlighting the importance of regional resistance patterns in treatment decisions.
Dr. Marshall also stressed that successful treatment should not be assumed simply because symptoms improve.
"Treating the patient is only half the job. We should confirm that the bacterium has actually been eradicated. Otherwise, the patient may continue to carry the infection and remain at risk," he said.
He said non-invasive testing could make detection easier and help expand screening.
Dr. Marshall has also invented PYtest, a C14 urea breath test that provides a 15-minute, non-invasive and quantitative method for detecting current H. pylori infection using a breath sample from the patient.
The patient-friendly test could help Indian doctors detect active H. pylori infection through a quick diagnostic procedure.
PYtest is available in India through Pylorium Diagnostics, part of Trimed Australia, founded by Dr. Marshall and headed by Bhanu Rahoni in India.
The need for prevention has gained urgency as gastric cancer remains a major global health burden, with the highest incidence concentrated in several Asian regions.

The Maharashtra government has reportedly directed all bike taxi aggregators, including Rapido, Uber and Ola, to transition to an all-electric fleet by July 2027. According to the Indian Express, the state transport department, earlier this month, wrote to the aggregators to phase out petrol-powered bike taxis in a phased manner in the next nine months. Following directions from chief minister (CM) Devendra Fadnavis, the platforms have been told to switch to electric bike taxis before the deadline. Under the proposed plan, ride-hailing platforms will initially be given six months to comply with the EV mandate. However, bike taxi operators, which have applied for provisional or temporary licences under the Maharashtra Bike Taxi Rules, 2025, will receive an additional three months to meet the requirement. This comes a month after the Maharashtra Bike Taxi Welfare Association (MBTWA) reportedly wrote to CM Fadnavis, state transport minister Pratap Sarnaik and transport commissioner over the EV transition. In its letter, the gig worker body had sought a deadline of one-and-a-half years for aggregators to comply with the EV mandate. “Most bike taxi riders hail from middle or lower-middle-class backgrounds, making it difficult for them to undertake a significant investment to purchase an EV bike at once. The lack of EV charging infrastructure and the smaller life of an electric vehicle also makes this decision more difficult,” MBTWA president Amit Gawde reportedly said. Meanwhile, sources reportedly said that ride-hailing platforms had also sought an extension until 2030, citing the need for more time to transition their fleets. The state government, however, appears to have granted them only nine months to switch to EV fleets. The development comes four months after Sarnaik said that the Maharashtra government would impose a temporary daily fee of ₹5 on bike taxi services operating illegally in the state. He had also said that aggregators would also be required to contribute 2% of fare of every ride to a welfare fund for bike taxi drivers. It is pertinent to note that bike taxis officially became legal in the state in July last year when the state government notified the Maharashtra Bike-Taxi Rules 2025. At the time, local authorities granted provisional 30-day licences to Ola, Uber and Rapido to transition to electric bike taxis. The rules mandated that only electric two-wheelers painted yellow and marked as bike taxis could operate commercially. However, the platforms allegedly failed to comply, leading the state government to revoke their licences in March this year. Afterwards, officials began undertaking enforcement action against aggregators for operating unauthorised petrol-powered bike taxi services. Local authorities collected fines totalling ₹16.25 Lakh for illegal bike taxi operations between April 2025 and March 2026, and another ₹2.31 Lakh during April and May 2026.

Owner, businessman & player: Messi has big plans as a golden era ends
- Published
Lionel Messi is about to play his last match for Argentina.
On what will be his 208th appearance, the country's most-capped player and record goal scorer will bid an emotional farewell in a friendly against Benin at the Monumental in Buenos Aires.
Arguably Argentina's greatest ever player - only Diego Maradona comes close - announced his retirement from the national team on 31 August, six weeks after the World Cup final defeat by Spain, saying he had nothing more to give.
Coach Lionel Scaloni insists that if Messi ever wants to carry on, he can, and there is no embarrassment in changing one's mind. But that chapter seems closed.
His club career though goes on. The contract with Inter Miami runs to the end of the 2028 season, but it is reviewed year by year, and nobody close to him expects him to walk away a day before he has to.
In fact, it is quite likely he will renew it if he feels, mentally and physically, up for it.
Ask the people around him what comes after that and they smile, because Messi has never really planned beyond his next game.
Even so, the shape of what lies ahead is already in front of us. He will stay inside football, because he would struggle to live without it, but his other business interests stretch far outside the game.
- Messi retires from Argentina duty with 'nothing left to give' 
  - Published31 August
- How Messi's decade of dominance almost never happened 
  - Published31 August
An owner who wants to be involved in everything
Messi used to like the idea of being a sporting director or an adviser to the president, close to the decisions without all the travelling and the phone calls.
And asked recently whether he would rather be a coach or an owner, Messi chose owner.
A coach lives and dies by every Saturday and has to worry about far too many things for Messi's liking.
An owner shapes the direction of a club from a little further back. Having said that, he would be an owner who does not stop at approving the appointment of a manager and stepping away. He would want to be involved in everything.
The groundwork is being laid in Spain. UE Cornella, on the edge of Barcelona and in the fifth tier, is the nursery where young players grow. He bought it in April.
CD Eldense, in the second division, announced Messi as its new owner on 1 October, subject to authorisation from the Spanish sports council, the CSD.
Eldense will be the club that leads his football operation, but the target this season is not to get relegated, so former Villarreal boss Javi Calleja got the job with the arrival of the new owner.
The plan is to run both through people he trusts, who will act as a link between Messi and the clubs until the day he can give them his full attention.
For now he follows every Eldense match closely on his computer. After Eldense beat Real Oviedo by four goals to one, his first message as owner was an Instagram post that read "Aupa Deportivo".
The pull of his name has been felt as well. Around a dozen sponsors came forward within a couple of days, some of them brands that had been talking to the previous owners without ever closing a deal, and some that already have a relationship with him.
In Uruguay he and Luis Suarez founded Deportivo LSM in May 2025, and they won promotion to the country's third tier in its first season.
A network of more clubs was discussed at the start. But the sums needed to lift them up the divisions have cooled that idea quickly, and it is not on the table today. Messi's focus is to see whether Eldense can establish itself in La Liga.
There is a link to Miami as well. As part of his contract with Inter Miami, he will have some shares in the club when he retires. A franchise of his own is not part of the plan.
Could he go home to Newell's Old Boys, the club where he played as a child in Rosario? The idea has never been formally discussed.
It may have crossed his mind while drinking mate with Suarez, in the way a return to Barcelona or a spell at Napoli, the club of Maradona, might have.
Nobody close to the player expects it though. Everything is built around Europe and Miami, and the perfect home is waiting for the family in Castelldefels, close to the sea and Barcelona.
- A rivalry that changed football 
  - Published5 June
- Goals, records, tears ... Messi's most iconic moments 
  - Published31 August
A growing business empire and love for youth football
Newell's will still be close, because the club is one of the sixteen academies at this year's Messi Cup.
If owning clubs is one love, youth football is the other, and his regular presence at his son's games and the Messi Cup are the proof.
He puts his money and his time into a tournament for Under-16 academies, which began in 2025 with eight teams.
Last year, the organisers expected him to come to one or two games, perhaps only the final, but to everyone's surprise, he sat through every match on every day.
This year the teams doubled to 16, from 25 October at Inter Miami's facilities in Florida, including Atletico Madrid, Chelsea, Barcelona, Inter Milan, Arsenal, UE Cornella, and others.
Away from the pitch, Messi has built a portfolio that helps explain why Forbes put his net worth at about $1.1bn, external in June, with earnings of around $140m over the previous year split between football and business.
His best known endorsement is the lifetime Adidas deal he signed in 2017.
The most visible piece is MiM Hotels, six boutique properties from Ibiza to Andorra, which Melia has run under a rental agreement since 1 November 2025.
MiM takes its name from Messi and the Majestic hotel group, and runs the hotels inside its Melia Collection.
In Rosario, his family firm invests in Carrasco M, a development of 24 homes by the Parana river, with Ángel Di María's property agency handling the sales.
He is also a partner in the restaurant chain El Club de la Milanesa which plans to open five branches in Catalonia, the first in Castelldefels.
He has a mate collection with the drinkware giants Stanley, the brand's first multi-year deal with an athlete, and he gave his opinion on materials and colours.
The business side began with his father. Jorge Messi, who died in August aged 68, looked after his son's affairs from the start, and some of his early advice led the family into trouble with the tax authorities in Spain.
The company then grew into branches for TV production, marketing, media and commercial partnerships, among others, all well established by the time Jorge fell seriously ill.
Messi trusts the people who run them, some of them with him since his early days at Barcelona, and a thorough filter means he only gets offered and chooses what he is comfortable with.
He sets his own relationship with the business world, and nobody imposes anything on him.
In Miami last November, Messi told the America Business Forum: "Business is something that interests me. I would like to keep learning because I know nothing and I am just starting out."
The portfolio his circle has prepared is already impressive while he finds more football targets to keep the flame alive.

A hot tip to battle performance anxiety? 'Pretend flush' a mistake down the toilet
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
In 2012, psychologist Cindra Kamphoff was running a marathon. Then at Mile 22, her self-doubt started to kick in. She remembers telling herself, "This is dumb. Why am I doing this?"
Life Kit
Beat performance anxiety with these quick tips
But Kamphoff, who works with top athletes on how to overcome performance anxiety — including from the Minnesota Vikings and USA Track & Field — was prepared. She had written positive phrases on her arm that she could read when she needed a boost during the race: "I'm strong, I'm fast, I'm fit, I'm ready."
This is just one of many techniques that Kamphoff shares in The Confidence Habit: 7 Core Practices to Transform Self-Doubt to Self-Belief, published in September. The book offers creative ways to manage fear and negativity — like pretend-flushing your mistakes down the toilet — before, during and after a high-stakes task.
These tools can be applied to any situation, whether it's a race, work presentation or a job interview. The goal is for people to "be their best in the moments that matter most to them," she says.
Kamphoff, who has a PhD in sport and performance psychology, shares four tools you can try today.
Move on quickly with "learn, burn, return"
Maybe you fumble the ball in a big game or forget the lines in your school play and can't stop thinking about it afterward.
If you make a mistake during a high-stakes moment, Kamphoff says it's important to move on quickly.
She suggests a tool she calls "learn, burn, return" to build back your confidence and keep your goals in reach. Try this if you fumble mid-performance, or as a way to reflect after the event.
Learn: Ask yourself, what did you learn? Use this prompt: Next time, I will _____.
Burn: Think of a motion or a cue you can use to remind yourself to move on quickly. Kamphoff says you can snap your fingers, say "that fast" or "you might literally pretend to flush a toilet."
She taught the toilet flush move to former Minnesota Vikings player Adam Thielen, who used it after he fumbled during a playoff game in 2020. He then went on to catch a 43-yard pass over his head that helped the Vikings win the game.
Using the same motion or phrase every time you "burn" helps your brain strengthen new neural pathways when it comes to moving through anxiety, she says.
Return: Now it's time to build yourself back up. Remind yourself, "you got this, you're doing the best that you can," says Kamphoff.
Speak to yourself powerfully
How you talk to yourself matters, Kamphoff says. According to the American Psychological Association, self-affirmations, even in small doses, can have lasting effects on our self-esteem.
When Kamphoff wrote positive messages on her arm to motivate her during her marathon, they worked because she was giving her brain evidence that she could be successful.
As Kamphoff repeated these phrases during her race, her pace picked up. She ended up not only winning the race in her division, but running her last four miles the fastest out of any part of the marathon.
To make what Kamphoff calls a "power phrase," choose a statement that starts with I will, I can or I am. Then ask yourself, How am I at my best? What does that look like? What does that feel like?"
Kamphoff chose phrases that reminded her of her love for running — and that she had trained for hundreds of miles to run the race.
Set gold, silver and bronze goals
Instead of focusing on one perfect outcome, set a range of goals for yourself. Kamphoff recommends creating a "gold, silver and bronze goal," she says.
Let's say you're running the mile in track. Your bronze goal might be running a time you're generally happy with, your silver goal might be to run a personal best, and your gold goal might be to win the race.
This can help decrease anxiety and increase confidence by removing the pressure of one ideal performance and shifting focus to the present moment. Especially because "an outcome is something you can't control," she says.
Fact-check your self-doubt
If you're feeling overcome with negative thoughts right before a job interview or a big test, ask yourself three questions:
- Is that thought true?
- Is that thought serving you?
- What would be a more empowering statement? 
This method is similar to other frameworks, like acceptance commitment therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy. It can pause negative thoughts and help you get back to the present moment.
For example, if you walk into a job interview thinking, "If I don't ace this, I'll never get another job," this exercise can challenge that thought. And it can help you find a more positive, grounded alternative: "Even if I don't get this job, I know I'm capable of success and that there are better opportunities for me."
Remember, she says. Confidence is a choice you get to make.
"You get to decide in the moment, are you going to be confident?" she says. "Many times the action of confidence comes before the feeling, and it's a skill."

Skydance will combine HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single streaming service
The newly merged media company plans to 'unify' its new streaming businesses.
Skydance, the new media entity made from Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, is also going to merge its streaming apps. The company shared its intentions in the same announcement that confirmed the $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. was complete, a nearly year's long process that was briefly blocked by a multi-state lawsuit until Paramount reached a settlement in late September.
While Skydance didn't get into specifics, it did share that its streaming services, which now include HBO Max, Paramount+ and Discovery+, "will unify into a single service over time." Plans to combine the streaming services have been on the table for a while. In March, Variety reported Skydance CEO David Ellison intended to combine Paramount+ and HBO Max into a single entity, giving the company "a little over 200 million direct-to-consumer subscribers." Ellison also stressed that HBO would continue to "operate with independence" after the merger. Based on Skydance's recent appointment of HBO CEO Casey Bloys to Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer of Skydance DTC, the company is hoping some of that prestige HBO quality can rub off on its other programming.
Reducing redundancies and combining catalogues of content is what all entertainment companies do after merging. HBO Max is a recent example: Since it launched as Max in 2023, the service has offered Discovery's catalog of reality TV and documentary programming alongside WarnerMedia's collection of movies and TV series.
That same merger process typically results in some negative outcomes too, like layoffs — which Skydance has already warned employees about — and higher prices. Skydance hasn't announced the name of its unified streaming service, let alone what it'll cost, but given the exorbitant amount of debt the company took on as part of the merger, there's a good chance it could be higher than what customers paid before.

Asos hit by extortion hack that may have compromised some customer data
The attackers sent a push notification to Asos shoppers announcing their activity.
UK-based fashion retailer Asos is doing damage control after its customers were sent a push notification claiming that its cloud services had been hacked. According to The Guardian, Asos users received mobile alerts that were addressed to the company's data protection officer and IT personnel.
The notifications read: "Dear Asos DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us or we will leak it." Snowflake is a cloud service that handles push notifications as well as managing data about transactions and customer demographics. A link in the message sent users to a Telegram channel claiming to be operated by Xuanye Group, a reportedly unknown name among most cybersecurity circles.
According to the company's statement, "We are investigating unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms that we use to communicate with customers. We took immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms and are working with our internal and external specialist advisers, as well as all relevant authorities."
Asos said that although customers' names and contact information may have been accessed in the hack, it did not believe payment details or passwords had been compromised. The company added that its app and website were operating as usual.

Jim Bakker’s death was confirmed by his second wife, Lori Bakker, on Monday

Jim Bakker, the televangelist who co-founded a lucrative media empire with his first wife, Tammy Faye, before a high-profile sex scandal and federal fraud convictions brought down his ministry, has died at the age of 86.
His death was confirmed in a statement on Monday by his second wife, Lori Bakker. The cause of death was not immediately disclosed.
"He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry," she said.
Based near the entertainment hub of Branson, Missouri, the couple had produced and hosted "The Jim Bakker Show" in the area since launching it in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020.
Decades prior, it was another evangelical broadcast that elevated Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker to national prominence. Their celebrity status routinely made them subjects of satire on late-night comedy programs and "Saturday Night Live," and their life story inspired the September 2021 feature film "The Eyes of Tammy Faye."
At its peak in the mid-1980s, the couple's religious organization reached up to 13 million viewers each night and operated the Heritage USA Christian theme park and hotel complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina.
Born in Muskegon, Michigan, Bakker studied at North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. After marrying in 1961, the pair left school to begin an itinerant ministry, traveling the country to perform at tent revivals and local churches, with Bakker preaching while his wife sang and played the accordion.
Their efforts caught the interest of televangelist Pat Robertson, leading to a children’s program on his Christian Broadcasting Network in 1965. By 1966, Bakker was hosting the religious talk show "The 700 Club."
Bakker departed CBN in 1972 and established the PTL Satellite Network two years later. Its centerpiece broadcast became "The PTL Club," short for "Praise the Lord."
At its height in the 1980s, the program generated millions of dollars annually from millions of devoted followers.
Filmed largely at their extensive resort south of Charlotte, North Carolina, the show blended guest interviews with Christian musical acts. Bakker delivered encouraging sermons, while Tammy Faye—distinguished by her dramatic mascara—performed music.
The couple’s prominent lifestyle and Tammy Faye’s recognizable appearance made them frequent targets for television comedy.
The ministry collapsed in March 1987 following Bakker’s admission of a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Bakker stepped down from his position, transferring control to pastor Jerry Falwell.
Tammy Faye remained supportive of her husband publicly during the scandal, which came to be viewed by critics as emblematic of 1980s televangelist excess.
Conditions worsened further.
Federal prosecutors indicted Bakker in 1988 on conspiracy, wire fraud, and mail fraud charges tied to PTL financial operations. Following his conviction, he received a 45-year prison term, which was later reduced to eight years.
At a media briefing after the verdict, Tammy Faye addressed reporters by singing the hymn "On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand."
The marriage ended in divorce in 1992 while Bakker remained incarcerated. Tammy Faye later wed building contractor Roe Messner, who had built the Heritage USA property and was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995. She died of colon cancer in 2007.
Paroled in 1994, Bakker married Lori in 1998, and five years later they established "The Jim Bakker Show" on the PTL network.
In June 2021, Bakker and his media company resolved a lawsuit over claims made in early 2020 that a health supplement called Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who purchased or donated to receive the product following claims made during 11 broadcasts.
Bakker had two children with his first wife, and he and Lori adopted five children in 2002.

Dentist recalls 45 minutes of trying to save Smit Machchhar's life: 'Please don’t sleep, we need you'
Dentist Shota Musaev recounted the 45 minutes of him trying to save Smit Machchhar, whom he said was bleeding profusely from the head and his left hand.
As Indian Captain Smit Machchhar bravely fought off his co-pilot after being stabbed on the flydubai FZ1073 flight to Tel Aviv, a dentist on board helped stop the bleeding.
In a conversation with UAE's The National, 47-year-old Shota Musaev recounted the 45 minutes of him trying to save Machchhar, whom he said was bleeding profusely from the head and the left hand.
“I told him, ‘Please don’t sleep, we need you.’ I asked how many children he had, their names. I kept telling him, 'Don't be afraid, you will go back to your family, we are landing soon,'” Dr Musaev told the UAE daily.
The dentist also said that Machchhar told him he was from India.
‘His pulse was too low, lips turned blue’
Recalling what happened on the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight last week, Musaev said he heard screams and calls for a doctor.
He said he used many T-shirts to press on Machchhar's wounds as he was heavily bleeding from some places, but asked for ice when the cloths didn't help. “He had very, very deep cuts and we needed many ice packets. But every time I opened the T-shirt to check the bleeding, it would bleed more. So I pressed not very hard and with ice. All through the 45 minutes I kept the pressure on," he was quoted as saying.
He also recalled how Machchhar's pulse went too low at one point and lips turned blue. “At one time, his pulse was too low, so I put his feet up and the pulse came back,” Dr Musaev said. “When I saw his lips were blue, I told the steward, ‘We need to land quickly. He doesn’t have much more time’," he was quoted as saying by The National.

Smit Machchhar was stabbed mid-flight by his Omani copilot, an incident that was later termed a "terrorist" attack by a UAE official. The co-pilot was identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national, according to multiple news agencies.
‘Help me’: Dentist recalls pilot's words
In an earlier interaction with ABC News, Musaev recalled how Machchhar sought help from him after being stabbed. "Everything will be good," Musaev said he told the pilot as he treated him. "He said to me, 'Help me, please. Help me, please. I don't want to die here.'"
During the same interaction, he also expressed his wish to meet Machchhar again one day and thank him for saving lives despite being injured. "We'll say thank you very much for all," he said.

According to UAE, Smit Machchhar was hit inside the cockpit with a crash axe as the accused co-pilot tried to take control of the plane. It was only after Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door that passengers were alerted to what was happening, and pinned down the co-pilot.
A crash axe is typically kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies such as crashes.
Smit Machchhar's first remarks after the flydubai incident came in a video call with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday. He said he could feel the aircraft going down even after he collapsed from his injuries, but was determined to not let the passengers die.

American tennis star Coco Gauff said on Tuesday she faced an “insane” amount of online racist abuse after defeating Chinese teenager Sun Xinran in a match that included a video review.
During Monday’s China Open match against 16-year-old Sun Xinran in Beijing, the former US Open champion requested a video review over flickering LED lights, prompting some boos from the crowd.

Trump orders military base mass shooter to be executed by firing squad
Former army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan faces death penalty for shooting dead 12 active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman in 2009

Donald Trump has ordered the rare use of a firing squad for the execution of a former army major who killed 13 people in Texas in 2009.
Former army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan’s method of execution was approved by the president at the recommendation of defence secretary Pete Hegseth, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said.
Hasan opened fire at Fort Hood on 5 November 2009, killing 12 active-duty but unarmed soldiers and a retired serviceman and injured 32 people. He was sentenced to death after being convicted on 45 counts of premeditated murder in 2013 for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility at the Texas military base.
The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to deploy to Afghanistan. Prosecutors said he was motivated by unwillingness to be sent to Afghanistan and the shooting was in retaliation for America’s wars in the Muslim world.
Hasan was left partially paralysed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police upon his arrest.
Parnell said the "judgment day for Hasan has finally come" and that the date and place of his death would be set by the secretary of the army.
Death by firing squad was one of the forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to the list of permissible methods of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with gas asphyxiation and electrocution. The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which had also proved challenging to carry out for other reasons at times.
Hasan is one of four military inmates awaiting execution, which requires approval from the president and an appellate review.
Hasan's military execution is different from the majority of executions, which are legal in 27 states of America.
Execution by firing squad is rare in the country, with the latest being carried out in March last year in South Carolina.
In 2024, the South Carolina Supreme Court had ruled that firing squad, lethal injection and electric chair were all legal methods of execution. The court noted the firing squad was not cruel because a prisoner would not suffer longer than 15 seconds.
Brad Sigmon became the first person in the state to be executed by firing state and the first across the country in 15 years. Mikal Mahdi was executed in a similar way on 11 April.
In all, at least six people have been executed by firing squad since the country reinstated the death penalty in 1977.
Since 1608, at least 145 civilian prisoners have been executed by shooting, nearly all in the state of Utah, according to the Associated Press.
Hasan will be the first person to face a military firing squad since the end of World War II. His will also be the first military execution, by any method, since 1961.
The last military execution, the Death Penalty Information Center said, was done by hanging, while the last-known execution by a military firing squad was likely carried out "by musketry" in November 1945.
Trump, a supporter of the federal death penalty, reinstated the execution method on his first day back as president in January 2025.
At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The Utah Supreme Court halted the scheduled 5 September 2025 firing-squad execution of death-row inmate Ralph Menzies.
Trump's approval for Hasan’s execution comes as plans by Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week.
Prison personnel botched an attempt to administer a lethal injection, leaving Christa Pike alive but unconscious and hospitalised on life support.
Pike's lawyers had previously urged the Tennessee Department of Correction to consider an alternative to lethal injection such as hanging or firing squad, in anticipation of the trouble executioners would face in establishing a sound intravenous line.
"There’s nothing Donald Trump loves more than the power to kill," Death Penalty Action, a campaign group opposed to capital punishment, said, pointing out that he oversaw more executions during his first term than any president since Franklin D Roosevelt. “Truly, this is just another distraction and a ploy to stem his record-low approval ratings."

India Mobile Congress begins on Wednesday, PM Modi to inaugurate on October 8
The India Mobile Congress, being held at Yashobhoomi from October 7 to 10, will be themed “Scale Without Boundaries” this year.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi will inaugurate the 10th edition of the India Mobile Congress (IMC) in New Delhi on October 8, with telecom operators, technology companies, policymakers and startups expected to use the four-day event to showcase new technologies and discuss the next phase of connectivity.
The event, being held at Yashobhoomi from October 7 to 10, will be themed “Scale Without Boundaries” this year. The formal inauguration comes on the second day, although the conference programme begins a day earlier, with a line-up of government and industry speakers.
What is lined up?
The opening day on October 7 will feature Lauren Dreyer, vice-president of Starlink Business Operations at SpaceX, alongside Hideo Fuseda, vice-minister for international affairs at Japan’s ministry of internal affairs and communications.
Minister of state for communications Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani, Department of Telecommunications (DoT) Secretary Amit Agrawal and C-DOT chief executive Rajkumar Upadhyay are also scheduled to speak.
Representatives from companies including Qualcomm, GSMA, Ericsson, Jio, Vodafone Idea, Bharti Airtel and Intel are also expected to participate in sessions throughout the day. Discussions will cover areas including next-generation networks, AI, 6G, digital infrastructure and satellite communications.
The second day, October 8, will begin with the formal inauguration by PM Modi. The programme will also feature keynotes from major industry leaders, including Reliance Jio chairman Akash Ambani, Bharti Enterprises founder and chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal and Aditya Birla Group chairman Kumar Mangalam Birla.
The day is also expected to see government announcements, partnerships and discussions around investment and business opportunities in the telecom and digital technology sectors.
The third day will continue with keynote sessions, panel discussions and industry conversations across multiple tracks. The programme includes sessions on 6G, AI-native telecom networks, intelligent RAN, cybersecurity, satellite communications, network APIs, cloud and edge computing, semiconductors and digital infrastructure. GSMA, for instance, has sessions planned on digital trust, satellite communications policy, AI-native telecom networks and the transition from connectivity towards digital infrastructure.
Over four days, an exhibition at Yashobhoomi will run alongside the conference programme, with companies showcasing products, technologies, and live use cases spanning 5G and 6G, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, satellite communications, cybersecurity, advanced manufacturing, and cloud and edge computing.
Focus on deep-tech
Startups will also have a significant presence through the ASPIRE programme, which this year places greater emphasis on deep-tech and frontier technologies, including support for startups to move from prototypes to market opportunities and investment.
The event will also feature international participation and technology demonstrations, with the broader programme spanning policymakers, telecom companies, equipment makers, technology firms, startups and investors.
The 2026 edition is the 10th iteration of IMC, which is jointly organised by the DoT and the Cellular Operators Association of India.

A surge in Russian jet-powered drone strikes on Ukrainian data centers has increasingly disrupted mobile phone and Internet services for thousands of people. Now Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and other government officials are warning of the need for more air defense capabilities, as such telecommunication outages could threaten Ukraine’s digital economy and undermine the country’s ongoing resistance to Russia’s invasion.
The Russian attacks on Ukrainian telecommunication infrastructure have focused on Ukraine’s capital of Kyiv since September 23, according to the nonprofit Reporters Without Borders. Ukraine’s digital transformation ministry reported that 100,000 households in the Kyiv region were temporarily experiencing Internet outages from those initial strikes—and Russia has only intensified its strike campaign against major Ukrainian data centers and mobile phone networks in recent weeks.
“Russian attacks on Ukraine’s telecommunication infrastructure are not new, with strikes and shelling previously damaging fiber optic lines, cell towers, and facilities belonging to mobile network companies,” said Tetiana Gaviuk, analyst for Europe at ACLED, in a post on October 1. “However, the recent concentrated attacks on Kyiv’s data centers and telecom networks stand out because multiple providers and facilities were hit within days, indicating Russia’s increased pressure on Ukraine’s digital infrastructure.”
Such repeated attacks could undermine the telecommunication networks that support Ukraine’s banks, payment systems, and public services, according to warnings from officials and industry figures, as reported by The Guardian.
Russia’s strike campaign
Russia has launched mass missile and drone attacks on Ukraine’s power grid infrastructure, railroad stations, shipping ports, and even residential apartment buildings since the first year of its full-scale invasion in 2022. But such long-range strikes have become even more damaging this year, as they have exhausted Ukraine’s supply of missile interceptors—and Russia has also upgraded many of its one-way attack drones to become faster jet-powered drones that are more difficult to shoot down.
For example, Zelenskyy stated on October 4 that Ukrainian air defenses currently intercept more than 85 percent of conventional Shahed-type drones originally developed by Iran and supplied to Russia. But such interception rates fall to just 50 or 60 percent when dealing with newer and faster jet-powered Shahed drones.

Egypt have left Mohamed Salah out of their Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against South Sudan because the match will be played on artificial turf.
The former Liverpool forward, now with Turkish club Trabzonspor, has not travelled with the squad to the capital Juba for Tuesday's game.

"The Egypt national team's technical staff, led by Hossam Hassan, has decided to rest Mohamed Salah for the match against South Sudan scheduled for 29 September because of the playing surface," the Egyptian Football Association (EFA) said.
"It was agreed between the national team's technical staff and Mohamed Salah before the Angola match that he would not play against South Sudan, and the technical staff preferred this approach in order to protect the player," it added.
There is a perception of increased risk of injury on artificial surfaces despite technological improvements, though studies have shown, external there is no evidence of a greater risk of injury.
Salah left Liverpool at the end of last season after nine years during which he made 442 appearances and scored 257 goals, winning nine major trophies.
In six Turkish Super Lig games for Trabzonspor this season he has seven goals and two assists.

Captain apologises for gloating over military service exemption
- Published
South Korea captain Lee Gi-hyuk has apologised for gloating about avoiding mandatory military service after winning gold at the Asian Games.
His side beat hosts Japan 1-0 in the final and, afterwards, Lee held up his gold medal and triumphantly announced he was "not going to the military".
In a social media post reported by local media,, external the 26-year-old later said he was "deeply sorry to the fans who are currently fulfilling their military duty, as well as to all those who sincerely supported us".
South Korean males are, in most circumstances, required to undertake between 18 and 21 months of active military service before the age of 28.
However, the government rewards Asian Games champions and Olympic medal winners of any colour with a service exemption bar basic training, which lasts less than a month.
Golfer Tom Kim also avoided military service by winning gold at the Asian Games.
Athletes who have previously secured the exemption include former Tottenham footballer Son Heung-min, who served for only three weeks in 2020 having won the Asian Games with his country two years earlier.
"As an adult I should have thought carefully before speaking," added Lee, who was one of the overage players in his country's Under-23 squad and plays for Gangwon FC in South Korea's K League.
"I deeply regret having spoken so carelessly, and I will continue to reflect on my actions.
"I sincerely apologise to all the fans who have supported us wholeheartedly and who are doing their utmost to fulfil their military duty."

Cable lobby groups notified the Federal Communications Commission that they will sue the agency to block its controversial repeal of the National Television Ownership Rule, which limits the number of broadcast TV stations a single company may own.
The cable groups said that larger broadcast TV station groups will have leverage to demand higher retransmission fees from TV providers, resulting in “higher monthly TV bills for consumers.” They said the FCC repeal order “arbitrarily and capriciously ignores the harms that will surely follow from allowing broadcast station groups to exceed the National Cap.”
The cable lobby groups represent top providers Comcast, Charter, and various other cable operators. Top cable companies have also expanded through mergers. Charter completed a purchase of Cox in August after the FCC rejected protests by advocacy groups that said the cable deal “would create unchecked gatekeeper power over Internet distribution” and make it easier for the biggest cable companies to raise prices.
The FCC voted to eliminate the TV ownership rule on August 6, and finally published the repeal order on its website on October 1 after an unusually long delay. The delay may be explained by the FCC shoring up its legal arguments in anticipation of lawsuits because the agency is claiming authority to repeal a limit set by Congress over 20 years ago.
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has said that replacing a strict ownership limit with a “case-by-case review” of each proposed merger will let the agency approve deals that promote the public interest while rejecting deals that do not. Given Carr’s history of threatening to revoke licenses from broadcasters disfavored by President Trump, case-by-case reviews would let Carr influence news coverage of the administration by allowing favored broadcast companies to expand.
Cable lobby petition
The TV ownership rule prohibits any single broadcast station owner from reaching more than 39 percent of all TV households in the US. Congress directed the FCC to set the cap at 39 percent in 2004. On Friday, cable lobby groups submitted a petition asking the FCC to keep the TV ownership cap in place until litigation over the FCC’s authority to repeal the rule is over.

Saudi Arabia urged to spare man sentenced to death over Facebook post
- Published
"I plead for mercy for the wrongs committed by my son. Please forgive him and send him back to us."
Speaking through tears, Rasamanickam Yogalakshmi made a desperate plea for the life of her eldest son, Anojan Sivarasa. The 24-year-old migrant worker is facing the death penalty in Saudi Arabia after an appellate court found him guilty of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over a comment he made on Facebook.
The case has sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, sparking widespread concern and civil society petitions across the country. Multiple political parties and government bodies have co-ordinated diplomatic efforts seeking clemency.
However, the family has had no updates on his condition since 28 September. The Sri Lankan government has instructed the family to refrain from making further statements while diplomatic efforts take place.
Saudi authorities have not published an official execution timeline, and it remains unclear when the sentence will be carried out. Saudi Arabia has a history of carrying out executions without warning families or foreign embassies, only informing relatives after the sentence has been carried out.
Anojan was prosecuted after a dispute on social media following an incident that took place during a Hindu pilgrimage in Sri Lanka. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online.
During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Anojan to post a response in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad.
Although Anojan promptly deleted his comment and posted an apology video, it was screenshotted and brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July.
His personal devices were subsequently seized, and his social media accounts were deleted by Saudi officials.
"People in Saudi Arabia knew nothing about this matter. It was individuals in Sri Lanka who sent emails to the company where my brother worked. I do not even wish to mention who those people are," Anojan's brother, Hamsidan Sivarasa, BBC Sinhala.
The company employing Anojan notified the authorities in Saudi Arabia who registered a case against him, according to Hamsidan.
Anojan was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of 3m Saudi riyals (about $0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. An appeal submitted on Anojan's behalf seeking to reduce his sentence was rejected, according to Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath.
The case took a drastic turn on 17 September after Saudi prosecutors filed an appeal for Anojan to be prosecuted under Sharia law instead of the country's cybercrime legislation. The appellate court granted the prosecution's request, increasing his sentence to the death penalty.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sri Lanka confirmed it is taking all available steps to assist Anojan.
His family met President Anura Kumara Dissanayake at the Presidential Secretariat on 21 September. The president assured them that the government would spare no effort to obtain a general pardon for him, instructing diplomatic channels to engage Saudi authorities.
The case has brought together cross-religious support. Senior Buddhist leaders, the Mahanayake Theros of the Ramanna Nikaya and the Amarapura Maha Nikaya, together with Hindu religious leaders, handed over a memorandum to the Presidential Secretariat calling for urgent state intervention.
In addition, a four-member Sri Lankan legal delegation is travelling to Saudi Arabia this week to meet Anojan's local defence lawyers.
"There are two law firms in Saudi Arabia handling Anojan's case. We are going there to meet the lawyers from these two firms, discuss the case and plan what can be done next," one of the team, Upul Kumarapperuma, MP, told BBC Sinhala.
Back home, communication between Anojan and his family has completely ceased.
"My brother hasn't called for two days." Hamsidan said on 28 September. "We informed the embassy and asked officials to look into the matter and update us. They said they would check. We are still waiting, as we have not yet received a response."
In Saudi prisons, inmates on death row typically lose access to personal mobile devices, with formal calls strictly facilitated through prison authorities.
Human rights organisations have repeatedly raised concerns regarding severe sentences for online speech in Saudi Arabia.
In July 2023, Mohammed Al Ghamdi, a retired Saudi school teacher, was sentenced to death over his comments on multiple social media platforms, according to the United Nations.
"The death sentence against Mohammad bin Nasser al-Ghamdi, who has a total of just 10 followers on both of his anonymous Twitter accounts and is accused of nothing other than expressing his opinions on social media, is ludicrous," Philip Luther, Amnesty International's Research and Advocacy Director for the Middle East and North Africa, said at the time.
Al Ghamdi's ruling was overturned, and he was sentenced to 30 years in prison, according to ALQST for human rights, an independent non-governmental organisation defending and promoting human rights in Saudi Arabia.
There are more than 10 million foreign workers in Saudi Arabia, according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM). Rights groups emphasise that low-wage migrant workers face distinct vulnerabilities in the Saudi legal system due to language barriers and lack of proper legal representation.
Executions for blasphemy are relatively rare compared with those for drug offences or murder handed down by courts in Saudi Arabia.

The Coalition’s migration plan risks breaching Australia’s free trade agreement with India, signed by the former Morrison government, allowing Indian students to stay and work for up to four years after completing their studies.
Angus Taylor on Tuesday announced plans to cut net overseas migration to 100,000 for the first two years of a Coalition government and up to 160,000 in year four, in a plan which would abolish temporary graduate visas, make major cuts to international student, bridging and temporary protection visas, and halve humanitarian places.
Under the plan, temporary graduate visas would be slashed from 271,200 to just 10,000 by 2031-32.
The shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, said any graduate wanting to remain in Australia would have to return home and apply for a separate temporary visa.
“Universities and other educational institutions have reverted to, sadly, selling a pathway to some form of permanency or perhaps even citizenship rather than education; that’s not what this scheme was set up for,” Duniam said.
“Abolishing the temporary graduate visa … means we can focus on skills we need in this country, not just whatever is churned out of our universities.”
Duniam said there would be a four-year transitional phase before the abolition of the temporary graduate visa. Some workers in priority areas such as health, education and in some regional areas would be allowed to remain.
Phil Honeywood, the chief executive of the International Education Association of Australia (IEAA), said this could breach the India free trade agreement.
A letter on the agreement, from the then Liberal trade minister Dan Tehan, in April 2022, states: “Australia agrees to maintain the following opportunities for former students to live, study and work in Australia temporarily after finishing their studies.” This includes allowing trade or diploma graduates to stay up to 18 months, bachelor graduates up to two years, bachelor graduates in Stem courses and master’s graduates up to three years, and doctoral degree graduates up to four years.
Honeywood said it was “ironic” the Coalition was targeting the visa when it had negotiated special conditions with India, the second largest cohort of international students in Australia, behind China.
He warned Australia would lose skilled workers in critical areas under the Coalition’s changes.
He said Australia would take “money off bright young people for their qualifications” before sending them home without having the chance to benefit from their high-demand health, IT and engineering skills.
Honeywood said the explosion in non-genuine international students coming to Australia was in part due to a post-Covid directive by the then Liberal prime minister Scott Morrison, who increased the number of hours international students could work in key industries.
“[Morrison] opened the floodgates to non-genuine students coming out of Covid without consulting the sector, promising more work rights for international students while they were meant to study full-time,” Honeywood said.
A Coalition spokesperson told Guardian Australia there would be no treaty breach, and the party would look at establishing different visa pathways for some of those graduates.
“Our treaty commitments are to provide temporary visa pathways for some students to stay post their study for short periods. Which visas are provided is up to Australia,” the spokesperson said.
“When we implement this policy in government we will work through with affected international partners which new visa pathways, including skilled visa pathways, their citizens can access.”
The Coalition’s plan would cut international student commencements to 240,000, below the current planning level of 295,000. But a spokesperson for the assistant minister for international education, Julian Hill, said the sector was now tracking towards 250,000 commencements for this calendar year.
Universities Australia said the changes risked doing “lasting damage” to Australia’s higher education sector and the economy. In a statement, its chief executive, Luke Sheehy, said removing the temporary graduate program could make Australia less attractive for students.
“Restricting post-study work rights also risks making Australia less competitive for talented students and graduates at precisely the time we need more skilled people contributing to our economy.”
Hill said removing the temporary graduate visa would make Australia a less attractive option and deny the country the ability to “select the brightest skilled graduates and would hurt Australian employers and industry”.
He said all comparable nations had competitive postgraduate work opportunities.
“Wiping out temporary graduate visas would mean many of the brightest students will simply never choose Australia, further trashing our fourth biggest export.”
