Player welfare, injury worries & boredom - has extended break worked?
- Published
The first international break of the 2026-27 season is almost over - and it has been a longer one than fans are used to.
For the first time, the Premier League and Championship paused for three weeks rather than the usual two with players returning to domestic action from Friday.
The idea was brought in by Fifa with player welfare in mind, but, with a growing list of injuries, has it really been a success?
Who benefits from an extended international schedule? And do people really want a three-week break from domestic action when the season has only just got going?
Why was extended break brought in?
In recent years, Fifa has used five primary international breaks during the season, all consisting of two-week gaps in March, June, September, October and November.
The switch to a three-week gap across late September and early October, alongside reducing the number of breaks down to four, was made for a number of reasons.
One was that the scheduling of the 2026 World Cup final on 19 July was the latest date for a summer World Cup since 1966.
Player welfare also featured in the discussions, this including travel considerations.
The reduction in the number of breaks will reduce the number of journeys some players face in having to travel from one continent to another for their international fixtures . One such example is African and South American players who play their domestic football in Europe and have to travel cross-continent to fulfil international fixtures.
But with the domestic season just starting to get interesting, fans tend to bemoan the interruption - no matter the length - and long for the return of club football.
Injury nightmares
The extended international break might have been brought in with player welfare in mind, but the reality is that a number of players will return to their clubs with injuries.
It is hard to quantify whether more injuries have been picked up during the past fortnight than during other international breaks and it must be factored in that this is a lengthier break with more fixtures. A full and fair comparison might have to wait until the end of the season, after all the international breaks.
However, there have been numerous injuries to players since players joined up with international team-mates.
On Monday, it was announced that Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott had withdrawn from the England squad with a thigh injury and the Cherries are unhappy with the way they believe England handled the injury.
Manchester City striker Erling Haaland asked to be substituted on 67 minutes, subsequently limping off in Norway's match against Portugal on Sunday before leaving camp on Monday while club team-mate Nico O'Reilly returned to City for further assessment.
Following the injury to Haaland, the Norwegian players' union (NISO) expressed concern over the increased demands.
"Over time, we have seen a worrying trend where the burden on top players has become far too high," NISO chief Kristoffer Vatshaug said.
"We want clearer guidelines for workload and recovery. It is about the time between matches, consecutive rest periods, travel strain and how much time players get to recover after a long season."
Liverpool duo Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak have both picked up injuries with Gakpo withdrawing from the Netherlands squad with an ankle injury and Isak pulling out of Sweden duty with a minor thigh injury.
Portugal boss Jorge Jesus revealed Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes had been playing through pain while Sunderland's Dan Ballard and Brian Brobbey both sustained hamstring problems.
Club managers will have their fingers crossed that no more names are added to that list with three days of fixtures still to be played.
England's Tino Livramento, Kobbie Mainoo, Cole Palmer, Marcus Rashford and Declan Rice all pulled out of Thomas Tuchel's squad before the start of the break.
Away from the Premier League, there have also been injuries to some of the biggest stars in the game with Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe sustaining an injury while on duty with France and Barcelona's Raphinha also returned from Brazil with a thigh injury.
'More challenging' but 'positives to take' - Tuchel
England boss Thomas Tuchel has previously been critical of the three-week break, saying it is "more challenging" than previous years, citing travel and having only two days of rest between games as problems.
In a news conference on Monday before England take on the Czech Republic on Tuesday he said: "I can assure everyone that player welfare is priority number one.
"But new training styles and training times, different positions to play maybe, increase the chance of injury."
On whether the extended break has had an impact on injuries, he said "we need to get the numbers right" before deciding.
"Is it really more or is it the same amount [of games] as in two shorter little windows? I don't have the answer to that," he said.
"The two-week window is not guilty for everything. If it is a thing, we will adapt and make the most of it as always.
"I didn't like the start of it after a long tournament to have a long window. There are also positives to it like we saw against Croatia after having three matches together.
"The team is together for longer, more training sessions, more meetings, more of the same language. You see improvements and automatisms clicking in. We made it a very good camp."
What do fans say?
Shay, Swindon: I don't think any Premier League or Championship fan backs this idea. It's just boring without your club in action for so long.
James McCreadie: Fans are getting sick and tired of losing players to what is a glorified friendly. Teams in Europe and Carabao Cup have nine games in 28 days or so before the next international break. Hope clubs pull players out, citing that player welfare comes first.
Matt, York: The amount of injuries during this break, most of them muscular, including the usually extremely robust Erling Haaland surely highlights it has been a mistake of an experiment. Whoever thought it a good idea after a long World Cup summer needs to be in for a performance review.
Kelvin Thomas: Too many players are being withdrawn due to injuries. But I am sure they will make a miraculous recovery when back at there clubs. Even with them gone England will win (bring it on).
James: Revealing that players came to camp with minor issues highlights the pointed comments about Cole Palmer (and I'm sure others) who seem to value their club more than country. Last chance saloon for a few of them come next internationals.
It's not all negative though...
The international break signals an opportunity for fans to swap their usual Premier League or Championship ticket for a trip to a local lower league club or Women's Super League match.
Women's teams associated with a Premier League club often take the opportunity to play their home matches at the larger men's stadium to allow more fans to attend.
Without tiers one and two of the football pyramid in action, it also means room on the television schedule for lower-league matches - a financial boost for those clubs.
While it is difficult to compare week by week attendances because of the number of variables, the international break does offer some fans the chance to watch other teams in action.
Across the 11 games played in League One and League Two on Saturday – nine postponed because of international call-ups – only three had attendances less than their home average for the season.
In the WSL, five of the seven games played over the weekend had a higher attendance than the home club's season average.

As renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern region of Ethiopia, reports are emerging that a new alliance of armed groups in Tigray has been forcibly recruiting men and boys to its ranks.
Renewed conflict erupted on 23 September between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which rules the region, shattering the fragile Pretoria peace agreement signed between the two sides in November 2022.
The latest fighting started after months of escalating tensions when the TPLF launched an attack in what it claims was a response to drone strikes by the federal government.
Witnesses who spoke to the Guardian described a broad campaign of forced recruitment in Tigray, targeting men and boys between the ages of 15 and 65.
The Eritrean Defence Forces and Amhara militias, which committed war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 2020-22 conflict, have switched allegiance and are now fighting in support of the TPLF.
Along with this new alliance, testimonies of forced recruitment, child soldiers and fresh humanitarian crises are emerging out of the already battered region.
Gezu*, 34, who fought with the Tigrayan forces in the 2020-22 war, lost many of his friends on the battlefield and was grateful to survive the deadly conflict. He was planning to start a family when he received a call from the TPLF authorities to join their armed group after the latest outbreak of hostilities.
“I refused to join the war,” he said. “I responded to them to kill me rather than ever force me back to the horrors of the battlefield.
“When they saw no one would join their army willingly, and people fleeing to the capital city, they started rounding up people from the streets. I didn’t want to leave my home town until things started getting worse.”
In the past few months, Tigrayans with the means to leave have been heading for the capital, Addis Ababa, fearing that war was coming. But on 23 September, Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to and from the Tigray region, stranding many people, after Tigrayan forces seized the airport in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray region.
Solomon*, a 52-year-old man who was able to flee to Addis Ababa, said: “The main targets are those between the ages of 15 and 40. I have seen the armed group of the TPLF rounding up people as young as 15 and 16 at gunpoint from the streets and public transportation areas.
“I know parents who tried to save their children by showing medical certificates. The officers don’t care whatever internal disease you have; they forcefully recruit anyone whose hands, eyes and feet work.”
Ephrem, 40, is a father of three who, fearing conscription, was planning to leave the region weeks before the fresh fighting erupted. “Every time I go outside the house, my wife and the kids are anxious. The kids cry fearing that I will be rounded up from the street.
“People who have money protect themselves and their children from the forced recruitment by bribing the officers. It is devastating; no one wants to join the war,” he said.
The Tigray region has been under siege for the past week, when citizens’ bank accounts were abruptly frozen by the federal government, leaving people unable to withdraw their money. The banks have since reopened with a daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr (£9) and with long queues forming outside.
Negus*, an elderly man in Mekelle, said: “We don’t know for how long the siege and the war are going to stay. A daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr can hardly afford to buy the skyrocketing food prices. It is impossible to leave this embattled region. There is no way for relatives outside to send medicine or cash. I am just hoping it all ends soon.”
Internet and phone communications were also cut off on the orders of the TPLF until this week, leaving families desperate for news of relatives in the region.
Meanwhile, the Ethiopian government has been accused of carrying out indiscriminate drone airstrikes and there have been reports of attacks by the opposition forces coming close to Addis Ababa.
An estimated 300,000 to 800,000 civilians died during the Tigray conflict, according to the British government. The Ethiopian army, Eritrean forces and Amhara nationalist “fano” militias, have previously committed grave atrocities against the Tigrayan population that amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity, according to the UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia. Tigrayan forces were also accused in an Amnesty report of committing atrocities during the war.

India is likely to have a much older population later this century, as the country’s age structure is beginning to shift and fertility has fallen “below replacement,” Moody’s Ratings said on Tuesday (September 29, 2026).
Moody’s said population growth has long been a tailwind for economic growth and creditworthiness, but falling fertility is now changing that picture.
Fewer workers will limit productive capacity, while fewer households and consumers will weaken demand. As a result, countries will have to rely more on productivity to sustain growth.
Moody’s said the global fertility rate had declined from 4.9 children per woman in 1950 to about 2.2 today, only slightly above the replacement rate of 2.1.
“What makes this episode particularly significant is that many of the world’s largest economies are ageing at the same time. In fact, more than 70% of the world’s population now lives in countries with fertility rates at or below replacement level,” Moody’s said in a report on global demographics.
It said fertility rates across much of Latin America were now comparable to those of Europe and Japan, while several East Asian countries had some of the lowest fertility rates ever recorded.
Japan has the most top-heavy population structure, with nearly 30% of its population over 65 and about 11% under 15.
South Korea is close behind, while China is moving rapidly in the same direction. Emerging markets, including Brazil, India, Thailand and Türkiye, are also progressing along the same path.
“Although India’s population remains relatively young, fertility has already fallen below replacement and the country’s age structure is beginning to shift, setting the stage for a much older population later this century,” Moody’s said.
Declining fertility ultimately reshapes age structures as well as population growth, it said. Countries experiencing the steepest fertility declines today will also age most rapidly in the coming decades.

In Summary
- Xiaomi released a number of power banks in the Indian market recently.
- The most eye-catching of the new power banks is the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank, which is the successor to the Ultra Slim power bank launched last year.
- The UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank is the slimmest power bank in its class – it is a mere 6 mm thin, and less than 100 grams in weight. It also comes with a super premium design, with a metal build and a fiberglass wireless charging area.
- It has a premium design and feel, but the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank comes with a stiff price tag of Rs 5,999, which many might find outrageous for a 5000 mAh power bank. But it could be perfect for many others!
Power banks and “beauty” are seldom used in the same sentence. They are notorious for being bulky, heavy, and brick-like. Even the ones that can be slapped on the back of your phone and attached magnetically often feel uncomfortable to use along with a smartphone. Unless one is using the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank.
Xiaomi pleasantly surprised us all with a super thin power bank last year, the Xiaomi Ultra Slim power bank, which was so slim and compact that many of us had mistaken it for a card holder. It, however, lacked wireless charging, so it could not be stuck onto the back of a phone. The UltraThin power bank fixes this shortcoming. It comes with a 5,000 mAh battery with up to 15W wireless charging support, and 22.5W charging support (up from 20W on the Ultra Slim). While these numbers are nothing to rave about, it is the design and build of the power bank that are showstoppers. But can its lightweight make up for its rather heavy price tag of Rs. 5,999? Let’s find out:
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Design and Appearance: A treat to hold and carry!
It is difficult to think that anything out of the ordinary can be done with the design of power banks, given just how simple and functional the devices are, but Xiaomi has managed to make the design of the UltraThin power bank its biggest USP. As the name suggests, the power bank is truly “ultra thin.” In fact, at 6mm, it is almost half as thin as the Ultra Slim power bank that impressed us last year, and is the thinnest power bank we have used to date.
The power bank is quite compact as well. It is 98.5 mm tall, 71.5 mm wide, and weighs just 98 grams, which means that it will not only easily fit on the back of any phone out there, but will add only about as much weight as a routine phone case. Even though the Xiaomi UltraThin powerbank is quite sleek, it still feels very sturdy. The body is made of an aluminum alloy shell, giving it that reassuring solid feel, and the wireless charging side comes with fiberglass.
The power bank is available in three different colors – Graphite black, Glacier Silver, and Radiant Orange. While we received the black color option, we think all three colors look very good – the bright orange is the exact shade of the iPhone 17 Pro series’ orange and will basically blend with your iPhone 17 Pro or Pro Max (Apple seems to have stepped away from the shade in its latest iPhones, though).
Our unit came with a matte finish, and the back has a small “Mi” logo in a glossy contrast. The thin sides curve softly around the edges, while the front (which is the part that connects wirelessly to your phone) has a huge circular mark to highlight wireless charging connectivity, along with some information. All the sides are bare except the base, which has a small power button, a USB Type-C port for charging, and four tiny LED lights highlighting the amount of charge in the power bank.
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic power bank is a treat to both hold and carry. It exudes premiumness, and its thin form factor makes it easy to carry around, regardless of whether you hold it in your hand, carry it in your trouser pocket, or in your bag. Or even on your phone. It was so thin and light that we actually used it as a bookmark from time to time.
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Specs and Hardware: Decent, rather than exceptional
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank is more about style and convenience than specs. It comes with decent enough specs, but nothing that will make people sit up in surprise. The power bank comes with a 5,000 mAh battery, which is a touch more than the UltraSlim, which had a 4900 mAh battery. Xiaomi has used an advanced silicon carbon battery instead of the usual lithium-ion one, which allows more mAhs to be packed in a much smaller form factor.
In terms of charging speed, the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank offers up to 15W wireless charging support and 22.5W wired charging support (up from 20W on the UltraSlim). That sounds brisk enough, but this 15W wireless charging speed is only delivered with the Xiaomi 17 series. For other smartphones that come with wireless charging support, you will get 7.5W charging speed, including the iPhones (MagSafe is supported, but the charging speed remains slow).
Xiaomi has added a number of safety features in the power bank as well. The brand says there are ten layers of safety protection on the device, including foreign object detection, overcurrent, short circuits, overvoltage, overcharging, overdischarging, and over-discharging, amongst other safety features.
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Performance: Super convenient, but not super fast
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank’s spec sheet means that it cannot fully charge most modern smartphones from 0-100 percent – while it has a capacity of 5000 mAh, its rated capacity is lower (3000 mAh), as in most power banks. As a result, it was able to take our iPhone 17 (which comes with a 3692 mAh battery) from 20 percent to nearly full only once. And as its wireless charging speed for iPhones is fairly sluggish, it took comfortably over an hour. And it took even longer to charge our Pixel 10 Pro XL. That said, thanks to its slim size and light weight, you can just stick it to the back of your phone and forget it.
If you need relatively faster charging, you can connect your phone to the power bank with a Type-C cable and enjoy 22.5W wired charging speed, which is pretty much three times the 7.5W wireless charging speed with non-Xiaomi 17 series phones, and does get the phone charged much faster in comparison. However, if your phone comes with a relatively big battery (and many phones these days are comfortably above 5000 mAh), the power bank might only be able to get them up to 40 or 50 percent charged before needing charging assistance itself.
While you can use the power bank to charge two devices at once – wired and wirelessly – that compromises speed and its charging capacity a fair bit, as both get divided. The power bank also gets fairly warm while charging a phone wirelessly, which can make the temperature of the phone attached rise too. Our iPhone 17 often got very warm while charging.
The magnetic hold of the power bank is very strong. It latched on very easily to our iPhone and did not budge when we kept the pair of them in our pocket or bags, or even while using the phone. This is by far the most comfortable and convenient power bank to use with a phone – you hardly feel its weight.
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Review Verdict: Pricey, premium and a convenience contender
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank comes with a very steep price tag of Rs 5999. You can get power banks with way more mAh, more ports, and much faster charging speeds at a lower price from Xiaomi itself. Other brands also have their version of slim power banks at far lower prices – Boat has the Magnacharge at Rs 1,599 and URBN the One Premium MagSafe at Rs 1,999. However, none of them brings the sleek form factor and the premium build that the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank offers, nor the long-term assurance that the brand offers. In fact, its only real competitor would perhaps be Samsung’s Galaxy Magnetic Wireless battery pack, which comes with a similar capacity and 15W wireless charging, but is bulkier and not exactly super affordable at about Rs 4,900.
If you are in the market for a power bank with more mAh in capacity and more Ws in charging speed, and what’s more, want both for a small price tag, the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank is not for you. However, if you are someone who wants to invest in an ultra-portable, very premium power bank which can simply give your smartphone a power-packed nudge without adding too much bulk to your gadget life, or even to your device itself, the Xiaomi UltraThin Powerbank might be perfect for you. Yes, it is expensive, but it brings with it terrific design, ease of use, and convenience, which is likely to be coveted by many premium phone users, especially those who use iPhones and Pixels!
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank’s style is its substance. And it is substantially stylish. Yes, it does have a big price tag, but then, convenience can also be a powerful feature of a power bank.

The story so far: India is working towards eliminating dog-mediated human rabies by 2030. Yet the country does not have a single, comprehensive national count of human rabies deaths. While the Health Ministry’s disease surveillance system recorded 54 deaths in 2024, an ICMR-led study estimates that 5,726 people die of rabies in India every year.
Is rabies a notifiable disease in India?
Rabies is not a notifiable disease nationwide. Unlike diseases for which there is a clearly established national notification mechanism covering every State and Union Territory, rabies notification has historically depended on State-level notification requirements and the disease surveillance system.
The National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) has been working to make human rabies a notifiable disease across the country. Communications have been sent to States to notify the disease under the relevant State legislation.
However, a disease being under surveillance does not necessarily mean that every case or death occurring in the country is automatically captured in one central database.
Rabies is a particularly difficult disease to count because a large proportion of deaths can occur outside the formal health system. Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is almost invariably fatal, but patients may die at home or in facilities that do not routinely report the death through disease-surveillance channels.
How is a disease chosen for notification in India?
Disease notification is largely a public-health surveillance and State-level regulatory function, while the Union government maintains national surveillance systems such as the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP).
A disease is generally prioritised for notification or surveillance when it has significant public-health importance — for example, high mortality or morbidity, epidemic potential, rapid spread, risk of international transmission, emergence of a new pathogen, or where early detection can trigger effective control measures. India’s disease-prioritisation exercises have considered epidemiological, clinical, economic and public-health factors, with expert consultation.
Once a disease/condition is designated for surveillance, health facilities, laboratories and health workers report cases through the surveillance system. Under IDSP, reporting includes suspected (S), presumptive (P) and laboratory-confirmed (L) cases. Data move from reporting units to District and State Surveillance Units and ultimately to the Central Surveillance Unit at the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC).
A rising or unusual cluster triggers investigation by Rapid Response Teams, which can lead to laboratory confirmation, containment measures and further reporting.
The exact legal notification requirement can depend on the State/UT and the particular disease. Leprosy, for instance, was declared a notifiable disease nationally in 2025.
So, how many people die of rabies in India?
There are different answers, depending on what is being measured. The Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme/Integrated Health Information Platform (IDSP–IHIP) recorded 21 human rabies deaths in 2022, 50 in 2023 and 54 in 2024.
The Registrar General of India’s Medical Certification of Cause of Death (MCCD) system, meanwhile, recorded 66 medically certified rabies deaths in 2022 and 271 in 2023.
But neither set of numbers represents all rabies deaths in India. The MCCD figures are based on medically certified causes of death. The system does not cover every registered death in the country. At the national level, medically certified deaths accounted for only about 22% of registered deaths in both 2022 and 2023.
The IDSP–IHIP figures serve a different purpose. They are generated through disease surveillance and are intended to identify and track cases and deaths reported through the surveillance network.
This is why the figures cannot simply be added together or compared as if they were measuring the same thing. Then where does the figure of 5,726 deaths come from?
An ICMR-led study published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases estimated that India has about 5,726 human rabies deaths every year.
The researchers did not arrive at this number by counting death certificates or hospital records.
They conducted a large community-based survey involving 337,808 people in 78,807 households across 60 districts in 15 States. The study estimated that India sees about 9.1 million animal bites every year, including around 5.6 million dog bites.
The researchers then combined information from the community survey and laboratory data with a probability decision-tree model to estimate how many people bitten by animals would develop rabies and subsequently die.
The 5,726 figure is therefore a modelled estimate of annual mortality, rather than a tally of deaths reported to the government.
Why is the difference so large?
This is because each system is designed to capture its own unique data.
IDSP–IHIP is primarily a disease-surveillance system. It depends on cases and deaths being detected and reported through the health system and surveillance network.
MCCD records medically certified causes of death. It provides valuable information on the causes of deaths that are medically certified, but it does not cover every death.
The ICMR-led study, on the other hand, attempts to estimate the actual burden in the population, including deaths that may never enter either surveillance or medical-certification systems.
This means that a low number in a surveillance database does not necessarily mean that the disease burden is low.
In rabies, the problem is compounded by the nature of the disease itself. Patients may not reach a hospital after symptoms begin; some deaths occur at home; and the animal bite that initiated infection may have happened weeks or months earlier.
There is also a critical point between the animal bite and a possible rabies death: post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). If a person receives appropriate wound care, rabies vaccine and, where indicated, rabies immunoglobulin promptly after exposure, death can be prevented.
What happens to a case of a notifiable disease?
India’s disease surveillance system works through multiple levels.
At the frontline are healthcare facilities, laboratories and other reporting units. When a suspected, probable or confirmed case of a disease covered by surveillance is detected, information is reported through the appropriate surveillance mechanism.
The information moves through district and State surveillance structures and is consolidated nationally through the IDSP/IHIP platform. The purpose is not simply to count cases. Surveillance is intended to detect unusual increases, identify outbreaks, understand geographical patterns and enable public-health authorities to respond.
But notification depends on detection, diagnosis and reporting. A person who never reaches a reporting facility, a death that occurs outside a medical setting, or a case that is not recognised as rabies may not enter the surveillance database.
This is why notification should not be confused with a census of every person who has the disease.
Does that mean the 5,726 figure is the “real” number?
The 54 deaths recorded by IDSP–IHIP in 2024 tell us how many deaths were reported through that surveillance system.
The 5,726 estimate attempts to answer a different question: how many people may actually be dying of rabies each year, including deaths that are missed by routine systems.
The study itself is therefore important not because it replaces surveillance data, but because it draws attention to what routine surveillance may be missing.
A senior Health Ministry official has also pointed out that the two figures are generated through different methods and should not be treated as directly equivalent. Together, however, they point to a substantial gap between reported surveillance deaths and estimated mortality.
Why does this matter when India wants to eliminate rabies by 2030?
Reliable surveillance is essential to rabies elimination. India cannot determine whether it is moving towards elimination if it cannot accurately establish where human rabies deaths are occurring, where dog-mediated transmission continues and which populations are not receiving timely post-exposure care.
The ICMR-led study also found important gaps after animal bites. About one in five dog-bite victims had not received anti-rabies vaccine, while only 66.2% had received at least three doses. Among those who received only one dose, nearly half did not complete the vaccination course. Only about one in 10 eligible victims received passive immunisation.
The gaps are therefore not confined to counting deaths. They extend across the entire rabies-control chain — from preventing dog bites and vaccinating dogs to recognising exposures, completing human post-exposure prophylaxis and recording outcomes.
As medical scientist and former ICMR Director-General Nirmal Kumar Ganguly puts it, the absence of consolidated data remains a challenge for rabies elimination. Cases and deaths can occur in places where they are difficult to measure, making stronger surveillance, dog vaccination and timely human post-exposure treatment critical.
Rabies is almost entirely preventable, but once symptoms appear, it is almost invariably fatal. That makes every missed exposure, incomplete vaccination course and unrecorded death significant.
For India, therefore, the question is not simply why one database reports 54 deaths while a study estimates 5,726.
The larger question is how many deaths the health system is failing to see — and whether India can close that surveillance gap before it attempts to declare dog-mediated human rabies eliminated by 2030.

Rows of hardware and car-part shops line Garstin Bastion Road, with faded signs crammed together above their shutters. By day, the street is one of Old Delhi’s busiest commercial thoroughfares. But as dusk falls, GB Road, as it is known locally, transforms into one of the city’s most notorious red-light districts.
An estimated 2,800 sex workers live and work in brothels that occupy the upper floors of the dilapidated buildings, their entrances tucked behind narrow stairways and unmarked doors. Women sit on plastic stools beneath the stairways, calling out to men passing on the street, while others watch from windows above, their eyes following the movement below before customers are directed upstairs.
The challenges the women of GB Road face are numerous and well documented – from health risks to abuse, debt to poor sanitation. Now they face a new struggle: India’s controversial electoral reform process. The Election Commission’s special intensive revision, or SIR, is a nationwide exercise in which electoral rolls have shrunk by more than 58 million voters across the 13 states covered in the first two of three main phases. In Delhi, covered in the third phase, the scale of exclusion is the highest recorded as a percentage: 4.76 million names – 33% of the city’s previous electorate – do not appear on the city’s draft roll published on 31 August.
The government says SIR is meant to “purify” the electoral rolls by removing ineligible voters, including alleged undocumented migrants, but critics have accused Narendra Modi’s government of using it to target minority voters and reshape electoral rolls in ways that could benefit his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
On GB Road, the proportion of those excluded is even higher. Data shared by officials overseeing about 1,300 voters in the area show that about 650 were sex workers on the previous electoral roll. Of these, at least 500 have either been marked as “shifted”, meaning they have moved home or location, or have been unable to establish their eligibility because of missing documentation – more than three-quarters of the sex workers on the local roll.
One of them is 36-year-old Beauty*, who has lived on GB Road for more than two decades. She got her first voter ID in 2008. At the time, the address where she lived and worked as a sex worker and verification by a government official called a booth-level officer (BLO) were enough to put her on the electoral roll. She voted in previous elections.
But under the new rules, voters had to establish eligibility by proving their link to the relevant previous electoral roll or by producing prescribed documents such as a passport, birth or education certificate – a paper trail Beauty struggled to reconstruct. Trafficked at 16 and brought to the brothels of GB Road, she has no contact with her family. She does have an Aadhaar card, India’s biometric identity document used widely to establish identity and access government services, with her GB Road address. But Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship and does not, by itself, establish eligibility to vote under the SIR process.
She tried to get a copy of her matriculation certificate, which is evidence of schooling, from the village in Rajasthan where she grew up. One of her regular customers of the past 10 years – a man she refers to as her husband, agreed to help track down the old record but failed.
“If I had the papers to show my father’s birth certificate, or even my own matriculation certificate, then I could prove who I am,” she says. “But how can I go back to my village to ask for these things when my trafficking has brought so much shame to my family that they no longer accept me?”
Now Beauty has lost hope – and, for now, her vote. Her name was left out of Delhi’s recent draft electoral roll. For her, the voter ID had meant more than a piece of identification. Sex workers, she says, are accustomed to being treated as immoral, degraded and less worthy than others.
“We all shit. That is what makes us equal as human beings. Voting is the same in the realm of rights. When I stand in that queue, nobody is more or less than me. It reminds me that whatever people think about my work, I am still equal to everyone else.”
Beauty is not alone in struggling to prove her eligibility. The SIR requirements have exposed the precarious paper trails of women across GB Road, a roughly 1.5km stretch running between two of Delhi’s historic landmarks, Ajmeri Gate and Lahori Gate.
Of the nine sex workers interviewed for this story, none had successfully completed the SIR process: six said they had never received the enumeration form distributed by BLOs to verify voters’ details and collect information for the electoral-roll revision, while the remaining three were unable to meet the documentation requirements.
According to Kiran Deshmukh, a sex worker and coordinator at the National Network of Sex Workers (NNSW), many have spent years, even decades, in Delhi but possess few documents establishing their family histories or links to earlier electoral rolls. “Some were trafficked as children and lost contact with their families; others never attended school or have moved between rooms and brothels without leaving a stable documentary trail,” says Deshmukh. “It is impossible in such circumstances to prove such rigid eligibility requirements under SIR.”
The process is so cumbersome that even people who are literate and have institutional and organisational support can struggle to establish their eligibility. “The process of receiving the enumeration form, knowing when you have not received it, reaching out, then trying to create a paper trail is so daunting that the entire burden of proving your eligibility is placed on the citizen to protect their own constitutional right,” says Deshmukh.
Sagrika Rajora, a researcher and member of Voter Adhikar Manch, a citizens’ collective, argues that the burden falls particularly heavily on people whose lives do not fit neatly into the categories used by the verification process. “To identify people of such marginality is a tedious task. These categories of ‘shifted’ become an easy way forward for booth-level officers, when finding people on the ground is already time-consuming.”
BLOs are often drawn from occupations such as auxiliary nurses or health workers, adding electoral duties to already demanding jobs. Some have raised concerns about the workload and unrealistic timelines of the exercise. Yet, Rajora says, there has been little effort to streamline the process to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out”, the aim outlined by the Delhi chief electoral officer, Ashok Kumar.
“There is so much discretion vested in one BLO. Even if you leave citizenship aside and talk only about voter rights, the entire process of delivering and collecting these forms depends on that one person. There are no grounds for entrusting one person with such a huge responsibility without any accountability at all,” Rajora says.
“It is not surprising that sex workers are among those being excluded. When people have lives that are so complex and mobile, you are going to be untraceable, absent from the system. These are the people for whom such a verification system is simply not designed to work.”
The gaps also cause problems for workers’ children when they reach adulthood. “Children may not possess documents establishing parentage in the manner expected for verification. Some are raised by relatives, guardians or members of the community, while others grow up in institutional care, making conventional family records difficult to establish,” says Deshmukh.
For 23-year-old Dinesh*, whose mother was a sex worker, the problem is not abstract. His mother died three years ago, but she never had a birth certificate. Without one, obtaining her death certificate became nearly impossible, leaving Dinesh with little documentation through which to establish his maternal lineage.
When Dinesh submitted his enumeration form, he relied on his matriculation certificate as proof of his identity. But the booth-level officer pointed out that it did not have his father’s name. “If my mother gave birth to me, why do I need a man’s name on any official certificate?” he asks.
Dinesh says his name is missing from the draft electoral roll. He is still unsure why, but suspects the absence of his father’s name may have been a factor.
The NNSW has written to the chief electoral officer seeking special measures to ensure that sex workers and their children are not excluded from the SIR. But the joint chief electoral officer, Balram Meena, told The Hindu there was no separate process for sex workers. “If their mapping can’t be done and there are no documents either, their names will be removed as per the process.”
The fear of losing the vote is not only about voting rights. In West Bengal, where the SIR has already been completed, the BJP government has used lists of voters deleted during the exercise to scrutinise eligibility for welfare schemes. The BJP chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, says welfare programmes will continue under a “transparent process”, but adds: “No deceased person, illegal infiltrator, or non-Indian individual will be allowed to avail benefits meant for citizens of the state.” The government has excluded about 3 million beneficiaries from its new Annapurna Bhandar welfare for women scheme, using SIR deletion data in its verification process.
In Delhi, the next stage of the SIR process – issuing notices to those whose eligibility or previous electoral-roll details could not be established or matched, and dealing with claims and objections – has now begun and will continue until 29 October. Those excluded from the draft roll can challenge their omission. But Dinesh says he does not intend to.
After years of being asked to produce documents that his family never had, he is unsure what more he can submit to prove that he exists.
“Even if my mother were alive today, I don’t think that would be enough to prove anything. She never had the documents they are asking for. So how am I supposed to get those documents now, especially after her death?”
* Names have been changed. Workers and residents did not permit any photography during the Guardian’s visit

The recent US-China summit yielded a narrow, caution-filled outcome for bilateral trade: a two-month extension of the Kuala Lumpur trade truce, which now expires on January 10 next year. This reprieve eases fears of immediate tariff escalation and shows that head-of-state diplomacy can still curb spiralling confrontation. Yet the short timeline exposes the wide gulf separating the two sides’ priorities.
China’s position has been unambiguous: removal of all punitive tariffs and restrictive measures imposed since 2018. Beijing has repeatedly stressed that no one wins in a trade war. Even so, it responded to the extension with goodwill. The Ministry of Commerce said the pause gave both sides time to take stock of implemented consensus and deliver stable, predictable policy conditions for businesses.
Washington offered a different narrative. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent portrayed the two months as a compliance review, accusing China of failing to fully meet its commitments. He and other US officials did not celebrate the pause, instead speaking of obstacles remaining before any longer truce could be agreed.

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
- Published
"I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk."
"I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her."
Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township.
"Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am."
At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust.
At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.
He raises his fist.
"We are men!" he shouts.
The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer.
"Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide."
Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women.
The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women.
The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women.
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer.
The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder.
A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners.
For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions.
"We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here."
Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation.
Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done.
The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases, are too little, he says, and too late.
"When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?"
He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again."
Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains.
"And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity.
"We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence."
He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men.
"You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe."
Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges.
Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women.
Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court.
But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever.
Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket.
"We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says.
"We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?"
It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko.
She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve.
"Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?"
Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other."
Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer.
Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up.
"As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this.
"And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends."
Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard.
"I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. "Our fathers and our uncles, they are there in prison. We must now become role models and help make this country better."

‘Brain fog’ is used to describe a feeling of mental slowness, difficulty concentrating, finding words, remembering information or processing things as quickly as before. But it is not a medical diagnosis, and persistent cognitive difficulties should not automatically be attributed to brain fog.
What brain fog feels like
Brain fog is a subjective description of changes in cognitive functioning. People may feel that their thinking has become slower or more effortful, that they cannot concentrate on a task, lose their train of thought, struggle to find words or read something without absorbing the information.
“Brain fog is basically a subjective feeling that you are cognitively slow, that you are mentally slow, that you are not able to do your daily activities as quickly or as deftly as before,” says Srividhya S., associate consultant, department of neurology, Rela Hospital, Chennai.
It is different from the occasional forgetfulness that occurs when a person is tired, distracted or stressed. Forgetting where the keys were kept or briefly forgetting a name, for instance, does not by itself indicate a cognitive disorder. Tiredness is also not the same as brain fog. Fatigue is primarily a feeling of reduced physical or mental energy, while brain fog refers more specifically to difficulties with attention, memory, processing or mental clarity.
T. Swathi, consultant, neurology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai, says people with brain fog are often aware that they are not functioning as efficiently as before. This also distinguishes it from some memory disorders, where relatives may be the first to notice changes such as repeated questions, difficulty managing regular tasks or getting lost in familiar places.
Health factors
The causes of brain fog can be varied, and more than one factor may be involved. Poor or inadequate sleep is a common contributor. Sleep apnoea can also disrupt sleep repeatedly without the person being aware of it.
Stress, anxiety and depression can affect attention and processing speed. Other possible contributors include thyroid disorders, diabetes, anaemia and nutritional deficiencies such as vitamin B12 and folate. Migraine and hormonal changes, including those during pregnancy, the postpartum period and menopause, can also be associated with cognitive symptoms.
Medicines should also be considered. Sedatives, some sleeping medicines, antihistamines, anticholinergic medicines and some anti-seizure drugs can affect alertness or cognitive function. Alcohol and dehydration may add to the symptoms.
“Brain fog has several possible causes and can be due to more than one,” says Arulselvan V.L., senior consultant in neurology, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai. “It is crucial to not think that all brain fog is neurological.”
Cognitive difficulties can also occur during or after infections. A recent systematic review of 47 studies involving more than 25,000 people with long COVID estimated the pooled prevalence of brain fog at 30%. However, various studies use different definitions and assessment methods. There is so far no comparable prevalence estimate because brain fog is a symptom description and not a defined medical diagnosis.
When tests are needed
There is no fixed duration after which every case of brain fog requires investigation. Persistence, progression and its effect on daily functioning are important.
Doctors advise evaluation when symptoms continue despite adequate sleep and lifestyle measures, recur frequently or gradually worsen. Repeatedly forgetting important information, struggling with previously familiar tasks, difficulty following conversations or unusual changes in work performance are also reasons to consult a doctor.
Symptoms lasting for several weeks without an obvious explanation, particularly when they affect work, studies or relationships, should be assessed. New symptoms such as persistent fatigue, weight changes, breathlessness, tingling, low mood or excessive daytime sleepiness can provide additional clues.
Evaluation usually begins with a detailed history. . A neurological examination may then be performed.
Depending on the history and examination, doctors may check blood counts, blood sugar, electrolytes, thyroid function, kidney and liver function and nutritional markers such as vitamin B12.
A brief cognitive assessment may be useful when there are concerns about memory, attention or language. Brain imaging such as an MRI is also not routinely required for uncomplicated brain fog. It may be considered when symptoms are progressive, the neurological examination is abnormal or there are other features suggesting a structural or neurological cause. A sleep study or EEG may be considered in selected cases.
Certain symptoms, however, require prompt attention rather than being attributed to brain fog. Sudden difficulty speaking, facial drooping, weakness or numbness on one side, sudden problems with vision or balance, seizures, fainting or severe confusion can indicate an acute neurological problem such as stroke. A sudden, severe or unusual headache also requires urgent assessment.

The Kerala High Court on Tuesday set aside the detention order issued by the Thiruvananthapuram Collector against councillor R. Sugathan under the Kerala Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act (KAAPA Act), 2007.
A Division Bench of Justices Anil K. Narendran and S. Murali Krishna set aside the detention order and directed the Superintendent of Central Prison and Correctional Home, Viyyur, to release Mr. Sugathan if he was not required in any other case.
The court held that his detention order lacked application of mind and that he had been served with several illegible pages in the documents pertaining to his arrest. The unexplained delay in considering his representation seeking cancellation of the order or his temporary release violated his constitutional rights against arbitrary arrest and detention.
The Collector had considered seven criminal cases registered at the Vattiyurkavu police station for ordering Mr. Sugathan’s preventive detention, classifying him as a ‘known rowdy.’ The court noted that final reports had been filed in six of the seven cases, and investigation was under way in the seventh one. The court had allowed anticipatory bail in one of the cases and had directed Mr. Sugathan to appear before the investigating officer within one week. Mr. Sugathan had sought an extension of time to surrender thereafter, which had been granted.
Mr. Sugathan informed the court that he had filed representations to the Additional Chief Secretary (Home) and the Chief Secretary against the detention order. He stated that there was delay on the government’s part since they allegedly waited till the receipt of the opinion of the advisory board, established under the KAAPA Act.
He contended that the authorities concerned failed to consider the sufficiency of bail conditions imposed in one of the cases, which prevented him from committing similar crimes. He claimed that the preventive detention proceedings were initiated due to “political malafides” as he was a councillor of the Thiruvananthapuram Corporation.
Director General of Prosecution T. Asaf Ali argued that Mr. Sugathan had been on the rowdy list since 2014. Altogether, there were 22 criminal cases registered against him. He argued that the councillor refused to receive the arrest intimation and service of documents, and he attacked the police personnel who went to arrest him, along with his co-accused. He also contended that even if some of the documents or pages were illegible, it would not vitiate the detention order.

The adoption of AI agents in millions of organizations is creating new opportunities for attackers to make them take malicious actions, such as exfiltrating database contents and sensitive business and personal information.
In the past five months, Google and four other organizations—with little in common except for their use of AI agents—have acknowledged vulnerabilities that exploit one agent inside a targeted network to spread harmful instructions to other internal agents. The technique is a special form of prompt injection that targets not the LLM but a particular agent, such as one for translation or data analysis. Guardrails inside such agents, if they exist at all, are often lax and will send the instructions to other agents down the chain. Because the latter agent explicitly trusts the first one, it follows the directions.
Unexpected and hard to mitigate
Independent researcher Syed Anas Mohiuddin tested agents from organizations including Google, JP Morgan Chase, Weviate, Rapid7, the French government’s interministerial digital directorate, and the US federal government. His proof-of-concept attacks exploit trust gaps in MCP, short for Model Context Protocol. The standard is one way AI apps and agents communicate with each other inside an internal network. The illustration below shows a simplified MCP in action.
Many special-purpose agents lack the guardrails that might normally mitigate the most harmful consequences of a prompt injection. And since MCP servers store credentials for each agent—and agents are built to trust every other internal agent—an exploit that would have been rejected by the LLM succeeds. In many cases, well-crafted prompts targeting the right agent will lead to a server-side request forgery, a vulnerability that causes a web server to make unauthorized network requests.

In the 53rd episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu, Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, and Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, discuss medicine pricing, drug safety and dengue surveillance.
The episode examines the Supreme Court’s concerns over the difference between the supply price and maximum retail price of essential cancer medicines. In one instance, the court was told that a cancer drug with a price to retailer of about ₹2,700 carried a maximum retail price of ₹27,000. The Bench described the difference as “broad daylight dacoity”.
The discussion also covers the court’s concerns about hospitals requiring patients to buy medicines from their own pharmacies, its suggestion of a uniform 16% margin and questions around generic prescriptions and the implementation of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order.
The episode also covers the risks of indiscriminate painkiller and antibiotic use, including kidney disease and antimicrobial resistance. While prolonged or inappropriate use of painkillers can cause kidney-related complications, unnecessary or incorrect antibiotic use can make infections harder to treat. The discussion highlights the importance of appropriate prescribing and responsible medicine use.
The final segment focuses on a Dengue Early Warning System being developed by researchers at the Institute of Advanced Virology in Keralam. The system combines disease surveillance data with rainfall, temperature and humidity to generate weekly, district-level forecasts using machine learning.
Trained on six years of data, from March 2020 to February 2026, the system aims to help health authorities anticipate increases in dengue transmission. If validated, the forecasts could support earlier surveillance, mosquito-control measures, healthcare preparedness and public alerts. The system is still under development and evaluation.
The episode ends with a fun fact about dengue mosquito eggs, which can remain dormant for months in dry conditions and hatch when water becomes available. Even seemingly dry containers can harbour eggs that may contribute to future mosquito populations.
The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

Environment Minister Ramalinga Reddy has directed forest officials to take immediate action against all illegally established resorts and homestays in the Eco Sensitive Zone (ESZ) and buffer zone of various tiger reserves and protected areas.
Mr. Reddy, who chaired a meeting of the Standing Committee of the State Board for Wildlife, sought details on the number of resorts, homestays and other commercial activities in the ESZ and buffer zone after the ESZ was notified for various tiger reserves and protected areas.
Silent zones
He also directed that there should be minimal disturbance in ESZ areas and that they should be declared as silent zones.
He also sought preparation for Zonal Master Plans to create awareness among people on the dos and don’ts in ESZ areas.
At the meeting, a proposal for the establishment of an eco resort on private land falling within the buffer zone of Bhadra Tiger Reserve was placed which was deferred.
No quarrying
Also, a proposal for allowing quarrying activities in the ESZ of Kappatagudda Wildlife Sanctuary in Gadag was rejected.
The proposals for electrification BSNL saturation towers, OFC cables and a small connecting bridge were approved for recommendation to the Standing Committee of the National Board for Wildlife (SC NBWL).
At the meeting, it was also decided to submit a proposal to the SC NBWL for rationalisation of the boundary of the Shettihalli Wildlife Sanctuary where the boundary was not properly demarcated while notifying it.
The Standing Committee of the State Board for Wildlife also decided not to alter the ESZ of the Bannerughatta National Park.
Opinion to Union govt.
“With regard to the ESZ re-notification for Bannerughatta National Park it was decided to submit an opinion to the Union government that since all the elephant corridors are already part of the ESZ and the ESZ has been notified after due deliberations the same may be continued, without any modification,” said a statement from the Minister.
It was also decided to review the existing buffer zone notifications for the tiger reserves through a Technical Committee and discuss whether any rationalisation of the existing buffer zones is required.

Kerala Health Minister K. Muraleedharan on Saturday (October 3, 2026) denied reports of a shortage of medicines in government hospitals and alleged that pharmaceutical companies were behind claims highlighting such a crisis.
Speaking to reporters, Mr. Muraleedharan described the reports as a “media creation” and maintained that adequate stocks were available in government hospitals.
“There is no crisis at all. There is sufficient stock of medicines. If needed, you can ask the Superintendent or anyone whether there is medicine stock or not,” he said.
He alleged that some pharmaceutical companies were attempting to create an impression of a shortage and accused sections of the media of highlighting their claims.
“Some pharmaceutical company representatives have come out with sticks and swords. And to highlight that, some big and small TV media people have also stepped out,” he said.
Reiterating that medicines were available in sufficient quantities at government hospitals, Mr. Muraleedharan said he would not be intimidated by such allegations.
“There is adequate stock of medicine. Furthermore, if any pharma company people come out brandishing sticks and swords, I am not someone who gets scared seeing that. That is all,” he said.
On the spread of infectious diseases, Mr. Muraleedharan said the number of cases reported so far was lower than during the corresponding period last year.
“Compared to last year, that many cases have not been reported. So far, infectious diseases haven’t been reported in such numbers,” he said.
On the proposed All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in Kerala, the Minister rejected Union Minister Suresh Gopi’s allegation that the State government was not cooperating with the Centre.
He said Mr. Gopi was unaware of the facts and that the Principal Secretary of the Health Department had already submitted a report to the Centre on the matter.
“If he asks for it, I can show him a copy. Then why unnecessarily blame the State Government?” Mr. Muraleedharan said.
He said Mr. Gopi was keen on establishing AIIMS at a particular location.
“However, we don’t have any such preferences. Our only demand is that Kerala should get an AIIMS,” he said.
On cases of alleged medical negligence, Mr. Muraleedharan said the Health Department had not received any direct complaints.
“If we receive a complaint about anything, we will investigate it. There is no doubt about that,” he said.
Sabarimala preparations
Mr. Muraleedharan, who also holds the Devaswom portfolio, said preparations for the upcoming Sabarimala pilgrimage season were progressing.
A meeting chaired by Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan would be held at Pampa on October 17 to review the arrangements, he said.
“The government is providing full support to the Travancore Devaswom Board. Therefore, what we expect is that things can be conducted without any issues,” he said.
The Sabarimala pilgrimage season begins on November 17.

Eight organisations from different parts of the world have come together to form the Global Alliance for Diabetic Foot Survival and Limb Preservation. This was announced at the Diabetic Foot Society of India’s (DFSI) national conference held in Bengaluru on Friday, October 2, 2026. The founding organisations also signed a joint declaration calling for diabetic foot ulceration to be recognised as a global public health priority.
The eight organisations are the DFSI, King’s College London, the International Association of Diabetic Foot Surgeons, D-Foot International, the Pan African Diabetic Foot Study Group, the American Limb Preservation Society, the International Federation of Podiatrists and the Podiatric Surgeons’ Society.
A 2023 review cited in the alliance proposal estimated that about 18.6 million people worldwide are affected by diabetic foot ulceration annually. It reported a five-year mortality of about 30% following a diabetic foot ulcer and over 70% following a major amputation.
The proposed alliance will focus on research, workforce training, comparable data collection and advocacy with the World Health Organization and national governments to secure greater policy recognition of diabetic foot disease.
The proposed framework also emphasises the involvement of people living with diabetes, those who have experienced foot ulcers and people living with amputation or disability in decision-making and programme design. It envisages regional demonstration programmes, a common measurement framework and an annual report on progress.
The DFSI Scientific Committee is proposed as the alliance’s interim secretariat, with a governing council representing the founding organisations overseeing strategy, finances and activities. The members are expected to meet within 30 days to discuss governance, collaboration, resource mobilisation and implementation.

'It's a nightmare.' Former refugee, professor on Trump's new Medicaid policy
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Mustafa Rfat has been getting frantic phone calls recently from refugees with disabilities. As of Oct. 1, refugees are losing access to Medicaid across the country because of H.R. 1, the Trump administration's major budget bill Republicans passed last summer.
"I spent these past two weeks just talking with so many of them, literally just terrorized by the reality that their children with disabilities are losing coverage," he says. "For example, a father is a refugee with disabilities, with two kids with disabilities, and he's just confused how he's going to get the medication."
Rfat is a professor of social work at the University of Nebraska at Omaha, and his research focuses on refugees with disabilities, an experience he knows firsthand.
When he arrived in the U.S. as a refugee from Iraq in 2011, the chronic condition that affects his spine was severe. "I was in a very bad situation," he says. "I couldn't walk. I was in so much pain. I missed my medications for a long time. I didn't see a doctor. So it was a very, very difficult and vulnerable situation."
As he moved from Alabama to Illinois to West Virginia trying to find housing and continue his education, Medicaid was a lifeline, Rfat says. "I had to climb this big mountain of acclimating into the culture here, learning English, dealing with the traumas of the war, the loss of family members, the challenges that I faced, being alone with a disability," he says.
"I was determined and in this determination, Medicaid was the big factor that made my dreams come true." In fact, he says one of the specialists who treated him wrote his first reference to apply for college. He has since become a U.S. citizen with a family, a doctorate, and a job as a professor.
Now, he's trying to help refugees with disabilities facing the challenges of navigating life in the U.S. without that lifeline. As of Oct. 1, refugees are among the groups that will lose Medicaid coverage.
Hundreds of thousands will lose coverage
Only a small portion of legal immigrants have been eligible to enroll in Medicaid, including refugees and asylum seekers. Because of the changes to "Alien Medicaid Eligibility" in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that Republicans passed last summer, an even smaller subset now have access. An estimated 280,000 people will lose Medicaid in October, according to an analysis by KFF Health News.
That includes immigrants admitted to the U.S. on humanitarian grounds who are waiting to be approved for a green card, explains Ben D'Avanzo, senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center.
"The people who are losing Medicaid and CHIP [the Children's Health Insurance Program] are among some of the most vulnerable immigrants — people who have experienced violence in their own homes or on their journey, who may have physical and mental conditions, who are fleeing persecution and war," he says. "These are people who we have long, in the United States, welcomed, and populations who have had very strong, historic bipartisan support."
Rfat points out that refugees are more likely to have serious health conditions than other groups. "More than one third of them have at least one type of disability — this is what the research tells us," he explains. In refugee camps and during war access to doctors and medication is difficult, and simple conditions can become serious and complex.
That was his own experience with an inflammatory condition called ankylosing spondylitis. "By the time I arrived in the U.S., a lot of doctors told me, 'You are one of the worst cases that we are seeing,'" he says. "And that is the case for a lot of refugees that come here."
In a statement to NPR, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services wrote that they are enacting the law passed by Congress working with states to accurately implement the policy. They did not respond to a follow up question about the effect of the policy on refugees with disabilities.
"Once these changes take place, these groups of immigrants will be left with very few options for affordable, comprehensive coverage," says Drishti Pillai, director of immigrant health policy at the nonpartisan health research organization KFF.
"They could still buy full price coverage from ACA marketplaces, but that is often unaffordable," Pillai says. "Employer-sponsored coverage is also an option, but many immigrants, especially those who are on Medicaid, don't work in jobs that don't offer employer-sponsored coverage, such as jobs in construction, agriculture, food service."
She says a few states are creating their own coverage options for these groups, but many have tight budgets and are facing even bigger Medicaid cuts in January. Most states have also opted in to allow Medicaid to continue to cover pregnant women and children who would otherwise be losing coverage.
D'Avanzo points out that the categories of people losing coverage now will eventually become green card holders who are eligible for Medicaid.
"So these are people who are going to put off preventative care, who are not going to treat their chronic conditions, who are going to forgo important medication," he says. "And then when they are Medicaid eligible again in the future, once they've received their green card, they're going to be needing much more specialized care and much more costly care."
Hope for change
Mustafa Rfat is headed to his alma mater Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri this weekend to meet with a few dozen refugees with disabilities and share some of his recent research. He says the loss of Medicaid and food benefits will hang over the event.
"It's a nightmare for the community," he says. He hopes Congress will reverse course.
He's decided to devote part of the event to teaching about civic engagement. "To understand the importance of voting when they become citizens, to understand the importance of being aware of the policies, being aware of who their representatives are, how to communicate with their representatives," he says.
"These are new Americans," he adds. "These people are going nowhere. By making their health and well-being worse, it's not going to benefit anyone."

ప్రధాన ఎన్నికల కమిషనర్ జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ కాక్రోచ్ జనతా పార్టీ (CJP) ముంబైలోని శివాజీ పార్క్ మైదానంలో 02 అక్టోబర్ 2026న నిరసన ప్రదర్శన నిర్వహించింది. ఓటర్ల జాబితా ప్రత్యేక సమగ్ర సవరణ (SIR)లో ఓటర్ల తొలగింపు ఆరోపణలు, ఎన్నికల ప్రక్రియలో పారదర్శకతపై నిరసనకారులు ఆందోళన వ్యక్తం చేశారు. ఈ సమావేశానికి ముంబై పోలీసులు అనుమతి నిరాకరించినప్పటికీ, వందలాది మంది నిరసనలో పాల్గొని నినాదాలు చేశారు. సమావేశంపై ఉన్న ఆంక్షలను ఉల్లంఘించారనే కారణంతో నిర్వాహకులతో పాటు, ఇందులో పాల్గొన్న 400-500 మంది గుర్తుతెలియని వ్యక్తులపై పోలీసులు FIR నమోదు చేశారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, ముంబైలోని శివాజీ పార్క్ మైదానంలో జరిగిన నిరసనకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో బాగా ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 02 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ముంబైలోని శివాజీ పార్క్ మైదానంలో సీఈసీ జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలంటూ CJP చేసిన నిరసనను చూపుతున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియోకి ముంబైలో జరిగిన CJP నిరసనలతో ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదు. ఇది మధ్యప్రదేశ్ అసెంబ్లీ ఆమోదించిన యూనిఫామ్ సివిల్ కోడ్ బిల్లుకు వ్యతిరేకంగా సెప్టెంబర్ 15న భోపాల్లోని సెంట్రల్ లైబ్రరీ గ్రౌండ్లో AIMIM నేత అసదుద్దీన్ ఒవైసీ నిర్వహించిన బహిరంగ సభకు సంబంధించిన పాత వీడియో. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 18 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నుంచి, అంటే CJP ముంబై నిరసన ప్రదర్శన కంటే రెండు వారాల ముందు నుంచే ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం.
ఈ వీడియోను ఫేస్బుక్, ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్లలో అమీన్ సిద్ధికి అనే భోపాల్కు చెందిన కంటెంట్ క్రియేటర్ 18 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026లో అప్లోడ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఇవే దృశ్యాలను చూపుతున్న మరిన్ని వీడియోలను (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కూడా అమీన్ సిద్ధికి తన ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పేజీలో అప్లోడ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. వీటి ప్రకారం, ఈ వీడియోలు మధ్యప్రదేశ్ రాజధాని భోపాల్లో జరిగిన AIMIM అధ్యక్షుడు అసదుద్దీన్ ఒవైసీ బహిరంగ సభకు సంబంధించినవిగా పేర్కొన్నారు. వార్తా కథనాల (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రకారం, మధ్యప్రదేశ్ అసెంబ్లీ ఆమోదించిన యూనిఫామ్ సివిల్ కోడ్ బిల్లుకు వ్యతిరేకంగా భోపాల్లోని సెంట్రల్ లైబ్రరీ గ్రౌండ్లో 15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న ఈ సభను నిర్వహించారు.
ఇక వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపించే దృశ్యాలను గూగుల్ స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూ ద్వారా పోల్చి చూడగా, ఈ వీడియో భోపాల్కు సంబంధించినదిగా స్పష్టమైంది.
చివరిగా, ముంబై శివాజీ పార్క్లో CJP నిరసన దృశ్యాలంటూ భోపాల్కు చెందిన సంబంధం లేని వీడియోను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

INDIA bloc to march to EC today over Gyanesh Kumar row: Traffic curbs, heavy security in place
Traffic would be regulated and diverted in and around Connaught Place, Patel Chowk, Parliament Street, the Patel Chowk-GPO stretch, and adjoining areas.
Security was tightened and traffic restrictions imposed across central Delhi on Tuesday ahead of the INDIA bloc’s proposed march from Parliament to the Election Commission of India (ECI) headquarters over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls and demands for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
According to police, the march is scheduled to begin at 11am, with Opposition MPs expected to walk from Parliament to the ECI headquarters. The Congress had also announced on Monday that its MPs would participate in the protest.
Track Live Updates on Opposition March in Delhi today
The Delhi Traffic Police said traffic would be regulated and diverted from 8am onwards in and around Connaught Place, Patel Chowk, Parliament Street, the Patel Chowk-GPO stretch, Windsor Place-GPO, Ashoka Road, Jantar Mantar Road and adjoining areas.
A senior police officer said elaborate security arrangements had been made along the proposed route and around Parliament and the ECI headquarters to prevent disruptions to traffic and maintain law and order.
"No permission has been granted for any such march or gathering," the officer said.
“Security personnel have been deployed at all sensitive points, and barricades will be installed wherever required. We have made arrangements to regulate the movement of protesters and ensure that commuters are not inconvenienced. Any diversion will be implemented depending on the movement of the protesters,” the officer added.
The traffic police advised commuters to avoid non-essential travel through the affected areas, particularly during the morning hours, and use public transport, especially the Metro, wherever possible.
Commuters were also urged to avoid stopping or parking near restricted areas and follow the directions of traffic personnel and road signage.
HT has learnt that Opposition leaders had requested the police not to obstruct the march, stressing that it would be a peaceful demonstration.
Around 4,000 personnel from the Delhi Police and Central Armed Police Forces have been deployed across New Delhi district amid heightened security following demonstrations by civil society groups demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, which began on October 2.
