Vietnamese police arrest 12 suspected of prowling city streets at night, snatching cats for meat
HANOI, Vietnam — Police in Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City arrested 12 men suspected of operating a citywide ring that stole and resold about 2,700 cats for meat, Vietnamese state media said.
Police identified 39-year-old Luu Thanh Binh as the alleged leader of the network. He and 11 others were being investigated for theft, state media said Monday.
Investigators said Binh bought stolen cats, kept them at a facility in the city's north and resold them for meat. He worked with suppliers who recruited others to ride motorcycles through residential neighborhoods between 11 p.m. and 4 a.m., hunting for cats and trapping four to 10 cats each night.
Eating dog and cat meat is not unique to Vietnam and has been practiced in parts of Asia, though it is not common practice. In Vietnam, cat meat traditionally is more commonly consumed in the north, among older generations.
The practice has declined with growing pet ownership and urbanization, and younger Vietnamese are more likely to regard dogs and cats as companion animals.
In 2024, more than 250,000 people signed a petition calling for an end to Vietnam's dog and cat meat trade. The city of Hoi An also pledged in 2021 to end the sale and consumption of dog and cat meat.
Some believe eating cat meat brings good luck, though there is no scientific evidence for such claims.
Police raided the network on July 8 and found about 50 cats and dozens of traps, state media reported.
The suspects told investigators they had stolen and sold about 2,700 cats, the reports said. Police did not say how long the operation had been running.
Police returned 13 of the cats confiscated in the raid to their owners. A nonprofit animal rights group was caring for the others while authorities sought to identify their owners.
Under Vietnamese law, dogs and cats are considered private property, and stealing them is considered theft. Criminal prosecution generally applies when the value of the stolen property exceeds 2 million dong ($77).
In a separate raid in June, police reported they had rescued more than 400 cats. At least 40 were reunited with their owners, but dozens of dead cats were found packed in ice.

What to know about nationwide protests in India over voter list changes
NEW DELHI — Protests have spread across India in the past week as opposition parties and civil society groups demand the resignation of the country's election chief over alleged manipulation of voter lists.
The campaign has been led in part by India's "Cockroach" youth movement, which previously organized street protests that forced the education minister to resign in July.
Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the poll body's ongoing revision of voter lists. They accuse the revision could disenfranchise millions of voters and benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP. The commission and government deny any wrongdoing.
Here's what to know:
Voter list changes fueling the protests
India is the world's largest democracy with hundreds of millions of people voting in national and state elections. The Election Commission plays a central role in determining voter eligibility and administering elections, making changes to electoral lists politically significant.
The dispute centers on a nationwide voter list revision known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR. It began last year in the eastern state of Bihar ahead of local elections and has since expanded to most of India's states and federally administered territories.
Under the process, voters are required to provide documents showing they are eligible to remain on the lists.
The Election Commission says the exercise is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible entries and ensure legitimate voters remain registered. Critics say it could instead exclude legitimate voters, particularly poorer and other vulnerable communities.
They also say the requirements are confusing and difficult for many people to provide, particularly those who lack older government records or other documents.
Critics say the changes could benefit Modi's party
India's Election Commission is an independent constitutional body overseeing elections and maintaining voter lists, but opposition parties accuse the commission of favoring Modi's party. They allege the changes could remove people more likely to support opposition parties while preserving or adding voters who favor the BJP.
The BJP and the Election Commission reject the allegations and say the revision has no political motive. Modi's party says the list is being updated to weed out what they call "infiltrators."
The issue was prominent in West Bengal's crucial state elections earlier this year after a voter list revision removed about 9 million names, or roughly 12% of the electorate. The deletions left millions of eligible voters unable to cast ballots. Modi's party won the state for the first time.
Politics can impact commission rulings
Indian law requires a majority vote of commission members to enact changes making disagreements among its members potentially significant.
The Indian Express newspaper reported in September that two of the three election commissioners had formally objected to several decisions involving voter list revisions, registration procedures and the commission's digital systems.
The newspaper reported Kumar, the election chief, rejected those objections.
The Election Commission said the report reflected "differing views and deliberations" rather than formal written objections.
Protesters seek end to changes that could reshape elections
The "Cockroach" movement, opposition parties and civil society groups have called for Kumar to resign or be removed and for an inquiry into his conduct, including possible criminal proceedings. They want the current revision halted and the previous electoral lists used for future elections.
They also demand a more independent and transparent process for appointing election commissioners.
Election Commission data indicates voter lists in some regions could shrink by as much as 30%, fueling concerns among opposition parties and protest groups over potential exclusions.
The dispute is likely to intensify as the changes resulting from the revision expand throughout India, which is facing a series of state elections early next year.

A passenger bus, linked to Madhya Pradesh Government’s recently launched public bus service, was gutted in fire on Tuesday (October 6, 202) near Ujjain with about 40 people in it who managed to get out without any injuries, officials said.
The incident took place in Ramwas area, about 15 kilometres from Ujjain when the bus was traveling from the holy city to Indore. Officials, however, said that it was a private operator bus, under contract with the government as part of the Mukhyamantri Sugam Parivahan Seva, that was launched on September 25.
Chief Minister Mohan Yadav and Union Minister for Road Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari had flagged off 351 buses, reintroducing a public bus service in the State after 21 years, under the public-private partnership (PPP) model.
Speaking to The Hindu, Madhya Pradesh Transport Secretary Manish Singh said that while the exact cause of incident was yet to be known, an inquiry has been initiated in the matter.
Mr. Singh denied media reports claiming that the fire was caused due to a tyre burst.
“It appears to have occurred due to a short-circuit in the bus. But all the passengers were evacuated safely before the blaze spread,” he said.
Mr. Singh said that the bus was already being operated by a private company and was recently brought under a contract with the the Madhya Pradesh Passenger Transport and Infrastructure Limited, a recently established State-owned company, for operations.
Mr. Singh also denied recent allegations that the government had “rebranded old buses as new”.
“We never claimed that the government is going to buy 15,000 buses [the targeted number by 2031]. We have started operations with the PPP model and it is still in the transition phase. We have started developing our infrastructure and are working to better regulate the operations like ticketing and maintain safety protocols but the buses will be brought in by private operators only,” said Mr. Singh, who is also the managing director of the company.
After the resumption of services, the Congress has alleged that the BJP government has pasted saffron colour vinyl sheets on old buses while raising questions on their fitness standards. Various videos also surfaced on the internet showing the sheet peeling off from the buses.
Mr. Singh said that there was “nothing wrong with it” and that the private operators had modified the outlook of the buses as per their budget.
“All the buses that were added have passed the fitness test but are in a condition to run about 5-10 years. Of all the buses that were flagged off, only about 50 were newly bought by some of the private operators,” he said.

A woman in the remote Siberian region of Irkutsk has died of plague, a regional official said Friday, as a Russian media outlet reported dozens were under quarantine.
Local media named her as 28-year-old laboratory technician Darya Shipilova.
The "People of Baikal" news outlet said she worked for the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute and may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.
As many as 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine, the outlet added, without elaborating.
There was no immediate statement from Russia's health ministry and AFP was not able to verify the reports.
Alexei Tsydenov, governor of Russia's Buryatia region, had reported in a social media post earlier that a woman in the neighbouring Irkutsk region had "died of plague".
The plague is an infectious disease caused by bacteria.
Pneumonic plague is highly infectious and can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization.

World Contraception Day on September 26 offers an opportunity to look closely at a part of family planning that receives very little attention: contraception for men. The key question here is why the range of methods available to men and women remains so different.
Women today have options including oral pills, injectables, implants, intrauterine devices and permanent sterilisation, though access and affordability to safe and reliable contraception in our country continues to remain a major challenge. For men, the practical choices are still largely limited to condoms for reversible contraception and vasectomy for permanent contraception. Male and female reproduction are governed by the same broad hormonal axis, yet the biology, anatomy and mechanics of preventing conception create very different problems. Understanding those differences helps explain why a male equivalent of the pill has remained elusive.

Traffic crawls across Lutyens' Delhi amid INDIA bloc march to EC
At several points, long queues spilled back onto adjoining roads as motorists struggled to find alternate routes through the heavily barricaded area.
Barricades, diversions and security restrictions turned key roads in Lutyens' Delhi into long stretches of slow-moving traffic on Tuesday, as the INDIA bloc's march towards the Election Commission disrupted movement across the New Delhi area.
From India Gate and Connaught Place to Parliament Street and Jantar Mantar, bumper-to-bumper traffic built up on several stretches, with vehicles inching forward amid diversions and intermittent stoppages.
At several points, long queues spilled back onto adjoining roads as motorists struggled to find alternate routes through the heavily barricaded area.
The congestion left commuters stranded for prolonged periods, with several saying they were stuck for at least an hour. Some commuters abandoned their vehicles and switched to the Metro or walked to reach destinations in central Delhi, while visuals showed vehicles packed tightly along stretches affected by the restrictions.
Traffic was severely affected on the Connaught Place, Patel Chowk, Rafi Marg, Parliament Street stretch, Motilal Nehru Marg, Teen Murti Marg, Prithviraj Road, Windsor Place, Ashoka Road, and Jantar Mantar Road.
"Traffic was moving at almost zero speed and the queue barely moved. We were stuck for nearly an hour before some of us decided to get down and take the Metro instead," a commuter stuck on Ashoka Road said.
Traffic was also affected across the New Delhi area, with movement hit on Krishna Menon Marg, Rajpath and Circular Road, while heavy congestion was reported at several roundabouts around India Gate. Another commuter reported a complete traffic jam from Mori Gate roundabout towards Hamilton Road and Pul Dufferin rail over bridge.
Another commuter said roads around India Gate were heavily congested, with restrictions and diversions on several routes making it difficult to move between adjoining areas.
"The entire road near the Taj and Marriott was blocked for VIP movement and thousands of vehicles were left stuck. There was heavy barricading and no easy way through," the commuter said.

The police also said restrictions around the Taj and Marriott hotels were linked to VIP/VVIP movements and were imposed according to operational and security requirements.
"We understand the concern regarding traffic restrictions in the vicinity of Taj and Marriott hotels and the resulting congestion. Traffic regulation during VIP/VVIP movements is undertaken as per operational and security requirements and efforts are made to keep such restrictions need-based and for the minimum possible duration," the police said.
The disruption followed special traffic arrangements put in place from 8 am for the INDIA bloc march from Parliament Street to the EC headquarters to protest against the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
The Delhi Traffic Police said vehicular movement was being regulated or diverted on several key roads in and around Connaught Place, Patel Chowk, Parliament Street and Jantar Mantar.
Commuters have been advised to avoid unnecessary journeys through Jantar Mantar, Parliament Street, Ashoka Road and adjoining areas and expect diversions, barricading and congestion.
Traffic personnel remain deployed at critical points to manage diversions and ease congestion, with normal movement being restored progressively after the completion of the movements, police said.
The traffic restrictions came as INDIA bloc opposition MPs marched towards the EC headquarters, with heavy security and barricading deployed around Parliament and the poll panel's office ahead of the protest.
High drama unfolded during the march when Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, along with other MPs and supporters, attempted to proceed towards the EC office. They were stopped near the NITI Aayog office on Parliament Street.
The INDIA bloc has been opposing the SIR exercise and has raised concerns over the revision of electoral rolls, while the Election Commission has rejected allegations of a split among its three-member body and maintained that decisions on the exercise were taken unanimously.

The setting for perhaps the country’s biggest exercise in public debate was quintessential rural India: fields of green paddy, a pond, a temple. On a normal day, as dusk falls in the village of Ajgara, in Uttar Pradesh, people gather beside the pond to chat about the price of crops, the weather, or the theft of a goat.
But for more than a month, metaphysics and ethical dilemmas replaced the usual topics. Is it permissible to use deceit to defeat an evil enemy? Is a lie justified to save a life? What is the nature of reality?
The debating tournament was the brainchild of Abhishek Pandey, district magistrate of Pratapgarh district in Uttar Pradesh. When he took up the post two years ago, he knew the area was rich in archaeological treasures connected to the ancient Indian epic, the Mahabharata.
Throughout the text, Yudhishthira, one of the central characters, debates the nature of human existence. In Ajgara he answers a string of philosophical questions to save the lives of his four brothers.
Pandey, 35, like most Indians, grew up on this story and was proud of the intellectual depth of the dialogues. When he attended Oxford University on a fellowship, he admired the debating society, which has a 200-year-long history. But India’s tradition of sophisticated public debate is much older, going back more than 3,000 years.
Pandey started to question why the tradition had not survived. “Indians have celebrated certain traditions for centuries,” Pandey says. “Why have we ceased to celebrate the legacy of debate and questioning?” Was it possible to revive this noble tradition, particularly when it was a vital component of a democracy?
He decided that the annual fair held in Ajgara in September would be a good time to stage the event. In the run-up to the fair, Pandey and his team arranged 1,500 debates across the district.
Age and education were no bar. The youngest participant was a 10-year-old schoolboy, the oldest an 80-year-old farmer. In debating for and against a motion, participants were judged on reasoning and moral clarity.
The overwhelming public response dumbfounded Pandey. Thousands of people participated in multiple rounds, and were whittled down to eight finalists – two women and six men.
While villagers milled around, enjoying the food, watching folk theatre, buying local crafts and taking a ride on a ferris wheel, a silence descended inside the debating tent.
The finale of the Great Ajgara Debate 2026 on 17 September lasted about six hours.
One topic was women’s rights. A finalist, Vivek Singh, argued that women might have equality on paper but society’s expectations of them impeded the exercise of these rights.
Another, Prajjwal Shukla, 24, argued that the real question was not what role society assigned to women but who had the authority to make those choices. Whether a woman chose a career, household responsibilities, or both, should be her choice and hers alone, he said.
“What amazed me the most was not the intellectual quality of the debates (which was great), but the atmosphere. Everyone listened respectfully, patiently, without interrupting. No one got personal. People sat for hours,” says Pandey.
Marx’s adage that history repeats itself, first as tragedy and then as farce, is a perfect description of how debate in India has descended from the sublime to the farcical.
In television studio debates everyone shouts at the same time. No one can finish a point. Personal abuse and gibes fly while the anchor whips them into ever greater frenzies.
Sadhana Dwivedi, one of the two women to progress into the last round of the Great Ajgara Debate, despises this new format.
“People need to learn to listen, to understand there may be value in another person’s point of view,” she says. “In a democracy, it is crucial for all opinions to be aired so that we can get to the truth.”
The turnout was a good demonstration of the thesis posited in economist Amartya Sen’s book The Argumentative Indian that India had a rich tradition of questioning authority and entertaining heterodoxy.
It is only in recent years that dissent has been suppressed, notably by the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party, which values conformity.
“It’s ironic, because the BJP wants to recreate a Hindu state but is not even acquainted with the traditions of ancient Hindu civilisation, such as that of debate and being open to different ideas,” says author and commentator Parsa Venkateshwar Rao Jnr.
At the end of the tournament, the eight finalists were garlanded and driven around in an open-top car to much cheering, feted as “intellectual heroes”. The winner was Shukla, who is preparing to sit exams to enter the civil service.
“I can’t believe I am the winner of a debate that took place at the exact same spot as in the Mahabharata all those centuries ago. I participated just because I wanted to hear other people’s thoughts,” he says.
Pandey is still processing the public enthusiasm. “My deputy asked me if we should get some police deployment because the turnout everywhere was so big, but I laughed and said no. That would be a sad affair.”
He hopes to spread the event across other Indian states and perhaps nationwide. “We have to inculcate a culture of debate. It’s the hallmark of a democracy.”
Meanwhile, he has planted his flag. The inscription on the stone slab he has installed at the site reads: “The Great Ajgara Debate. First Debate 3152 BC: Yudhishthira. Second Debate 2026: Prajjwal Shukla.”

The MRP debate, which has been recently triggered where a hospital purchased a product for ₹11 and billed it for ₹325, is misplaced and lacks the context we need to understand the issue properly.
Hospitals rightly point out that the gap between procurement and billing is not all profit: storing supplies, maintaining sterility and ensuring availability carry costs. But patients are entitled to ask a more basic question. How did ‘maximum’ become the price they routinely pay?
Understanding maximum retail price
MRP was designed as a ceiling to protect consumers. In healthcare, it can, however, also conceal how a price is built. The printed figure tells a family little about the manufacturer’s returns, the margins taken along the supply chain, or whether the product offers any advantage over a cheaper alternative. A patient in an emergency cannot shop around. When choice disappears, a ceiling risks becoming the default charge.
This is a serious problem, and price controls can help. In 2019, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority applied trade-margin rationalisation to 42 non-scheduled cancer medicines. The government estimated that this could save patients 200 crore annually. But the wider lesson is not that every medicine and device should have the same permitted margin. It is that India needs to decide what each margin is paying for.
Different products, therapies
A standard syringe sold by multiple suppliers does not justify the same return as a therapy developed for a rare disease after years of research and clinical trials. Nor should a familiar medicine acquire an innovation premium simply because it has a new brand name and a large marketing budget.
India needs a differential profit and margin strategy. Routine, high-volume products should have modest, transparent distribution and hospital margins, informed by comparable procurement prices. Bulk purchasing should benefit patients, insurers and public programmes. Genuine costs of stocking, safe handling, wastage and round-the-clock availability should be recognised openly, rather than recovered through an inflated price for the item itself.
Companies that take substantial scientific risks deserve a different approach. Those investing in original research, rare and neglected diseases, or products that demonstrably improve outcomes while reducing hospitalisations and total care costs should be able to earn higher profits. Fair returns give investors a reason to fund difficult work. But the premium should go to the organisation creating the clinical value, not automatically to every intermediary between the factory and the patient.
Science must earn
‘Novel’ must not be a label a company awards itself. A claim for a higher return should be tested against existing treatments: Does the product help patients live longer or better? Does it prevent complications? Is it safer or easier to use? Does it lower the total cost of treatment, even if its purchase price is higher? A product that costs more upfront but prevents repeated admissions may be better value than the cheapest item on the shelf.
Societal impact should count too. Research into diseases affecting small or neglected patient groups, reliable supply in underserved areas, and meaningful differential pricing for vulnerable patients merit consideration. These commitments must be specific and measurable. A patient-assistance scheme that reaches a handful of people cannot excuse a price that excludes everyone else.
India has an institution on which to build: Health Technology Assessment already evaluates clinical effectiveness, costs and equity to inform public decisions. Its evidence could help distinguish genuine advances from claims designed to justify a higher price.
Margins under microscopes
The government should establish an independent Healthcare Pricing and Value Panel with clinicians, scientists, health economists, patient representatives and pricing regulators. It should assess products against published criteria: clinical benefit, research risk, development investment, disease burden, total health-system cost and access for those least able to pay. Its members should disclose conflicts of interest, explain decisions and provide an appeal process.
A higher return would come with obligations. Companies seeking one should submit evidence and relevant costs for independent review. Premiums should be reconsidered as products mature or competitors enter the market. Where promised benefits remain uncertain, agreements could link part of the payment to observed outcomes. Concessional access for eligible patients and public programmes should be enforceable, rather than left to goodwill.
The panel must also separate manufacturer profits from trade and hospital margins. Otherwise, a policy intended to reward research could simply enlarge the amount captured downstream. Regulators need visibility into invoice prices, rebates and patient charges. Patients need itemised bills showing the product charge and any separate handling fee. Small and rural pharmacies, meanwhile, need viable returns to keep essential products available. A pricing policy that closes the last-mile supplier has failed its patients.
Profit, but not profiteering
MRP should remain a shield against overcharging, but it cannot be our entire definition of fair price. Companies should be able to make a profit, but not profiteer. India can protect a family buying an IV set and reward a company developing a breakthrough for a child with a rare disease. To do both, we must ask what the price rewards, what benefit the patient receives, and who can actually afford it. In healthcare, margin should follow proven value and access, and not bargaining power over a captive patient.
(Dr. Rajendra Pratap Gupta is the chairman of Health Parliament, a global executive think tank on healthcare, and former advisor to the Health Minister, government of India. founder@parliament.health)

Sinner out for rest of season with knee injury
- Published
World number one Jannik Sinner will not play again in 2026 because of an ongoing right knee injury.
The Italian has not played competitively since defending his Wimbledon title in July.
Five-time Grand Slam champion Sinner said he "needed to think about my long-term career" when deciding to end his season early.
"Me together with the doctors have decided that I need a course of treatment for my knee," the 25-year-old said in an Instagram video.
"The last couple of years gave me so many beautiful feelings and emotions, which this year is going to be way different.
"I will do everything possible to get back 100%."
Sinner was the dominant player for much of the year, winning 44 and losing just three of his singles matches.
He won five Masters 1000 titles in a row between March and May, becoming the youngest man to complete the 'career Golden Masters'.
Sinner's injury means that Alexander Zverev is highly likely to replace him as world number one by the end of the year.
Second-ranked Zverev, who has won the French Open and US Open this year, trails Sinner by 1,280 points in the live rankings.
However, Sinner will be unable to defend the points he claimed with title triumphs in China, Vienna, Paris and the ATP Finals at the end of last year.
Sinner won six titles in 2026 on all three surfaces and lost just one singles match between March and July.
He reached the semi-finals of the Australian Open, losing in five sets to Novak Djokovic, but suffered a shock second-round exit at the French Open in May.
The loss to Juan Manuel Cerundolo in hot and humid Paris conditions ended Sinner's 30-match winning streak.
However, he bounced back superbly at Wimbledon. Despite being taken to five sets in the first round - and bleeding through his shoes at one point - he recovered to eventually beat Zverev in the showpiece and defend his title.
Sinner and generational rival Alcaraz, having met in three of the four Grand Slam finals last year, only played each other once in 2026.
Sinner came out on top, beating the Spaniard in the Monte Carlo Masters final to replace him as world number one.
He finishes the year with a 10-1 record against top-10 players, with his sole defeat coming against Djokovic in Melbourne at the start of the year.

South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
- Published
South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself.
"Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it.
His response to the US president's claim is blunt.
The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.
Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted.
In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African.
Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas.
Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property.
"Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said.
She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside".
The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.
In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa.
"While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart."
SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme.
Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms".
"There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says.

An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".
Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners.
"I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."
Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject.
The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.
He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner".
"But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.
Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.
Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.
While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".
Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".
He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.
The programme has its critics among Afrikaners in South Africa too.
"Why single out the white Afrikaner to say this group qualifies to flee to the US? This country suffers gender-based violence. Why not single out women?" Rudi Swanepoel, a pastor from Johannesburg told the BBC.
Swanepoel thinks it is not persecution but a "loss of privilege" that is causing some Afrikaners to feel aggrieved.
"To use the metaphor of a cake, 30, 40 years ago the white people of South Africa controlled the cake," he says. "Since democracy came, the obvious reality was we had to now start sharing that cake and those privileges."
Alongside "rural safety", the Trump administration has raised other concerns about South Africa, including targets for companies to increase non-white employment and a law allowing the state, in exceptional circumstances, to expropriate land without compensation. These are aimed at redressing historic racial inequality.
Meyer wants Trump's executive order against South Africa, which underpins the refugee pathway, revoked.
He said South Africa had never prevented people from leaving and had addressed all the US concerns, stressing that the land expropriation law is awaiting a court judgement.
"South Africa has challenges with the prevention of crime and with the combatting of crime," he said.
But he added: "It's a problem all around. It's not rural. It's not farm attacks only. If you look at the total picture, the huge levels of crime in the black townships of South Africa are the biggest concern, proportionally, far more than anything else."
He said he would encourage the US to help South Africa with resources on combatting crime, including by providing equipment to speed up reaction times.
Meyer also has a message for Afrikaners protesting against "farm attacks" by laying white crosses in Washington.
"It doesn't help us to raise a voice outside, if we are not committed to doing something inside the country," he says.

NAMSCON 2026, the 66th annual conference and convocation of the National Academy of Medical Sciences (India), will bring together medical professionals, researchers and academicians from across the country in Chennai from October 8 to 11.
Hosted by SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre, SRM Institute of Science and Technology, Kattankulathur, the conference will focus on the theme ‘Synergy of Science and Technology in Healthcare for a Healthier Tomorrow’.
Tamil Nadu Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar will inaugurate the conference as the chief guest.
The four-day programme will include pre-conference workshops, symposia, keynote addresses, National CME sessions, and oral and poster presentations.
The scientific sessions will cover antimicrobial resistance, CAR-T cell therapy, biosimilars and biologics, senolytic therapies, rare genetic disorders, emerging infections, pandemic preparedness and the Indian diabetes phenotype. Discussions will also focus on medical education, robotics in surgery, organ donation and transplantation, and evolving approaches to tuberculosis management.
Eight workshops on October 8 will cover trauma care, neonatal resuscitation, AI in clinical research, spine surgery, endoscopic gastroenterology, palliative care, diagnostic reasoning, and physician entrepreneurship.
Among the speakers are Shekar C. Mande, president, Indian National Science Academy; Abhijat Sheth, Chairman, National Medical Commission; Mohan V., Chairman, Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, Chennai; Mohan Kameswaran, Managing Director and Senior Consultant, Madras ENT Research Foundation; Vivekanand Jha, Executive Director, The George Institute of Global Health, India; and Gobardhan Das, Member, NITI Aayog.
M. Srinivas, member (Health), NITI Aayog, will deliver a plenary lecture on ‘Good Governance for Transforming Medical Institutions in India and Quality Research during Residency’. He will also interact with undergraduate and postgraduate students on research during residency.
Founded in 1961, NAMS is a non-statutory body that advises the Government of India on health policy and planning. NAMSCON 2026 will be the first annual conference of NAMS to be hosted by SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre.
The conference is being organised under the leadership of R. Jayanthi, Organising Chairperson and Dean, SRM MCH&RC, and Melvin George, Organising Secretary and Head, Centre for Clinical Pharmacology and Clinical Trials Research, with Rajarajan Swaminathan as State Convenor.

Shreyas Iyer’s meticulous preparation, sharp tactical understanding and ability to assess the opposition’s strengths make him well-equipped for a successful stint as India’s captain, said VVS Laxman, who served as the team’s head coach at the Asian Games.
Shreyas led India to the men’s cricket gold medal in Japan, and Laxman was particularly impressed by the way the middle-order batter approached the leadership role, saying he was already showing the qualities needed to stay ahead of the opposition in the fast-paced T20 format.
India edged out Pakistan by 19 runs in a high-scoring final to defend their title.
“It’s just the start of his captaincy career, but I’m sure that he’ll achieve a lot of success. He’s a player’s captain. He makes everyone very, very comfortable and leads by example,” Laxman told BCCI in an interview.
“Whether with the bat or on the field, even before the team meetings, he sits down with the plans, strengths and opposition’s weaknesses. And he’s very thorough in the way he prepares. Puts a lot of emphasis on fitness. I’m sure that he’ll have a very successful tenure as captain.”
A classy batsman in his playing days, Laxman also highlighted Shreyas’ tactical acumen and his understanding of the players at his disposal, qualities that he believes helps him get the best out of the team.
“He’s a fabulous leader of players. Tactically, very, very smart, very sharp. He understands the strengths of each and every player on his team. And he knows how to get the best out of them,” he said.
“Especially in T20, you’re required to be one or two steps ahead of the opposition. And the way he assesses the opposition’s strengths and weaknesses, prepares really well. And that’s something which I’m very happy about.”
The coach’s praise came after India negotiated a difficult build-up to the Asian Games, with weather, travel and limited opportunities for outdoor practice posing challenges to their preparation.
Laxman said the squad’s ability to adapt to those circumstances was one of the most pleasing aspects of their campaign.
“From the time we came to Japan, we were challenged by weather, travel, lack of good practice session and preparation. But not even once did I feel that the team, all the players in the squad were not eager to get ready for the big matches,” he said.
“We know that the semifinal (against Sri Lanka) was on a tough wicket, but they showed positive intent and again in the finals, with the bat, with the ball, I thought they were very professional.”
Laxman was also pleased with how the players adjusted to conditions that were different from those they encounter in international and IPL cricket. He cited the example of the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023 where the conditions were completely different from Japan and players adapted well.
“Both the games in China and in Japan had their own set of challenges. And I’m happy that both the group of players, again, adapted and adjusted and got the desired result for the country,” he said.
For Laxman, the gold medal was particularly significant because of the rarity of the experience for cricketers of standing on a podium at a major multi-sport event.
“The ultimate aim and goal for all of us, whether in China or here in Japan, was to win the gold. Because not very often do we as cricketers experience being on a podium and receiving the gold medal,” he said.

Why drones for stubble? Farmers question Punjab govt in Sangrur protest
BKU Ekta Ugrahan farmers blocked all three gates of the Sangrur DC office over their 13 demands. Women protesters questioned the government's promises, while the standoff now turns on a proposed meeting.
Farmers led by the Bharatiya Kisan Union (Ekta Ugrahan) continued their protest outside the Deputy Commissioner’s office in Punjab’s Sangrur, questioning the state government over its plans to use drones to monitor stubble burning while demanding a concrete solution for stubble management.
The farmers have blocked all three gates of the Deputy Commissioner’s office and are sitting in protest over 13 demands. A large number of farmers, including women, have joined the demonstration, with protesters preventing officials and employees from entering the premises.
BK Ugrahan state president Joginder Singh Ugrahan questioned the administration’s approach to stubble management, saying that while officials were preparing to deploy drones to monitor farmers’ fields, there was no adequate arrangement for the disposal and management of stubble.
Ugrahan said farmers know how to cultivate their fields and also understand the problems they face. He questioned why the administration was focusing on surveillance instead of ensuring effective arrangements for stubble management.
The farmers said their protest had been continuing since Tuesday. On Tuesday night, protesters also demonstrated outside Sangrur Deputy Commissioner Poonamdeep Kaur’s residence until around 10 pm before burning an effigy to register their protest.
WOMEN FARMERS TARGET PUNJAB GOVERNMENT
Women farmers participating in the protest also criticised the Punjab government over its proposed Rs 1,000 financial assistance for women ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections.
They said women want their rights and solutions to their problems rather than merely financial assistance. They also urged Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann to address the drug problem in villages, saying addiction has caused several families to lose their sons.
The women farmers also questioned the Deputy Commissioner for not coming to the protest site and addressing their concerns.
FARMERS SEEK ACTION ON 13 DEMANDS
The farmers have said they will continue their protest until the government gives them concrete assurances on their 13 demands.
Ugrahan said the Punjab government had sent a letter regarding a meeting with the farmers’ organisation. According to him, Finance Minister Harpal Singh Cheema, Cabinet Minister Aman Arora and Agriculture Minister Gurmeet Singh Khuddian are expected to participate.
However, there is a discrepancy over the date of the proposed meeting. One piece of information mentions October 13 at 11 am at Punjab Bhawan, while Ugrahan’s statement refers to October 11. The final date is yet to be officially confirmed.
Meanwhile, Ugrahan also raised the issue of rising farmer debt and alleged that government policies were making farming increasingly difficult.

Cornell names former acting U.S. attorney general to review rape case
Cornell University named Sally Yates, a former acting U.S. attorney general and career federal prosecutor, as head of an independent internal review into how the school handled a former student's rape allegations.
The announcement comes as the school continues to face outrage on campus and nationally after a former student filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was drugged and gang raped in 2024. The woman, identified in the suit as Jane Doe, also alleged failings by the school in how it handled her complaint and the aftermath.
Yates, a partner at King & Spalding who served as the U.S. deputy attorney general under President Barack Obama, was picked by the newly formed Special Committee of the Cornell University Board of Trustees. She will also examine the school's policies related to how it "prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus," the school announced Tuesday.
"Sally Yates brings extraordinary experience, independence and judgment to this work," said Anne Meinig Smalling, chair of the special committee, in the school's announcement. "The questions raised by the Jane Doe matter warrant a rigorous examination of Cornell's response to that case, but our responsibility is broader. We have asked Ms. Yates and her team to examine Cornell's overall approach to preventing and responding to sexual misconduct, identify where we are doing things well and where we can do better, and recommend changes that will help make our community safer."
Doe filed her lawsuit in mid-September. In it, Doe alleges that seven men drugged and assaulted her for several hours in October 2024 at their Chi Phi fraternity house on campus. No criminal charges were ever filed against the men. Those named in the lawsuit have denied all wrongdoing. Cornell University is also named as a defendant in Doe's suit.
The university has maintained that Cornell University Police investigated the case thoroughly and that the school held its own Title IX investigation, which resulted in suspensions and expulsions.
But in the weeks that have followed the lawsuit's filing, students have protested the university's response to the case. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed state Attorney General Letitia James to lead a criminal investigation into the rape case, after sharp criticism of its handling by campus police and the local prosecutor, Matthew Van Houten. The case also has renewed national conversations over consent and sexual assault on college campuses.

At full-time in India vs Brazil, Akash Mishra looked completely devastated – sunken shoulders, head down, and he often shook his head in disappointment.
Eight days ago, he was a hero: he assisted Ryan Williams as India scored against Panama — a gorgeous long ball from the left flank that perfectly landed for Williams to latch on and shoot.
For 68 minutes, he was one of the reasons India dared to believe it could beat a team ranked 94 places above it. Against Brazil, he did not get that much time – 45 minutes, two goals conceded and subsequently replaced by Jay Gupta.
India lost that match 0-4, and unlike most national team players, he did not post anything on Instagram, posing with Brazilian stars like Vinicius Junior and Bruno Guimaraes.
“I’m a sore loser. After the loss, as a player, we never feel good,” Akash told reporters. “I didn’t sleep. I was watching the game all night. I slept in the morning, and then, I had to wake up early and do my recovery.”
Akash may have replayed his mistakes again and again in his head, but he knows he can’t dwell on it for too long. Uruguay, another former world champion, awaits.
“As a team, or as football players, we don’t have to sit down with the results. We have a very good upcoming game, so we have to prepare for that and do our best. This is what the game demands. We have to play with whatever rest we get. As a player, I’ll always be prepared to perform well,” he said.
India plays Uruguay in its third and final match in this international window on Tuesday, at the Salt Lake Stadium, at the same venue where Akash had to endure a difficult night three days ago.
The full-back will now have a shot at redemption, and one to get his sleep back.
“Uruguay is as good as the other teams, so we have to keep our focus for the 90 minutes and any extra (stoppage) time that follows,” Akash said.
“When we came to this camp, we got to know that we were playing Panama, Brazil, and Uruguay. We knew the calibre of those teams, and we have been prepared for them. It was never as if we were only prepared for Brazil. Two are done, one more to go, and we have to finish on a very good note.”

In a country where cricket eclipses every other sport, the recently concluded Asian Games offered a much-needed reminder of India’s breadth of sporting talent. In this edition of the games, in Japan, India won 85 medals: 21 golds, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. I admit I did not know many of the players competing, or even some of the sports they play before putting this piece together. Learning about the stories, I wonder why not.
There were individual breakthroughs, records broken and history made. There were also hard-fought team victories, including the Indian women’s hockey team gold medal after a 44-year wait.
Sports broadcaster Siddharth Pandey cited an old saying in the world of sport: “You cannot be what you cannot see.” For Pandey, one of the most heartening sights was families and communities rallying around the four female players from the north-eastern states. (The region has endured decades of conflict and is often overlooked in the national conversation.) “We simply cannot underestimate the impact these games and medals have on future generations taking up non-cricketing sport and wanting to excel in it,” he told me.
Recognition is also important. Vidya Pillai, the first Indian woman to win a snooker world championship has spoken about her sport not getting the attention or respect it deserves. She felt unacknowledged following her 2023 feat, despite the fact that it came after six unsuccessful world finals and she beat two former world champions along the way.
Behind India’s medal glory are dozens of athletes and families who have struggled financially, trained with limited facilities, and often without much institutional support.
So this week, I am sharing a sample of the many extraordinary stories from different parts of the country. These are only a fraction of the champions to emerge from the games, yet they provide a glimpse of the possibilities that can open up when a country sees and celebrates sporting talent across the spectrum.
Neeru Dhanda (gold in trap shooting): Dhanda’s family in Haryana’s Jind relies on the government’s food subsidy programme and she began her sporting journey using a borrowed shotgun with tin cans as targets. Right before the games began, the 26-year-old spent a few days in a hospital recovering from an illness instead of training. But last week, as rain lashed the shooting range in Urenocho, she became the first Indian woman to win an individual gold in trap shooting at Asian games. She won a second gold in mixed team trap event as well as a silver in the women’s team trap event.
Vithya Ramraj (gold in 4x400m): Ramraj was one of the breakout stars of the event with a three-medal haul. NDTV reported that her father had to borrow money to support Ramraj and her twin sister’s athletic careers. Alongside the team gold in 4x400m, she won a silver in the mixed 4x400m relay. She also broke Indian legend PT Usha’s long-held national record in 400m hurdles which won her a bronze medal.
Sahil Jadhav (gold in compound mixed archery team and men’s compound team): Not long ago, Jadhav contemplated quitting archery, frustrated by not making the progress he had hoped for. He had been forced to compete with borrowed arrows for selection trials, the New Indian Express reported, adding that his mother sold her jewellery to buy him professional compound bows. Now, the 25-year-old has two gold medals and an automatic entry to the 2028 LA Olympics.
Lalremsiami Hmarzote (member of the gold-winning women’s hockey team): The women’s hockey team forward once had to travel about 100 miles from her home to reach the only hockey academy in Mizoram. When she was growing up, her parents had no idea about what hockey and she played barefoot on dirt pitches. This month, playing her 200th international appearance, the 26-year-old struck gold. She scored the lone goal of the final against China, which Hockey India described as a “stunning reverse-stick strike”.
Ancy Sojan (silver in long jump): With colourful beads glistening in her hair, Sojan flung herself 6.53 metres in long jump, to win the silver medal. Earlier this year, the 25-year-old broke the national record set in 2004. Her journey, from a village in Kerala’s Thrissur district to the international stage, has not been straightforward. Last year, she was diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome, forcing her to drastically change her diet and manage the medication-related weight gain she had before the tournament.
Aslam Inamdar (a member of the gold-winning men’s kabaddi team): Inamdar came to kabaddi, a south Asian contact sport combining elements of tag and wrestling, from humble beginnings – he was partly drawn to it because it was affordable and didn’t require expensive equipment. Coming from a village in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar, he worked odd jobs – from cleaning washrooms to working in the fields – so he could spend evenings training. “It still feels like a dream to me,” Inamdar told the Indian Express. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.” The 26-year-old was instrumental in helping India win their gold-medal match against Iran.
I would love to hear from you: which sportsperson from the Asian Games did you find most inspiring and why?
What else we’re reading about
Flydubai incident | Indian pilot Smit Machchar is being hailed as a hero for helping to save 174 passengers on the flydubai flight to Israel last week, after his co-pilot made an apparent effort to crash the plane. After being stabbed, Machchar opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to enter and overpower the attacker. He is recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia, where the plane eventually landed.
Datacentres | Protests against water-guzzling datacentres erupting from the US to Australia are gathering momentum in India. South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen travelled to the small village of Tarluvada, in Andhra Pradesh, where the state government has been accused of fast-tracking plans for a $15bn AI datacentre for Google, allegedly to avoid stringent environmental scrutiny.
Art and design | Designer Vikram Goyal, celebrated for his signature repoussé brass work, brings his installation Wings and Tales to a Georgian townhouse in London’s Mayfair from 12 to 16 October. The exhibition includes furniture designs inspired by landscapes from the Indian epic Ramayana.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shireen Gandhy, director of Mumbai’s pioneering Chemould Prescott Road Gallery, founded in 1963, recommends the work of artist Al-Qawi Nanavati. “[She] is a young artist from Bombay whose practice is rooted in printmaking and making her own paper. Her mother’s passing left her with a void,” says Gandhy. Nanavati created Letters to My Mother, an epistolary artwork crafted in, as Gandhy puts it, “a deeply personal language that is not known to anybody but her. Using fabrics and saris that belonged to her mother, she creates this tactile imagery for these letters. I find it very moving and like alchemy.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
13,626
This is the number of students from disadvantaged communities who dropped out of some of India’s most prestigious institutions: central universities, Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management between 2018 and 2023, according to Anubhuti Vishnoi of the Economic Times. The figure comes from an interim report by a committee set up by the supreme court last year to examine mental health and suicide prevention in higher education.
Vibe check
Nitesh Shetty’s sketches find absurdity in everyday life, turning familiar characters and social interactions into unexpected punchlines. This is what makes his work powerful: you’re laughing one moment and moved the next. There is a reel for every character imaginable: the person perpetually trapped in the limbo of land disputes, the man who is strangely knowledgeable about funerals, or the friend who has a unique dressing sense.
The 35-year-old from Mumbai didn’t plan on a career in comedy. “When you don’t know what to do, you try anything,” he told me. Now, Shetty rejects more conventional formats such as television in favour of challenging himself creatively. His advice for those who look up to him? “It’s a great time to build something. The [online] audience is ready-made for you. Be original and don’t follow trends.”

Mumbai, October 7, 2026: The Bombay High Court has ruled in favour of Punjab National Bank (PNB) in a 42-year-old dispute over a Cuffe Parade flat, holding that a 1982 transaction was a genuine agreement to sell and not merely security for a loan.
Justice Sharmila Deshmukh overturned a 2023 City Civil Court decree favouring the original owner, M/s Mohan Gandhi & Company, and directed specific performance of the agreement, paving the way for PNB to secure the property after paying the balance Rs 1 lakh.
Dispute Over Cuffe Parade Flat
The dispute concerns Flat No. A/1 in Cuffe Castle Co-operative Housing Society. In July 1982, the partnership firm agreed to sell the flat to the then New Bank of India, which later merged with PNB, for Rs 15 lakh.
PNB’s advocates Shanay Shah and Anuj Loya submitted that the bank paid Rs 14 lakh and was handed possession, with the balance payable upon execution of the sale.
The firm later challenged the transaction, claiming the flat had been given as collateral security for a Rs 14 lakh loan taken by Argee Textiles Pvt Ltd, a company associated with one of its partners. Its advocate Prasad Pathare argued that the property was to be returned after repayment of the loan.
Court Rejects Security Claim
The firm also alleged that the agreement was executed late at night under pressure and without proper legal advice, and questioned the validity of signatures of two minor partners.
Rejecting the claims, Justice Deshmukh relied on bank records, payment vouchers and Debt Recovery Tribunal proceedings. The court noted that the Rs 14 lakh paid by PNB was directly credited towards reducing Argee Textiles’ loan liability on the firm’s instructions.
The court held that the payment, coupled with transfer of possession, indicated consideration towards sale.
“The agreement when read holistically indicates that the agreement between the parties was a transaction of sale of flat for total consideration of Rs. 15 lakhs,” the court observed, adding that possession after receipt of substantial consideration was a “strong indicia of sale transaction”.

The High Court dismissed the firm’s suit and directed PNB to pay the remaining Rs 1 lakh, with 12% annual interest from June 30, 1987, within four weeks.

Temperamental traits and adverse experiences during childhood may together offer clues to vulnerability to major psychiatric disorders, a transdiagnostic study by researchers at NIMHANS has found.
The study, published recently in the Journal of Affective Disorders, examined 1,162 adults, including 532 people with psychiatric disorders, 457 unaffected first-degree relatives (FDRs) and 173 healthy controls. The participants were drawn from 393 multiplex families - families in which multiple members had been diagnosed with psychiatric disorders - involving schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD).
The researchers examined four broad dimensions of adult temperament - negative affectivity, extraversion/surgency, effortful control and orienting sensitivity - along with adverse childhood experiences (ACEs).
“Our findings suggest that temperament does not map onto psychiatric disorders in a simple, one-to-one manner. Rather, different combinations of temperamental characteristics are associated with different disorders, and some of these characteristics are also seen among unaffected family members,” said Srinivas Balachander, corresponding author and one of the lead researchers of the study.
Temperament shared within families
Using data from the erstwhile Accelerator programme for Discovery in Brain disorders using Stem cells (ADBS) project, (funded by the Department of Biotechnology and Pratiksha Trust), now known as the Rohini Nilekani Centre for Brain and Mind, at NIMHANS, the researchers found evidence of familial sharing across all four temperamental domains.
This was observed despite considerable variation in the psychiatric diagnoses within the same families. The finding is of interest because temperament is known to have a substantial heritable component, although the study did not directly establish that the temperamental characteristics observed were caused by specific genetic variants.
“In our study, considering the significant within-family heterogeneity in terms of different diagnoses, there was still a significant degree of shared temperament,” Dr. Balachander said.
Among affected participants, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder were associated with lower extraversion/surgency and orienting sensitivity. OCD was associated with higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity, along with lower effortful control and extraversion/surgency. Participants with AUD showed higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity and lower effortful control.
Some of these patterns were also observed among unaffected first-degree relatives. Relatives of people with schizophrenia showed lower extraversion/surgency, while relatives of people with OCD showed higher negative affectivity and lower effortful control.
“These findings are particularly interesting because some temperamental characteristics were evident even in individuals who did not have the disorder but belonged to families carrying a higher degree of familial risk,” Dr. Balachander said.
Childhood adversity and alcohol use disorder
The researchers also examined whether adverse childhood experiences altered the relationship between temperament and psychiatric disorders.
The clearest evidence for an interaction between temperament and childhood adversity emerged in alcohol use disorder. The overall ACE score was significantly associated with AUD, and interactions between childhood adversity and two temperamental domains - extraversion/surgency and effortful control - were also observed.
“Childhood adversity appears to add another layer to the relationship between temperament and psychiatric vulnerability. In our study, the evidence for this interaction was particularly apparent in alcohol use disorder, rather than uniformly across all four disorders,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers, however, cautioned against interpreting the findings as evidence that a particular temperament or childhood experience causes a psychiatric disorder.
The study was cross-sectional, meaning that the assessments were made at one point in time. The adult temperament measures were self-reported and could be influenced by current illness, treatment, illness duration or an individual’s perception of their own past Reports of childhood adversity may also be affected by recall and measurement biases.
Testing the findings
To examine whether the findings extended beyond the genetically enriched family sample, the researchers tested their statistical model using an independent community-based cohort from the Consortium for Vulnerability to Externalizing Disorders and Addiction (c-VEDA).
The analysis included 2,485 adults aged 18 to 23 years for whom the relevant temperament, ACE and psychiatric assessments were available.
The model showed an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.822 for alcohol use disorder, 0.742 for bipolar disorder and 0.752 for OCD. Its performance for schizophrenia was close to chance level, with an AUC of 0.526.
“The external validation gives us some indication that the associations identified in the family-based sample may extend to community populations for some disorders. However, the findings for schizophrenia did not replicate well, which is an important limitation and needs further investigation,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers said the findings point to the need for prospective studies that follow unaffected family members over time. Such studies could help determine whether particular temperamental characteristics precede the onset of psychiatric illness or are partly consequences of illness and its treatment.
“Temperament and childhood adversity may eventually become useful components of broader risk assessment frameworks, but we need prospective longitudinal evidence before we can say that they have predictive or preventive value,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers said that studying temperament alongside childhood adversity could eventually provide a more nuanced understanding of psychiatric vulnerability than considering family history alone. However, they stressed that the present findings do not establish that these measures can predict who will develop a psychiatric disorder.
The researchers said continued longitudinal follow-up of the cohort would be important to establish whether the observed temperamental patterns have value in identifying individuals at increased risk before the emergence of clinically significant symptoms.

Spain lifts arrest warrant for Catalan separatist Carles Puigdemont
Spain has lifted the arrest warrant for Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont, allowing the politician to return home without fear of detention for the first time in nearly a decade
MADRID -- Spain has lifted the arrest warrant for Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont, allowing the politician to return home without fear of detention for the first time in nearly a decade.
Puigdemont fled Spain for Belgium in 2017 after his failed bid to lead an illegal secession attempt for Spain’s northeastern Catalonia.
Judge Pablo Llarena lifted his arrest warrant on Tuesday moments after Spain’s Constitutional Court announced it has decided to apply a government amnesty for the Catalan separatists to one of Puigdemont’s cohorts who had been found guilty of misusing public funds.
Llarena said he was lifting the arrest warrant for Puigdemont while awaiting the opportunity to study the Constitutional Court’s decision, which he said would likely affect the warrant.
Puigdemont's party in Catalonia, Junts, said that he will give a press conference later on Tuesday from Waterloo, where he resides as a self-proclaimed exile.

When the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.
Google, one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech companies, would soon be bringing a “golden opportunity” to this tiny village in south India: a $15bn AI datacentre.
The project, being built in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, is set to be Google’s largest “hyperscale” AI datacentre outside the US and would, officials said, make the village of Tarluvada into a world-famous tech hub. Jobs, usually scarce in this impoverished community, would become bountiful, real estate prices would soar and compensation for any land would be generous.
Few in the village – which sits on a dusty unpaved road and is surrounded by farms and forest – had even heard of AI or knew what a datacentre was. Yet it did not take long for local jubilation over Google’s arrival to turn to suspicion.
Just as protests have erupted globally over AI datacentres – from California and Texas to Scotland and Australia – communities in Andhra Pradesh, too have been gathering in opposition to the project, fearing that the people will end up bearing a crippling environmental and economic cost.
“We have learned that America does not want the problems of datacentres and so now Google is bringing them here,” said Tarluvada’s village head, BRB Naidu, who admitted he was torn about whether the datacentre would bring prosperity or ruin to their community. “Many in the village are very worried. But the government has refused to answer our questions.”
Pointing up to the nearby hillside – where bulldozers recently stripped the land bare of trees to ready it for Google’s mega AI campus – Naidu adds: “The work just continues every day.”
The state government, which is allied with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s party, have been accused of trying to obfuscate the true scale of the vast AI hub being built in Andhra Pradesh, to push the project through at lightening speed and avoid more stringent environmental scrutiny. Google has partnered with the Adani Group, one of India’s largest and most politically powerful conglomerates with a reputation for getting approvals through quickly, to build the project.
Publicly it was announced as a 1GW project – already a larger energy requirement than most AI datacentres. In its response to the Guardian, Google referred to it only as an unspecific “gigawatt scale AI hub”, that was “comparable to other projects”.
But state environmental clearances reveal that permission has been granted for it to be more than double that size – 2.51GW; the power equivalent of two large nuclear reactors at full output. Over a year, it amounts to upwards of 30% of the current energy consumption of the whole of Andhra Pradesh, a state home to more than 55 million people.
Activists fear that meeting the datacentre’s vast energy demands will lead to seismic environmental consequences for the region, including driving up fossil fuel emissions. While Google has pledged to help generate “new, clean energy” to power its AI hub, currently 75% of the country’s electricity grid is run on coal.
The state government argues AI datacentres will be essential to India’s growth and long-term digital competitiveness. According to the government of India’s Economic Survey 2025–26, India generated nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global datacentres.
But locals and activists say that building one of the world’s largest AI datacentres in a region of India already struggling with issues over extreme heat, water, land, forests, power shortages and environmental regulation comes at a heavy cost.
Google’s project will in fact encompass three separate datacentres around the state capital of Vizakhapatnam. One other site nearby to Taluvada is a few metres from reserve forest, a drinking water reservoir and a wildlife sanctuary home to endangered species such as leopards.
Despite the AI datacentre’s expansive footprint, the state government issued environmental clearances to Google in just nine days, with no public consultation.
Three petitions challenging the state’s quick approval of the project have now been filed to India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT), the country’s top environmental court. The petitions allege that government’s assessment of the risks to the environment and water supplies were “grossly inadequate, scientifically unrealistic, and misleading”. A public litigation has also been filed in the Andhra Pradesh high court.
“This datacentre will be unprecedented in scale but there was no public hearing and no substantial evaluation of the ecological damage or the economic cost for local communities,” said VS Krishna, an activist with Human Rights Forum, the organisation which filed the NGT cases.
Krishna alleged that their campaign to protest against the datacentre had been met with a deliberate silencing, including videos and social media pages being taken down. The government did not respond to this allegation.
“We just have to look at the protests happening across the world to understand how environmentally catastrophic this will be,” Krishna added.
In Tarluvada, temperatures regularly soar to about 45C during the summer and there are concerns the datacentres – documented emitters of heat – could make this even worse. The mass deforestation required for the project – more than 100 acres, could drive up temperatures even more. In response to the Guardian, Google said the project would have “no expected impact” on the local community.
The strain on water supplies in this already water-stressed area has also been a cause of concern. In similarly water-stressed cities in the US, datacentres have been accused of exacerbating drought while polluting the water supply. Google said this project would use air-cooling instead of water, and would therefore have no impact on local drinking water supplies.
Venkat Surynarayana, 40, a farmer in Tarluvada, said that when officials had initially come to measure land for the datacentre “they never mentioned anything about risks of pollution or water or heat, they didn’t even tell us what the project was.
“We are sick with worry since we learned about the problems a datacentre can bring. This area can not afford to be any hotter. What if this makes our land dry and worthless? What will happen to my crops and my livelihood?”
Surynarayana claimed attempts to get answers from the local administration had been met with police threats and protesters such as himself had been routinely detained. “When we raised our voices, they ignore us and then they shut us down,” he said. “But if this is not stopped, it could be the end of Tarluvada.”
For the state government of Andhra Pradesh, the deal struck with Google to build this vast datacentre on its turf is a source of enormous pride, part of a wider policy to make the state into India’s most advanced and affluent tech hub. “Artificial intelligence is becoming foundational infrastructure for the global economy,” said Sribharat Mathukumilli, a local MP with the ruling state government, who rejected the environmental concerns.
The subsidies and incentives they offered to Google, from decades-long tax breaks and discounted land to access to cheap electricity and water, are estimated to amount to 220bn rupees ($2.2bn) over 20 years.
“Our objective is not simply to host a datacentre, but to create an AI and digital ecosystem,” said Mathukumilli. Late last year, the state granted permission for another 1GW AI datacentre, to be built by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries.
Google insisted the design choices of its AI datacentre have been tailored to local conditions and that it had “engaged deeply” with local communities, claiming it would generate thousands of jobs around Vizakhapatnam.
But swathes of villagers in Tarluvada allege they were forced to give up land for the project against their will, and say they have not been given all they were promised in return.
“No one will tell us the truth about this project,” said T Applaraju, 40, who was one of the 520 local families in Tarluvada who recently had land taken back that the government had allocated to him 20 years ago. He claims he was given no notice that his land was to be taken until April this year, when security guards working for the Adani Group erected fences and blocked locals from entering the plots they had farmed for years.
“They took land that we thought belonged to us, it’s a big shock,” he said. “Why are Google building this here and not in America?”
The state government claims no lands were forcibly taken and that it gave “generous compensation” to those who were eligible. The Adani group says that all necessary legal approvals were given. But many of the 47 farmers from the impoverished Dalit community who were compensated for their land are also unhappy.
One farmer, P Venkat Rao, alleged he was pressured by the government into giving up his only acre of land against his will. He received $40,000 in compensation, but said the government’s promise to give them a replacement piece of land and one job per family had not materialised. Without land to farm, Rao described the compensation as “worthless”.
“I am a farmer, without my land I am nothing,” he added. “They have taken my livelihood and broken their promises.”

President Donald Trump suggested on Monday that reporters from The New York Times and other media outlets should be “arrested” following their coverage of his weekend campaign event in Ohio.
