An Oct. 2 video shows Trump fielding reporters' questions outside the White House. Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy asked, "What do you think about New York's governor appointing a special prosecutor in the Cornell rape case, Letitia James?" (James, New York's attorney general, previously led a civil fraud case against Trump.) Trump thrice called James corrupt, saying he feels "badly" for "whoever" James prosecutes and alleged that defendants she targets "won't get a fair shake."
A rumor circulated online in early October that U.S. President Donald Trump said he feels "badly" for the seven current or former male Cornell University students whom a female former student accused of rape.
Trump purportedly made the remarks while answering a question about New York Attorney General Letitia James' appointment as a special prosecutor to investigate the case.
Snopes readers asked about this claim via email, with one person inquiring, "I saw something that says Donald Trump said he feels bad for the 'Cornell 7,' but can't find reputable sources. True??"
In sum, people correctly attributed this statement to Trump. A C-SPAN video shows Trump standing outside the White House on Oct. 2 and responding directly to a reporter's question about the Cornell case, thrice calling James corrupt and saying he feels "badly" for "whoever" James prosecutes, alleging that defendants she targets "won't get a fair shake."
James previously sued Trump and his associates in a civil fraud case beginning in 2022, leading to Trump repeatedly targeting her on social media.
In an emailed response, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis referred us to Trump's own comments, adding that the White House believes James has weaponized the justice system to unjustly target the president.
Digging into the rumor
The Cornell accuser, identified in court documents only as Jane Doe, claims the seven men sexually assaulted her at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Oct. 19 and 20, 2024. She filed a lawsuit against the seven men, the university, the fraternity and others, in mid-September.
On Sept. 28, Tompkins County, New York, prosecutors announced they were reopening the criminal investigation, citing a "discrepancy" between Doe's original statement and the allegations in the lawsuit.
Prior to New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointing James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case on Oct. 1, James posted a statement of compassion for Doe on her official social media accounts, writing, "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I'm holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you're not alone. We stand with you."
In an example of the claim from Oct. 2, a Facebook post (archived) displayed a meme reading, "This is disgusting: Trump just said he 'feels badly' for the people accused in the Cornell rape case because Letitia James is now overseeing the investigation. Not one word for the victim."
(Really American via Facebook)
Other users shared the rumor about Trump's remarks on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived) and X (archived). Some posts didn't mention James but did include a video showing a reporter's question about James and Trump's answer. Examples of those posts appeared on Bluesky (archived), Threads (archived) and X (archived).
The remarks occurred when Trump spoke to a group of reporters outside the White House. Videos show Fox News' Peter Doocy asking Trump about Hochul appointing James as a special prosecutor:
DOOCY: What do you think about New York's governor appointing a special prosecutor in the Cornell rape case, Letitia James?
TRUMP: Letitia James is a corrupt person. She's totally corrupt and I can't imagine it. And, I feel badly for whoever she's looking at because they won't get a fair shake. But Letitia James is a corrupt person.
C-SPAN posted remarks on social media. (Readers can also watch the full press gaggle on YouTube, with the pertinent moment beginning at 6:24.)
Trump has made other remarks about the Cornell case. During a similar gathering of reporters on Oct. 1, a video shows an unidentified reporter asking Trump, "Mr. President, do you think that Cornell University has done enough to investigate the alleged rape on campus?" Trump answered, "Well, I don't know that much about it but Cornell is a fine school, and I'm sure they'll do what's right." (Readers can watch that full gaggle on YouTube, with the Cornell question occurring at 11:43.)
Trump has also posted about the case on Truth Social (archived), labeling it "the highly controversial Cornell University rape case" and questioning why Hochul would appoint James.
For further reading, we previously reported Trump authentically expressed well wishes to Ghislaine Maxwell, the close associate of deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, prior to her conviction on federal sex-trafficking charges.

In early October 2026, a rumor spread that a worker at a Russian lab that studies Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes the plague, had died of the pneumonic plague.
Some social media users said the lab worker's death resulted from an accident at the lab. One X post reads, in part, "A lab worker in Russia has died from pneumonic plague."
Meanwhile, several Snopes readers emailed us asking for details about the story.
The claim stems from various news reports about a 28-year-old woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia. Around 200 people have reportedly been isolated as a precautionary measure. The articles cited Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian public agency responsible for "federal state sanitary and epidemiological supervision," according to the Russian government.
In short, it has not been possible to independently verify the rumor without access to primary sources or confirmation from Russian authorities. Therefore, this claim is unrated. We will update this article if we learn more.
Russian authorities reportedly implement containment measures
Snopes could not reach the website of Rospotrebnadzor, therefore we could not confirm the details of the lab worker's death. On Oct. 4, Russian news agency Interfax reported that the Russian government said she had died of a pneumonia pathogen of "unknown etiology," meaning its origin is not clear.
The same report adds that Rospotrebnadzor said no microorganisms associated with the individual's professional work were detected in that person's samples following "extensive testing." If true, it would suggest the lab worker did not die of pneumonic plague.
Local authorities have reportedly implemented preventative measures. Interfax cites the Rospotrebnadzor health agency as saying:
Due to the patient's professional activities, upon receiving information, a comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures was immediately and fully implemented in accordance with sanitary legislation. This included identifying the widest possible circle of people who had been in contact with the patient, inpatient medical observation, and daily laboratory testing. The results revealed two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection. No other infectious agents were detected.
View from U.S. Department of State
"We are aware of reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia," a U.S. Department of State spokesperson said via email. "We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners."
We contacted the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety of the European Union Commission requesting updates on the situation. We will update this report if we receive responses.
There are three main types of plague: bubonic plague, which infects lymph nodes; septicemic plague, which infects the blood; and pneumonic plague, which infects the lungs. The bubonic and septicemic plagues are most commonly transmitted via flea bites and handling infected animals, while the pneumonic plague spreads through the air via infected droplets.
The pneumonic plague "has a nearly 100% case-fatality rate when untreated," according to the CDC. The illness requires antibiotic treatment that should start as soon as the plague is suspected, even before test results, per the U.S. health agency.
"Plague is a known disease and is treatable with common antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early," the State Department spokesperson said via email. "Cases occur naturally in many parts of the world."

- Published
A lawyer for one of the seven men accused of participating in a Cornell University gang rape has called for the special prosecutor on the case to recuse herself over past public comments.
The lawyer had said a social media post from New York Attorney General Letitia James throws into question her investigation's "integrity and independence".
In the 28 September post, James wrote that "what this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable" and told survivors that "we stand with you".
The university's administration is under fire over its alleged mishandling of the October 2024 incident and, according to US media, now faces a no-confidence vote by Cornell faculty.
The university's Faculty Senate, a governing body comprised of professors and other academic staff, will vote on a resolution of no confidence next week, according to reports. Cornell is an Ivy League university, alongside Harvard and Yale, and its faculty includes Nobel laureates and other distinguished researchers.
A majority no-confidence vote would be a largely symbolic gesture, signalling the broader faculty's discontent and applying pressure on university leadership to act.
Cornell University announced on Tuesday that it was hiring Sally Yates, a former deputy attorney general, to lead an independent review of the university's practices and procedures on sexual assault and related conduct.
"Yates and her team will conduct a detailed review of the University's response to the allegations involving Jane Doe", the university said in a statement, "including whether Cornell followed its policies and procedures in responding to the matter".
Allegations made in a lawsuit against seven men and the university have rocked the campus in New York state, with hundreds of students and faculty members gathering there on Monday in protest, and sparked anger across the country.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul last week appointed James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case and how law enforcement and the university initially responded to the allegations made by a woman identified in the lawsuit as Jane Doe.
Jane Doe has accused the university of failing to protect her, after she was allegedly drugged and raped by the men for several hours at a fraternity party.
Days before she was appointed special prosecutor, James wrote on X: "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable.
"I'm holding her in my heart and in my prayers," she continued. "To her, and to all survivors: you're not alone. We stand with you."
The lawyer for one of the seven accused said these remarks were disqualifying.
In a statement sent to the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the lawyer said her comments conflict with the need for "independently evaluating the evidence".
"This is not an accusation that Attorney General James is corrupt, acting in bad faith or incapable of performing her duties professionally," the statement said.
"Nor am I suggesting that a court has determined that she is legally disqualified. The point is much narrower: an avoidable question now hangs over this investigation, and voluntary recusal would remove it."
Governor Hochul and James were questioned about impartiality concerns during a news conference, and Hochul said James would "follow the facts".
"She'll examine the evidence and go wherever it leads, and if the evidence supports charges, she will pursue them," Hochul said.

"If the impugned judgement is not stayed, CBI will register an FIR against high public functionaries of the state on untested material... and the situation will become irreversible," it said.Senior advocate Vikas Singh, appearing for the state govt, said HC had brushed aside the state's preliminary objections, declined three weeks to Punjab Police to complete the preliminary inquiry, which it initiated based on ED's communication levelling "cash-for-transfers postings" allegation, and directed a CBI probe, contrary to the federal scheme of governance mandated by the Constitution."Please hear the petition today itself at 2pm," Singh requested a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana.
When the bench said it was impossible to take the appeal for hearing Tuesday itself, Singh said the appeal must be heard Wednesday, suggesting the development can have potentially a huge political fallout in the poll-bound state and arguing that the order marked a breach of the federal scheme of governance.The bench said the state's petition will be listed for hearing either Wednesday or Thursday.In its appeal, the state govt revealed ED's Jalandhar zonal office on July 30 sent a 150-page communication to Punjab DGP under PMLA, alleging it was found that one Nihal Gohal, whose premises were searched in May, influenced transfers, postings, tenders and policy decisions "through an officer on special duty in the office of CM".DGP marked the communication, large parts of which were illegible, to Punjab Bureau of Investigation on Aug 3. The bureau began its preliminary inquiry within two days and started collecting evidence from different departments. It sent reminders to ED on Aug 28, Sept 2 and Sept 5, asking it to depute an officer with complete records, but no cooperation was received till Sept 7, the state claimed.
HC had ordered a CBI probe because of what it held to be inaction in the registeration of an FIR on the material evidence sent by ED and had said, "Prima facie allegations with regard to scams including cash for transfers, cash for getting favourable policies, cash for tenders, and such other illegal activities corruption in high public offices have been substantiated by ED with reference to various WhatsApp chats and other information..."Punjab govt said the high court erred by sending CBI into a state which had withdrawn consent to the agency needed to carry out an investigation in the state's jurisdiction, without citing any exceptional circumstances that warranted a CBI probe.In 2010, SC had ruled that SC and HCs can direct a CBI probe in exceptional cases even in states which have withdrawn general consent.

Trump says Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego, drawing backlash
The US president said this would be a ‘very small price to pay’, as he insisted that the war with Iran was almost over
US President Donald Trump suggested to a crowd of his supporters in Nebraska that Iran could “take out” a major US city like Los Angeles or San Diego, drawing a swift rebuke from California’s Democratic leaders and some fellow Republicans.
Trump, speaking at a political rally in the state’s farm belt on Monday, discussed American wartime economic sacrifices and said he was determined to “see a tremendous victory, because it verifies all the things we did”.
“And again, remember, with the war, it’s just artificial, it’s a little bit high, it’s a small price to pay,” he told the crowd in Grand Island, Nebraska, apparently referring to rising prices of fuel, fertiliser and other products attributed to energy market disruptions from the war.
“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let ’em take out Los Angeles, let ’em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon,” he said.

007 fans, rejoice: Every film starring the world's most famous spy is finally streaming in one place, the franchise's new home, Amazon.
Longtime "James Bond" producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli ceded creative control of Bond, James Bond, to Amazon MGM Studios in February 2025, so it makes sense that Bond's films would live there.
Wilson had been involved with Eon Productions, the original studio behind "Bond," since 1972, and Broccoli's family had cinematic stewardship of the franchise since it began in 1962.
Amazon officially acquired MGM in 2022, but the studio hasn't produced any 007 content since then; it hasn't even picked a successor to Daniel Craig after his 2021 exit.
The Broccoli family's fierce protectiveness of the character was widely believed to have stalled franchise development, but that could change now that Amazon MGM Studios has full creative control. Announcements have been slow, though — all we know is that "Bond 28" will be directed by Denis Villeneuve.
In honor of the new James Bond, who's hopefully coming our way soon, we used Rotten Tomatoes to see how all 27 films in this storied franchise stack up, according to critics.
27. "Casino Royale" (1967)
The lowest-rated Bond movie by critics is 1967's "Casino Royale," starring David Niven as the titular spy.
This version of "Casino Royale" is a parody of spy films, rather than a straightforward Bond caper. It's also one of two films about James Bond that wasn't produced by Eon Productions.
"Casino Royale" also starred Peter Sellers, Ursula Andress, Joanna Pettet, Daliah Lavi, Barbara Bouchet, and Terence Coop in double roles — all of them play different versions of Bond. Woody Allen also appeared as Bond's nephew, Jimmy.
"Unfortunately, after the introductory sequences, 'Casino Royale' begins a downhill slide. It gets progressively sillier and more incoherent until it's impossible to keep any of the plot elements straight. Worse, with only occasional exceptions, the humor ceases to be funny, and the whole production degenerates into absurdity," wrote James Berardinelli of ReelViews.
26. "A View to a Kill" (1985)
Roger Moore's seventh and final outing as 007 was also his worst, according to critics.
The film sees Bond travel to San Francisco to save Silicon Valley from a former KGB agent played by Christopher Walken. His bodyguard and lover, May Day, was notably played by Grace Jones.
The classic "Bond girl" was played by Tanya Roberts, of future "That '70s Show" fame.
"It's not double-oh-seven anymore, but double-oh-seventy, the best argument yet for the mandatory retirement age," wrote The Washington Post's Paul Attanasio.
25. "The Man with the Golden Gun" (1974)
"The Man with the Golden Gun" starred Moore as Bond and legendary actor Christopher Lee as the titular man with the golden gun, Francisco Scaramanga. Meanwhile, Bond's love interest, Mary Goodnight, was played by Britt Ekland.
Bond and Scaramanga engage in a game of cat-and-mouse for much of the movie, as no one knows what Scaramanga looks like, outside the fact that he has a third nipple.
"If you enjoyed the early Bond films as much as I did, you'd better skip this one," wrote Nora Sayre of The New York Times.
24. "Octopussy" (1983)
Let's get it out of the way: Yes, this movie is really called "Octopussy." Its titular character, a successful businesswoman and jewel smuggler, was played by Maud Adams. Bond and Octopussy have personal business: Years earlier, Bond arrested her father for treason.
The two form an uneasy alliance to defeat an exiled Afghan prince, Kamal Khan, played by Louis Jourdan.
"It's an easy film to hate (and often paints a big target on its back encouraging you to do so), but it works perfectly as a piece of entertainment, where the good ultimately outweighs the bad," wrote Jake Tropila of Film Inquiry.
23. "The World Is Not Enough" (1999)
Critics think the worst Bond film starring Pierce Brosnan is 1999's "The World Is Not Enough," Brosnan's third.
Bond shares the screen with an American nuclear physicist named Dr. Christmas Jones. Equally improbable, she's played by Denise Richards. His other female costar is Elektra King, an oil heiress played by Sophie Marceau.
The classic Bond villain, Renard, an ex-KGB agent who became a terrorist, was played by Robert Carlyle.
"What do the James Bond series, the Chicago Cubs, and Master P's No Limit empire have in common? All owe their considerable commercial success more to loyalty, marketing, and tradition than to quality," wrote Nathan Rabin for the AV Club.
22. "Die Another Day" (2002)
Brosnan's fourth and final appearance as Bond, 2002's "Die Another Day," saw him get overshadowed by Halle Berry.
"Die Another Day" plays as a classic early 2000s film: heavy on the CGI and the product placement. But it's notable for its casting of Berry as Jinx Johnson, an NSA agent, whose entrance in an orange bikini remains iconic over 20 years later.
"Die Another Day" was also the first Bond movie in 39 years to not feature Desmond Llewelyn's Q as the head of the British Secret Service's fictional research and development division — in other words, he provided Bond with all of his nifty gadgets.
Llewelyn died in 1999, just a few weeks after the premiere of "The World Is Not Enough." He was replaced as Q by John Cleese for "Die Another Day," which would end up being Cleese's only appearance as the character.
"In a year when 'Austin Powers' has scoffed at 007 as a joke and 'xXx' has scoffed at him as an anachronism, 'Die Another Day' is a fluffed opportunity to assert that nobody does it better," wrote Nicholas Barber for The Independent.
21. "Tomorrow Never Dies" (1997)
Brosnan suited up for his second Bond film in 1997 with "Tomorrow Never Dies," which introduced international audiences to Michelle Yeoh — for that alone, it remains an important cultural moment.
The film follows Bond as he attempts to stop power-hungry media tycoon Elliot Carver, played by Jonathan Pryce, from engineering events that will bring about World War III.
The Wall Street Journal's Joe Morgenstern criticized the film for its overuse of product placements.
"In the latest James Bond, our hero saves the world from brand-name unawareness. 'Tomorrow Never Dies' is a dramatized trade show; imagine Comdex or the Geneva Automobile Salon with a plot," he wrote.
20. "Moonraker" (1979)
It took four movies for Moore's Bond to blast off into space, which he does by the end of "Moonraker."
He takes on an all-time Bond villain, Hugo Drax (Michael Lonsdale), who somehow wants to kill the entire population of Earth with nerve gas and use his own space station as Noah's Ark to repopulate the planet with a "master race."
"The space-age plot is spread dangerously thin, the fights all tend to slapstick, and the wanton destruction has become rather too predictable. But it's held together by likable performances," wrote Chris Auty for Time Out.
19 (tie). "Spectre" (2015)
One of Daniel Craig's lowest-rated Bond movies is 2015's "Spectre."
It was the first Bond film since "Diamonds Are Forever" to include Bond's most famous villain, Blofeld (now played by Christoph Waltz), and his criminal organization SPECTRE.
Also notable was Sam Smith's Bond song, "Writing's on the Wall," which became the second consecutive Bond theme to win an Oscar.
"'Spectre,' Sam Mendes' latest entry in the James Bond franchise, is a real oddity: the first 007 film that's more enjoyable to think about than to watch," wrote FlavorWire's Jason Bailey.
19 (tie). "Quantum of Solace" (2008)
Craig's second outing as Bond, 2008's "Quantum of Solace," received a similar critical response.
The movie picks up almost immediately after the events of Craig's first Bond installment, "Casino Royale." He once again faces off against Jesper Christensen as Mr. White, an assassin.
Bond also faces environmental entrepreneur Dominic Greene (played by French filmmaker and actor Mathieu Amalric), who claims to want to stop deforestation but is actually trying to stage a coup in Bolivia to take control of the country's natural resources.
"Although it's not the most crushing disappointment of all time — finding you have won the lottery but lost the ticket is probably more crushing, I imagine — it is still a crushing disappointment," wrote Deborah Ross for The Spectator.
17. "Diamonds Are Forever" (1971)
After starring in five Bond films, Sean Connery left the role and let someone else take a (relatively successful) crack at the character. But he returned for Bond No. 7, which you might recall from its iconic theme song sung by Shirley Bassey.
Connery would once again leave the role until 1983, when he appeared in the second non-Eon Productions Bond movie, "Never Say Never Again."
In "Diamonds Are Forever," Bond faces his archenemy Blofeld (Charles Gray).
"The movie's momentum is such that one never has much time to react to its lack of reason, only to its sensations of speed and narrow escape, and to the splendor of its crazy gadgets and decor," wrote The New York Times' Vincent Canby.
16. "Live and Let Die" (1973)
"Live and Let Die" (1973) might've been Moore's first outing as Bond, but it's most remembered for the Paul McCartney song of the same name.
In total, Moore played Bond seven times, the same number of appearances as the first-ever Bond, Sean Connery.
"Live and Let Die," per IndieWire, was released during the height of the blaxploitation movement in cinema, and therefore led to a supporting cast of mainly Black actors, including the first Black Bond girl, Rosie Carver, played by Gloria Hendry
"It is good, lively, mindless entertainment, slow to warm up but once embarked upon its improbable story quick to appreciate its own absurdity," wrote The Guardian's Derek Malcolm.
15. "For Your Eyes Only" (1981)
"For Your Eyes Only" is Moore's fifth Bond movie, and a real course correction from the campier, sci-fi tone of "Moonraker."
In this installment, Bond's love interest, Melina Havelock, played by Carole Bouquet, is dead set on getting revenge for the murder of her parents. Meanwhile, Bond teams up with a former smuggler, Milos Columbo, played by Chaim Topol, to recover a dangerous piece of submarine tech.
"No. 12 in the phenomenally durable James Bond series. 'For Your Eyes Only' is undeniably easy on the eyes. Maybe too easy to prevent the mind from wandering and the lids from drooping," wrote Gary Arnold for The Washington Post.
14. "Never Say Never Again" (1983)
"Never Say Never Again" is the result of some complicated rights issues from the Ian Fleming novels on which the Bond movies are based. It's a remake of the 1965 movie "Thunderball," which also starred Connery, which was in turn based on the 1961 Fleming novel of the same name.
Due to conflicts between Fleming and producer Kevin McClory, McClory ended up with the rights to "Thunderball" and anything introduced in that story, including SPECTRE.
So, in 1983, McClory commissioned a remake of "Thunderball," titled "Never Say Never Again," starring Connery once again, for a non-Eon Bond film. The title was reportedly inspired by Connery's wife, who told her husband he couldn't say he'd "never" return to Bond again, per Screen Rant.
"In 'Never Say Never Again,' the formula is broadened to accommodate an older, seasoned man of much greater stature, and Mr. Connery expertly fills the bill," wrote Janet Maslin for The New York Times.
13. "You Only Live Twice" (1967)
Fun fact about "You Only Live Twice": Children's author Roald Dahl, the mind behind "The BFG," "The Witches," "James and the Giant Peach," and "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory," wrote the screenplay.
The biggest legacy of "You Only Live Twice" is the performance of Donald Pleasence as Bond's enemy, Blofeld. In just two minutes, you can see where Mike Myers got the idea for Dr. Evil in the "Austin Powers" movies.
"What I can say for sure is 'You Only Live Twice' is the Bond film I have seen most often and I have enjoyed the hell out it every single time," wrote Phelim O'Neill for The Guardian.
12. "The Living Daylights" (1987)
Timothy Dalton's first entry into Bond lore, 1987's "The Living Daylights," was well-received.
After Moore left the role, the British actor stepped into Bond's very prolific shoes. The only constant remaining from Moore's tenure was Desmond Llewelyn as Q.
The plot, as usual, involved Bond investigating shady activities by the KGB. In this case, he was investigating suspicious deaths of KGB defectors, which put him directly in the path of Brad Whitaker, an American arms dealer played by Joe Don Baker.
"'The Living Daylights' is different; even from a quarter of a century away, there's nothing to sully the romantic air. It's no coincidence that the most recent Bond films are the closest in tone," wrote The Guardian's Les Roopanarine.
11. "Licence to Kill" (1989)
Dalton's second (and final) outing as Bond, "Licence to Kill," was even more well-received than his debut.
The film was, at the time, the darkest Bond movie ever released — it followed Bond as he was suspended from MI6 in order to help his friend and CIA agent Felix Leiter, played by David Hedison, avenge the murder of his new wife … all while trying to take down a Latin American drug kingpin.
"Dalton revives the cool, ironic detachment of the Connery years, but he also allows a touch of obsession to show through Bond's surface aplomb," wrote the Chicago Reader's Dave Kehr.
10 (tie). "GoldenEye" (1995)
After six Bond-less years, Irish star Brosnan brought the world's most dashing spy back to the big screen with 1995's "GoldenEye." His version of Bond began his tenure taking down a rogue MI6 agent played by Sean Bean and romancing a Russian programmer played by Izabella Scorupco.
This movie also marked the first appearance of Judi Dench as Bond's boss at MI6, M, who would go on to appear in the Craig movies.
The most lasting legacy of this movie, though, may be the Nintendo 64 game based on it, simply titled "GoldenEye 007," released in 1997. It became the third-best-selling Nintendo 64 game of all time, per VGChartz.
"With a dynamite opening reel that showcases the series' renewed vigor, 'GoldenEye' is two hours of well-executed thrills, high-tech mayhem and one-of-a-kind comedy," wrote David Hunter for The Hollywood Reporter.
10 (tie). "On Her Majesty's Secret Service" (1969)
It wasn't critically beloved at the time, but George Lazenby's one and only Bond movie has been reevaluated in the following five decades. Now, it's one of the most critically admired Bond films.
Part of what makes this film so different than any other Bond movie, besides Lazenby, who is Australian, is that it ends in true tragedy: After Bond falls in love with Diana Rigg's Countess Tracy di Vicenzo, the two wed at the end of the movie, only for Tracy to be shot by Bond's nemesis Blofeld (Telly Savalas) immediately after.
"'On Her Majesty's Secret Service' is pure poetry. It transcends the idea of a Bond film. Gorgeously photographed, thrillingly executed, and wonderfully performed, this is the franchise zenith," wrote Jake Tropila for Film Inquiry.
8. "The Spy Who Loved Me" (1977)
"The Spy Who Loved Me" was Moore's third outing as Bond, and his best, according to critics. It covers similar territory as other Bond movies, including a megalomaniac villain dedicated to starting World War III — this time a shipping tycoon named Karl Stromberg, played by Curt Jürgens.
This movie was also the debut of Jaws, one of the most memorable henchmen in Bond history, played by Richard Kiel.
"The end result is unquestionably one of the Bond series' brightest spots, and includes a good deal of its finest moments," wrote Gerardo Valero for RogerEbert.com.
7. "No Time to Die" (2021)
After five movies and 15 years, Craig drank his final shaken, not stirred, martini in the epic conclusion to his series, "No Time to Die."
While Craig, as usual, performed his role admirably, audiences left "No Time to Die" talking about Ana de Armas' CIA agent, Paloma, and Lashana Lynch's new 007 agent, Nomi.
The less we say about Rami Malek's performance as the film's nanobots-obsessed villain Lyutsifer Safin, the better.
"No Time to Die" also became the third Bond film in a row to have its theme — this time sung by Billie Eilish — win an Oscar.
"With this fifth and final go-round, it's clear who the best Bond is. It's Craig, Daniel Craig," wrote Mark Feeney for The Boston Globe.
6. "Thunderball" (1965)
"Thunderball" is the second-highest-grossing Bond film ever, accounting for inflation, only behind "Skyfall," per Screen Rant. At this point in history, Connery's Bond had become a full-blown phenomenon.
In the movie, Bond's mission was to recapture two atomic bombs stolen by the evil criminal organization SPECTRE. Much of the film's action takes place underwater, an impressive feat for the '60s. Bond also, of course, falls in love with the girlfriend of a SPECTRE agent, Domino, played by Claudine Auger.
"The color is handsome. The scenery in the Bahamas is an irresistible lure. Even the violence is funny. That's the best I can say for a Bond film," wrote Bosley Crowther for The New York Times.
5. "Skyfall" (2012)
The highest-grossing Bond film of all time is 2012's "Skyfall," starring Craig.
"Skyfall" was Craig's third Bond film, and, to many, a high point of his Bond tenure. The film delves into Bond's past in a way that hadn't been done for many years, and introduced viewers to the super-spy's ancestral home in Scotland, fittingly named Skyfall.
Javier Bardem's performance as Raoul Silva, a former MI6 agent (and now cyber-terrorist), instantly solidified Bardem as one of the top-tier Bond villains.
"Skyfall" also introduced audiences to the new versions of Q (Ben Whishaw) and Miss Moneypenny (Naomie Harris).
The film's theme, "Skyfall" by Adele, also started the three-film streak of Bond themes winning the Academy Award.
"Bond traditions haven't just been updated — they've been intelligently modified and rethought, giving us the franchise's inherent pleasures in a new package," wrote Tim Grierson of Deadspin.
4. "Casino Royale" (2006)
"Casino Royale" kicked off an entirely new generation of Bond after a multi-year break. The film follows a newly appointed 007 as he joins a high-stakes poker game at the Casino Royale in Montenegro, in order to bankrupt the terrorist financier Le Chiffre (Mads Mikkelsen).
Bond is paired with Vesper Lynd (Eva Green), a British Treasury agent. Their relationship would haunt Bond until Craig's final installment, "No Time to Die."
"Daniel Craig, an excellent actor, has more than earned his Walther PPK," wrote Stephanie Condron and Sinclair McKay for The Telegraph.
3. "Dr. No" (1962)
The very first Bond movie, 1962's "Dr. No," is still a high bar that the franchise rarely clears.
Without the success of "Dr. No," which was released 64 years ago, it's unlikely that we would've ever gotten 26 more films about the most debonair spy on his side of the Atlantic.
But "Dr. No" was successful, much due to Connery's iconic take on the character.
Does the plot, in which Bond teams up with a seashell diver in Jamaica named Honey Ryder (the first Bond girl ever, Ursula Andress) to take down a mad scientist determined to stop a rocket launch with a radio beam named Dr. Julius No, make the most sense? No, but we love it anyway.
"[The] first screen adventure of Ian Fleming's hard-hitting, fearless, imperturbable, girl-loving Secret Service Agent 007, James Bond, is an entertaining piece of tongue-in-cheek action hokum," wrote Variety.
2. "From Russia With Love" (1963)
Connery's second outing as Bond follows him as he goes up against multiple SPECTRE agents who want him dead after the events of "Dr. No." He also falls in love with a Soviet clerk, Tatiana Romanova, played by Daniela Bianchi.
Notably, this was Desmond Llewelyn's first appearance as Bond's technology supplier Q. He'd play the role until his death in 1999.
"A highly immoral film in every imaginable way but it sure is fun...," wrote Richard Roud for The Guardian.
1. "Goldfinger" (1964)
It seems increasingly unlikely we'll ever have a Bond movie that tops "Goldfinger," a movie in which Bond meets a female pilot (played by Honor Blackman), investigates a sociopath obsessed with gold named Auric Goldfinger (played by Gert Fröbe), and sleeps with a woman named Jill Masterson (played by Shirley Eaton) who gets painted in gold for her betrayal and dies from "skin suffocation."
Not all of it has aged well — specifically, the scene where Bond forcibly kisses Galore in a barn comes to mind — but it's still where many of the tropes we've come to associate Bond with began.
"Perfection. Farty critics may scoff, but 'Goldfinger' should take its place among the greats," wrote Ian Nathan for Empire.

Russian authorities denied Tuesday that special restrictions had been introduced over reports that a laboratory technician died of plague, even as Washington said it was closely monitoring events.
Reports on Friday that pneumonic plague had killed 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who had been working for the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region, sparked alarm.
Russia's consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor however insisted Tuesday that a document circulating online indicating heightened sanitary-epidemiological measures and restrictions in the Irkutsk region was fake.
"We wish to clarify that the document and information in question do not originate from official sources and are untrue," it said on Telegram.
"No such decisions have been made at this time," it said, stressing that "the sanitary-epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk Region ... remains stable".
The Russian news outlet People of Baikal, citing unnamed sources close to the regional security services, said Friday the dead woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.
Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.
As many as 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine, the People of Baikal outlet added, without elaborating.
But Russian officials have stressed that postmortem tests had not detected the disease.
Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said Monday that a special Rospotrebnadzor expert commission inspection in the region had found that "the cause of death was pneumonia of undetermined aetiology".
The health watchdog, he said, had determined that "no microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples".
And there had been "no new cases of staff from the anti-plague institute seeking medical attention" since the death, he added.
Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization.
US President Donald Trump said Monday that his administration was closely monitoring the situation.
"We're looking at it very strongly," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague coming from Russia.
"We'll help them as much as we can."

Telangana to issue notices to KCR family in Siddipet's missing 45-acre probe
Revanth Reddy ordered notices to K Chandrashekar Rao and his family over land records linked to the Erravalli survey gap. The move comes as the government widens its scrutiny of missing acreage and Dharani-linked land irregularities.
Telangana Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy has directed officials to issue notices to former Chief Minister K Chandrashekar Rao (KCR) and his family members seeking land records as part of an ongoing probe into a 45-acre discrepancy in Survey No. 325 at Erravalli village in Siddipet district.
The direction came during a review meeting chaired by Revanth Reddy at the MCRHRD Institute on Tuesday night, where officials briefed him on the status of the survey ordered after the issue was raised during the Assembly session on September 16.
According to officials, government records show 388 acres under Survey No. 325 in Erravalli village. However, the recent survey could account for only 343 acres, leaving a discrepancy of 45 acres.
Taking serious note of the issue, the Chief Minister directed officials to issue a notification for a fresh survey covering Erravalli and neighbouring Venkatapuram villages to establish the whereabouts and ownership status of the missing 45 acres.
Officials informed the Chief Minister that KCR and his family members own land near Survey No. 325. Revanth Reddy consequently instructed authorities to issue notices seeking the relevant land records from the former Chief Minister and his family.
The review meeting was attended by Chief Secretary Sanjay Jaju, CMO Principal Secretary Seshadri and members of the committees appointed to investigate land-related irregularities and issues linked to the erstwhile Dharani portal.
LAND FOR FARMERS, TELANGANA MARTYRS' COLONY
The Chief Minister directed officials to distribute the government land identified in Survey No. 325 among eligible local farmers.
He also ordered the establishment of a 'Telangana Martyrs' Colony' for families of those who sacrificed their lives during the Telangana movement. Housing plots would be allotted to eligible martyrs' families and the colony would be developed with all necessary infrastructure.
The Housing Department has been tasked with executing the project, with the Chief Minister directing officials to complete it by June 2.
EDUCATION HUB AT VELIKATTA
Revanth Reddy also proposed setting up a Young India Integrated School and an education hub at Velikatta village in Kondapaka mandal.
Officials were asked to identify suitable government land for the project while excluding assigned lands and land earmarked for the Mission Bhagiratha programme.
The Chief Minister further directed officials to closely monitor the utilisation of water from reservoirs and tanks in view of El Nio conditions. He also ordered officials to identify those drawing water from Mallanna Sagar without authorisation and take stringent action against them.
The government is also examining possible irregularities linked to land records and the erstwhile Dharani system.

The story so far: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has warned against the indiscriminate, repeated, or prolonged use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and antibiotics, linking inappropriate use to avoidable renal complications and chronic kidney disease (CKD).
In its September 21 circular, it also reminded doctors, pharmacists, hospitals, and the public that these medicines are subject to prescription and other regulatory safeguards.
What does the latest directive mean?
The CDSCO circular is, in significant part, a reminder that existing rules already require medical supervision for these medicines and doesn’t amount to any new ban on painkillers or antibiotics.
Most NSAIDs are classified under Schedule H of the Drugs Rules, 1945. Most antibiotics are under Schedule H1. These medicines are therefore not meant to be sold at retail without a prescription from a Registered Medical Practitioner.
Schedule H1 medicines also carry a specific warning that they should be taken only on and according to medical advice.
The regulator has asked the public not to take NSAIDs or antibiotics indiscriminately, repeatedly or for prolonged periods without medical advice.
“Antibiotics should not be self-medicated or used for illnesses where they are not clinically indicated,” it said.
Also, doctors have been asked to prescribe them only when clinically justified, in the appropriate dose and for the appropriate duration, and to follow antimicrobial stewardship principles. Pharmacies, hospitals, and healthcare institutions have also been put on notice.
The kidney warning is particularly relevant to NSAIDs. These drugs can reduce blood flow to the kidneys and are associated with acute kidney injury, particularly among people who already have kidney disease, diabetes, or hypertension. Longer-term use has also been associated with CKD occurrence or progression.
Importantly, the warning does not mean that all painkillers or antibiotics are inherently unsafe. The concern is inappropriate selection, dose, duration, and unsupervised use.
How extensive is antibiotic misuse?
There is no single national figure that captures all inappropriate antibiotic use in India. Available studies, however, show that self-medication remains a significant problem.
A systematic review covering 66 Indian studies and nearly 30,000 participants estimated overall self-medication at 64.4%, although this included medicines generally and not antibiotics alone. Analgesics, antipyretics, antibiotics, and cough remedies were among the commonly self-medicated drug categories.
A community study from South-East Delhi found that 35% of 200 participants reported antibiotic self-medication. Fever, cold, and flu were common reasons, while pharmacies were the main source of antibiotics.
While these studies cannot be interpreted as a national prevalence estimate and represent different populations and locations, together they illustrate why prescription enforcement and antibiotic stewardship remain concerns.
What does antibiotic misuse do?
Antibiotics work against bacterial infections. They do not treat viral illnesses such as most common colds and influenza.
When antibiotics are used unnecessarily, incorrectly or for an inappropriate duration, bacteria can be exposed to the drug without being eliminated. Resistant organisms can then survive and multiply. This contributes to antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
The consequences extend beyond the individual who takes the antibiotic. Resistant organisms can spread to other people and through healthcare and environmental pathways.
WHO estimates that bacterial AMR was associated with more than 4.7 million deaths globally in 2021. In 2023, approximately one in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections globally was resistant to antibiotics. WHO says misuse and overuse of antimicrobials are important drivers of the problem.
What does WHO say about antibiotic use?
WHO has increasingly moved towards antimicrobial stewardship — ensuring that antimicrobials are used only when necessary and that the right drug, dose and duration are selected.
Its AWaRe classification divides antibiotics into three groups: Access, Watch and Reserve. Access antibiotics are generally preferred for common infections because they have a narrower spectrum and lower resistance potential. Watch antibiotics have greater resistance potential and therefore require more careful use. Reserve antibiotics are intended for infections caused by multidrug-resistant organisms when other options are inadequate.
WHO’s analysis of 2022 antibiotic-use data found that only about one in three reporting countries/territories/areas met the target of having at least 70% of antibiotic consumption from the Access group. WHO has called for stewardship policies to reduce unnecessary antibiotic use and encourage Access antibiotics when they are clinically appropriate.
WHO’s 2025 global AMR surveillance report, based on more than 23 million laboratory-confirmed cases reported by countries, also underlines the continuing global burden of resistance and the need for better surveillance.
Which drugs are commonly misused, and who is most vulnerable?
NSAIDs are among the medicines of concern because they are widely used for headaches, fever, body pain, arthritis, dental pain, and other painful conditions.
Common NSAIDs include ibuprofen, diclofenac, naproxen, and similar anti-inflammatory painkillers. Their risks become more important with prolonged or high-dose use and in people with kidney disease, diabetes, hypertension, dehydration or other risk factors.
Indian pharmacovigilance data, although based on reported adverse events rather than population prevalence, provide an important signal: in one analysis of NSAID-associated CKD reports, 82% of cases were among people aged 40–80 years, with diclofenac implicated in 43% of the reports.
For antibiotics, children are an important vulnerable group, largely because parents or caregivers may administer medicines based on previous prescriptions or advice from pharmacies and family members. The recent Indian meta-analysis found substantial antibiotic self-medication among children.
Older adults and people with chronic diseases also require particular caution because kidney function may already be reduced and multiple medicines may be involved.
What measures is the government bringing in?
India has been working on AMR for more than a decade. The National Programme on AMR Containment was launched in 2013, with surveillance, monitoring of antimicrobial consumption, infection prevention and control, and promotion of rational antimicrobial use among its objectives.
India launched its National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance 2.0 (NAP-AMR 2025–2029) in November 2025. It adopts a One Health approach, bringing human health together with animal, agricultural, and environmental sectors. It includes surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention and control, research and monitoring.
The government has also used the Drugs Rules to control antibiotic sales. Schedule H1 requires records of the supply of listed medicines, including details of the prescriber and patient, with records maintained for three years.
There is also a recent regulatory development in August 2026, when CDSCO issued a draft notification proposing four additional drugs for inclusion in Schedule H1.
Why have rules not worked so far?
The central difficulty is that regulation has existed for years, but implementation has been uneven.
India’s NAP-AMR documentation itself records earlier CDSCO awareness and enforcement drives concerning Schedule H and H1 medicines, including restrictions on selling antimicrobials without prescriptions. Yet studies continue to document antibiotic self-medication and access through pharmacies.
Similarly, antimicrobial stewardship programmes have been part of India’s AMR strategy since the first National Action Plan. The 2017–2021 plan called for stewardship programmes, treatment guidelines, multidisciplinary stewardship committees, and training.
The continuing problem, therefore, is less about the absence of rules and more about translating those rules into routine practice — ensuring that prescriptions are actually required at the point of sale, that doctors prescribe antibiotics appropriately, that patients do not demand or reuse medicines, and that hospitals monitor antibiotic consumption.

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

Amazon has disabled Alexa control of devices plugged into the company’s Echo smart speaker’s AUX port.
Users have reported receiving an email from Amazon this week informing them of the change. “This is a reminder that as of today, voice commands to control your Echo device’s Aux input are no longer available. Requests like ‘Alexa, play from line in” or “Alexa, set aux input’ will no longer work,” an email that Amazon sent reads, according to a screenshot a Reddit user shared this week.
An Amazon spokesperson confirmed the news to Ars Technica today.
Amazon hasn’t made an Echo with a 3.5 mm port in years. The change affects only some older Echo devices: the Echo Plus 2nd Gen (released in 2018), Echo 3rd Gen (released in 2019), Echo Studio 1st Gen (released in 2019), and Echo 4th Gen (released in 2020).
The physical AUX inputs continue to work, so users can still listen to audio from a device connected to an Echo’s 3.5 mm port. They can also continue to use the Alexa app to enable or disable a supporting speaker’s AUX input.

"This is for her - we just want to live and go running and come back home without having to think that it may be one of us", said Nonhle Mpohlo.
In Cape Town, people gathered in a vigil to honour the victims and called on the government to act.

I've been to Italy 16 times, and if you give me an opening, I can work it into just about any conversation.
But surprisingly, it wasn't Venice, Rome, or the Amalfi Coast that made me fall head over heels for the country. It was Bologna, the capital of northern Italy's Emilia-Romagna region.
Bologna has it all — food, wine, art, history, architecture, and the kind of energy that makes you seriously consider missing your flight home. Sure, seeing the Colosseum is cool, but I prefer eating perfectly made tortellini with a glass of pignoletto in Bologna.
Here's why I always recommend tourists add Bologna to their itinerary, even if they can only spare one glorious, carb-loaded night.
Bologna's food is truly unlike anything else I've ever had.
Every Italian I know tells me their region's cuisine is the best, but I'm here to tell you that Bologna is home to the best food I've had.
I fell hard for the mortadella, the tortellini, and the Bolognese, and I've spent practically every trip to Italy since chasing those foods.
One of my favorite things I did in the city was wander through the Quadrilatero, the city's historic market district, where butcher shops, cheese merchants, and specialty food stores practically demand that you stop every few feet.
When I was there, I grabbed a mortadella sandwich and a glass of Lambrusco, then sat in one of the stunning cobblestone alleyways to people-watch.
The region is also well known for producing Parmigiano Reggiano, which always seems to taste freshest here.
For a traditional Emilian dinner, I always recommend A Balùs. The Bolognese was the best pasta dish I've ever had in all of Italy, and the sardines served on bread with butter literally melted in my mouth.
The city's got history, too.
Bologna isn't just a city where you eat extraordinarily well. It's also a place where visitors can stumble into hundreds of years of history while walking off lunch.
One place that particularly moved me was the Archiginnasio Municipal Library, which houses rare books, centuries-old manuscripts, and other special collections.
Although, in my opinion, it might not be as visually impressive as the Trinity Library in Dublin, knowing that some of these manuscripts date back more than a thousand years made this place feel pretty extraordinary to me.
It's a university city, but it doesn't feel like a typical college town.
One of the city's highlights is the University of Bologna, which dates back to 1088 and is widely recognized as the oldest university in the Western world.
But Bologna isn't a typical college town where the bars are packed with rowdy students and every night feels like a fraternity party.
Instead, the city has a much more sophisticated energy. I saw students mingling with professors, artists, young professionals, and longtime residents, creating this incredible mix of old-world Italy and youthful enthusiasm.
I also loved visiting the Piazza Verdi, a square filled with students catching up with friends after class.
I still can't get over how stunning the architecture in Bologna is.
One of the unique things about Bologna's design is its porticoes. I love these eye-catching archways that line the streets, many of which date back to the 12th century.
In fact, Bologna has about 38 miles of porticoes, with the most famous being the Portico di San Luca, a pathway that extends for about 2 miles and has more than 600 arches.
Bologna is ridiculously easy to visit, even if you only have one night.
I always recommend Bologna to travelers because they don't have to sacrifice seeing other parts of Italy to go there, since the city is one of the country's main railway hubs.
By train, Florence is only 30 minutes away, Milan is about an hour away, and Venice is just about 90 minutes away.
Overall, I think Bologna is one of Italy's greatest culinary and cultural destinations, and I couldn't recommend it enough.

'I reduced my running because of urine leaks' – Commonwealth finalist Korir
- Published
Naomi Korir's career on the track reached a high point in August when she finished fifth in the final of the mile at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
But things could have been very different for the Kenyan middle-distance runner.
The 28-year-old was born with fistula, a medical condition in which abnormal openings develop between organs and can lead to uncontrolled leakage of urine or faeces.
While Korir loved athletics as a child, it initially forced her to rethink any plans to be a runner.
"I played most of the sports activities: football, netball, athletics, even rugby," she said.
"But it was difficult because [of] the training, and the urine is flowing continuously. It's bad.
"I reduced my running to shorter distances to reduce the leaking.
"I began doing 100m hurdles."
Despite the challenges, Korir's love of sport also offered a form of escape and belonging.
"I could do it because I loved it," she explained.
"Because most of the people could avoid me, I did a lot of activities just to pass time and not to feel that I'm excluded."
Three surgeries and a second chance
The charity Doctors Without Borders estimates that 500,000 women live with fistula globally.
Some develop a fistula after childbirth while for others, like Korir, it is congenital.
Access to good obstetrics, or to simple surgery, means that the condition has all but disappeared in some countries, but it remains a problem in sub-Saharan Africa, where high quality medical care can be hard to access.
Korir was born with genitourinary tract fistula - an opening between bladder and vagina which caused her urine leakage.
Surgery was required, but her first two operations failed to solve the problem.
In August 2013, a third operation finally brought relief for the then 13-year-old.
The procedure was carried out in her home town Eldoret by the Gynocare Hospital, which specialises in fistula, obstetrics and reproductive health.
"It's a difficult condition to live with every day," Gynocare director Caroline Mabeya told BBC Sport Africa when discussing the stigma and isolation women with the condition suffer.
"They are ostracised in the society. That's the psychological torture that they face with the fistula."
The hospital has treated patients from across East Africa since opening its doors in 2011. Its work extends beyond surgery, with a post-operation programme designed to help women rebuild their confidence.
"We offer free treatment for these women at Gynocare because most of them are very poor," Mabeya explained.
"When they come into the facility, they are crushed, they have low esteem. So, there's a huge amount of effort that is put in to make them at least be strong enough to be reintegrated and get back into the community."
'A champion in sport'
For Korir, successful surgery offered a second chance, both on the track and in the classroom.
As well as allowing her to run properly again, she continued her education through Gynocare's Beyond Fistula programme.
"I have a family in GynoCare, a fistula home," she said.
"That is where I schooled after my surgery until I finished my secondary level."
In 2019, Korir began competing professionally and two years later was part of the Kenyan duo which claimed a silver medal in the 2x2x400m mixed relay alongside her partner Ferguson Rotich at the World Relays in Poland.
A year later she went one better, bagging gold as part of Kenya's 4x400m relay team at the African Championships in Mauritius.
The mile at this year's Commonwealth Games was her first appearance in major global final.
"I'm giving hope to young women maybe who have lost hope," she said of her achievements.
"They need to come back again in living and enjoying life."
Mabeya says Korir's transformation makes her a powerful example to the women currently receiving support at Gynocare.
"She makes them realise that you can actually pull yourself out of these struggles and still make it in life and succeed.
"Naomi actually is one of those patients that inspires us to continue working very hard, because we struggle with this condition and these women. The work is not easy."
As a young girl, Korir sang in church and played the keyboard, convinced that music was a more likely career than athletics.
"But now I'm in different career and I'm so happy," she beamed.
And with the World Championships in Beijing next year and the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, Korir believes there is another chapter to write.
"I know I'm a champion in life, because conquering fistula alone is being a champion.
"Now I'm looking forward to be a champion in sport."

A purported Dainik Jagran newspaper clipping (here & here) claims that the Rajasthan High Court has given a judgment that provides for six months of imprisonment and a ₹50,000 fine for any candidate who fails to secure at least 100 votes in the Sarpanch elections. Let us verify the authenticity of the claim made in this post.
Claim: A Dainik Jagran newspaper clipping claims the Rajasthan High Court has ordered a six-month jail term and a ₹50,000 fine for Sarpanch candidates securing under 100 votes.
Fact: The viral newspaper clipping is an AI-generated fake image. The Rajasthan High Court has given no such judgment, Dainik Jagran published no such report, and Indian electoral laws contain no provision imposing jail time or fines for low vote counts. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
First, an initial search confirmed that the Rajasthan High Court has not issued any such judgment regarding low vote counts in Panchayat elections. Additionally, we found no news reports published by Dainik Jagran corroborating this matter. Moreover, no such law, Court order, or judicial mandate exists under the Election Commission of India or Indian electoral statutes (such as the Representation of the People Act, 1951) penalising candidates with imprisonment or fines purely for receiving a low vote count. Under current election rules, the only major consequence for a poor electoral performance is the forfeiture of the security deposit, which applies if an unelected candidate fails to secure more than one-sixth of the valid votes polled.
Further, we ran the viral newspaper clipping through the OpenAI content detection tool, which confirmed that the clipping is an AI-generated image created using OpenAI tools. Earlier, we debunked a similarly fabricated clipping that falsely claimed a woman gave birth to puppies in the United States.
To sum it up, the viral newspaper clipping is a fabricated AI-generated image, and there is no legal provision or court order mandating jail time or fines for securing low votes in a Sarpanch election.

Guru Randhawa drops new Punjabi single ‘FOSHO’: “We wanted to take the energy literally to the skies”
At the centre of ‘FOSHO’ is the recurring line ‘pakki pakki gal aae’, which reflects the certainty of pursuing someone who has caught the protagonist’s attention. The song follows the idea of trying to win over a woman who appears out of reach, while maintaining a playful and self-assured tone.
Written and composed with a mix of romantic and street-inspired elements, the track opens with a bass-heavy sound as Randhawa describes a woman who attracts attention wherever she goes. The lyrics include references to fashion and Hollywood, including a comparison to actor Scarlett Johansson, while also touching on the possibility of developing a deeper connection beyond casual messages.
The song also features references to Gurjit Gill and Guru Randhawa, adding another layer to its storytelling. The overall composition maintains a light and energetic approach while focusing on attraction and confidence.
Speaking about the song and its music video, Guru Randhawa states, “With ‘FOSHO’, we wanted to take the energy literally to the skies! The track has a very fresh and fun vibe to it, which is why shooting the entire music video inside an airplane felt perfect. Working with Bhushan Sir has always been a great creative experience, and together we wanted to create something that feels fresh, larger-than-life and instantly connects with the audience. ‘Pakki Pakki Gal Aae’ is that ultimate confident statement we all make when we know something is bound to be a hit. I can’t wait to see the fans vibing to this one mid-flight or on their own road trips!”
The music video, directed by Preet Singh and Harry Singh, takes the airplane setting further by turning a flight into the backdrop for the track. It features Randhawa along with a group of passengers and crew members dancing through the aisles before the celebrations continue with a dance sequence at the airport after landing.

A US marine stationed on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa is accused of murdering a Japanese woman and has been arrested on suspicion of murder, police said on Sunday.
The suspect allegedly “killed [a] 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha and stole her wallet” as well as her backpack, local police told news media outlets.
Citing police, NBC News reported that the suspect charged in the case was identified Lance Cpl Devin Jacob Ballard, 20. Anna Yagi was identified as the victim.
Ballard denied the allegations, police said, according to NBC.
Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving accidents by US personnel have long sparked protests on Okinawa. The island bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of US military facilities in Japan.
US ambassador George Glass posted on social media that he had spoken with Japan’s foreign ministry and Okinawa’s governor, offering “sincere condolences to the victim’s family” and pledging cooperation into the investigation of her death.
The Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said Japan had lodged a protest with US authorities and called the crime “exceptionally brutal and vicious”.
The government has urged the US “to provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among US military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes,” Takaichi said.
Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.
Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station where he was arrested, NHK reported.
“We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened,” Yagi’s brother said through local police, according to the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper. “My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter.”
The US has about 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
Crimes committed by US personnel in Japan have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.
“Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen,” Japan’s defense minister Shinjiro Koizumi said.
In June 2025, a Japanese court sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton – then 22 – to seven years in prison after being convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
Earlier, in 2017, former US marine and civilian military base worker Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, US forces in Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated American marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.
According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since Okinawa was returned to Japan from the US in 1972 after the second world war.
The number of arrests in a year hit 80 in 2024, the highest in 20 years.

Tamil Nadu is recording around 200 cases of dengue a day. Fresh cases are being reported in places including Chennai and its neighbouring districts and cities such as Coimbatore and Madurai.
Officials of the Directorate of Public Health (DPH) and Preventive Medicine said the caseload remained steady and was not at outbreak proportions. A. Somasundaram, Director of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, said cases had not risen exponentially, with the numbers remaining broadly steady. “We are seeing nearly 200 cases a day. The numbers are not doubling or tripling, which usually happens in an outbreak. Right now, there is a static trend in the number of dengue cases, and we are expecting the cases to decline soon,” he said.
Cases are being reported across cities including the Chennai belt (Tiruvallur and Kancheepuram), Coimbatore, and Madurai. This could partly be due to a “natural bias” with these areas having more hospitals and testing facilities, Dr. Somasundaram said.
“We have specifically instructed staff to increase the number of tests for dengue for better surveillance and patient management. This is so we don’t miss a case, and when samples are tested, we can identify pockets of cases or clusters, which are likely to bring about an outbreak,” he said. There are over 4,500 government and private laboratories in the State, he added.
Surveillance measures to identify Aedes mosquito breeding pools are continuing, but the number of pools detected has started to decline as a result of source reduction measures. The mosquito density is slowly coming down, the official said. About 25,000 Domestic Breeding Checkers (DBC) have been engaged across the State, with 20 persons covering one block.
Dr. Somasundaram said while preventive measures had been intensified, they had been holding daily monitoring meetings with District Health Officers via video conferencing. “We are analysing the case trend, whether increase or decrease or static, and number of laboratory tests conducted. We are also monitoring fever triaging, patient management, and discharge policy. Patients are being categorised as having mild, moderate, or severe symptoms and treated appropriately. Right now, the severity of infections is less. Fogging operations and source reduction measures, along with work taken up by DBCs, are being supervised. We are also looking at creating awareness among the public,” he said.
With October and November being crucial months, he said, there could be intermittent or heavy rain and people should ensure that their household environment is clean. “Avoid storing water unnecessarily. If you have too, keep containers closed properly,” he added.
