Turning artificial intelligence research into real-world tools isn’t always straightforward, despite the remarkable progress in recent years ranging from self-driving cars to large language models. Systems that perform well in controlled lab settings often fall short when deployed in homes, in hospitals or on city streets.
Vision-based systems, for example, hold promise for improving safety, monitoring health and aiding rehabilitation. For example, a camera-based system could help a clinician assess a patient’s gait or rehabilitation progress.
In the future, an assistive robot in an older adult’s home might need to recognise when the person is struggling to stand or reaching for an object. But a major challenge is ensuring these robots perform reliably beyond the lab, particularly in messy, unpredictable or low-visibility conditions.
As a computer scientist who studies AI systems designed to understand human behavior – especially through visual cues like body movements and interactions with objects – I see three main challenges to taking AI from the lab to the real world: generalisation, human behavior and resources.
Challenge 1: The generalisation gap
Most AI vision systems are trained on well-lit, high-quality images, often from curated sources like motion capture studios or daytime recordings. But when these systems are deployed in real-world settings, such as in a dimly lit home, hospital room or nighttime street, they often struggle. This is not because the technology is flawed, but because the data used to train it cannot fully represent the enormous variability of the real world.
Take human pose estimation, for example. This task involves detecting key points on a person’s body, such as joints, to understand how they’re moving. The result resembles a digital skeleton that represents the positions of a person’s arms, legs and other body parts. Pose estimation has been studied for health and rehabilitation applications, including measuring a person’s gait, monitoring rehabilitation exercises and assessing movement patterns associated with the risk of falling. In well-lit environments, modern AI models do this with impressive accuracy. But in low or uneven lighting, performance can drop sharply. That’s because the model has learned from clean, consistent data and isn’t prepared to generalise to tougher conditions.
Would collecting more nighttime training data solve the problem? More labeled data would certainly help, but collecting it is especially difficult. When a person’s joints are hard to see in an image, they are also hard for a human annotator to label accurately. Low light can also obscure visual information rather than simply make an image darker, and nighttime conditions vary with cameras, shadows, glare and other sources of noise. Collecting and manually labeling examples that cover all these conditions is therefore difficult and expensive.
We’ve been working to close this gap by developing AI systems that perform better in low-light scenarios. One method we use is unsupervised domain adaptation, where a model trained on well-lit, labeled data is adapted to handle low-light settings, without needing manual body-joint labels for the low-light images. This helps bridge the “domain gap” between clean training data and the messier world where these systems are actually used.
In our 2026 study on low-light human pose estimation, we generated realistic low-light training images and designed the system to balance uncertain visual evidence with its learned knowledge of human body structure. The method substantially improved performance on two low-light benchmarks, although the broader challenge is far from solved.
Challenge 2: Human behavior
Another major hurdle is the sheer variety of human behaviors, especially when people interact with objects. In computer vision, this is known as human-object interaction detection. Teaching an AI system to recognise actions like cutting a tomato or passing a basketball requires not just object detection, but an understanding of context and intent.
The real challenge is scale. The number of objects is large, and the ways humans interact with them are even greater. You can sit on a chair, carry it, drag it or stack it. Each is a distinct interaction. A cup might be used for drinking, washing, pouring or handing something to another person. An assistive robot would need to distinguish among these actions to respond appropriately. It’s simply not feasible to collect and label data for every possible combination.
In my research, we study how an AI system can detect interactions it has never seen during training. Researchers call this a generalisation-to-unseen-classes problem, and it’s a key challenge for building models that don’t just memorise patterns, but can adapt to new situations. Our work has explored how foundation models can help recognise previously unseen interactions. In a more recent study, we used large vision-language models, models that combine computer vision and natural language processing, to identify the parts of an object that support particular actions, without training the system on labeled examples for that specific task. This matters in areas like assistive robotics and safety monitoring, where AI needs to respond intelligently to behaviors it wasn’t specifically trained on.
This challenge is different from the low-light problem. In low-light pose estimation, the system is trying to recognise a familiar type of movement under unfamiliar environmental conditions. In human-object interaction detection, the action-and-object combination itself may be new. Both are generalisation problems, but they require different solutions.
Challenge 3: The resource gap
Even when researchers know how to make models more robust, applying those improvements isn’t always easy, especially in academic or smaller research settings. Today’s most powerful AI systems depend on massive computational resources in the form of data centers that contain huge numbers of specialised computer chips.
These are often too expensive for university labs or public-sector researchers, and the computing power needed to train leading models has continued to rise. According to the 2026 AI Index Report, the technology industry produced more than 90% of the notable AI models introduced in 2025.
At the same time, a model developed using large computing clusters may ultimately need to operate in a clinic, school, robot or home device, which means running on much smaller hardware. Such systems may also need to respond quickly without continuously sending sensitive data to the cloud. This mismatch creates a widening gap between what’s possible in theory and what’s practical in deployment. Bridging that gap requires not just better models, but more efficient algorithms and open-source tools that broaden access to advanced AI.
Why it matters
These challenges aren’t just academic. They affect how and whether AI tools can be trusted in the real world. Imagine a fall-detection system that fails at night, a workplace safety monitor that misses a crucial action or a robot that misunderstands what a person is doing because it’s never seen that exact interaction before. These aren’t just minor bugs – they’re breakdowns in trust, usability and sometimes even safety.
AI systems are being deployed in homes, hospitals, factories, vehicles and other everyday environments. If they can’t adapt to different environments or recognise new human behaviors, their usefulness becomes limited and their risks amplified. That’s why researchers are increasingly focusing not just on accuracy in ideal conditions, but on robustness, generalisation and real-world readiness.
Looking ahead: Closing the gap
Closing the gap between lab-trained AI models and messy, unpredictable real-world environments won’t happen overnight, but it’s possible. In my research, we’ve explored techniques like using augmented data to simulate challenging conditions and help models adapt. We’ve also worked on enabling AI systems to better generalise to new, unseen situations by using knowledge from foundation models to distinguish unfamiliar interactions from similar ones encountered during training.
Ultimately, I believe that making AI systems more reliable in everyday settings is a challenge worth solving, not just to improve gadgets and apps, but because AI has the potential to support human well-being, whether that means safer streets, smarter healthcare or more secure homes.
Bo Wang, assistant professor of Computer and Information Science, University of Mississippi

Israel’s ambassador to Australia says the third anniversary of 7 October is an opportunity for both countries to return to “traditional friendship” as hundreds gathered in Sydney’s east to mark the day.
But, in the lead-up to commemorations on Wednesday marking Hamas’ terror attack, leaders of Australia’s Palestinian community say the federal government should do more to help the diaspora suffering since the war on Gaza.
Hillel Newman spoke to the Australian Jewish community at Bondi Pavilion, saying it was moving seeing so many gathered in solidarity with Israel at 6.29am, the moment the massacre in Israel began three years ago.
“I will never forget that hour in my entire lifetime … the trauma of that day will be with us for all eternity,” he told the crowd. “The events of the last three years have revealed the deep hatred for Israel and Jews.”
Michael Gencher, the executive director of StandWithUs Australia, said the events of October 7 and in the intervening years, notably the massacre at Bondi beach, had shown hatred towards Israel and the Jewish people had become “more visible, and more dangerous”.
“It has changed the way many of us have seen the world, and it has changed the way we see our place in the world,” he said. “But the future does not have to be defined by the hatred of the past three years”.
Speaking ahead of the anniversary, Newman acknowledged relations had become “strained” between Australia and Israel but wanted to see improvement.
“We have challenges, but I have come with a lot of goodwill in order to try and make a positive change in the relationship, perhaps even reset the relationship and return both sides to the initial historical traditional friendship,” the Israeli ambassador told Guardian Australia.
“There have been issues between our two countries. We can have differences of opinion, but we should not allow differences of opinion to overshadow and overcrowd the overall relationship. We can understand if Australia has criticism of this issue or another.”
The comments come despite Israel’s foreign ministry publicly criticising foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, on social media in recent weeks, branding comments she made to the United Nations about settler violence in the West Bank a “blatant lie”.
It follows an earlier intervention into domestic Australian politics, where Israel urged Labor to soften criticism in a draft policy platform that condemned settler violence and a controversial death penalty law.
Since the 2023 attack – in which Hamas militants killed about 1,200 Israelis and 250 people were taken hostage, in what is considered the single deadliest day for Jewish people since the Holocaust – there has been a near breakdown in ties between the Israeli government and federal Labor.
Israel’s response to the attack and bombardment of Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.
Australia has joined other countries in taking an increasingly stronger stance against Israel, including action alongside the UK, Canada and New Zealand to sanction Israeli politicians Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, accusing the two of inciting violence against Palestinians.
But the federal government last month stopped short of joining the UK and other partners in imposing a ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Relations deteriorated further when Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom was killed in a humanitarian convoy struck by Israeli drones in April 2024. Albanese and Wong slammed a decision by the Israel Defense Forces in August not to pursue criminal proceedings over Frankcom’s death.
Pressed on Israel’s failure to release audio from the strike, Newman stressed it was an issue for the Israeli military, but that his country remained open to any request for potential reparations for Frankcom’s family and remained in favour of continued discussions.
Wong has been working with the Frankcom family on an appropriate response to the decision not to press criminal charges.
She said in a statement that the Australian government had condemned the Israeli government’s decision not to pursue criminal proceedings against those responsible for killing Frankcom and her World Central Kitchen colleagues.
“The Australian government will not stop pressing Israel for justice for Zomi and her colleagues. We continue to engage closely with the Frankcom family on further action,” Wong said. 
“7 October is a day of profound grief and remembrance. We mourn those who were killed in the Hamas terrorist attacks, including Australian Galit Carbone, and all those who have suffered from antisemitic violence around the world.”
The Australia Palestine Advocacy Network president, Nasser Mashni, said the impact from three years’ of war was measured in two places at once: Gaza and in the diaspora.
“In Australia, the impact is a quieter but a relentless erosion of our place in this country,” he said.
“Underpinning every discussion that happens about ‘us’, but without ‘us’, is a nagging suggestion that we don’t belong, that we must prove we are Australian, and even human.
“This is the domestic footprint of genocide: protesting a demand for its end, and stopping Australia’s complicity in it, is more controversial than supporting it.”
In 2025, a UN commission found that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, citing tens of thousands of civilian deaths and massive destruction. Israel strongly denies accusations of genocide.
The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, said Australians would reflect on the devastating toll of violence.
“The attacks on October 7 were condemned by the Greens at the time, as our party has a deep belief in peace and non-violence,” he said.
“It is that same core value that means we condemn the ongoing genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.”
The cooler relations between Israel and Australia come against a backdrop of antisemitic attacks in Australia, as the nation prepares to face the first anniversary of the Bondi massacre on 14 December.
Fifteen people were killed in an antisemitic terror attack on a Hanukkah celebration.
A royal commission sparked by the Bondi attack is due to release its final report on 18 December.
The Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Alex Ryvchin said the 7 October attack and the “unsatisfactory responses” to it meant “troubled, uncertain times lie ahead for us all”.
“But if the jihadists thought mass terror at home and abroad would bring about some global capitulation by Israel and Jewish communities or that the majority of Australians would turn on their Jewish friends and neighbours, they have failed dismally,” he said.
The shadow defence minister, James Paterson, said the 7 October attack had changed Australia in “terrible ways” and culminated in the Bondi attack.
“Fixing this societal cancer will take years of sustained effort from the entire community, from the prime minister down,” he said.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday (September 29, 2026) expressed concern over the sharp disparity between the prices charged to retailers and consumers for essential medicines, particularly cancer drugs, observing that steep mark-ups placed an enormous burden on taxpayers and amounted to “carnage”.
A Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta questioned the Centre on why the 16% retailer margin provided for under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013 should not be applied uniformly to essential medicines to curb steep mark-ups over the price to retailer (PTR).
“Why not keep the 16% margin on MRP, which is prescribed in the DPCO, on everything? ... Ultimately, the loser is the taxpayer. This is carnage, as simple as that,” the Bench remarked.
The observations came while the top court was hearing petitions filed by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha, seeking its intervention to regulate the prices of drugs, medical equipment, and generic medicines, and make them more affordable.
Justice Mehta pointed, in particular, to the nearly ten-fold mark-up on an essential cancer drug, which was supplied to retailers for around ₹3,000 but sold to consumers for ₹27,000. He questioned who ultimately benefited from the nearly ₹24,000 difference. “You tell us why this difference... Where does this chunk of money go? Ten times...” Justice Mehta remarked.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, acknowledged the concern and said the government would have to find a way forward while “balancing equities”. He, however, said it was private hospitals, rather than pharmaceutical companies, that benefited from the steep mark-ups. “The pharma company is not the gainer. The gainer is the private hospital,” the Solicitor General submitted.
The Bench also flagged the practice of private hospitals insisting that patients purchase medicines from their in-house pharmacies, leaving them with little choice to procure the same drugs at lower prices elsewhere.
It also pointed to the impact of such inflated prices on public finances, observing that when treatment is covered under government-funded health schemes such as Ayushman Bharat, the cost is ultimately borne by taxpayers.
“Suppose the patient is taking treatment through government services... The government doesn’t pay, the taxpayer pays. This affects a larger section of society,” the Bench remarked.
Mr. Mehta sought time to place before the court details of the existing mechanisms governing drug pricing and assured the Bench that he would make his submissions on the next date of hearing. The Bench accordingly posted the matter for further hearing on October 12, 2026.
The petitions have sought directions to make drug formulations more affordable by curbing alleged overpricing of essential medicines by pharmaceutical companies and retailers. They have also sought stricter enforcement of price controls under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013 to prevent violations of the prescribed pricing mechanism and disproportionate profit margins across the drug supply chain.
Earlier, the top court had described the wide difference between the price to retailers and the MRP of medicines as “dacoity”, while drawing attention to the financial distress faced by patients struggling to meet treatment costs.
“The MRP is 10 times the rate at which it is provided to the retailers. If this is not extortion, then what is it? People sell their houses, ornaments to get treatment,” the Bench had remarked.

Uefa investigating Republic of Ireland-Israel row after spitting accusation
- Published
Uefa has confirmed it is investigating the half-time incident during Sunday's Nations League game between Republic of Ireland and Israel following an accusation of spitting.
The teams clashed at half-time in the 1-1 draw behind closed doors in Serbia, with the Irish Times, external reporting that Republic of Ireland head of athletic performance Damien Doyle alleged he had been spat at by an Israel player.
Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later confirmed there was an "accusation of spitting" during the fracas.
On Tuesday, Uefa confirmed it was opening an investigation "following a review of the official reports".
"An Uefa Ethics and Disciplinary Inspector has been appointed to conduct the appropriate disciplinary investigation regarding potential misconducts from player(s) on the occasion of the Uefa Nations League 2027 League Phase match between Republic of Ireland and Israel, played on 4 October 2026 in Backa Topola, Serbia," added European football's governing body.
The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) has been contacted for comment.

- The claim that an all-female team led the botched execution of the Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike on Sept. 30, 2026, is still under investigation.

In early October 2026, after the Tennessee Department of Correction failed to execute death row inmate Christa Pike on Sept. 30, 2026, a claim circulated online that Pike's execution team had been all female.
Pike was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death in 1996 for the killing of her Jobs Corp training program classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. She also was convicted of attempted first-degree murder in 2001 after attacking another inmate.
The department halted Pike's execution in the evening of Sept. 30 after she appeared to survive receiving two doses of the sedative pentobarbital. Pike was taken to a hospital and her lawyers said on Oct. 1 that she was in critical condition, The Associated Press reported.
Some social media users appeared to suggest that there was a connection between the failed execution and the alleged all-female lethal injection team. One X user wrote (archived), "I'm just going to say it, I think that the all-female execution team botched this on purpose."
I'm just going to say it, I think that the all-female execution team botched this on purpose.
— Cassandra MacDonald (@CassandraRules) October 1, 2026
The claim also circulated elsewhere on X (archived). Snopes readers searched our site for more information about the rumor.
At the time of this writing, conflicting claims circulated about whether an all-female team had carried out Pike's botched execution.
Speaking at a news conference after the execution attempt, Pike's lawyer Randy Spivey appeared to confirm that her execution team had all been women by saying that the team he saw at the execution was "consistent" with a reported request Pike made for an all-female team.
However, local media in Tennessee reported that Dr. Mark Fowler, a man who also was involved in the botched execution of Tony Carruthers in Tennessee in May 2026, administered the lethal injections or "oversaw" Pike's attempted execution.
When reached by Snopes via phone on Oct. 2, Fowler would not comment on whether he was involved in Pike's attempted execution. The Tennessee Department of Correction also declined to comment on whether Pike had an all-female execution team.
Given the lack of confirmation from official sources to settle conflicting claims, we leave this claim unrated.
The Tennessee Department of Correction had not confirmed at the time of this writing exactly what led to the failure to execute Pike. Therefore, it was impossible to say whether an all-female team affected the outcome of the execution.
Snopes contacted reporters for WSMV and WVLT, the two local news stations that reported Fowler's apparent involvement in Pike's attempted execution, to ask how they knew Fowler was present. We also contacted lawyers for Pike for the latest update on her health and case. We await replies to our queries.
The New York Post reported in September 2026 that Pike had requested an all-female execution team "citing past sexual abuse." Pike reportedly also said that if her request was not possible she would prefer to be executed by hanging.
Snopes contacted lawyers for Pike to access a copy of this reported request and await a reply. Spivey appeared to acknowledge the existence of the request when he responded to a question about it during a news conference (archived) after the failed execution (at 33:41):
MODERATOR: We have a question from Heather Derell. Was she granted the all-female execution staff she requested?
SPIVEY: I want to be careful with that because I understand the rules around identifying that, and I will say that I think what TDOC has said is that they would make every effort to comply with that, and what I saw was consistent with that.
At a news conference on Oct. 1, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said (at 0:54, archived) he had called for a "thorough and comprehensive and third-party review and investigation into the protocol" at the execution attempt. Lee also said that the state's last planned execution of the year would not take place while that investigation was ongoing.
Pike appealed to Lee for clemency and to have her death sentence converted to life in prison without the possibility of parole on Sept. 14. Lee rejected that appeal on Sept. 28.

Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel are the joint recipients of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm, Sweden announced on Monday.
Deisseroth, a professor at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University, Hegemann, a professor at Humboldt University in Berlin and Nagel, a professor at the University of Würzburg, Germany, developed a method that uses light, combined with genetic modifications of neurons, to switch on or off individual cells in a living brain. This makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behavior in the brain, and is being studied as a treatment for disease.
The work started in the early 2000s, when Hegemann and Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, a light-sensitive algal protein that allowed a single-cell alga to swim toward light. They found that this protein worked in any cell they injected it in.
Deisseroth then introduced the gene for the protein into nerve cells from rats, becoming able to trigger a nerve signal in the living brain with blue light.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine.
The committee was able to reach all three winners, starting with Deisseroth, who was “definitely asleep, but he woke up”, said Thomas Perlmann, the sSecretary for the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine. “All three said the same thing, that they thought it was absolutely wonderful to receive the prize with the other two; they called them ‘my friends,’” he said.  
There have been 235 award winners since the first medicine prize was awarded in 1901, of which 14 have been women. The youngest recipient was 31, the oldest 87. 
The award has been given 117 times: 40 times to a single individual, and has been shared among two winners 36 times, and among three (the maximum allowed by the Nobel statute) 41 times.
The winner will receive 12 million Swedish Kronor (SEK), or roughly $1.2 million.

Trump brings Natalie Harp on stage to sign executive order to bring diesel prices down at Nebraska rally
The president unveiled his multi-pronged strategy during a campaign appearance in Nebraska, where farmers and ranchers have been hit hard by high fuel costs

President Donald Trump has brought his close aide, Natalie Harp, on stage at a rally in Nebraska to sign an executive order in a desperate attempt to reduce diesel costs ahead of the crucial midterm elections.
In Grand Island Monday night, Trump asked Harp — known as the “Human Printer” for giving the president physical copies of social media posts and news clippings while on the go — to bring him the executive order that will allow anyone to purchase tax-free red-dyed diesel.
Harp walked on stage and handed Trump the executive order, which he signed in front of his supporters. When he was done, he threw his pen into the crowd as they chanted, “Trump, Trump, Trump.”
He then handed the executive order back to Harp and said, “She reminds me of The Price Is Right,” referring to the game show where an announcer asks contestants to “come on down” to the stage.
“This perfect person comes up, hands it, walks off,” Trump said, seemingly comparing Harp to a model who shows off the prizes on The Price Is Right. “We should go on television with this show. Right?”
Harp’s unusually personal relationship with the president has drawn scrutiny in recent weeks afterThe Washington Post reported that she was one of the select few who got to ride with Trump during a secret escape from Air Force One while they were leaving the NATO summit in Turkey amid a potential assassination threat from Iran.
Marc Beckman, senior advisor to Melania Trump, dismissed any rumors that her husband’s relationship with Harp was inappropriate, telling conservative media personality Stella Escobedo on her YouTube show earlier this month that the “liberal media” was “attacking this hardworking, very talented, very intelligent person in Natalie Harp.”
Trump announced the new executive order in Nebraska, where farmers and ranchers have been hit hard by record diesel prices. Red-dyed diesel is commonly used in farming, construction and other industries.
Trump will also urge states to increase the availability of dyed diesel and order the Treasury Department to review federal diesel taxes, according to Politico. The new executive order comes as new polls show Democratic gubernatorial candidates surging in four traditional Republican strongholds.
The White House didn't immediately respond to an inquiry from The Independent.
Trump's announcement came after he said Friday that he wouldn't impose a diesel export ban because the U.S. and other leading industrialized nations, known as the Group of Seven, had agreed to release stockpiled diesel.
"Europe has a lot of diesel, and they’re going to be making a major world contribution, and so are we," Trump said.
Monday's national average price for diesel was $6.32 a gallon, down from the record high of $6.53 on September 22, according to AAA.
Trump appeared Monday at the Nebraska State Fair with Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, who faces Democratic Party-backed independent challenger Dan Osborn.
Two recent polls showed the candidates jockeying for the lead in a state that Trump won by more than 20 percentage points in 2024.
Other polls show Democratic candidates ahead of Republicans running for governor in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas, even though none of those ruby-red states has been led by a Democrat in at least two decades.
And the Silver Bulletin polling-analysis website said Monday that the Democratic edge in the so-called generic congressional ballot had risen to 8.9 percentage points, marking a new high for this year’s election cycle, and that with adjustment for likely voters, that lead increases to 9.6 percentage points.
Patrick De Haan, chief petroleum analyst for the GasBuddy price-tracking website, said on social media last week that expanding access to red-dyed diesel could save some drivers about 60 cents a gallon, but noted that “farmers already use dyed diesel and are still paying record prices.”
“Taxes aren't the problem, supply is,” De Haan wrote.
The global availability of diesel has been pinched by Trump's war against Iran, now in its eighth month, as well as Ukraine's targeting of Russian refineries as it continues to battle the full-scale invasion that Russian President Vladimir Putin launched in February 2022.
Shuting Pomerleau, director of energy and environmental policy at the center-right American Action Forum think tank, responded to Haan's post by saying, "There are no effective ways to quickly bring down the diesel prices."
"It's like using a bucket to empty a river," she added.
As of Friday, 10 states that account for about one-third of all diesel sales in the U.S. had already taken steps to increase the availability of dyed diesel, Politico said, citing analysis by the independent ClearView Energy Partners research company.
Denton Cinquegrana, chief oil analyst for Dow Jones Energy, told Politico that suspending fuel taxes could provide short-term relief with long-term consequences.
“When you’re not collecting taxes, you’re just kicking the can down the road, because you have to fix roads and stuff like that,” Cinquegrana said.

Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls.
The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC.
Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.
Writing in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, Dr Roselyn Campbell, author of the study from Purdue University in the US, notes: “While Aha, the first ruler of the First Dynasty, seems to have only had a few subsidiary burials, his successors included hundreds of subsidiary graves around their tombs and enclosures.”
The graves of the retainers were excavated in the 1920s by the English Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, who believed them to be an example of human sacrifice – a view some later experts agreed with.
But there was a snag: Petrie did not find any evidence of trauma on the remains. While he suggested the individuals may have been buried alive, others suggested the retainers died naturally and were later reburied at Abydos when their ruler died.
Campbell re-examined the skulls of 46 retainers excavated from graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of three different royals – King Djer, King Djet, and Queen Merneith – from the Duckworth Collections at the University of Cambridge.
“This question of whether or not retainer sacrifice was practised in Egypt has been debated for over a century, but this is the first study to examine the human remains from the tombs themselves,” Campbell told the Guardian.
Campbell reports that 18 of the skulls showed signs of potentially lethal trauma such as fractures and – in one case – a chopping injury to the eye.
Campbell believs Petrie may have seen the skull fractures but did not realise they were injuries that occurred around the time of death, rather than arising as a result of later damage.
The fractures, she adds, are unlikely to have been caused by a mace – a weapon often depicted in ancient Egyptian art as being used by a victorious king to smite his enemies. Instead they are more likely to have been caused by flat, wide objects made of wood or antler.
“For the crania without trauma, we cannot be certain they were sacrificed. It’s quite possible that some of the retainers were sacrificed, while others were not,” she said. “With such a small sample size of the original burial population, we simply can’t see the full extent of these funerary rituals, nor can we be sure that this sample is truly representative of all the retainers.”
Campbell noted the number of subsidiary graves tapered off quickly and seems to have disappeared with the beginning of the Second Dynasty.
Salima Ikram, a professor at the American University in Cairo, said while the idea of retainer sacrifice was not totally new, “this paper is one of the few times that rigorous current methodologies are being used to evaluate these remains”.
She added: “The practice was short-lived, with people being replaced by statuettes. Possibly some or all retainers felt that this was a boon and that they would enjoy an eternal life in the service of the god-king, though they might also have resented it, been terrified, and tried to escape this fate.”
Dr Dawn McCormack, an Egyptologist at Samford University, Alabama, said similar sacrifices had occurred across different cultures and times, adding that not everyone at the Egyptian site may have been compliant.
“If you really think about what those scenes would have looked like, it would have been very gruesome,” she said. While noting that the study only involved a small number of skulls from the burial site, “the idea that some of the people may have been violently killed, I think, is something that in reality we might expect”, she said.

Tear gas in Paris and Marseille as school protests grow across France
- Published
Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France, as a wave of protests by high-school pupils spread to their parents, university students and unions.
Crowds of teenagers marched from the Place de la République in Paris, calling for more resources for schools, and what they called less repression from police.
Police clashed with demonstrators in Lyon, used tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes, but there was little of the serious trouble that marred previous protests.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned the earlier violence and said since the protests had begun 215 students and 85 staff had been hurt as well as 715 police officers.
The government said there had been disruption in 891 high schools on Tuesday - almost a quarter of all lycées - and said more than 250,000 demonstrators had taken to the streets during the day.
Students' unions put the number at 450,000, and said the number of high schools blockaded was 1,800 on what the protesters dubbed "Act Three" of their movement.
In Marseille, thousands of demonstrators moved around this city, stopping momentarily to chant before moving on as police changed direction.
A group of masked protesters grabbed bollards and bins and tried to barricade themselves off from police. Riot officers fired tear gas, and the protesters dispersed.
"Most of us aren't violent," said Alissa, a student in Marseille. "We're going to the streets because they've closed our schools... schools are falling apart."
Her friend, Sacha, said the ceilings in Marseille's schools were leaking and conditions were generally rather poor, "so we can't really work a lot of time". "We will keep doing this until good measures are taken," he added.
In parliament, the prime minister accused the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of seeking to "sow chaos" ahead of presidential elections in seven months' time.
President Emmanuel Macron is nearing the end of his second and final term in office and LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon is currently runner-up in the opinion polls behind Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally.
Macron was due to chair a meeting with ministers at the Élysée Palace on Tuesday evening to assess the situation.
Education Minister Édouard Geffray said that from the start he had appealed for dialogue rather than school blockades and complained that "ultra-violent elements infiltrated the high-school student movements".
He is now under pressure to respond to the students' demands. What has been offered, including a website for students to express their grievances and an afternoon of internal discussion in schools on Friday, has made little impression so far.
There seems little chance of the protests coming to an end just yet. France's biggest union, the CGT, has said that further protests involving school and university students are being planned for Thursday.
There is widespread concern over allegations of "disproportionate force" by police, and France's IGPN police inspectorate has been investigating a number of cases.
One police officer who fired a tear-gas grenade at a high school student at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, last week has now been charged by prosecutors with "violence... resulting in mutilation or permanent disability".
Eden, 14, was part of a group blockading the Château d'Épluches lycée for 15-18-year-olds when he was hit in the face. His lawyer said he suffered a fractured jaw, and that his upper teeth were broken and four of his lower teeth were gone.
On Monday, a 15-year-old's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near a school in the northern city of Lens.
Authorities say he picked up the "sting ball" grenade which then exploded, but students allege he was hit directly after an officer fired.
The grenade is considered a non-lethal weapon and the local prefect has said the incident took place when police were confronted by a group of 200-250 students throwing stones and fireworks.
What began with local anger at overcrowded classrooms, a lack of teaching staff and dilapidated school buildings in the northern Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis in mid-September has since spread across the country, and extended to some universities too.
Late on Tuesday, the French interior ministry said a total of 6,547 had been stopped or arrested by police since 28 September.
Tuesday's protests drew people of all ages. One couple in their 70s, Alain and Michèle, joined the march in central Paris, to show their support for young students, explaining that as former teachers they understood the problems that France's education system was facing.
"We are the grandparents of three students who are all mobilised. They have protested peacefully in front of their respective high schools in Paris in recent days, but they were still tear-gassed," Alain told the BBC, his voice trembling.
Additional reporting by Manon Prat in Paris.

France's police fire tear gas and water cannons as school protests sweep the country
PARIS — Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support school pupils demanding more education funding, according to government figures. The protests increased pressure on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.
As pupils again blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron's nearly decade-long tenure.
"We need to listen to them," said Léa Monimart, a demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. "They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It's important to show that there are adults who support them."
The Interior Ministry estimated that 256,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square during a largely peaceful march through the city.
The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fueling defiance and angering some parents and teachers.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in "almost all cases" and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school leaders must listen to students' concerns and find solutions.
Questioned in parliament on Tuesday about the protest movement, Lecornu denounced "ultra violence" threatening schools. Responding to criticism of police tactics, he pledged that any "accidents" would be investigated and described allegations that the police are racist as a "lie."
Class boycotts with police making thousands of arrests
More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,100 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign.
Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn't make "any sense to hit minors."
"Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas," said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests.
The violence is "absolutely unbearable," Le Coq said.
Nuñez defended police tactics despite a growing number of severe injuries blamed on officers' riot-control weapons. In the latest case, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade. He said 715 officers had been injured.
The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties, such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war, to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron, who can't run for a third consecutive term.
Against that backdrop, pupils' complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience.
"You say 'young people are the future,' so listen to them," read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school.
Ministry offers online portal for complaints
At the Hélène Boucher lycée, or high school, in Paris' 20th district, protesters tipped over trash cans and bicycles onto their sides to create a makeshift barricade.
Like hundreds of others around the country, the school was closed. Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry.
Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see.
Student protests have drawn attention to rundown classrooms
At Hélène Boucher, parents and other adults positioned themselves on Tuesday between protesters and police keeping watch.
"They are our children. Teachers, parents, federations, we all share the same goal: the protection of children's rights, and it is a legitimate right to demonstrate and to make demands," said Emilia Sichili Suriam, who is a member of an association of parents.
Demonstrators have voiced a range of grievances, often centering on a lack of resources and opportunities for students in disadvantaged schools, despite the promise of France's national motto: "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity."
Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats. Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students' compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.
Suzanne Nijdam, president of the federation of student associations, vowed that demonstrations would continue until authorities address the complaints.
"So, we really need to act now, and it's in the government's hands, to see these demands through to the end," she said. "It's a matter of political priority, a matter of prioritizing the youth and the future of our country."

Child accidentally locks himself inside car, rescued by locals in MP's Sagar
A child was accidentally locked inside a car in Sagar's Tehsil area while his father had stepped away briefly. The safe rescue by locals underscored the risks of leaving children unattended in vehicles.
Panic gripped a locality in Madhya Pradesh's Sagar city after a young child accidentally got locked inside a car when the vehicle's doors shut from the inside, triggering anxious moments for family members and bystanders.
The incident took place in the Tehsil area of the city when the child's father was on his way to drop him at school. According to reports, the father stopped near a stationery shop to buy some items and briefly stepped out of the vehicle, leaving the child seated in the driver's seat. The car key was reportedly left inside the vehicle.
While his father was away, the child accidentally locked the car from the inside. When the father returned and tried to open the door, he realised the vehicle had been locked and the child was trapped inside.
Alarmed by the situation, the father sought help from people nearby. Within minutes, a crowd gathered around the car as concerned residents tried to assist in rescuing the child.
People approached the vehicle and attempted to guide the child into unlocking the door from inside. However, the youngster was unable to understand the instructions and began to panic, making the rescue more difficult.
As time passed, anxiety grew among family members and onlookers. Residents continued to reassure the child while simultaneously searching for a safe way to open the vehicle without causing harm.
After several attempts and careful efforts, locals managed to unlock the car door and safely bring the child out. No injuries were reported.
The child's father and those present at the scene heaved a sigh of relief after the successful rescue. What had briefly turned into a tense and chaotic situation returned to normal once the child was safely out of the vehicle.
The incident has once again highlighted the risks of leaving children unattended inside vehicles, even for a short period. Authorities and safety experts often advise drivers to ensure keys are not left inside parked vehicles and to avoid leaving young children alone in cars under any circumstances.

A British father asks a Cyprus judge to avoid prison after son's fatal hotel fall
The lawyer for a British man who pleaded guilty to a charge of negligence in the fatal fall of his 3-year-old son from a hotel window in Cyprus has appealed to a judge to avoid a prison sentence
PAPHOS, Cyprus -- The lawyer for a British man who pleaded guilty to a charge of negligence in the fatal fall of his 3-year-old son from a hotel window in Cyprus appealed to a Cypriot judge on Tuesday to avoid a prison sentence, saying his loss was punishment enough.
According to evidence heard in court, the 38-year-old defendant, his son and father-in-law got ready for dinner after a day at the pool and were making their way to the elevator from their fourth-floor room at the King Evelthon hotel on July 12. The father lifted the child to check out the hotel's waterpark visible from a window when the boy somehow slipped and tumbled 12 meters (about 40 feet), falling to his death.
His lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told the Paphos District Court that his client's guilty plea acknowledges a momentary lapse of judgment but that he wasn't “willfully negligent.”
“That fraction of a second will haunt him for the rest of his life,” Alexandrou told judge Froso Christodoulidou during mitigation proceedings. “This is punishment he and his family will carry with them for the rest of their lives.”
Alexandrou said the defendant — who prosecutors and the defense haven’t named throughout the proceedings — didn’t recall the circumstances of the fall because it happened so quickly. But he and his father-in-law had told investigators that they thought the glass window pane was shut.
The defendant, sitting in the dock, was visibly distraught and constantly wiped tears from his eyes as he heard the translator next to him recount the details. His parents were also sitting in the rear of the courtroom, his mother's eyes red from weeping.
Addressing the judge, Alexandrou said he wasn't arguing that the defendant be absolved of responsibility but that the court must consider “what kind of mistake was made at that point in time.”
“Justice can be served without imposing the utmost severity in sentencing,” the lawyer said.
Prosecutor Chryso Perganti said that the boy was pronounced dead in hospital a couple of hours after his fall, suffering multiple skull and bone fractures and damage to his vital organs.
He also said a blood sample taken from the defendant roughly six hours after the boy's fall showed that he had consumed alcohol but was under the legal limit. However, experts estimated that this blood alcohol level at the time of the fall may have been more than twice the legal limit.
Alexandrou countered that the defendant's alcohol consumption had no bearing on the case because there's nothing to suggest that he was impaired at the time of the incident.
The lawyer told the judge that his client, an auditor at a major U.K. firm, risks losing his job because of the disciplinary hearing and the prison sentence. He also said even if the sentence is suspended, the man could lose his license to practice.
The charge carries a maximum of four years’ imprisonment and a minimum of a fine. Imprisonment can be suspended if the sentence is three years’ imprisonment or less.
Judge Christodoulidou said she would rule on the matter on Oct. 16.
Cyprus, a former British colony, is very popular with tourists from the U.K., who make up a significant portion of the roughly 4 million holidaymakers the island nation received in recent years.

Ronaldo wants Portugal 'punishment' but not retiring
- Published
Cristiano Ronaldo says he is not retiring from international football but deserves to be punished for walking out on Portugal after he committed a "breach of the coach's trust".
The 41-year-old captain left his country's Nations League camp after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark.
Al-Nassr forward Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances - both world records - helping them win Euro 2016 and the Nations League twice.
In a lengthy statement, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United player said he should be held accountable for his actions.
"The Portuguese Football Federation must assess the consequences of my actions and punish me for them. I believe the punishment should not be reduced," Ronaldo said.
"I have already apologised, but I know that actions have consequences."
Portugal manager Jorge Jesus said on Sunday that the door was still open for Ronaldo to play for the country's national team.
Ronaldo said that, provided he was "physically fit, playing with my team, and hopefully scoring goals", he would like to continue to play international football.
"After my suspension period ends, I will be available, as I always have been, to compete and win with our national team," he added.
'Manager had broken his word'
Ronaldo's statement, which ran to nearly 2,000 words, struck a conciliatory tone in places but was also critical of Portugal coach Jesus as he provided his version of the dispute which prompted him to walk out on the squad last week.
He said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness.
However, on the day of the Norway game, the 72-year-old coach told him he would play for 30 minutes.
"Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn't called on," Ronaldo said.
"The manager had broken his word to me."
A later meeting with Jesus produced an agreement for the coach to clarify matters at his next news conference.
Ronaldo said an eight-point document was prepared saying he had never demanded playing time, had respected Jesus' decisions and that the coach asking him to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake.
Portugal'a all-time appearance holder said the agreed notes did not require Jesus to apologise to him but said the coach's public remarks did not reflect their private discussion.
"It was the second time he had broken his word to me," Ronaldo explained.
"I decided to leave the training camp without waiting for any further broken promises."

Bahrain Grand Prix software glitch: FIA to blame for Sepang 'farce', says David Croft
Sky Sports F1's David Croft discusses the chaos caused by a software glitch at the Bahrain Grand Prix, labelling the scenes in Sepang a "farce"; watch F1's first ever Singapore Grand Prix Sprint weekend live on Sky Sports F1, with Sprint Qualifying at 1pm on Friday
Tuesday 6 October 2026 20:12, UK
David Croft has criticised the FIA for the chaotic formation lap scenes at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, describing a software glitch that saw several drivers slowing to a crawl or stopping completely as a "farce".
F1 and the FIA have new technical regulations this year which saw the introduction of a new power unit which is almost 50 per cent electric.
Sepang saw the first wet conditions of the season, and the FIA later confirmed that a combination of low engine speeds, low grip, wet-weather energy-management settings and the configuration of the circuit had caused an unintended loss of power.
Speaking on the F1 Show podcast, Sky Sports F1 commentator Croft questioned why such a scenario had not been simulated before the season began.

"We had a shakedown in Barcelona and six days of testing in Bahrain before the season started. Why on earth were situations like this not tried out before we went racing?" he said.
"Nikolas Tombazis [FIA single-seater director] says there are bugs all the time with software. Behind the scenes, people are working on those bugs, and what they try and do is do updates during the night time when people aren't actually using their computers.
"Not during the course of a Grand Prix, when someone has now suddenly realised we've got a situation on our hands.
"Before the start of the race, it looked like it was the day where we were going to break the duck and have some wet weather running.
"We've had dry weather all the time, so we've had plenty of time to simulate this, to stop it happening in front of hundreds of millions of people during the course of a race.
"This falls on the FIA. I'm sorry, but you are the governing body. You are supposed to have the upper hand when it comes to these rules and regulations, the directives, the power units and everything.
"You weren't on top of things when it came to that race, and it was a farce."
When the drivers left the pit lane following a rain-delayed start, several almost ground to a halt, including race leader Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, with numerous other drivers in the midfield also experiencing issues.
The unusual scenes left spectators and viewers unsure what was happening, with the aborted start followed by a lengthy wait while the problem was resolved.
The FIA said its emergency software fix took around 20 minutes to issue and install, although the overall disruption was considerably longer.
"We had no idea why those cars were going so slowly," Croft said. "We had no idea why we were waiting around for 40 minutes to get a race on.
"There's a lot going on, and we need to understand and appreciate that the FIA are trying to keep across a million and one different things.
"But sometimes taking a step back, identifying issues that could come during a season, during a scenario, and taking preventative measures is the best way forward, rather than just trying to react on the spur of the moment.
"I want to see a bit more strategic thinking when it comes to these sorts of issues.
"Let's go through other simulations, FIA, and other things that could go wrong with these power units. Let's get the bugs fixed and get the simulations in place now."
Tombazis acknowledged after the race that the software had not been tested sufficiently in the specific conditions encountered at Sepang.
The FIA added that the issue had not been detected during testing or the laps to the grid and has promised a full review with the teams and power-unit manufacturers.
The controversy ultimately overshadowed what became an eventful and competitive Grand Prix as Verstappen emerged victorious, with Kimi Antonelli second and Hamilton completing the podium after a dramatic recovery.
"I'm just really frustrated that I've come away from Sepang - a brilliant weekend commentating, talking about a great track, brilliant drivers, some sensational racing - and what's dominating the headlines is F1 farce because we see cars slowing down and stopping," Croft added.
"I don't want that for the sport that I love. I actually want people to be talking about great racing.
"That's what we should be talking about, but these issues need addressing."

Three storms are churning simultaneously across the western Pacific, an unusual October clustering that’s generating high waves around parts of Japan.
Typhoon Choi-wan, Typhoon Nolo and Tropical Storm Koguma were all active on Tuesday, marking the first time in five years that three systems have existed at the same time in the month of October, according to the Japan Weather Association (JWA).
The three storms are at different stages of development and are spread across a wide swath of the Pacific.

) India is among the top countries with 90% of the world's chewing tobacco-related health burden, and South Asia is the "epicentre" of chewing tobacco, according to new research published in The Lancet Global Health journal.
Researchers estimated that chewing tobacco contributed to 251,000 deaths globally in 2023 -- there were 241 million chewing tobacco users globally, with use peaking among individuals 60 to 64 years old, they said.
The analysis, part of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 (GBD 2023) and covering 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023, distinguishes the burden of chewing tobacco from that of other forms of smokeless tobacco, the team said.
"Chewing tobacco is not a uniform public health problem, and our findings show that a relatively small number of countries bear an overwhelming share of its health burden," lead author Gabriela Gil, research scientist at Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), University of Washington, US, said.
"Understanding how patterns of use differ within these populations is critical to designing more effective prevention and tobacco control strategies," Gil said.
The researchers said despite decades of progress in tobacco control, the global prevalence of chewing tobacco use has remained relatively unchanged. Stroke and lip and oral cavity cancer were found to comprise much of the health loss attributable to chewing tobacco use globally.
South Asia had the highest concentration of chewing tobacco use, with 14.6% of people aged 15 years and above chewing tobacco products in 2023.
The region accounted for 2,10,000 chewing tobacco-related deaths -- about 84% of the global total, the study estimated.
However, more than 90% of chewing tobacco-related deaths and disability burden among men was found to occur in 10 countries, including India, Bangladesh, China, Pakistan and the US.
Among women, more than 90% of the burden was concentrated in countries, including India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Indonesia, Myanmar and China.
The researchers said the figures reflect total deaths and disability, meaning countries with larger populations may account for a greater share of the burden even if their rates are not the highest.
Patterns of chewing tobacco use also varied substantially by age and sex.
"These findings show why chewing tobacco control cannot take a one-size-fits-all approach," senior author Emmanuela Gakidou, professor in the department of health metrics sciences at IHME, said.
"Prevention and cessation strategies need to reflect how patterns of use differ by country, age, and sex, as well as the cultural and social factors that shape tobacco use in each setting," Gakidou said. PTI KRS

New Delhi, Oct 06: INDIA bloc MPs, including Leaders of Opposition Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi, on Tuesday marched from Parliament House complex towards the Election Commission but were stopped by police on Parliament Street, where they sat on a dharna demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
The MPs were stopped in front of the NITI Aayog office, on the stretch between NITI Aayog and Akashvani Bhavan leading towards the Election Commission headquarters.
After being prevented from proceeding further, they sat on the road in protest. Opposition MPs carried cutouts depicting Kumar in an RSS uniform and raised slogans, including “BJP hai CEC hai”, “Vote chor, gaddi chhod” and “Democracy not for sale”.
In a post on X, Gandhi posted, “Gyanesh it's done bro. Time to resign".
TMC leaders Abhishek Banerjee, Derek O Brien, Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, SP chief Akhilesh Yadav and CPI (M) leader John Brittas were among those who took part in the march.
Heavy security deployment and barricading had been put in place in and around Parliament and the Election Commission headquarters ahead of the march.
Security personnel were stationed in the area much before the MPs began arriving. The MPs gathered at Parliament's Makar Dwar before setting off towards Nirvachan Sadan, the Election Commission headquarters.
Ahead of the march, opposition MPs questioned the security arrangements and stepped up their demand for Kumar's resignation, citing the Supreme Court's observations on changes to Form 6, the statutory application for enrolment as a voter. Congress MP Imran Masood accused Kumar of eroding public trust in the Election Commission.
"Across the country, the institution that Gyanesh Kumar headed was an institution the entire country trusted, an institution the entire country took pride in and felt proud of. Questions were never raised over its impartiality. One person has broken that trust," he told PTI Videos.
"And an entire nexus is working together. We will question Gyanesh Kumar, and the BJP chief ministers will start giving the answers," he alleged.
CPI MP P Sandosh Kumar said the Supreme Court's observations on Monday had strengthened the opposition's objections to the additional declaration attached to Form 6 during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
"On September 26, there was a press statement by the Commission and it was stated that the entire process related to Form 6 has been ratified by the Supreme Court. Whereas it has been proven that it is an entirely misleading statement," he alleged. Calling the CEC a "Cheating Election Commissioner", the CPI leader said opposition parties had been agitating against the provisions since 2025 and would intensify their movement.
Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut questioned the scale of security deployment ahead of the march, saying the MPs intended to proceed peacefully.
"We are MPs. We are members of Parliament. We are also citizens of this country. Why is there a need to deploy such a large force to stop us? We will walk and go. We are unarmed," he said.
Raut claimed that Border Security Force and CISF personnel had been deployed and security outside ministers' residences increased.
Accusing Kumar of misleading the public over the Supreme Court's position on Form 6, he said the CEC had "no moral right" to continue in office.
The Supreme Court on Monday said it had not approved any modified version of Form 6 and would examine the Election Commission's records to ascertain whether changes had been made and who had authorised them.
The observations were made while hearing a petition challenging alleged unilateral decisions by Kumar.
In its September 26 statement, the Commission had said the declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR had been upheld by the Supreme Court, while forms prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, would be used outside the SIR period.
The protest comes amid an opposition campaign over alleged irregularities in the SIR exercise and reports of differences within the three-member Commission. The poll body has rejected suggestions of a split and maintained that decisions relating to SIR were taken unanimously.

Anyone with ovaries who lives long enough will experience menopause. While menopause is a natural transition in midlife, it can strongly affect a person’s quality of life and their current and future risk of heart disease, osteoporosis and other issues. So you might think that whether someone is experiencing or has gone through menopause would be noted in their medical records.
But when we and our colleagues examined the electronic medical records of almost 240,000 women, only 12% included mention of menopause, even though more than half the women reported separately that they were experiencing this transition. Our findings, published in the journal Menopause, reveal a major gap in how clinicians capture basic information about women’s health.
The menopausal women we examined are from a broader group of 400,000 who participated in the All of Us Research Program, a nationwide study run by the National Institutes of Health to compile a wide range of health data from at least 1 million Americans. We looked at how information about menopause was included in electronic health records and how this information differed by demographics, such as age, education, race and income.
Because study participants filled out health surveys upon enrolling, we could track discrepancies between their own reports of menopause and what was in their medical records. Age at menopause and symptoms, such as hot flashes or sleep disturbances, were also largely missing from the medical records and survey.
Missing links
Many aspects of menopause, and the diversity in women’s experiences with it, remain poorly understood.
For example, when menopause begins, as well as how disruptive its symptoms are, can vary greatly. Some women experience extreme hot flashes, sleep disruptions and brain fog, while others do not. One woman may go through natural menopause at age 45, and another at 54. Both ages would be considered normal, but that timing can affect current and future health in distinct ways.
Electronic medical records offer an unmatched opportunity to investigate these knowledge gaps, enabling researchers to study the experience of hundreds of thousands or even millions of people using routinely collected data.
Such large-scale studies may shed light on how menopause symptoms change over time and who is more likely to experience them; how markers of heart disease, bone health or mental health track with menopause; how social determinants of health, such as ethnicity and access to healthcare, affect someone’s lived experience of menopause; and countless other unanswered questions.
Closing the data gap
Our study is not the first to point out how inconsistently menopause status and symptoms are recorded in healthcare settings and electronic health records. But it systematically highlights the enormity of the gap, showing that menopause is often not even recorded at all.
It’s not clear why menopause is so rarely documented in electronic health records. It may be because menopause is not a disease, so it does not generally occur to clinicians to note it as a diagnostic code. It may feel obvious or irrelevant to diagnose or measure. It’s possible that patients themselves often don’t bring it up unless their symptoms are severe. Healthcare providers routinely ask middle-aged patients about their reproductive health – for example, when they had their last menstrual period – but this information rarely ends up getting documented in the electronic health record.
As we see it, not capturing this information is a colossal missed opportunity to drive vital research and improve personalized healthcare. Our team is developing a short, simple questionnaire about menopause status and symptoms for patients to fill out as they check in for medical appointments. These responses could then be added to their medical records for use by both their healthcare team and researchers. We are also developing a computer-based approach to infer menopause-related information from other data in a woman’s health record or genetics.
Finally, we are exploring the All of Us dataset to identify systematic differences – for example, in patients’ cultural background or income level, specific health system practices, urban versus rural settings – that might be linked with whether menopause data gets recorded in medical records. These associations can point to targeted ways to encourage its collection.
It’s impossible to research, and treat, what’s not measured. Capturing the menopause transition is an essential step to improving healthcare for women in midlife.
Audrey Hendricks, University of Colorado Anschutz and Nanette Santoro, University of Colorado Anschutz
