EU wants to track potential rogue efforts to block out the sun
Rising temperatures are sparking fears that governments or private actors could launch unsanctioned experiments to try to alter the climate
The European Union has launched a €35 million (US$39.4 million) tender to fund research and coordination on, among other things, detecting rogue efforts to alter the Earth’s atmosphere by blocking out the sun.
The EU’s Horizon Europe arm, which funds research and innovation, launched the call for projects on Tuesday as part of an early stage effort to coordinate action on so-called Solar Radiation Modification, a nascent and controversial technology that could be used to cool the planet should temperatures rise to critical tipping points.
In a report last month, the UN warned that global temperatures are set to cross the key 1.5 degrees Celsius (1.8 degrees Fahrenheit) threshold above pre-industrial levels within the next few years, and could climb as high as 2.6 degrees without changes to current policies.
The effects of climate change are already being felt with wildfires, droughts, hurricanes and severe floods happening increasingly frequently.

Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?
- Published
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.
Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.
There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.
This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.
Why has fighting broken out now?
It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.
The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.
This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.
This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.
Who are the TPLF?
For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.
It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.
At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.
When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.
Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.
The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.
An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022.
Why has the peace deal faltered?
There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray.
The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army.
Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991.
When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa.
The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum.
For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms.
The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy.
But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy.
This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions.
Who is backing the TPLF?
A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies.
Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army.
Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power.
So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside.
TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated.
Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests.
What is the government's position?
As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country.
It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies.
During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out.
Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports.
Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force.
What do we know about the bombing in Tigray?
Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces.
The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify.
Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war.
This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces.
The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks.
What is being done to stop the fighting?
The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks.
It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently.
The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict.
The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume.
The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated.
Could the fighting spread?
Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia.
The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia.
The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily.
There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government.
The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters.
The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.

Artificial, the new comedy-drama about OpenAI and the artificial intelligence arms race, is a movie of weird walks.
As OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever, Russian actor Yuri Borisov clomps around, like a geeky Frankensteinian monster. As the controversial OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Andrew Garfield bounces and skips boyishly—a gait that Altman himself recently commended for its accuracy. And as Elon Musk, Ike Barinholtz puts on a loping swagger, commanding rooms of computer nerds like some sort of alpha gorilla (a semblance matched by his long, pouting faces, which call to mind those old Bored Ape NFTs).
During the movie’s post-premiere Q&A earlier this week at the New York Film Festival, Barinholtz wryly described his character as “a person who walks normally.” Such are the awkward saunters of the march of history in the making.
Artificial, directed by Luca Guadagnino, waltzed into NYFF with some controversy clinging to it. The film was originally set to be released by AmazonMGM, which conspicuously dropped it this summer after Amazon struck a $50 billion deal with OpenAI. (Indie house Neon swooped in to pick it up.) NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim referenced “the circumstances” around the film in his onstage introduction.
That OpenAI may have brooked issues with Artificial makes sense. The film is almost completely unflattering, depicting Altman and other OpenAI stakeholders—as well as all the major drivers of the AI boom—as vain, reckless, and insufferably boring. Where 2010’s The Social Network succeeded in making Silicon Valley computer savants look like robust titans of industry and architects of the future, Artificial works to opposing ends. It depicts its tech titans as self-regarding dweebs.
Comparisons to David Fincher’s Facebook drama are inevitable. There’s the subject matter, of course. And the fact that both films feature Garfield in a lead role. (It should be said that Artificial is really more of a biopic of Sutskever, here depicted as both the prime mover of the current AI wave and its nagging moral conscience, than it is of Altman.) But Guadagnino and writer-producer Simon Rich’s approach to the material feels diametrically opposed to Fincher’s. The Social Network was a steely, polished, wordy drama. Artificial is pitched as a black comedy that verges on the surreal.
Guadagnino, best known in Hollywood for the coming-of-age drama Call Me by Your Name and the three-way tennis romance Challengers, has mastered a strain of tense eroticism. There are shades of that in Artificial, in Altman’s seductive wooing of Sutskever’s character. But the film is, for the most part, literally and figuratively sexless.
The images are plain, and even a little ugly. You can almost feel Guadagnino’s more rococo style begging to break out. A slo-mo sequence of a room of gawky programmers dousing each other in bottles of Jarritos, celebrating their AI’s latest self-learning benchmark, is stickily unsexy. A climactic scene of Altman and his OpenAI lackeys confronting Sutskever on a sloping San Francisco street recalls the green-screen backdrops of Tommy Wiseau’s cult classic The Room. After the screening, Guadagnino claimed the story captured a different strain of desire—what he described as “the desire to prevail.”
It’s a need many viewers might share, as leaders in the AI industry (including Altman) appear united in tamping down the technology’s acceleration. Artificial intelligence, we are told, is developing so rapidly, and is becoming so sophisticated, that it risks compromising life on Earth as we know it. In a recent interview with WIRED, former Anthropic AI employee Jacob Coxon alleged that his former colleagues have described the next few years as the potential “endgame” for humanity itself. Another Anthropic researcher claimed that there’s a chance that AI could “kill all humans” within a decade. (The odds were set below 10 percent, which still seems extremely high.)
Artificial stages these tensions as a kind of a high moral drama. Borisov’s well-meaning researcher—depicted as being temperamentally incapable of lying—pleads for safeguards, slow-downs, and AI’s “alignment” with humanity’s broader interests. Meanwhile, the case for exponential technological and capital growth is argued by, well, basically everyone else.
Even the idea of safety itself as saleable. In one scene, concerns about OpenAI’s capacity for serious harm is framed as being beneficial only to the company’s bottom line. Sounding alarm bells signals transparency and due diligence. And the harmful capacity itself is seen as proof positive of the technology’s advancement. It’s win-win. And it’s also no-win.
Artificial makes a persuasive, and frustrating, point about the ongoing AI contest. Pick a metaphor: The train has already left the station, the horses have fled the barn, the toothpaste is out of the tube. The technology already exists. And so, as with nukes in the last century, it becomes not a question of the power itself but who is allowed to harness it, and how. (In his post-Anthropic exit interview, Coxon directly compared the company to the Manhattan Project.)
Questions of ethics become academic, or just annoying, when everyone involved is playing by a different rulebook. If it’s not OpenAI that controls computing’s future, it will be Anthropic, or Google, or Elon Musk. Or, worst of all—at least according to the Trump administration—China. (An early scene in Artificial sees Sutskever and his mentor, Nobel laureate computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, played by Mark Rylance, rebuff the advances of a Chinese investor eager to use their neural network technology for drones and face-recognition systems.)
It may be hard for the average moviegoer, who may only engage with AI for email rewriting or calendar organization, to gauge just how seriously to take Artificial’s alarmist warnings. Not least of all because basically every character in the film is depicted as at least completely self-serving, if not sociopathic. And of course, one may naturally wince a little bit at a star-studded Hollywood movie raising these alarms, with a lavish premiere at a Rolex-sponsored film festival and a glitzy afterparty attended by stars, famous comedians, and notable filmmakers (including octogenarian Taxi Driver screenwriter Paul Schrader, who recently publicly confessed to being dumped by an “AI girlfriend”).
As a message movie, Artificial seems likely only to confirm the worst misgivings of AI doomers, while riling its diehard boosters. It is, however, genuinely funny in places, regarding the bulk of our future’s self-appointed engineers with withering contempt, from their dorky parties to their weird walks.
It was a stance embraced by Barinholtz, who offered the premiere-night audience his own half-hearted, sarcastic reassurance: “The future is bright! We’re all gonna be fine!” Cue a round of very nervous laughter.

- Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 3 adds the new Ice Caves biome to the Java Edition.
- Frostbite is a new hostile mob that uses Ice Balls and can apply the Freezing effect.
- Ice Crystals, Icicles, new freezing mechanics, and Friends list improvements are also included.
Minecraft’s upcoming winter game drop experimental features are finally live for Java Edition players. Mojang has released the Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 3, bringing the Ice Caves biome and the terrifying Frostbite mob, a zombie variant, after they were previously added in the last Preview. So, if you’re a fellow PC player, check out the rest of the Minecraft Winter update features here.
Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 3 Finally Brings Ice Caves to Java
One of the main additions to the Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 3 is the new Ice Caves biome. These caves generate underneath the colder Minecraft biomes and are primarily made up of Packed Ice and Calcite blocks, giving them the distinct frozen appearance.
Once you enter inside, you’ll spot the Icicles hanging from the ceiling that can naturally grow up to five blocks long and become a dangerous environmental hazard. If you wander around with a Minecraft torch or any heat-emitting block long enough in these caves, the Icicles can fall from above, dealing damage to any entity present under them.
Another feature introduced in the Minecraft Ice Caves is the Ice Crystals. These resemble the Amethyst Clusters, and you’ll see them generating on the ground, adding a beautiful decoration to the Ice Caves. Due to that faint glow, the Ice Crystals are the safest light blocks in Minecraft that can be used as an alternative to torches.
Minecraft Frostbite Mob Can Freeze Players with New Ice Ball Attacks
Alongside the Ice Caves comes the brand-new zombie variant, called the Frostbite in Minecraft. The most unique feature of this zombie is that it can switch between melee and ranged combat depending on whether it’s far away from its target and whether it spawns with the Ice Balls.
At close range, the Frostbite zombie can attack by punching, applying the Freezing mob effect to its target. Whereas from a distance, it can throw Ice Balls that deal damage and knock targets backward.
Now, the Freezing effect can cause players to become frozen while also making them shake. One way to counter this is wearing Leather armor that provides protection against Freezing, just as it does with Powder Snow; however, the effect is applied nonetheless.
Moreover, Zombies and Husks can also transform into Frostbites when they remain inside the Powder Snow for a while. Also, Frostbites are immune to freezing and Powder Snow themselves.
Other than the new Minecraft Winter update features, there are several small changes, including Snow being placeable on Packed Ice, Snowballs gaining knockback against players, and a redesigned Friends list with improved search and sorting options.
So, the new features are out for Java, and you can try them out now by downloading the latest Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 3. How do you like the new features? Tell us in the comments below.

Wildfire smoke affects animals in unique ways. Scientists are trying to understand it
Olivia Sanderfoot stands on a flower-freckled hillside in Amherst in Western Massachusetts. She listens for a moment — and a volley of birdsong flutters forth.
An Eastern Wood-Pewee. A goldfinch. A downy woodpecker.
"It's just magical," she says with an air of reverence. There are birds foraging among the flowers. Fluffy fledglings are darting about, learning the ways of the world.
"Every day that I get to start birding is a good day," she says. "If you want to get the widest range of species and hear the most songs, you want to be out here in the morning."
For new discoveries, everyday mysteries, and the science behind the headlines, follow NPR’s Short Wave podcast.
Sanderfoot, a global change ecologist at Cornell University, knows that for the birds that live here, not every morning is this idyllic. Over the summer, this area was suffused with toxic smoke from distant wildfires in Canada. It's an increasingly common problem, even in places untouched by flames. Fire season is starting earlier, lasting later, burning more land — and as a result, producing far more smoke.
"Smoke can blow hundreds to thousands of miles away from that burn site," Sanderfoot explains. "That means that the footprint of a smoke event greatly exceeds that of any fire. How do birds deal with that?"
This is the central question animating Sanderfoot's desire to form a new field of study called "smoke ecology." The goal, she says, is to understand how the smoke billowing off of wildfires may be disturbing wild places and creatures — and whether anything can be done to prevent possible harm.
Air today, gone tomorrow
Sanderfoot's curiosity about how birds cope with smoke emerged in 2018 when she was living in Seattle and wildfires blazed in Eastern Washington. "The air smelled acrid," she recalls. "The city was just blanketed in this sickly yellow, gray haze."
She was told it was a one-time event — yet the same thing happened two years later.
"I remember walking outside and my eyes were just burning," Sanderfoot says. "And I thought, 'What on earth are animals doing? Are they OK?'"
Very little was known apart from anecdotes — like the absence of birdsong or the arrival of droves of birds to a backyard, famished and parched.
"Smoke is a toxic soup of substances," she says. "It's not just about what [birds are] inhaling, which is inevitably bad for them. It's also about how the cues that they use to navigate their world are upended when it gets smoky outside."
To puzzle out what was going on, Sanderfoot realized that she needed to collaborate with researchers from a range of other disciplines, including conservation biology, statistics, ecophysiology, and atmospheric chemistry.
"Real-world problems don't map cleanly onto the same academic silos that have been set up for decades," says Tracey Holloway, an atmospheric chemist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, the lead of NASA's Health and Air Quality Applied Sciences Team, and a colleague of Sanderfoot's. "We need to be tackling new problems with new partnerships."
For instance, in order to understand what birds are inhaling, one has to know what's moving through the air in time and three-dimensional space. "It depends on which way the winds are blowing," says Holloway, "what chemical processes are happening in the air, and also patterns of rainfall and where the emissions are coming from." The science depends on air quality monitoring, satellite data, and evermore sophisticated computer modeling.
Birds are especially sensitive to smoke in large part because of how they breathe. A human being has soft lungs that allow inhalation and exhalation of air. By contrast, birds have rigid lungs surrounded by a collection of air sacs that act like bellows, pushing air continuously through the system.
"This allows birds to take up about twice as much oxygen with each breath that they inhale compared to us," says Sanderfoot. "This means that they're vulnerable to all the other things that are in the air, too."
Morgan Tingley, an ecologist at UCLA, is another member of the burgeoning smoke ecology cohort. "What we're trying to do is getting smoke to be recognized as a disturbance in and of itself distinct from fire that is worthy of our concentrated attention," he says.
For much of his career, Tingley has studied wildfires — events with a clear start and stop, and defined borders. But the smoke produced by those wildfires can present its own unique set of problems, as it can spread far from the original blaze.
"Smoke is extremely hard to predict and it's highly variable," he says. "It can be there one day, one hour, and gone the next. Which means that it's hard to actually disentangle what its impacts are because you can't really control it."
This means that it's not possible to anticipate where smoke will appear, or when. Scientists also prefer not to subject animals to smoke intentionally.
So when it comes to studying wildfire smoke and birds, the trick is to gather data everywhere. To do so, the researchers rely on legions of amateur birders and professional conservationists and ornithologists across the country who are already on the ground collecting data when smoke happens to blow in.
Big army, little birds
One such individual is Pam Sowizral, the bird project coordinator at Mass Audubon's Drumlin Farm Wildlife Sanctuary in Lincoln outside of Boston. On a sunny morning in late August, she walks up to a bluebird nest box and gently raps on the outside.
"Always give a little knock first," she advises quietly. "Let them know you're coming." When she lifts the side panel, she reveals two feathery puffballs huddled on a bed of pine needles. These baby bluebirds are the last of the season here.
Sowizral says that nearly every year for the last 20 years, three times a week in spring and summer, she and her volunteers check the bird boxes here and count the nests and the eggs and how many chicks fledge. They check when the weather's good, when it's bad (within reason) — and when the smoke rolls in.
"Those periods of time when the smoke was here, the air somehow felt a little different," she says. But "that didn't stop us from doing our usual monitoring of our boxes."
That's key. Nationally, counts like this one provide a portrait of bird activity and behavior before, during and after smoke events.
Sanderfoot of Cornell University says she's using these kinds of observations, alongside observations of breeding behavior, to help her understand how birds are coping with wildfire smoke in a variety of places.
She's revealed three distinct strategies, depending on the species and the individual birds. They either hunker down and stay put, fly away, or shift their behavior — by not vocalizing as much or venturing out less often, say.
"This could be an attempt to mitigate their exposure," says Sanderfoot. "It might also be how they are forced to respond if they feel unwell."
In addition, she and her colleagues have observed that repeated exposure to smoke appears to impair the body condition of a variety of birds, leading to lower weight overall.
"They all respond in different ways," she says. "And we need to figure out what those ways are and how effective they are in order to design effective conservation strategies for a rapidly changing world."
This is one of Sanderfoot's top priorities: determining what might constitute what she calls smoke refugia for birds — safer spots where they can hunker down until conditions improve. "I want to know where birds are going when it's smoky," she says, "what resources they're seeking out, and what we could provide to help them during a risky time" — like water and perhaps shelter or food.
"I would like to be able to give people something they can do to help," she says.
Sanderfoot's personal experience with wildfires didn't end in Seattle. "I almost feel like the smoke is following me," she says.
In early 2025, she and her family fled the fires in Los Angeles where they were living at the time. And this summer, she watched as a blanket of smoke descended upon parts of the U.S., including Ithaca where she lives now, blowing off the remote Canadian infernos. She says she doesn't think it's a coincidence.
"Let's put it this way," she says: "We can expect that the future will be smokier."
It's a fact that's true for birds and people, which means that what Sanderfoot and her colleagues learn about smoke ecology may reveal a clearer way forward — for us all.
"By learning more about birds," she says, "I think we might learn something about how we can take care of ourselves and each other."

Other Desert Cities, the starry Broadway revival of Jon Robin Baitz’s Tony Award-winning play featuring Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Ed Harris, Allison Janney, Joe Keery and Lily Rabe, grossed a smashing $1,879,441 in its first week of previews. All seven performances at the Hudson were sold out for the week ending October 4.
The $1.8M gross puts Other Desert Cities, directed by John Benjamin Hickey, at #2 on this week’s Broadway grosses chart, second only to Hamilton‘s $2,704,838 (enjoying a boost with the return of Christopher Jackson to the cast). Other Desert Cities‘ average ticket price of $275.66 edged out usual front-runner Hamilton ($251.78) as the week’s costliest seat. (Average paid admission for all 28 shows was $122.51.)
Those two shows were the week’s only sell-outs, though Chicago, Hadestown, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Just in Time, MJ, Paranormal Activity, Schmigadoon!, and School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play all came close with attendance at 95% of capacity or more.
Watch on Deadline
Overall it was a fairly strong week on Broadway, with all but five of the 28 productions reporting box office gains over the previous week. Most of the five bucking the upward trend showed only minor slips, with the exceptions of Oh, Mary!, which was down $241,332 to a still-healthy $1,216,930, and The Lion King, which had a cancelled Saturday matinee and accordingly dropped $202,402 from the previous week to $1,498,471.
In addition to Other Desert Cities, two productions were new to the roster: Billy Crystal’s solo show 860, which filled 83% of seats at the Imperial for five previews and a take of $854,574; and non-prof The Imaginary Invalid, starring Bill Irwin, doing 92% for seven previews at the Haimes for a gross of $352,824. Opening night for 860 is October 21, and October 22 for Invalid.
Going strong was recent non-prof arrival School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play, filling 96% of seats at the Friedman and grossing $351,072.
Chicago, with Reece Weaver as Roxie, continued its strong run with 98% of seats at the Ambassador filled and a gross of $1,030,366. Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, with Tom Felton as Draco, was an impressive 96% and $1,671,543.
On the lower end of the spectrum, Six and Stranger Things: The First Shadow were each at about 68% of capacity, with grosses of $562,105 and $571,076, respectively. Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) was at 65% and $503,692. All three productions have posted closing dates: November 29 for Two Strangers, and January 3, 2027, for both Six and Stranger Things.
Rounding out the Top Five Earners for the week, after Hamilton, Other Desert Cities and Harry Potter, were MJ, $1,588,467; and The Lion King.
In all, the 28 Broadway productions grossed $27,735,569 for the week ending October 4, a jump of 15% over the previous week but down 12% over last year at this time. Total attendance was 226,390, up 8% from the previous week and down 3% year-to-year.
In the 19th week of the 2026-27 season, Broadway has grossed $593,216,158 season-to-date, down about 7% from last year at this time, with total attendance of 4,906,881 down 2% year-to-year.
All figures courtesy of The Broadway League. For more box office information visit the League’s website.

Indian police accused of sexually harassing journalists at protest
- Published
Three female journalists have accused police officers in India of sexual harassment during street protests in the capital Delhi.
The claims were made on Saturday after the force detained scores of young people calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner.
In a post on social media, Delhi Police said its New Delhi District had received the complaint, and it had been transferred to its crime branch for a "fair and impartial" inquiry.
Thousands of protesters gathered in Delhi and Mumbai cities for a third day on Sunday demanding that Gyanesh Kumar step down over large-scale changes to voter rolls.
The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.
Videos online show people being physically dragged away from the Jantar Mantar protest site in central Delhi.
The accusations by the women journalists include inappropriate touching by some police.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said women fear for their safety and the home ministry must "answer for this".
"Police dragged me by my hair," Aahna Singh, an activist and student at Jawaharlal Nehru University told Reuters news agency during the protests.
She said the police were resorting to "brutality".
The Press Club of India has demanded immediate action on the complaints against police officers, saying it was "shocked and dismayed" by the treatment of journalists.
"Behaviour of this kind cannot be normalised in a democracy. Journalists must be allowed to work freely, without fear, and document those who gather to raise various issues," it said in a statement.
The protesters say the voter-roll revision will benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.
It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address.
But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour the BJP during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.
The protesters have included supporters of the influential Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) that began as an online satirical movement.
The pressure group recorded its first major victory in July when it forced the then Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign after weeks of protests calling for education reforms.
The CJP called for the latest protest after a report in The Indian Express, external said that Kumar's two fellow election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had formally objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders they said had been issued without their knowledge.
The differences were reported to be mostly over the controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.
The Election Commission has defended its way of working and said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process" and that all the decisions were taken unanimously.
But the revelations sparked a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation.

Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far
- Published
Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months.
The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police.
Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer.
The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
Here's what we know.
Busisiwe Mahlangu
Case 1
Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties.
Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed.
Itumeleng Kekana
Case 2
Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026.
The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park.
No arrests have been made so far.
Nomfesane Mjobo
Case 3
Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park.
Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises.
No arrests have been made.
Unknown woman
Case 4
Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear.
No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made.
Gracious Nkomo
Case 5
Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area.
Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death.
Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo
Case 6
Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park.
Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case.
Unidentified woman
Case 7
Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed.
No arrests have been made.
Dineo Motapane
Case 8
The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive.
Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni.
She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case.
Jabulile Ntimba
Case 9
The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni.
According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence.
The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice.
Ntombifuthi Nxumalo
Case 10
The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.
This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death.
A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge.
Unidentified woman
Case 11
The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni.
The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area.
The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared.
No arrests have been made.
Boitumelo Gift Mashita
Case 12
Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken.
Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand.
Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies.
While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September.
The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg.
It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni.
President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience".
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day.
Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests.

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners.
“Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.
As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together, in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”
The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi university, by three men who posed as police officers.
Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood, after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year old were also reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by the bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.
Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.
Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say that nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic underreporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and they could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.
Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi university, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.
While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country requires a deep societal shift where men no longer feel they have ownership over women’s bodies.
“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,’ she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”
Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.
“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”
Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women; as one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.
Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old a graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender-equality initiative, said she has experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.
She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”
The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before – but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.
“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago, but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe.’”
Many of the Delhi university students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.
“Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades,” said Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for her masters in English at Delhi University. “It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”
Many on the marches said that it was no coincidence the protests took place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, which saw hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians take to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): A large number of private hospitals in Bhopal face the risk of losing MP-ABN empanelment because they have not obtained full NABH accreditation despite extensions and a final notice issued in March 2026.
Bhopal has a higher concentration of private hospitals than other major cities in Madhya Pradesh or state capitals elsewhere in the country.
As per Madhya Pradesh Ayushman Bharat Niramayam (MP-ABN), there are 813 private hospitals and 1,140 government hospitals (total 1,953) which are empanelled under MP-ABN in MP. Around 423 out of them are in four major cities - Bhopal, Indore, Jabalpur and Gwalior.
Bhopal has 213 private hospitals, accounting for 26% of the state's private hospitals. In comparison, Indore has 100 private hospitals and Lucknow 200.
Among the four major cities of Madhya Pradesh, 51 private hospitals in Bhopal do not have full NABH accreditation, compared with 30 in Indore, 12 in Jabalpur and 33 in Gwalior.
These health facilities have been operating since mid-2024, and a final notice for obtaining full NABH accreditation was issued in March 2026.
MP-ABN CEO Dr Arvind Shah said, Bhopal has excess private hospitals in comparison to other major cities of Madhya Pradesh including Indore or other state capitals and state capitals of other states like Lucknow.
The final order was issued in March this year for renewal of accreditation, he informed Free Press.
On the accreditation issue, Shah said hospitals had already been given extensions. These hospitals have been given two extensions, but they even did not apply for renewal.
Renewal of entry-level accreditation has not been permitted, as once their entry-level accreditation has expired, they will have to apply for full accreditation of NABH certificates.

As bipartisan backlash against Flock grows, some cities are asking anti-surveillance advocates and media outlets to pay eye-popping fees—including charging tens of thousands or even millions—to get information about how police departments are using and potentially abusing AI-enabled camera systems that track every vehicle that passes them.
On Monday, the Texas Tribune reported that city officials in a Fort Worth suburb, North Richland Hills, asked one group to pay $2.3 million before it would fulfill a public records request for Flock data. To reach that high fee, officials claimed that searching “about a terabyte worth of communications about errors, misuse, and effectiveness of the Flock system” would take approximately 14 years of labor at a rate of $15 per hour.
Phil Mynona, who filed the request using a pseudonym on behalf of his group, the Texas Privacy Coalition, told the Tribune that the fee seemed “ludicrous” and designed to stifle his public records searches.
Mynona has sought similar records from more than 200 law enforcement agencies across the US, and he said it was impossible to predict how cities assessed fees for Flock records. Some cities provided more than 400,000 pages of documents for free, while others charged $5,000. Other groups, including a Houston news station called KPRC, have seen officials quote up to $121,000 for Flock records, the Tribune reported.
The high price tags may be hiding data that anti-surveillance groups note have triggered audits, arrests, and changes in how law enforcement uses cameras, including decisions to get rid of cameras. Many cops have been found using the cameras to stalk strangers and people in their personal lives, and so far, Flock has yet to introduce meaningful reforms to confront its stalker cop problem.
Texas is a perfect example of how increasing transparency about police use of Flock cameras works to protect the public from invasive searches that serve no lawful purpose. Last week, an ex-Texas cop, Zachary Anthony Klein, reportedly pled guilty to 100 felony counts of misuse of official information, which he agreed to do in exchange for the state not pursuing charges related to stalking several people. Klein’s Flock abuse—along with another cop’s—was outed after USA Today submitted a public records request that sparked a probe, then his arrest. Disturbed by the case, Texas Governor Greg Abbott quickly halted Flock funding and stopped issuing permits, the Tribune noted.

Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.
The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.
Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:
‘Climate risk maps’ in China
In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.
Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.
In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.
The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.
Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater
El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.
The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.
In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.
But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.
Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.
The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.
Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia
In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.
During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.
“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.
The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”
With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.
To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.
“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”
South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system
South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground.
The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.
Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.
Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons
Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.
El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.
Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.
Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.
The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.
This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

Gauff condemns racist abuse after China Open win

Coco Gauff says she suffered racial abuse on social media following an incident in her win over 16-year-old Sun Xinran at the China Open.
The American had been serving at 4-5 in the first set her Chinese opponent thought she had hit a winner.
However, Gauff raised her hand to halt play because of a flickering light in the side panels surrounding the court.
Gauff won the next three points to hold for 5-5 before she closed out the set, and then dropped just one game in the remainder of the contest as she claimed a 7-5 6-1 victory to reach the last 16 in Beijing.
The world number four gave a lengthy explanation of why she stopped the point in a post on X and said it was "an unfortunate situation" but "out of my control", adding that Sun had understood and accepted her apology.
Gauff then responded to a reply to her original post which included racist language.
"You can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff wrote.
"The amount of racist comments/direct messages I've received in the last few hours is insane. Lastly, I'm not a cheater or a thief."
Gauff is far from the first player in the women's game to suffer social media abuse.
A report in July said female players were subjected to more than 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media in 2025.
The WTA and World Tennis said "collective action" was required to make "significant progress" in tackling abuse.

When Blue Cross Blue Shield recently published research suggesting that hospitals use artificial intelligence tools to extract more money from insurers without providing additional care, people were mad. Amid growing concerns about AI, one glimmer of hope has been its potential to improve health — and yet, here it was: inflating health care costs without yielding any benefits.
As a doctor who has used the kinds of tools being criticized, I’m frustrated, too: We can document honestly and still wind up inflating hospital bills. This is because comorbidities function as an on-off switch with respect to billing, even though they affect patient care in nuanced ways.
Although the problem warrants a systemic fix, the best short-term solution is for hospitals to create more nuanced documentation tools, and for clinicians to exercise judgment when using them.
What did the research show?
BCBS suggested hospitals are using automated tools to document secondary diagnoses — like anemia, malnutrition, and low sodium — which allow them to charge more for caring for these patients.
For instance, a patient might be admitted for diverticulitis (primary diagnosis), but found on post-op labs to have acute blood-loss anemia (secondary diagnosis). Hospitals can use these secondary diagnoses to label a patient as having a comorbidity or a complication, allowing them to bill more for the hospitalization, whether or not they treated the patient’s anemia. These “bump codes” have cost BCBS hundreds of millions of dollars over the past two years, and these costs are presumably passed along to patients in the form of higher premiums.
BCBS claims that bump coding has become more widespread because hospitals are using AI tools to identify secondary diagnoses. Automated tools can skim a patient’s chart and prompt physicians to document that the patient is, for instance, anemic, and what they are doing about it.
Are doctors to blame?
A few weeks after I started medical residency, I began getting emails from hospital administrators I had never met, whose signatures said they were risk adjustment specialists. The emails were generic and polite, advising me to review clinical documentation integrity (CDI) queries on inpatients I was caring for. If I didn’t respond quickly, the request would be forwarded to the attending physician supervising me. A typical CDI query would point out that my note hadn’t commented on, say, a patient’s low sodium level, and would ask me to document that they had low sodium and what (if anything) we were doing about it.
Like most residents, I was already spending far more time on my computer than I was with my patients. Soon, CDI queries streamed into my inbox with such regularity that I turned to a more senior doctor to ask how I might stave them off. That doctor showed me an automated tool that I could include in my notes. This tool would assess a patient’s lab results, automatically detect any additional diagnoses a patient had (like anemia, malnutrition, or low sodium), and prompt me to specify whether we were monitoring, evaluating, or treating.
I assumed it was lucrative to the hospital for me to document these diagnoses (why else would they be paying risk adjustment specialists to email me about them?), but we almost always were at least monitoring the secondary diagnosis in question, and I accurately documented as much.
Including this tool’s outputs in my notes kept the risk adjustment specialists from hounding me and won me back several minutes of each day — enough time to poke my head into a patient’s room before I went home, or call a patient’s family member to give a quick update. I always answered the questions included in my tool honestly, but in the back of my mind, I wondered whether I was doing my patients a disservice: Was I inflating the cost of their hospitalizations without actually improving their care?
Where bump codes come from
In general, hospitals are reimbursed for hospitalizing patients on the basis of diagnosis-related groups, or DRGs. DRG payments are set by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services by analyzing claims data. (Medicare uses DRGs to set payments, while many commercial insurers, including BCBS, use the DRG system to negotiate reimbursement rates with hospitals.) Let’s say a patient is admitted with diverticulitis requiring surgery (typically billed as DRG 331 if there are no complications). CMS has estimated how much it usually costs to care for one of these patients and insurers prospectively pay hospitals on that basis; a hospital generally won’t get reimbursed more for keeping the patient longer, administering more drugs, placing more IVs, and so on.
However, some hospitals care for sicker patients than others. The typical diverticulitis patient at a tertiary medical center in a poor area will require more support than a diverticulitis patient at a community hospital in an affluent area. The government does not want to penalize hospitals that see more complex patients, and so it allows hospitals to seek additional reimbursement forcomorbidities or complications that increase the cost of their care.
This is where bump codes come from: Hospitals can bill more complex diverticulitis admissions as DRG 330, which is reimbursed at a higher rate. Not all comorbidities or complications count: In 2007, the last time DRGs were substantially changed, CMS analyzed claims data and used this analysis to decide which conditions qualify and set reimbursement rates. CMS pays hospitals more for patients with conditions like low sodium because it has found that it costs hospitals more to care for these patients (perhaps because they tend to be hospitalized longer and more often require ICU admissions).
However, although CMS adjusts DRG payments from year to year, the list of bump codes hasn’t been overhauled in nearly two decades.
Bump codes can help identify complex patients and ensure hospitals are paid more for caring for them. These are good things, in part because they reduce hospitals’ incentive to seek out healthier, more advantaged patients. While BCBS claims that hospitals are increasingly using these codes to bill more without actually providing more care, hospitals would presumably counter that they were being insufficiently reimbursed before, and that their coding is accurate. After all, the BCBS study does not claim that hospitals are engaging in fraud; the question is just whether the lab abnormalities hospitals are billing for warrant higher reimbursements.
So who’s right?
This issue boils down to the following question: How much more does it cost to care for a patient with a secondary condition, and do current coding rules accurately reflect this?
The answer is that it depends. For instance, not all low sodium levels are created equal. If a patient briefly has a sodium level that falls below the normal range, but their sodium immediately corrects once they’re able to eat again, they probably don’t require any additional resources, and hospitals shouldn’t be reimbursed more for caring for them.
By contrast, a patient with dangerously low sodium levels requiring an ICU stay, frequent lab checks, and carefully titrated IV fluids undoubtedly does use more resources.
This leaves doctors in a tough spot: Risk adjustment specialists ask us to document real diagnoses that we know could increase the cost of a patient’s bill, but we have no idea by how much. Moreover, there’s no medical school module on how much any of these comorbidities affects the true cost of the hospitalization. Against this backdrop, it makes sense that doctors try to just tell the truth: yes, this patient has low sodium, and we are monitoring it, even though this probably allows hospitals to code some patients as being more resource-intensive than they truly are.
What we can agree on
This entire enterprise — risk adjustment specialists spamming doctors, who are already nose-deep in documentation burden, to document diagnoses that often do not affect patient care, while insurers publish reports that fail to capture the nuance of the issue, leaving the public angry and confused — highlights a more general problem with respect to how the U.S. health care system works.
By design, hospitals and insurers are meant to compete with each other, with hospitals trying to collect as much money as they can for providing care, and insurers trying to pay as little as possible. Hospitals bolster their side by hiring risk adjustment specialists and employing AI tools, while health insurers hire payment integrity specialists and employ different AI tools.
Patients lose out because the administrative bloat inflates the cost of medical care, while making costs less transparent and harder to contest. Ultimately, the fix should be structural: At a minimum, we need to overhaul the list of secondary conditions that are eligible for bump coding. CMS attempted to do this in 2019, when it proposed downgrading or eliminating many bump codes based on new data showing they were not associated with increased costs. But hospitals pushed back, and the effort eventually stalled.
What should we do in the meantime?
Secondary diagnoses are supposed to be billed only when they are clinically significant — for instance, when they require further evaluation, treatment, diagnostic procedures, or monitoring. But in practice, the bar for clinical significance is probably lower than it should be. (Even rechecking a lab may qualify as monitoring.) Accordingly, I suspect the BCBS study is tracking a real problem, and that much of the documentation of secondary diagnoses isn’t linked to patient complexity.
Early in residency, I was caring for an immunosuppressed patient who kept spiking fevers. My colleagues and I wondered whether he might have an indolent infection lurking somewhere and ordered an echocardiogram to rule out endocarditis. His heart valves showed no signs of bacterial growth, but trace backflow was detected across one of his valves, a finding present in most people.
Soon, I received a CDI query inviting me to document his valve dysfunction in my note. I did not do this, because his incidental valve finding was irrelevant to his hospitalization. Instead, I typed out a response indicating as much. However, it would have been easier and quicker to click through the check boxes, and, despite answering them honestly, potentially inflate the patient’s bill.
At least some CDI tools built into electronic medical records — including the one I have used — default to including secondary diagnoses in ways that are likely to lead to bump coding. One way to improve the status quo would be to ensure that such tools give physicians the option to document whether a secondary diagnosis is clinically significant or not, rather than simply asking them how they are addressing it (on the presumption that it is clinically significant).
Hospitals should build such tools, and regulators should ensure they do. In the meantime, I’ll exercise clinical judgment when using my CDI tool — if the low sodium seems important, I’ll document it, and if it doesn’t, I’ll politely decline when a risk adjustment specialist invariably asks me to.
Leah Pierson is a resident physician.

As the Union government continues to host the ‘Seva Sankalp Abhiyan’ — a month-long celebration of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday and 25 years in public service, from September 17 to October 17 — one among the various events planned is the ‘Namo Seva: Untold Stories’.
Part of the larger celebrations aimed at promoting public participation towards the ‘Viksit Bharat’ vision, the theatrical performance has been carried out by students in functions across various schools and colleges. Several cultural forums, theatre groups, volunteers, and BJP workers themselves put up the play in events organised by state authorities to reportedly raise awareness about the welfare schemes launched by PM Modi as well as his life and work.
Also called ‘Namo Seva Gatha’, the play has been staged across several states, including Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Chattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, West Bengal, and many others. In the performances so far, despite its many forms — street play, cultural performance, panchayat event, school drama, puppetry show, and more — the script remained more or less the same, albeit in different languages.
Alt News read the script and instructions sent out by West Bengal school education department to primary, secondary, and higher secondary schools, as well as colleges and universities in the state. Further, a report by Ei Samay states that district school inspectors (DIs) had sent out instructions for the play to some schools.
Student participation in the play was reportedly voluntary. However, the performances have drawn criticism over the use of educational institutions to stage what a section of students and academics described as a politically charged celebration of the Prime Minister. Critics have questioned the appropriateness of asking students, especially young children, to enact a script that repeatedly praises Modi and his government, while also incorporating political and religious slogans such as “Modi hai toh mumkin hai” and “Jai Sri Ram”.
What’s There in the Script?
The script has “untold stories” about the Prime Minister were narrated in the form of a conversation between five school friends — Mohit, Raman, Kajal, Disha, and Sonali — who have reunited after many years at a cafe. They recall the days they have left behind and reflect on changing times, portraying Narendra Modi as the architect of ‘Viksit Bharat’ — a vision he has set for India to achieve by 2047.
Modi’s first appearance in the play comes in the aftermath of the 2001 Gujarat earthquake which killed over 20,000 people. He emerges through a screen of smoke amid the ruins of a collapsed structure, waving the Indian flag as a beacon of hope amid the devastation, before taking oath as Gujarat’s chief minister in his mother tongue.
The friends then turn to discussing range of topics from the advent of digital payments and UPI and the spread of modern technology into India’s hinterlands, to “Operation Ganga” during the Russia-Ukraine war, the abrogation of Article 370, the consecration of the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya — presenting them as beneficial and “grounbreaking” schemes and measures undertaken by Modi as the Prime Minister.
The script further represents the country as plagued by terrorism in the years preceding Modi coming to power. “Militants would carry out attacks whenever they felt like it. Bomb blasts, serial blasts, had become a daily affair,” a character reminisces. A scene that shows the Uri surgical strike of 2016 invokes the usage of “weeping, sounds of gunfire, and the notes of a bugle”. In one of the street plays staged in Varanasi, a character links the surgical strike to an alleged rise in the sale of diapers in Pakistan around that same time.
