‘We Were Coerced Into Participating’
The play stirred a controversy at Kolkata’s Scottish Church College. Some members of the college’s drama club spoke out against the college authorities, alleging that they were being coerced into participating in this play.
A student, requesting anonymity, informed Alt News that in an online meeting between faculty members and students organised on the evening of September 24, the matter came to a head, with students allegedly being reprimanding for not agreeing to take any part in the play. “As students of a college as prestigious as ours — one that counts Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose among its distinguished alumni — we cannot compromise on our individual convictions of what is right and what is wrong. Students should not have to face any undue pressure simply for exercising their fundamental right to act according to their own conscience and free will,” they said.
Posters stuck on walls around the college area on the evening of September 28, upholding the ideals of free expression by students, were allegedly removed within half an hour of them being put up, college sources who spoke to Alt News claimed.
Ultimately, the play which was scheduled to take place on September 29 at Scottish Church was cancelled after several students protested, The Telegraph reported. The report also quoted the mother of a student as alleging that college adminstration was pressuring students as well as the teachers to “act in a propaganda play”. She told the news outlet: “This resistance means a lot. It will also send a strong message to heads of other colleges that they cannot force their students to act in a play against their will.”
However, Madhumanjari Mandal, the principal of the college, squarely denied the allegations that there was any degree of pressure was involved. “Acting in the play was voluntary,” she told The Telegraph.
‘Propaganda’ Masked As Cultural Event?
Anwesha Sengupta, author and assistant professor of history at Institute of Development Studies, Kolkata (ISDK), believes that these plays represent a more effective form of propaganda.
Speaking to Alt News, she said, “When children come across the mention of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in their textbooks, they consume it dispassionately. This is not the case with performing a script, where it gets more internalised, as it is a group activity.”
“The play is a part of the same machinery which has been in the making for years now, and which tries to project the Prime Minister as a God-like figure. Since these directives come through teachers, and children usually grow up revering and trusting their teachers, the move comes across as more immediate, as compared to encountering Modi in a curriculum text, which seems to have mandated from a more distant, abstract authority,” she added.
Another student from Scottish Church College told Alt News, “It is unbelievable that an event so overtly political in nature was even allowed to be organised by the college.”

Next Generation Collective (NGC), a new group built around helping young people in entertainment with their mental health, was launched today at Hollywood & Mind’s inaugural summit in New York City.
Founded by Hollywood PR veteran Lilah Kojoori, NGC brings together clinical mental health expertise, entertainment industry leadership, and lived experience to provide guidance on mental health, boundaries, pressure, and the realities of working on set, performing, creating content and building a public profile at a young age. It will also serve as an additional resource for studios, productions, agencies, managers and platforms supporting young talent. The Kids Mental Health Foundation will provide clinical guidance and insights.
“Young people in entertainment often grow up in the public eye, and they deserve real support along the way,” Kojoori said. “With The Kids Mental Health Foundation’s clinical expertise, Hollywood & Mind’s reach across the industry and an advisory board that has lived this life firsthand, our hope is to give young talent and their families guidance and resources to navigate the industry while prioritizing their wellbeing.”
Popular on Variety
NGC’s founding advisory board includes: Angel Carter Conrad, Logan Henderson, Isabela Merced, Kel Mitchell, Artists for Artists, Soleil Moon Frye, Carmela Wallace, Hudson Yang, and Breanna Yde.
“We are excited that the Collective is beginning their work by first learning from the community they want to support” said Dr Ariana Hoet, Executive Clinical Director of The Kids Mental Health Foundation and a pediatric psychologist at Nationwide Children’s Hospital. “There are so many directions this important work can take shape and it’s wonderful that it’s being launched in such a thoughtful way.”
Beginning in 2027, NGC, its board and partners will work to develop expert-informed resources, education and support for young people, their families and the studios, productions, agencies, managers and platforms that shape their professional environments.
	“Supporting the wellbeing of those who work in entertainment is at the heart of Hollywood & Mind’s mission. We’re thrilled to be a founding partner of Next Generation Collective, where we can provide young people and their support teams with the resources and community they need to thrive both personally and professionally,” said Cathy Applefeld Olson, founder and CEO of Hollywood & Mind.

How Ceuta, football and Israel are shaping Morocco's election
- Published
Disillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections.
Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality.
"I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC.
The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber.
Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body.
The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs.
Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena.
Hamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda.
"As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC.
He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July.
Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history.
"We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says.
He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%.
El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031.
"As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government."
Fouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight.
Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July.
Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal.
The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals.
Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team.
Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031.
Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise.
"The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC.
He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision.
Also seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters.
Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.
Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021.
Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence.
During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended.
Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their respective countries.
This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations.
"We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh.
"If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people," he added, warning of "the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco".
I think young people should focus on the microscale: rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top"
More than half of Morocco's total population of roughly 38.8 million is under the age of 35 - though only 4% of the more than 15.8 million registered voters are aged between 18 and 24.
"I am not keeping up much with the campaigns - but I noticed the same faces as usual," says Hiba, a 27-year-old Moroccan living in Canada who preferred not to use her last name.
She lives in Montreal which has a large Moroccan diaspora of about 104,000 people, according to the 2016 census.
Many of last year's Gen Z protests were more vocal outside the country, where young Moroccans were able to express their anger without fear of repercussions.
Hiba, who co-organised several Gen Z protests in Montreal, says she would have considered voting had she been able to find a proxy in Morocco - which is how those in the diaspora can cast their ballot.
"Gen Z protests didn't go in vain. We achieved something. At least now we see more debates with young people on state TV," she says.
Azeroual, the environmental activist, agrees.
But having lived through both the 20 February movement in 2011 that changed the constitution and the recent Gen Z movement, she believes change must come from a multi-faceted approach.
"I think young people should focus on the microscale - rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top," she says.
Despite not being fully convinced by any political campaign, she says she will be heading to her local polling station to cast her ballot.

The Nobel Prize for Physiology for 2026 was awarded to scientists Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for “discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics,” the award-giving body said on Monday (October 5, 2026).
Karl Deisseroth, a 54-year-old American, Hegemann, a 71-year-old German, and Georg Nagel, a 73-year-old German, were selected by the Nobel Assembly of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute medical university and receive a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million), which is shared if there are multiple winners.
Optogenetics “makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain,” the prize-givers said.
“This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries.”
Last year, US scientists Mary E. Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell, and Japanese scientist Shimon Sakaguchi won the prize for their discovery of regulatory T cells. Their discovery has helped blaze new paths into treating cancer as well as auto-immune disease – a condition by which the immune system ends up harming healthy cells they are meant to protect.
The announcement of medicine Nobel kicks off the Nobel announcement week with physics being announced on October 6, followed by chemistry, literature, and peace. The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, popularly known as Economics Nobel will be announced on October 12.
The winners will get a cash award of 10 million Swedish kronor (nearly $900,000) and the award will be presented on December 10, the Nobel Prize day.
The Nobel Prize was created by Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel, who in his will dictated that his estate should be used to fund “prizes to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind”. December 10 is Nobel’s death anniversary.

Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
- Published
The co-pilot of the Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe in an attempt to take control of the aircraft, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying more than 170 people plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey.
Capt Smit Machchhar said he was lying on the cockpit floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside."
Passengers aboard the aircraft were then able to enter the cockpit and overpower the attacker, while on-duty crew travelling on the flight landed the plan safely.
A crash axe is usually kept in the cockpit in case of emergencies.
The UAE attorney general told state media that investigations were ongoing to determine the full circumstances and motives of the incident.
The co-pilot who launched the attack was an Omani national, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday that, after being subdued, the attacker called out to the crew, "Kill me, kill me!"
He added: "So, it's clear that he was suicidal… It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane."
He also said the attacker "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination".
The UAE has begun investigating whether the "incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose", according to the country's state news agency.
Machchhar, who was stabbed in the attack, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.
He was in "good health and recovering well", the Indian embassy in the UAE said on Thursday.
The pilot said: "I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again."

Barapullah Phase-III gridlock: Traffic Police ask PWD to redesign merger point
Police sought the redesign of the merger point where Barapullah Phase-III Flyover connects with the existing corridor
The Delhi Traffic Police have written to the Public Works Department (PWD) seeking the redesign of the merger point near the Sundial Park, where the newly opened Barapullah Phase-III Flyover connects with the existing corridor, citing repeated traffic congestion.
Barapullah Phase-III opened to the public on Wednesday last. By Thursday evening, the eight-km drive from Safdarjung Hospital to Sarai Kale Khan was taking over an hour. A Delhi Traffic Police drone survey found two three-lane roads feeding into a single three-lane corridor at several points. A lane ends abruptly where the new spur joins the existing flyover over Sundial Park.
The HT last week explained how traffic obeys physics that scientists have studied since the 1950s, and design manuals worldwide turn that physics into rules, and how Barapullah’s merges break several of them, and the science shows how predictable this jam was.
In an October 1 (Friday) letter, a copy of which HT has seen, the office of the deputy police commissioner (southern range) flagged major geometric and structural defects to the executive engineer of PWD’s flyover project division F-21.
It noted that “after opening of the flyover, a joint inspection of the newly opened flyover and its adjoining stretches was conducted on October 1, by senior officers of Traffic Police along with officials of PWD”. The letter cited the inspection and noted that certain geometric and traffic-flow related issues at the merger point near Sundial Park are contributing to significant traffic congestion, particularly in view of the exceptionally high volume on the newly opened corridor.
The joint inspection detailed critical design flaws responsible for the daily choke points on the crucial stretch connecting Mayur Vihar to South Delhi.
Under the heading of structural and geometric issues, the letter highlighted that the merger point of the Barapullah Phase-III Flyover with the existing flyover near the Sundial has a relatively sharp/rectangular geometry instead of a smooth curvature. “This results in an abrupt merging of traffic and creates a bottleneck at the junction.” An aerial photo taken by a drone was attached to the letter to demonstrate the extent of the defect.
The letter cited a severe mismatch in lane capacities where multiple heavy traffic streams converge, further compounding the crisis. “The new Phase-III Flyover has three lanes, while another three lanes of traffic from the Sundial side, coming from Sarai Kale Khan/Ring Road side, merge at the same location. Further, three lanes of traffic coming from the Ashram/DND side also merge towards the existing Barapullah corridor.”
The letter pointed out that the existing Barapullah Flyover has only two lanes at the relevant stretch. “Thus, a substantial mismatch in lane capacity occurs, resulting in congestion and slowing down of traffic at the merging point”.
The Traffic Police asked PWD engineers to execute prompt modifications to ease commuter distress and ensure road safety. “...it is suggested that the merger at the Sundial should be redesigned by providing a smooth curvature instead of the existing rectangular/sharp geometry to facilitate smooth and safe merging of traffic.”

CHICAGO — I was walking briskly on a steep treadmill, wearing a mask that evoked the villain Bane from “Batman.” Prince crooned back-handed compliments over an iPad speaker to keep my energy up, promising I had to be neither rich nor cool to be his girl. Every so often, the woman standing next to me asked me to point at the color-coded sheet ranking my state of exertion from 1 (roughly, “I could do this all day”) to 10 (“I not only hate this but am about to keel over if you don’t slow this thing down”). The goal was to get to 10. Pushing myself to achieve difficult physical goals does not come naturally. I can’t go on, I thought. I went on.
This was the VO2 Max test, which shows how efficiently the body uses oxygen (“V” stands for volume, “O2” for oxygen) and is considered medicine’s most accurate measure of cardiorespiratory fitness. It was the last in a barrage of assessments I’d undertaken at a shiny longevity clinic affiliated with Northwestern University — part of a $5,500 annual package. 
The quest to defeat the indignities of aging has long provoked costly and questionable practices, from the 1920s doctors who believed in the rejuvenating power of grafted monkey testicles to Bryan Johnson’s since-abandoned blood transfusions from his teenage son. Now some of the nation’s most prestigious health systems are jumping into the growing business of longevity. They promise a rigorous scientific approach to helping people preserve their youthful vigor for as long as they can, with assessments that give patients more detailed pictures of their current physical conditions and aging trajectories than they’d get at a typical doctor’s visit.
Some critics, however, question how to reconcile the clinics’ high out-of-pocket costs with hospitals’ nonprofit status and charitable missions, and warn that in their zeal to attract paying customers, they’re offering tests that lack sufficient evidence showing they actually improve people’s health.

OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
- Published
OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June, saying it had added more precautions to its training environments.
The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox.
"We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said.
Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation.
Executives from Microsoft and Google were also present.
An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June, in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind.
When asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake.
"In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said.
"The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties, but it's not good enough."
Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents.
"Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party."
OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee, which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators looking at AI and its impact on Australia.
The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI", it said.
Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and that an alarm was triggered if they interacted with the internet in a way they were not meant to.
This meant that OpenAI had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours.
The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations".
"We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… Based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well."
Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said that in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI.
"We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee.
The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials. AI companies want Australia to relax copyright laws so they can use books and music, for example, to train their AI models.
An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could mean artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard.
"In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association.
Anthropic's special envoy Jeff Bleich told the hearing the company had "never tried to dictate" to Australia on its copyright laws.

The Newport-Mesa Unified School District in Costa Mesa, California, announced it placed a teacher — whom it did not identify — on administrative leave for posting a video of herself saying the U.S. flag made her "uncomfortable" and suggesting to one student, possibly jokingly, that he recite the Pledge of Allegiance to a pride flag displayed on her classroom wall. However …
The video was recorded in 2021, a fact some people omitted from their "breaking" social media posts in 2026. No evidence showed the teacher, who taught English at Back Bay High School, "forced" any students to pledge allegiance to the pride flag, as was falsely claimed in memes and posts using fake, AI-generated images.
A district spokesperson said at the time, "The teacher is no longer in the classroom. We follow due process and our investigation continues." The statement didn't identify the teacher by name, nor did it specify whether she departed the school because she resigned or because she was fired. People who claimed she was fired didn't offer evidence to support it.
A rumor that a California school district fired a teacher for forcing students to recite the Pledge of Allegiance while facing an LGBTQ+ pride flag circulated online in September 2026.
For example, on Sept. 29, a Facebook user posted a meme (archived) showing three images of a woman smiling, laughing and wearing a rainbow-striped shirt and jacket. Pride flags also appeared on the wall in the background. The meme read, "A California teacher has been fired after forcing students to pledge allegiance to the pride flag. Do you believe she deserved to be fired?"
(David J Harris Jr. via Facebook)
The same user previously shared (archived) the same rumor in late August 2026 with a different image and marked it "BREAKING." Other people shared the same meme, or a similar one, on Instagram (archived), X (archived) and other platforms.
We found these posts contained a mixture of truth, falsehood, speculation and artificial intelligence.
The Newport-Mesa Unified School District in Costa Mesa, California, did once announce (archived) it had placed a teacher — whom it did not identify — on administrative leave for posting a video in which she could be heard saying the U.S. flag made her "uncomfortable" and suggesting to one student, possibly jokingly, that he recite the Pledge of Allegiance to a pride flag displayed on the classroom wall.
However, this all took place in 2021, a fact some people omitted from their "breaking" social media posts in 2026. No evidence supported the claim that the teacher, who was reportedly named Kristen Pitzen and worked as an English teacher at Back Bay High School, "forced" any students to pledge allegiance to the pride flag. Images used in the above meme and other posts that supposedly depicted the educator were in fact AI-generated and inauthentic.
At the time of the incident, a district spokesperson said, in part, "The teacher is no longer in the classroom. We follow due process and our investigation continues." The statement didn't identify Pitzen by name, nor did it specify whether she departed the school after submitting a resignation or whether she was fired. People who posted the claim she was fired didn't share evidence that the district had terminated her employment.
Via Messenger, Snopes contacted an account possibly belonging to Pitzen to ask questions. We will update this article if we receive further information.
Here are the facts
On Aug. 27, 2021, an educator — reportedly Pitzen, who was listed at the time as an English teacher for Back Bay High School in Costa Mesa — allegedly shared a video on her personal TikTok account in which she said she had packed her classroom's U.S. flag away and appeared to indicate she didn't intend to display it again.
In the clip, she laughed when recalling a story in which a student said her class was reciting the Pledge of Allegiance without a flag, then pointed the camera at a pride flag on her wall. She said she told him, "We do have a flag in the class that you can pledge your allegiance to." She laughed at several moments during the video, suggesting she may have been at least partly joking. No students or other staff were visible in the clip.
People then reposted the video and named Pitzen as its originator, with some X users organizing and calling for her firing that same day. Some users claimed her (now-defunct) TikTok handle on the account on which she shared the video and other clips was @mrsgillingsworth. We could not independently verify whether she truly owned the handle or if the videos originated from a different account.
In the video, she says the following:
Ok, so during third period, we have announcements and they do the Pledge of Allegiance. I always tell my class, "Stand if you feel like it. Don't stand if you feel like it. Say the words if you want. [You] don't have to say the words." So, my class decided to stand but not say the words. Totally fine.
Except for the fact [laughing] that my room does not have a flag. It used to be there but I took it down during COVID because [whispering] it made me uncomfortable. And I packed it away and I don't know where and I haven't found it yet. [laughing] But my kid today goes, "Hey, it's kind of weird that we just stand and then, you know, we say it to nothing." And I'm like, "Oh, well, you know I've gotta find it. Like I'm working on it. I got you." [laughing, shaking head]
In the meantime, I tell this kid, "We do have a flag in the class that you can pledge your allegiance to." And he like looks around and he goes, "Oh, that one?" [laughing, pointing to pride flag]
Following a wave of social media backlash, someone posted on the district's Facebook page the next day — a Saturday — posting (archived) that a teacher had been placed on administrative leave after causing "alarm and concern related to saluting the American flag." The post did not identify Pitzen by name.
(Newport-Mesa Unified School District - NMUSD via Facebook)
On the following Monday, Aug. 30, the district reportedly published a statement saying the teacher (still not identified) was "no longer in the classroom." The statement appeared in news articles, including in the Los Angeles Times:
We are aware that one of our teachers posted a video on her personal social media that caused alarm and concern related to saluting the American flag. We assure you that we take matters like this seriously. Showing respect for our nation's flag is an important value that we instill in our students and an expectation of our employees. The teacher is no longer in the classroom. We follow due process and our investigation continues.
Via email, district spokesperson Annette Franco confirmed the authenticity of the statement. We also asked whether the district fired the teacher mentioned in their statement — or whether the educator resigned. Without naming the teacher, Franco told us, "I can confirm that she is no longer with the District." We also requested comment from current Back Bay High School principal Scott Mazurier, who started at the school in 2024 and was not present during the incident. We will update this article if we receive more details.
The school district's policies include information about "patriotic exercises," including "the reciting of the Pledge of Allegiance." One part of the policy documentation says, "Individuals may choose not to participate in the flag salute for personal reasons."

Ship sinks and crew missing after Black Sea drone attack
- Published
A civilian cargo ship has sunk and its crew is missing after being attacked by drones in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say.
A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its 18 crew were rescued.
Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine.
Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks were "unacceptable".
Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said.
The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said. Named the Alfa Watan, it was a Turkish-owned general cargo ship and was reportedly heading for Sulina, Romania.
It is not clear what the Alfa Watan was carrying or how many people were on board.
A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. A search operation has been launched.
Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. That ship, the Able, was flying the flag of Palau and transporting grain.
Its last reported position was five nautical miles (9km) from the Alfa Watan.
Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law".
He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable."
He did not accuse Russia of carrying out the strikes, but referred to the war in Ukraine, saying: "As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning.
"Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea," she said. "While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning."
"Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable."
Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea.
A separate attack on Tuesday, near Odesa, saw a crew member killed and seven more injured. The ship was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, according to Ukrainian media.
On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The Karnataka government has flagged the disparity between the institutional landing costs and the Maximum Retail Prices (MRP) of high-value medicines, cancer drugs, antibiotics and hospital consumables supplied to hospitals across the State.
The department has raised the issue with the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA). Health and Family Welfare Minister U.T. Khader, in a letter dated September 23, wrote to the Union Health Minister seeking action.
Massive markup
Recent investigations by the Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) have revealed that pharmaceutical companies are supplying medicines to hospitals at heavily discounted institutional (landing) prices, while patients are being billed at or near the printed MRP, resulting in markups ranging from 10 times to over 52 times the actual procurement cost.
During inspections, the FSDA found extreme pricing anomalies in 253 drugs. For the cancer drug Cytax 100 mg, the landing cost was ₹342, while the MRP was ₹3,836, reflecting a markup of 11.2 times.
In the case of Gufipol, manufactured by Criticare, the markup was as high as 52.6 times, or 5,165%.
| Drug/Consumable | Landing Cost (₹) | MRP (₹) | Mark-up | 
| Gufipol (Criticare) | 86 | 4,528 | 52.6 times | 
| Guficycline-50 injection (GUFI) | 160 | 7,110 | 44.4 times | 
| Terlitis (AEQU) | 118 | 4,416 | 37.4 times | 
| Taxocare 120 mg (Intas) | 1,000 | 21,617 | 21.6 times | 
| Canmab 440 mg | 6,600 | 57,457 | 8.7 times | 
| Bevatas 400 mg injection | 5,850 | 62,690 | 10.7 times | 
| Cytax 100 mg (cancer drug) | 342 | 3,836 | 11.2 times | 
| Adult Nebuliser Mask | 44.50 | 950 | 21.3 times | 
| IV Set | 14.75 | 295 | 20 times | 
| Polysafety PRO IV Cannula | 33.21 | 548 | 16.5 times | 
11-point letter
The Karnataka government has requested the Centre to mandate transparency in institutional pricing by requiring hospitals to display both the landing cost and MRP on patient bills, expand the list of drugs under price control under the Drug Price Control Order (DPCO), and regulate trade margins on essential high-value medicines and consumables.
The State has also sought the constitution of an inter-ministerial expert group, a national data study, and amendments to, or supplementation of, the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013.
Other demands include rationalisation of trade margins, mandatory cost-to-MRP transparency, expansion of the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM), and creation of an audit and enforcement mechanism.
Drive to continue
Another special verification drive was conducted on September 25 and 26, 2026, at various wholesale premises, hospitals and other establishments in Bengaluru and district headquarters across Karnataka. According to the FSDA, preliminary observations indicate substantial differences between the landing cost, the MRP and the actual sale price of certain high-cost drugs, medical devices and hospital consumables. The inspections covered more than 768 consumable items and 189 high-cost drugs. The findings will be brought to the notice of the Central Government, the FSDA said in a statement.
According to the FSDA, the special verification exercise will continue in a phased manner. In the next phase, enforcement and verification activities will focus, among other categories, on antiretroviral drugs, higher-generation and critical antibiotics, medical devices and hospital consumables with substantial financial implications for patients.
Khader unveils SuMi
Health and Family Welfare Minister U.T. Khader released the new mascot for the Karnataka State AIDS Control Society on Thursday.
The mascot, SuMi, short for Suraksha Mitra, was selected from around 1,500 entries. The winning mascot was designed by Navya of Athena College of Nursing, Mangaluru.
The competition was organised by the AIDS Control Society to raise awareness about HIV/AIDS. It was conducted across all districts for people above the age of 16.

Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, at the start of a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
The Yemeni military also said in a statement that National Shield, Giants Brigades and Tihama Resistance forces had captured the Red Sea city of Mokha on Monday afternoon with the help of Saudi air strikes.
But in conflicting reports, unnamed Yemeni government and military sources told news agencies Reuters and AFP that the forces have only reached the city's outskirts.
The Houthis said they had struck Riyadh's international airport and other sites, but did not comment regarding Mokha.
Saudi Arabia condemned the attacks and reiterated calls for the UN Security Council's permanent members to support Yemen's government.
Four government sources told Reuters that Yemeni forces had reached the outskirts of Mokha late on Monday, and that Houthi fighters were now retreating.
Government military sources who spoke to AFP would not confirm the capture of the city, but said "our forces took control of the Dhubab military airfield and cut the road linking the Dhubab district to the Bab al-Mandab area".
Earlier, the Yemeni military also said its forces had seized Dhubab airport, 45km (27 miles) to the south, and were besieging Houthi fighters inside the nearby town.
Houthi-run media denied reports that government forces had also made advances in Dhubab.
The government said operations had also begun on other fronts on Monday, including the capital Sanaa, which fell to the Houthis at the start of the civil war 12 years ago.
Meanwhile, a Saudi-led military coalition said its fighter jets were providing "round-the-clock" air support to the pro-government forces and had destroyed 324 "high-value" targets since the start of the offensive.
Turkey and Pakistan, allies of Saudi Arabia, held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday and agreed to rapidly deploy military forces in Saudi Arabia in an invocation of their Mecca defence pact, according to a joint statement shared by Pakistan's foreign ministry.
Saudi air strikes killed a schoolgirl and a woman in the Sanhan and Saawan districts of Sanaa on Monday, according to Houthi-run Al Masirah TV.
Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdul Salam said Saudi Arabia was committing "dozens of massacres" and that it must "bear all the consequences".
The Houthi-run Humanitarian Operations Co-ordination Centre warned civilian airlines that Saudi airspace, except for the skies above the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, was no longer safe because it had become "a theatre of operations".
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting", in a statement to AFP.
On Sunday, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council announced the beginning of an offensive, dubbed Operation Yemen Dawn, aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Rashad al-Alimi insisted that all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted and called on all forces to carry out their assigned missions "until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia".
It came after the Houthis reportedly cut a mountain road near the south-western city of Taiz, effectively leaving government forces and residents there surrounded.
The Houthis also said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in retaliation for dozens of Saudi strikes on their territory.
In addition to the strikes on Riyadh's international airport, the Houthis attacked an Aramco oil refinery, and Abha airport, as well as other sites, according to Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree in a statement on Telegram.
According to BBC Verify, satellite imagery from Saturday shows thick, dark smoke coming from the site of a strike at the Aramco Riyadh Refinery, in the city's south-east.
A similar plume of smoke can be seen rising from the Khurais Central Processing Facility as well as from a potential strike point in satellite imagery from Sunday.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and quickly ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim (Mayyun) Island.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
At least 959 people have been killed and 5,000 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.
The UN says another 197,000 people have been displaced.

In 1972, so the internet story goes, the award-winning American actor Jane Fonda traveled to Hanoi, North Vietnam, in the midst of the Vietnam War. At some point in her visit, Fonda met with U.S. soldiers being held by the North Vietnamese military as prisoners of war. While a camera allegedly recorded the meeting, the POWs supposedly managed to pass Fonda scraps of paper containing their Social Security numbers in the hopes they could be smuggled back to the U.S. to confirm they were still alive.
Instead, the story goes, Fonda handed the slips to a North Vietnamese officer as soon as the camera shut off. Three prisoners purportedly died from subsequent beatings and a fourth barely survived, living to tell the tale of Fonda's traitorous behavior.
It's a rumor that's been spreading for decades as of this writing, and we consistently receive reader mail requesting a fact check. We have in fact debunked the rumor, all the way back in 2000. This update takes a fresh look at that investigation. 
Our conclusion, however — that the specific tale about Fonda handing over the messages is false — hasn't changed in the past 26 years.
Fonda did visit North Vietnam
The story is loosely rooted in a context of truth, as many myths are. Fonda did visit North Vietnam as an antiwar activist in 1972, and, while there, she did meet with U.S. prisoners of war. She acknowledged this in a page on her website separating truth from fiction about her visit.
According to Fonda's account, she was one of roughly 300 Americans who traveled to Vietnam with the aim of ending the war throughout its course. One of her main goals was to tour and document a series of dikes and levees in the agriculturally important Red River Delta. The U.S. Air Force had reportedly bombed the dikes on purpose, possibly hoping to cause a catastrophic flood.
Upon seeing the dikes, Fonda concluded — as did some other observers — that the U.S. was intentionally bombing them. She shared her conclusion at a news conference in Paris not long after returning from Hanoi, according to contemporaneous reporting from The New York Times.
While in North Vietnam, Fonda also made statements on Radio Hanoi, a radio station that broadcast English-language propaganda aimed at demoralizing U.S. troops. "I implore you, I beg you to consider what you are doing," The New York Times reported her as saying.
The anti-aircraft gun photo
But the most likely reason the secret messages story struck such a lasting chord is because of an infamous, widely published photograph of Fonda sitting on a North Vietnamese anti-aircraft gun. As soon as the photo was released in the U.S., many began calling Fonda a traitor and referring to her by the nickname "Hanoi Jane."
Fonda has said repeatedly in the years since the picture's release that she regrets being photographed in that pose. She recalled online that the photo was taken of her on her last day in Hanoi. Exhausted from her trip, she was taken to meet North Vietnamese soldiers, Fonda said. They sang her a song in Vietnamese, and then she sang them a Vietnamese song she had memorized for the occasion. The soldiers loved it, applauding and laughing.
Amid the revelry, according to Fonda, someone led her to the anti-aircraft gun and snapped the photo without her being fully aware of what was happening.
"It is possible that it was a set up, that the Vietnamese had it all planned," she wrote. "I will never know. But if they did I can't blame them. The buck stops here. If I was used, I allowed it to happen."
The photo was published and Fonda gained a longstanding reputation in some circles as anti-American and treasonous. That reputation, deserved or otherwise, made it easier for some to believe that she might have quite literally betrayed U.S. prisoners of war by revealing secret messages entrusted to her to their captors.
Debunking the 'secret messages' myth
Since 1999, the story about the POWs' messages has generally appeared in the form of this copypasta. It is relatively unchanged from its email chain message origins in the late '90s:
From 1963-65, Col. Larry Carrigan was in the 47FW/DO (F-4E's). He spent 6 years in the "Hanoi Hilton". . . The first three of which his family only knew he was "missing in action." His wife lived on faith that he was still alive. His group, too, got the cleaned-up, fed and clothed routine in preparation for a "peace delegation" visit.
They, however, had time and devised a plan to get word to the world that they were alive and still survived. Each man secreted a tiny piece of paper, with his Social Security Number on it, in the palm of his hand. When paraded before Ms. Fonda and a cameraman, she walked the line, shaking each man's hand and asking little encouraging snippets like: "Aren't you sorry you bombed babies?" and "Are you grateful for the humane treatment from your benevolent captors?" Believing this HAD to be an act, they each palmed her their sliver of paper.
She took them all without missing a beat. . . At the end of the line and once the camera stopped rolling, to the shocked disbelief of the POWs, she turned to the officer in charge and handed him all the little pieces of paper...
Three men died from the subsequent beatings. Colonel Carrigan was almost number four but he survived, which is the only reason we know of her actions that day.
As previously stated, Fonda did meet with prisoners of war — exactly seven of them — at one point on her visit. But Larry Carrigan (a real POW), wasn't one of them. In 1999, he told Snopes editor David Emery (working for About.com at the time) via phone the rumor was a "figment of somebody's imagination" and that in fact he had never met Fonda. 
The Minnesota Star-Tribune ran an article (part 1, part 2) debunking the claim in 2005, quoting Edison Miller, who did actually meet with Fonda while a POW. "The whole email story about Jane Fonda is just malarkey," he said.
Miller told the Star-Tribune he didn't pass Fonda a slip of paper, nor, to his knowledge, did any of the other POWs who met with her that day. He said Fonda didn't ask them any questions beyond their names — which raises another point: Why would the POWs have needed to pass Fonda their Social Security numbers?
By the time of Fonda's visit in 1972, some prisoners of war released back to the U.S. had described horrid prison conditions and torture at the hands of the North Vietnamese, which later memoirs and reporting confirmed but also suggested had began to improve around 1969.
(This, in and of itself, is another discrepancy. The Star-Tribune also spoke to Mike McGrath, a former Navy pilot who ran the NAM-POWs veterans group in the late 1990s. He said there had been no known cases of U.S. prisoners of war in Vietnam being beaten to death since 1969, three years before Fonda's visit.)
Even assuming the torture had continued (and had not been documented in the following 50 years), the North Vietnamese would have wanted to maintain appearances of at least decent conditions within the prison camps. That would have included letting Fonda (and through her, the outside world) know with whom she was meeting. Fonda would have had time to memorize the names of the people she met and report them afterward — and Miller noted that she did specifically ask their names.
As one final note: The full copypasta also purported to relate accusations made by a different prisoner of war, Jerry Driscoll. According to the text, he spat at Fonda and was beaten for it when she visited in 1972. Speaking to the Star-Tribune in 2005, Driscoll not only denied those claims but denied ever meeting Fonda at all.

Flávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, leaving progressive voters reeling.
The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.
“Miracles are possible in politics. But I don’t see that happening,” the political scientist Miguel Lago said of Lula’s chances of snapping back. “I don’t see Flávio losing this election now.”
The far-right surge was a triumph – albeit an incomplete one – for the Bolsonaro clan and its 71-year-old patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro.
The disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, saw four relatives elected to congress. His 44-year-old wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, won a seat in the senate, as did his second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, who is 43. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, 28-year-old Jair Renan Bolsonaro, and the ex-president’s 62-year-old brother, Renato Bolsonaro, both won seats in the lower house of congress.
Across Latin America’s biggest democracy, key congressional and gubernatorial races were also won by staunch Bolsonaristas including Tarcísio de Freitas, who was re-elected as the governor of São Paulo state, and Sérgio Moro, who was elected governor of the southern state of Paraná. Both men were ministers during Bolsonaro’s 2018-22 government.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) will now boast the largest caucus in the senate with 28 of its 81 seats. Combined with the seats of other hard-right parties, that number rises to 43, giving the movement an upper house majority.
Meanwhile, pro-Lula senate candidates, including the former environment minister Marina Silva, the leftwing veteran Benedita da Silva, and the centrist former planning minister Simone Tebet, suffered bitter defeats.
Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, two young Bolsonarista social media warriors, became the best-voted congresspeople in Brazilian history, securing more than 3m votes.
“We are experiencing a revolution … The far right is growing in a very consistent way, election after election,” said Lago, calling the election the worst for progressive and moderate centrist parties since the late 80s.
Lago believed Lula had managed to interrupt the advance of Bolsonaro’s populist movement in 2022, thanks to positive voter memories of his first two terms, from 2002 to 2010. Back then, a global commodities boom allowed Brazil’s first working-class president to fund major social welfare programmes that helped millions escape poverty. “But it was just an interregnum,” Lago said.
Control of the senate should allow pro-Bolsonaro politicians to approve an amnesty for their movement’s charismatic leader, allowing the former president to emerge from the Brasília mansion where he is living under house arrest and reassert his leadership of the far right.
“I think he will be freed and I think he will be very important during Flávio Bolsonaro’s [presidency],” said Lago. “Flávio will be running the country and [Jair] Bolsonaro will be doing what he has always done: leading the revolution.”
The senate majority may also help Bolsonaro’s third son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, return from self-imposed exile in the US. The 42-year-old, who has close ties to Donald Trump’s Maga movement, was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison earlier this year for coercion – the result of his lobbying the Trump administration to interfere in his father’s coup trial. Eduardo Bolsonaro reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.
Trump, who has been accused of trying to sway the election in Bolsonaro’s favour, has yet to comment on Sunday’s result, although writing on his Truth Social network, he praised the speed of the vote count. But the US president will be delighted by the strong rightwing showing, a major boost to his attempt to expand the conservative “orange wave” sweeping Latin America to its biggest democracy and economy. Recent years have seen a succession of pro-Trump presidents win power in the region, from Costa Rica, Honduras and El Salvador to Chile and Colombia.
One of Trump’s most enthusiastic regional cheerleaders, the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, celebrated Bolsonaro’s “historic” victory against “the communist Lula”. “The American continent belongs to citizens who want to live in freedom,” Milei wrote on X.
The prime minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, wished Bolsonaro “good luck in the final” and celebrated his “great victory”. He wrote on X: “I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil.”
Speaking after Sunday’s result was confirmed, Lula put a brave face on what analysts called a catastrophic night for the left. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil,” he said, vowing to expose his rival’s “dark past”, which involves well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld and corruption allegations, which Bolsonaro has denied.
But the mood at Lula’s post-election event was reportedly funereal and Bolsonaro goes into the second round as the firm favourite. He is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates – Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema – who, between them, won more than 5.5m votes.
Santos quickly announced he would endorse neither candidate, considering both Lula and Bolsonaro to be “crooks”. Zema has vowed to vote against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) in the runoff, while Caiado has yet to declare his intentions.
Lula’s best hope may be convincing some of the record 33 million Brazilians who did not vote to turn out next time. “He will need to mobilise these apathetic voters who, in a sense, have already abandoned politics, which will be an extremely difficult task,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right.
Rocha has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters and identified “a great deal of voter apathy, especially among those who are not aligned with Bolsonarismo, and who could potentially vote for Lula”.
Although Flávio Bolsonaro has held political office for more than 20 years, “for undecided voters, his main positive characteristic is this idea of ‘renewal’, despite his possible involvement in corruption and with paramilitary groups,” Rocha added.
Lago believed only a dramatic shift from Lula’s campaign – such as changing the candidate, or a severe scandal involving Bolsonaro – could change the election’s outcome. But he was doubtful that would occur.

Maanvi Gagroo has once again drawn attention for her performance in Heer Sara, with a monologue from the film focusing on body image and societal expectations gaining traction on social media. Known for her roles as Siddhi in Four More Shots Please!, Chanchal in TVF’s Tripling and Riya in Half Arranged Half Love, Maanvi plays Heer in the film.
Maanvi Gagroo’s Heer Sara monologue on body image strikes a chord online: “The messages and response I’m getting for the monologue is honestly amazing”
While her overall portrayal has received appreciation, it is a particular scene addressing the way women are often judged based on their appearance and body size that has resonated with viewers. In the monologue, Heer speaks about how a woman’s worth can sometimes be reduced to her physical appearance, bringing attention to the pressures surrounding conventional ideas of beauty.
The scene has been widely shared online, with viewers discussing the expectations women continue to face based on their bodies and appearance. For Maanvi, the response has been a mix of happiness and concern. While she is glad that audiences have connected with the performance, she also feels the response highlights how relevant the issue remains.
“It brings me so much joy to see people relating to the scene and being moved by it. The messages and response I’m getting for the monologue is honestly amazing. But also a little sad. While I am tremendously happy and grateful that people like my performance, it’s hard to ignore that this is still a reality for so many people,” shares Maanvi.
The actress also hopes the scene encourages viewers to look beyond external appearances and question the standards used to assess women. She believes that the larger impact of the monologue would come from audiences reflecting on the ideas presented in the scene.
“I truly wish people would learn to look beyond these superficial things and focus more on something deeper. THAT would be the best compliment. THAT would be impact. THAT would be how I’d want people to remember Heer’s monologue in Heer Sara,” she added.
Heer Sara is currently streaming on Amazon Prime Video. The response to Maanvi’s monologue has brought further attention to the film’s exploration of body image, acceptance and societal expectations, with the scene becoming a talking point among viewers on social media.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): A week after the murder of retired IAS official Rakesh Agarwal, police have yet to arrest the prime suspect, caretaker Varun Kumar. Police have now released a poster of the suspect and increased the reward for information leading to his arrest from Rs 30,000 to Rs 50,000.
The posters will be put up across Bhopal and five states at police stations, public places, railway stations, bus stations and other locations where the suspect is believed to have a presence.
The move is aimed at seeking information from the public that can help the police trace and arrest him.
Police officials said that the tattoo of a scorpion on the throat of the suspect is a crucial clue as it cannot be removed so easily. People may easily recognise him through the tattoo and inform police in case he is spotted.
Even on Tuesday, police failed to get any concrete clue about Varun Kumar. Police sources, however, said he could be in Delhi or Gwalior. As the suspect is reportedly not using a mobile phone, tracking his location has become difficult for the investigators.
Retired IAS official Rakesh Agarwal was murdered by Varun Kumar last Wednesday. The suspect allegedly slit Agarwal’s throat before fleeing with cash, the latter’s mobile phone and other valuables.
The mobile phone was later recovered by the police from one of Varun Kumar’s acquaintances in Agra.
However, the recovery has not yet helped investigators locate the suspect. Police teams have been searching for Varun Kumar in other states and are also examining his contacts and movements to trace his whereabouts.

Liberal-National Coalition vows to bring annual net overseas migration down to 100,000 for two years, roughly a third of current rate

Australia’s conservative Liberal-National Coalition has unveiled plans to drastically lower temporary and humanitarian visa numbers while prioritising skilled workers, in a move described by the party as the largest reduction in immigration in the country's history.
Under the proposed policy, temporary visas would be reduced by 650,000 across a four-year period, bringing annual net overseas migration down to 100,000 for two years, roughly a third of its current rate.
The sweeping proposal comes amid growing anti-immigration sentiment across Australia, driven by high living costs and housing shortages. The Coalition has faced intensified pressure from the far-right, anti-immigration One Nation party, which recently outpolled it in surveys after pledging to decrease temporary migration by 750,000 over three years.
"What we’re proposing today is the biggest cut to immigration in the history of this country. It will be putting Australia first and it will be putting our national interest first,” opposition leader Angus Taylor told a press conference on Tuesday.
"The net overseas migration numbers will be 100,000 year one, 100,000 year two, going to 160,000 in year four. That’ll take pressure off roads, off schools, off infrastructure, off houses, and that will ensure that our country has the breathing space it needs."
Under the Coalition's framework, humanitarian visa allocations would be halved to 10,000.
International student enrolments would be limited to 240,000, alongside the elimination of Australia's temporary graduate visa programme allowing post-graduation study and work. However, the Coalition promised to expand temporary skilled visas by 100,000 and also clear a backlog of construction worker applications.
"We have also seen under Labor a shift away from skilled migration to mass migration. We’ll reverse that shift," Mr Taylor added.
The plan represents a sharper reduction than the target set by the centre-left Labor government last month, which sought to bring annual net migration down to 225,000 by 2028.
Migration surged after Australia reopened its borders in February 2022 following over two years of Covid closures, largely driven by international students, backpackers and temporary workers. Intake has nevertheless dropped over the past two years, with net overseas migration standing at 306,000 in the year to 30 June 2025.
Australia's next general election is not due until 2028.

How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
- Published
Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a better economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China.
Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%.
Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked.
Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300m (£227m) in 2020 to $100m this year, while exports rose from around $129m to $200m in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market.
The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world.
Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year.
"India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC.
More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period.
"China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI).
If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava.
On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address, external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues".
But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC.
That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods.
To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones.
"Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava.
It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment.
Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank.
"Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production.
Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends.
China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output.
Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year.
A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava.
On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies.
"Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li.
"If normalisation [of ties] continues without a serious push for reciprocal market access, India risks a situation where the political relationship improves but the economic dependency stays the same."
The long term solution to both reducing avoidable imports and improving exports performance will be to strengthen manufacturing, says Srivastava.
But that requires sector-specific industrial policy and stronger fundamentals – affordable power and credit, efficient logistics and stable regulations – areas where India still falls short.
India has also recently softened foreign direct investment rules, which could open the door to Chinese companies wanting to expand Indian investments. But these too will need careful vetting, he adds.
"Investment that merely expands distribution networks or assembles products using Chinese parts could increase imports and deepen dependence. Approvals should therefore prioritise technology transfer, local value addition, domestic component production and exports from India."
More immediately, India could focus on targeting higher exports to China in specific sectors to reduce its trade asymmetry, says Li. Sectors like pharmaceuticals could be a natural fit with China's population aging and healthcare costs rising.
"But narrowing a $112bn deficit won't come from finding niche export sectors alone," he adds.
"The key question is whether Beijing is ready and willing to make concessions on market access as part of the broader normalisation. Alternatively, India will need to find its own leverage to force that conversation."
